Cakrasaṃketaḥ Prathamaḥ. These two, Gaṇeśa and Baṭuka, are worshipped by the world and praised by the universe.
May the two Discus-bearers— whose nature is the protection of the world, who bestow the fruit of proximity for those devoted to the recitation of mantras,
who are mounted upon their chariot, whose eyes blaze like the sun, the moon, and fire,
and who are composed of excellent qualities— be intent on protecting me with minds devoted to my welfare. (1.1)
Victorious is that eternal light of lights, the one and unsurpassed, which neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines. (1.2)
The supreme power of this Teacher of the Universe, whose nature is reflective awareness, though one, vibrates as the form of manifold names and meanings. (1.3)
Born from the sequence beginning with Paśyantī in the form of question and answer, these two unfold the introduction to the Tantra everywhere out of a desire to bestow grace.
Now, in this *Yoginīhṛdaya*, I strive to manifest the higher and lower meanings indicated in that *Vāmakeśvara Tantra*. (1.5)
Not even a single mortal understands the human heart in its true essence;
who, other than Śiva, is capable of knowing the Heart of the Yoginī? (1.6)
The inner treasury of the divine scriptures, which has not been opened by anyone else, is now being opened by me; let the wise take hold of this great meaning. (1.7)
I, Amṛtānanda, explain this work—which is crowded with various conventions and composed of many meanings—solely by the command of Śiva and Śivā. (1.8)
Otherwise, why was this not predicted long ago in beginningless saṃsāra? Were there no virtuous ones at that time, or what purpose was lacking here? (1.9)
This knowledge, which has come down through the lineage of succession from Śiva to the Gurus, has been obtained by me; it is beyond the reach of those who do not follow the traditional sequence.

In this regard, the Blessed One, the supreme Śiva whose form is luminosity, having divided his own self into the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), asks [the Goddess] through the sequence beginning with Paśyantī:
the venerable Goddess said:

Thus: "I am Śiva alone," meaning that having pervaded everything up to the level of *vaikharī* speech, I have questioned [you] by means of the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). The form *uvāca* is the third person singular of the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Its status as a past action is due to the eternality of what is to be said; its non-recentness is due to its being undivided by time; and its non-evident nature is due to its not being within the range of the senses. By this, it is meant that the venerable Bhairava spoke.

This too has been explained: the meaning is that I myself, who am Paramaśiva, whose nature is light (*prakāśa*), and who am intent upon bestowing grace upon the universe, having become active through the sequence of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, act as the questioner by means of the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and as the giver of the reply by means of the aspect of light; thus, I bring down the Tantra. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīmahāsvacchanda*:
"Abiding in the roles of teacher and disciple, the Lord Sadāśiva himself brought down the Tantra through dialogues consisting of questions and answers" (Svacchanda Tantra 8.31).
O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who consist of perfectly full renown: in this Vāmakeśvara Tantra, there are many meanings that remain unknown. (1/1)
O Bhairava, you ought to explain those various matters in their entirety.

Bhairava is Paramaśiva, the agent of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, so called because he sustains (*bharaṇa*), delights (*ramaṇa*), and emits (*vamana*) the universe. "Devadeva" means the God of gods; the "gods" (*deva*) are the luminous ones such as the Sun and others, and he is their "God" (*deva*), the illuminator.

Mahādeva is the essence of great light. The meaning is this: because you are the essence of great light, you alone illumine the universe; no one else is capable of illumining you. Regarding this, there is a scriptural verse:
"There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire."
"Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15).
Here, "expansion" (*prathā*) consists of fullness; expansion is knowledge (*jñāna*), and fullness is the consciousness (*jñapti*) whose object is the universe—of that [consciousness] it consists.

O Thou of such form! Since You alone are omniscient, it is You who are worthy to enlighten all; no one else is capable of enlightening You. Therefore, in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, the scripture of four hundred verses (*Catuḥśatīśāstra*), there are many points whose meaning is unknown or not understood. You ought to speak of, and clarify, those various meanings in their entirety and in full detail.
The meaning is: "You ought to bring [this] to the stage of my deliberation. || 1/1 ||
The luminous portion responds:
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme and great secret, the Heart of the Yoginīs. (1.2)

Out of affection for you, I shall today speak that which is especially to be kept secret. O Goddess! You who are intent upon the play of worldly activity such as the creation of the universe, whose very form is *vimarśa* (reflective awareness)—this is a great secret to be concealed in the world. To whatever extent the mind does not engage with a particular object, to that same extent it remains beyond the range of the senses.

However, because this [reality] is always beyond the faculties of mind and speech, it possesses the state of being a great secret (*mahāguhyatva*). It is the *Yoginīhṛdaya* (Heart of the Yoginī) because it is the ground of manifestation for the heart of the Yoginī’s own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), just like a physical heart. Here, "yoga" refers to the relationship of the coalescence of all things; she shines by means of that, and thus she is the Yoginī. As it has been said by the learned:

"Whatever object there may be—whether its nature be space, time, or substance—and however it exists, I take refuge in that digit of consciousness (*sāṃvidī kalā*) which shines in that very form. (Saubhāgyahṛdaya 4).
It is "supreme" (*param*), because it transcends all knowledge. Therefore, he will say: "Having known this, O beautiful lady..."
"One shall immediately attain the state of moving through the sky"—hear this and bring it to the level of reflective awareness. 1/2

Out of affection for you, and for the sake of our singular state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*), I shall speak. This has not been told to anyone before, because it is an extreme secret; therefore, for this reason, it must be especially guarded. The meaning is that it should be cultivated through the contemplation of the sense of "I" as one's own self.
In order to further strengthen the necessity of extreme secrecy, he says:
"It has reached the surface of the earth through oral instruction from ear to ear. (1.3)

"From Karṇa"—the ablative case is used here with the elision of the suffix *lyap* (meaning "having reached"); thus, it means having reached Karṇa, it was subsequently obtained by Karṇa himself through the sequence of instruction, that is, through the sequence of tradition (*pāramparya*). The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the inception of an action (*ādikarman*). By the word "surface of the earth" (*avanītala*), the humans residing there are indicated, just as in the expression "the platforms are shouting. Therefore, this is the resulting meaning: [it was obtained] by divine beings, perfected beings, and humans—

Because it is extremely secret in its gradual progression, this [teaching] is to be understood solely through the oral tradition from ear to ear (*karṇaparamparā*). Here, the mention of "human" (*mānava*) is intended as an illustration for both the divine (*divya*) and the perfected (*siddha*) [beings]. (1.3)
He states that it should not be given to those who are unworthy:
"It must not be given to the disciples of others, nor to atheists, O Sovereign Lady;
nor to those who are indolent in service, nor to those who bring about misfortune. (1.4)

Who indeed are those "disciples of others" (paraśiṣyas) to whom [the teaching] must not be given? Those who have attained the entirety of the ultimate secrets through the lineage succession in other sciences (*vidyā*), and who have received the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), are the disciples of others; [the teaching] must not be given to them. Having properly found a *kula*-guru, one should not resort to another guru.

Because of such statements as [found in] Kulārnava-tantra 13.130, it should not be accepted even by them. However, it should be given to those who have not yet acquired the entirety of the secrets through the traditional lineage of other sciences (*vidyā*), and who have not received the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*); by them, too, it should be accepted.
"Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to another flower, so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, should go from one guru to another guru.
(Kulārṇava 13.132). According to this statement, they are not the disciples of others; rather, [the object of veneration] is the sandals of that very guru who performed the full initiation.

And because of the statement: "(Kulārṇava 13.129). From atheists. Those who think "there is no other world" are atheists, devoid of faith. The meaning is that one should not give [the teachings] to them by creating a desire for them based on wealth, grain, and so forth.
As it is said in the Bhagavad Gītā:
"One should not create a division of intellect among the ignorant who are attached to action;
rather, the wise man, acting with disciplined composure, should cause them to engage in all actions" (Gītā 3.26).
Nor [should it be given] to those who are indolent in service; it should not be imparted to those who are lazy in serving.

The meaning is this: it should be given even to those who cause harm; it should be given to those who, though lazy in service, bestow wealth; and it should not be given to those who are both lazy in service and do not bestow wealth. As it has been said:
"Knowledge [is acquired] through service to the teacher, or by means of abundant wealth."
Or rather, knowledge [is attained] through knowledge; a fourth [means] does not exist at all. (1.4)
He states that [the teaching] should be given only after examination to one who is worthy:
"It should be given to one who has been examined and has resided for half a year.
By residing together for half a year, it is possible to examine whether defects such as being a disciple of another [teacher] exist.
Because the guru possesses discernment.
Reinforcing the very meaning already stated, he declares the fruit [of this knowledge] for the sake of the disciple’s engagement:
"Having known this, O beautiful lady, one immediately attains the state of moving through the sky" (1.5).

However, because of its great significance, this [teaching] should be given only to one who has been thoroughly examined. By the complete knowledge of this alone, the disciple becomes a *khecara*—one who moves in the sky (*kha*), that is, in the supreme void (*paramavyoman*)—which is Śiva. As it is said in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*:
"That which, situated between the moon and sun of vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*), moves in the sky as the abode of the fire-vision (*analadṛṣṭi*)."
"O Ambikā, show me that supreme Śiva who is in the sky above the highest peak" (verse 32).
The meaning is that one would immediately attain the true reality and become liberated while living. This has been stated in the *Vedarahasya*:
"Having known the path and the self of that very [Atman], one is not smeared by evil action" (Ishavasya Upanishad 20). Thus ends the fifth section.
He begins the treatise:
"O Supreme Goddess, the symbolism of the wheel, as well as the symbolism of mantra and worship—such is the threefold symbolism of the goddess Tripurā. (1.6)

The *saṃketaka* is like a convention (*saṃketa*). A convention is an agreement (*samaya*). Just as a lover and his beloved who have made an agreement may dwell anywhere, so too are these two Śivas. There is the convention of the wheel (*cakrasaṃketaka*), the convention of mantra (*mantrasaṃketaka*), and the convention of worship (*pūjāsaṃketaka*)—thus the convention is threefold. It is the abode of the Goddess Tripurā.

The Goddess Tripurā, who exists prior even to the triad of *tattva*, *pīṭha*, *liṅga*, and *mātṛkā*, is the Supreme (*parā*) whose nature is the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Her convention (*saṃketa*) is threefold.
O Supreme Goddess, she is she whose sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and command (*ājñā*) are supreme and most excellent, being protected even by Indra and the other gods. As it has been said:
In the Vedarahasya: "Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises;
out of fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on. (1)
(Tai. U. 2.8) thus [it is said]. 1/6.
He states the reversal of results for one devoid of this knowledge:
"As long as one does not know these three supreme conventions, so long shall one not become a bearer of the supreme command within the wheel of Tripurā. (1.7)

As long as one does not know these three conventions that are about to be described, so long will one not be a bearer of the supreme command (*paramājñādhara*) within the wheel of Tripurā—the supreme self-consciousness—which consists of the collection of principles (*tattva*) characterized by the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
"Command" (*ājñā*) refers to the power of both restraint and grace; such [power] exists even among kings in the world. Thus it is said:

"Supreme" means that the command (*ājñā*) of the Supreme Lord alone is supreme and unimpeded throughout all worlds. One who upholds the supreme command becomes the Supreme Lord. The meaning is that this is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): he who understands this shall immediately attain the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratā*), whereas he who does not understand this shall not attain that state.

This mention of the purpose (prayojana) is also an indication of the qualified person (adhikārī), the subject matter (viṣaya), and the relationship (saṃbandha). The one desiring liberation (mumukṣu) is the qualified person;

the deity of one's own consciousness (svasaṃviddevatā) is the subject matter; liberation (mokṣa) is the purpose; and the relationship is that between the thing to be explained and the explainer (pratipādyapratipādakabhāva).
Therein, first, he begins to explain the convention of the wheels (*cakrasaṃketa*):
"That pentad of powers, through emanation and dissolution, forms a quartet of fires;
from the union of the five powers and the four fires, the wheel arises. (1.8)

That wheel, by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), consists of the five powers (*śaktipañcaka*). A triangle with its apex facing oneself is called "power" (*śakti*); such is the pentad of powers. By way of dissolution (*laya*), there is the tetrad of fires (*agnicatuṣṭaya*). Fire, by way of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), refers to a triangle with its apex turned away; that is the tetrad of fires. Thus [is the nature] of the five powers.

And from the conjunction of the four fires—*saṃyoga* being a *samyak-yoga* (perfect union)—according to the method taught in the *Catuḥśatī-śāstra*, beginning with the verse "having pierced power with power" (1.29), the drawing [of the diagram] in such a way that the tip of the power (*śakti*) of the equilateral triangle has its lines perfectly aligned through the process of breaking the knots (*granthi-bheda*) is *saṃyoga*; from that, the manifestation of the wheel (*cakra*) occurs. || 1.8 ||

Having generally described the arising of the assembly of wheels (*cakra*), he now declares the origin of the wheels in terms of their individual parts: "O sinless one, I shall tell you this descent of the wheel (*cakrāvatāra*).
This refers to the descent (*avatāra*)—the term *avatāra* meaning... [of] this wheel of the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī, that is, her wheel of worship (*pūjācakra*).

In the world, there is the descent from elevated places such as palaces to lower ground; here, however, there is an emanation through the sequence of the *tattvas* from Paramaśiva, who is the light transcending the universe—such is the descent of the *cakra*. "O sinless one" means free from defects such as being a disciple of another. "Of you"—of me, whose nature is light, who am the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) and constitute your own portion.
"I speak" means "I lead [it] to the state of being heart-pleasing.
Now, one might ask: how can a wheel consisting of the *tattvas* arise from Paramaśiva, who is beyond all action? To this he says:
"When that supreme Power, by her own will, [assumes] the form of the universe... (1.9).
One should perceive the throbbing of one's own self; then the emergence of the wheel occurs.

When, at whatever time, by the power of the unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings, that very Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), desiring to emit the universe withdrawn within herself, creates the universe in its universal form through her own will—while Śiva remains indifferent and detached.
This is the meaning. On this point, the Śruti says:
"For him, there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither equal nor superior to him is seen.
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and his knowledge, strength, and action are innate" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).
It is also stated in the *Ājñāvatāra*: "By her own will alone, she swallows and also emits the entire universe.
The very creation of the universe is the vibration (*sphurattā*) of the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), because its nature is that of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). At that time...

At the time of the emanation of the universe consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), there occurs the manifestation of the wheel—the wheel of the Supreme Deity—which comprises the entire universe.
This very point is stated [in the following verse]:
"From the Point (*bindu*), which has the form of the void (*śūnya*) and terminates in emission (*visarga*), and which is the consciousness of vibration (*praspanda*). (1.10)

It is "of the form of emptiness" (*śūnyākāra*) because it is both empty and the letter *a*. Furthermore, its emptiness here consists in the fact that all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) has been cast out. For this very reason, it is Paramaśiva. As it is said in the *Saṃketapaddhati*: "The letter *a* is the foremost of all phonemes; it is the Light, the supreme Śiva. Regarding this, there is a Vedic scripture: "A is Brahman" (*aitareya-upaniṣad*).
(Ā. 2/3/8). "From that which ends in *visarga*," meaning from that whose end is *visarga*.

From the *bindu*, which is the consciousness of vibration (*praspanda*). The *bindu* has arisen as the sun called Kāma, consisting of Agni and Soma, and characterized by the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti. As it is said in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*:

"O Goddess, by bestowing upon me—that which has entered into the reflective awareness consisting of the enjoyed and the enjoyer—the firm state of the ocean of consciousness, the expansion of the Sun (Bhānu) here intends to express that [state] through the blending of Fire and Moon. (Śloka 212).
Thus, the vibration (*praspanda*) is the refinement of the Bindu known as Kāmākhya, whose nature is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti.

The meaning is as follows: consisting of two dots, white and red, in the form of fire and moon; from the vibration of the bindu—which is the state of equilibrium between the letters *a* and *ha*, arising from the pair of white and red dots—the digit of consciousness (*citkalā*), which consists of pure awareness and takes the form of fire and moon, is born. (1/10)
Because its ultimate reality is light, which is joined with the waves of its own vibration,
it has issued forth as the locus of the waves of the universe, consisting of the three subjects.

From the contact of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), like fire, with the *bindu*-wheel, a flow of the power of reflective awareness arises, just as a stream [flows] from clarified butter;

for this very reason, light possesses the status of ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*). From that which is joined with the wave of vibration (*sphurattā*), there is the wave of the power of reflective awareness, which is that very vibration.

[The Bindu] has issued forth from the space between the two dots, having the form of the half-moon (*kalā*) of the Heart; thus, from such a syllable of *Kāmakalā*, there has emerged the *Baindava-cakra* (the wheel of the Bindu), which consists of the three Mothers and is the locus of the waves of the universe. "Locus of the waves of the universe" means that the "waves" (*laharī*) of the universe are the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), and it is their locus because it is the cause of their origination.

It consists of the three Mothers in the form of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī. Thus, because it has arisen from the fourth Bindu known as Sadāśiva—which is the nature of the Supreme Self (Paramātman) as the totality of those [three]—the Baindava Cakra, the central triangle, has emerged. This very point will be stated here: "One should perceive the vibration of the Self" (1.36), and so forth.
This is shown by the passage ending with "Vaikharī has the universe as her form" (1/40), and also by "The wheel, in its ultimate sense, is the expansion of the form of Kāmakalā" (1/24).
This has also been elaborated upon by our teachers in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"The Supreme Power (*parā śakti*) takes the form of the sprout of the seed of the manifest union of Śiva and Śakti."
She shines forth, her form characterized by the script of unsurpassed contemplation upon the supreme form.
When the multitude of rays from the Sun of Supreme Śiva reflects in the pure mirror of self-awareness (*vimarśa*),
the Great Bindu does not enter the wall of the mind, which is as radiant and beautiful as a gemstone.
Victorious is the egoity consisting of consciousness, whose form is the perfectly manifest fusion of the phonemes,
the mass of the union of Śiva and Śakti, which has swallowed the entire circle of the worlds.
The pair of white and red dots, representing the distinct yet mutually interpenetrating contraction and expansion of Śiva and Śakti,
is the clear cause for the creation of both speech and meaning.
The Bindu is the essence of the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the Sun is the form of this union in the state of samarasa;
Kāma is so called due to his desirability, and the Kalā consists of the forms of Fire and Moon—the two Bindus.

"Thus, this Goddess Kāmakalāvidyā, whose nature consists of the sequence of the wheels (cakras), by whomsoever she is known, he becomes liberated and takes on the form of Mahātripurasundarī. (Kā. Vi. Ślo. 3–8), and so forth. 1/11.
Furthermore, this [wheel] would possess a threefold nature;

that is, this wheel, which consists of a triangle, would again have a threefold nature. By the word "again," it is understood that another quality of what was previously mentioned is being stated. This very same essence of the triangle is, moreover, the principle of Śakti.
The meaning is that through the process of emanation it attains the state of fire, and through the nature of withdrawal it becomes threefold.
When this has been accomplished, the wheel of nine sources (navayonicakra) together with its latent impressions (savāsana) is produced; thus he says:
"Virtue and vice, as well as the two selves, the knower and the knowable, and likewise valid cognition. (1.12)
This great [reality] consists of nine wombs (navayoni) and is a mass of consciousness and bliss (cidānandaghana).

Dharma and adharma refer to merit and demerit. The selves (ātmānaḥ) are fourfold: the self (ātmā), the inner self (antarātmā), the supreme self (paramātmā), and the self of knowledge (jñānātmā). The knower (mātṛ) and the object of knowledge (meya): the knower is the individual soul (jīva), and the object of knowledge is the category of perceivable things. The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)...
The motion. 1/12.
Thus it is: this wheel consists of nine parts and has nine wombs (*navayoni*), and is a solid mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandaghana*). Consciousness (*cit*) is the digit of pure awareness;
bliss (*ānanda*) is the transformation of universal egoity (*viśvāhaṃtā*). It is "solid" (*ghana*) by virtue of these two, being dense both internally and externally, like a mass of salt.
It is "great" (*mahat*), not delimited by space, time, or form, because its nature is pure consciousness.

Having first established that the Triangle is identical with [the Absolute] because it is the cause of the triad beginning with Paśyantī, he now describes how the external wheel consists of Vaikharī and its nature as the essence of the principles (*tattva*), starting from the verse beginning with "The Wheel" and ending with "the three revolutions in the form of Vāmā" (verses 13–19).
This wheel consists of nine aspects, with its mantra divided into nine parts.

This wheel, consisting of nine parts in the form of three triangles, has evolved into the nature of the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana; it possesses nine distinct mantras, corresponding to the ninefold division of the mantras of the Nine Goddesses of the Wheels (cakreśvarīs) to be described, such as the purification of the hands and so forth. || 1.13 ||

This very form of Ambikā, established upon the Baindava seat, is the seed-syllable of consciousness consisting of the fire of universal dissolution; it resides within the eight-spoked [lotus] and is encircled by the vowels. (1.14)

The *baindavāsana* is the seat consisting of the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*), which is Sadāśiva. As it will be stated in this very context: "O Goddess, the supreme *sadāśivāsana* consists of the Great Bindu" (2.56). Because Śiva and Śakti abide above the *sadāśivatattva*, they are established upon the *baindavāsana*. *Saṃvartānala* is the fire of dissolution (*layānala*), in which—

That which begins with earth and ends with Śiva dissolves into that form of fire—the unsurpassed (*anuttara*), consisting of light, which is the primordial source of all phonemes. This is the fire of universal destruction (*saṃvartānala*). Consciousness itself is *kalā*; this *citkalā* consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and takes the form of the half-*kalā* within the heart, which is the final phoneme of all. As it is said in the *Saṃketapaddhati*:
"The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, the supreme light, the ultimate Śiva;
the letter Ha is the final one, whose form is the *kalā*, proclaimed as being called *vimarśa*.

Thus, that [triangle] is established upon the seat of Bindu (*baindavāsana*), wherein the digit of consciousness (*citkalā*) is like the fire of universal destruction (*saṃvartānala*). In this very way is the triangle.

It has the form of Ambikā because it arises from the central wheel consisting of the Great Bindu (mahābindu), which is the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti. It resides within the eight-spoked [figure] because the triangle arises from the three pulsations (spanda) of the eight-spoked [figure]; therefore, this triangle is situated within the eight-spoked [figure]. It is "encircled by vowels," meaning its three lines are fashioned by the fifteen vowels—from *a* to the bindu—divided into three groups.

The center is occupied by the vowel *aḥ*. As it has been stated by the learned: "Having visualized the great triangle, whose interior consists of the vowels and whose lines are equal" (Sūtra 41). This is the meaning: this very triangular wheel, having transformed itself into the nature of the nine wheels, is situated in the middle of the eight corners, conjoined with the ninefold mantras beginning with the purification of the hands (*kara-śuddhi*) and ending with the Mistress of the Nine Wheels of Tripurā and the rest.

It is surrounded by the sixteen vowels; it is mounted upon the throne of Sadāśiva, which consists of the Great Bindu (mahābindu) representing the state of non-dual equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Ambikā and Śāntā; and it is presided over by Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, whose nature is illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
He brings forth the upper wheel together with its latent impressions—
a ten-spoked wheel consisting of the form of radiating light from nine triangles,
which causes the manifestation of the ten phonemes beginning with Śakti and ending with Nava. || 1.15 ||

Because they have as their objective support the illumination of the ten elements (*bhūta*) and subtle essences (*tanmātra*), there are nine triangles; by the word "triangle," the *baindava* (the point) situated in the center of the triangle is indicated. The ten rays perceived as vibrating all around the nine triangles and the *baindava* are—
That form is the ten-spoked [wheel] wherein [it resides]. Whatever transforms in whatever manner, it is of that very nature. *Śakti* is the letter *ra*.

As it is stated in the *Uddhārodhva-tantra* regarding the extraction of the seed-syllable of the power *Ramā*: "The Moon (*candra*) is *Śakti*, the Great Power (*mahāśakti*), Brahmāṇī, Kālikā, and so forth. The beginning of the power *ra* is the letter *ya*; starting from the letter *ya*, which is the beginning of *Śakti*, there are nine [syllables].
The letter *kṣa* reaches the end of the phonemes (*varṇas*); it is that which brings about the manifestation (*sphūrti*) of those ten [phonemes].
Manifestation means reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). The meaning is that it is the reflective awareness of the ten phonemes beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa*. (1.15)

The elements (*bhūta*) are earth, water, fire, air, and ether; the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are the five—smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. There are ten manifestations (*prakāśa*) of these ten, because they serve as their objective supports.
This is because the objects, such as earth and the rest, consist of the nature of Śiva, while the phonemes, beginning with *ya*, consist of the nature of Śakti.
The meaning is that this wheel is surrounded by a ten-cornered figure consisting of both manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
By describing it as being composed of the ten phonemes from *pṛthivī* (the letter *pa*) to *kṣa*, the nature of the first three wheels— beginning with the ten-spoked one—
as the state of maintenance (*sthiti*) is illuminated.
He describes the second ten-spoked wheel: "The form of the second ten-spoked [wheel] consists of the ten syllables beginning with Krodhīśa. (1.16)

The second ten-spoked [wheel] is the "twice-ten-spoked" (*dvidaśāra*). It is so called because its forms (*rūpa*)—the objects of the senses, namely the ten beginning with sound (*śabda*), as well as the ten beginning with speech (*vacana*)—manifest as the second set of ten spokes; that [wheel] in which such forms appear is of that nature. *Kṛdhīśa* refers to the letter *ka*. It is like the ten phonemes beginning with *ka*. What is the meaning? [It resides] within the circles of the *bindu*, the triangle, the eight [petals], and the six [spokes].

The meaning is that, illuminated by the two lamps consisting of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) situated in the center, there arose a pair of ten-spoked wheels (*daśāra-cakra*) composed of two sets of ten: one consisting of the ten [elements] beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*) and the ten [organs] beginning with the hands (*kara*), and the other consisting of the ten [objects] beginning with sound (*śabda*). This is because they are manifested by the radiance and shadow of those two tenfold groups.
As it has been said in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"In this group of ten, which is illuminated by the lamp of consciousness and contains the center of the nine-cornered [figure], these two shadows are seen in the form of two wheels. (Verses 29–30).

[Objection: Since it was already stated in the verse "nanu-bhūtatanmātradaśakaprakāśālambanatvataḥ" (1.16) that sound and the other [subtle elements] are intended by the term *rūpa*, why are they again included by the word *rūpa* in the verse "dvidaśārasphuradrūpam" (1.16)? [Response: Not so; for by the term *tanmātra*, the subtle elements (*tanmātras*)—which are the minute constituents of the gross elements and are not within the range of the senses—are meant.

Regarding "grahaṇa" (perception), by the word "rūpa" (form), the qualities of the elements—sound and so forth—which are perceivable by the ear and other senses, are included; therefore, there is no contradiction. || 1/16 ||

He speaks of the fourteen-spoked [wheel]: "Through the transformation resulting from the union with the form of the light of the four wheels, it exists in the form of fourteen spokes by means of the nature of the instrument of consciousness. (1.17)

Consisting of the manifestation of the ultimate reality of the letters beginning with Khecarī and ending with Jayā, there are four wheels (cakras) in the form of the Bindu, the Triangle, the Octagon, and the first Decagon;
their splendors are four. Because they are remote, only their splendor is perceived, just as when many trees [are seen from afar].

"Forest" (*vana*) does not imply a distinction of parts; likewise, because it is proximate to the second ten-spoked wheel (*daśāra*) conjoined with the fourfold radiance of that [first] wheel, there is a perception of parts, since it is a transformation of the ten spokes belonging to the second ten-spoked wheel which are inherent in those four radiances. This occurs by means of the fourteen-spoked form, whose nature is consciousness (*saṃvit*).

Consciousness (*saṃvitti*) is knowledge. By the word "consciousness," action is also indicated. The instruments (*karaṇas*) are the fourteen: the ten senses beginning with the ear and the voice, as well as mind, intellect, ego, and thought; [the Lord exists] by means of them. (1.17)

*Khecarī* is the letter *ṭa*, and *Jayā* is the letter *bha*; these fourteen letters, beginning with *ṭa* and ending with *bha*, have as their cause the manifestation of ultimate reality (*paramārthaprathā*), which is the manifestation of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), and [the Wheel] consists of that. What is the meaning?
It is the central wheel itself, appearing in the sequence of the triangle, the eight-spoked figure, and the twelve-spoked figure.

The meaning is that it has transformed into the form of a fourteen-spoked wheel, consisting of the fourteen instruments— namely, the five organs of knowledge such as hearing, the five organs of action such as speech, mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness— which correspond to the fourteen phonemes beginning with *ṭa* and ending with *bha*, and which are composed of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Regarding the triangle wheel: having previously described its nature as Ambikā in the verse, "This very form of Ambikā, situated in the eight-spoked [wheel] and surrounded by the vowels" (1.14), he now describes the nature of the Śrīcakra— from the eight-spoked wheel up to the fourteen-spoked wheel— as Raudrī:
Thus, it consists of the radiance of Raudrī, flashing forth in the form of power and fire.

In the manner thus described, the meaning is that the throbbing wheel— consisting of five powers and four fires, having the form of forty-two wombs, composed of the radiance of Raudrī, and manifested through the expansion of the power (śakti) of Raudrī— shines forth in the form of the fire of power.
He describes the remaining wheel:
"The four-cornered [wheel] in the form of Jyeṣṭhā, and the triple circle in the form of Vāmā.
This means that its four corners—the squares—are the forms of the power (śakti) of Jyeṣṭhā, and there are three such [circles] in the form of Vāmā.

That [mandala] has four corners in the form of the *Jyeṣṭhā* [power]; it is that which possesses three circles in the form of the *Vāmā* power and three spirals (*bhrami*). By the word "three spirals," the two lotuses situated within them are also indicated. As he will state here: "There may be another [form] with two lotuses and with three earth-houses" (1.74). Here, there are three spirals in the form of *Vāmā*.

Although the reading "the quadrangle in the form of Jyeṣṭhā" would be logical, the Lord has stated that "the quadrangle is in the form of Jyeṣṭhā and the three circles are in the form of Vāmā," following the sequence of the recitation of the powers beginning with Ambikā.
Furthermore, he states another internal impression (*vāsanā*) of this very wheel:
"The triangle within the portion of consciousness, and the eight-cornered [figure] of Śāntyatītā. (1.19)
The portion of Peace (Śāntyamśa) has twelve spokes and likewise contains the worlds;
it is surrounded by eight petals consisting of the forms of the light of the Kalās of Knowledge (Vidyā).
It possesses a clearly manifest eight-petaled lotus through the form of *pratiṣṭhā*,
and it is adorned with four corners shining with the form of *nivṛtti*.

The aspect of consciousness is the *citkalā*; that which consists of it is the internal triangle. *Śāntyatītā*, *Śānti*, *Vidyā*, *Pratiṣṭhā*, and *Nivṛtti* are the *kalās* of the five elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*). The meaning is that this wheel consists of these;
the meaning of the individual components is indeed clear. (1/19–21)

Regarding this very wheel, he states another tradition concerning the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), from the words "But in the Trailokyamohana and the others" up to "the remainder of the ritual" (verses 22–24):
"But in the nine wheels beginning with the Trailokyamohana, O Sovereign of the Gods..."
Nāda, Bindu, Kalā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and likewise Vāmā. || 1/22 ||
Viṣaghnī, Dūtarī, and Sarvānandā are situated in sequence.
Here, the word "tu" (but/however) marks the conclusion of the context concerning the demonstration of the previously mentioned nature of Kāmakalā.
In the phrase "Trailokyamohanādyes tu," the word "ādi" (beginning/first) refers to the cakras beginning with Sarvāśāparipūraka and so forth. Of these...

The names [of these powers] will be stated later. Regarding the phrase "in the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana," the singular number is used in the sense of a class (jātāvekavacana); thus, the meaning is "in the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana. The meaning is that the nine powers, beginning with Nāda and ending with Sarvānanda, reside respectively in the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana and ending with Bindu. This is the meaning of the words.
This is indeed clear. || 1/22–23 ||

Having previously stated, in the passage beginning with "This is indeed the form of Ambikā" (1.14), that the four [deities] beginning with Ambikā— who constitute the aspect of manifestation (*prakāśa*)— consist of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the mandalas ranging from the triangle to the square, he now describes the latent impressions of the four [deities] beginning with Śāntā— who constitute the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— as consisting of the mandalas ranging from the square to the bindu.
Nāda and bindu are partless, and kalā has the nature of will.
Jyeṣṭhā is knowledge (*jñāna*), while the remainder is action (*kriyā*).

Śāntā is the partless power (*niraṃśā śaktiḥ*); its partlessness arises from its nature as consciousness (*cidrūpatvāt*). Therefore, both Nāda and Bindu, being partless, consist of the power Śāntā. The form of Nāda and Bindu consists of a square and sixteen petals.
The meaning is that the two wheels consist of the power of Śāntā.

"Kalā" has the nature of Will (icchā); the meaning is that the form of Will is the form of Kalā, and thus the eight-petaled lotus consists of the power of Will. Jyeṣṭhā is knowledge; she is indeed the power of knowledge.

The form of Jyeṣṭhā consists of fourteen spokes; this means it is composed of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). The remainder, consisting of the five powers known as Kriyā, Raudrī, Vāmā, Viṣaghnī, Dūtarī, and Sarvānandā, constitutes the five wheels (cakras) known as the twelve-spoked, the eight-cornered, the triangle, the trident, and the bindu.
The meaning is that it consists of the power of action (kriyā-śakti). || 23 ||
Having previously established the nature of the *kāmakalā* starting from the verse "Because the Wheel is of the form of emptiness" (1/10), he now concludes:
"Thus, it consists of a triad."
The wheel is, in its ultimate sense, the expansion of the form of Kāmakalā. || 24 ||
In this manner described, the wheel (*cakra*) consists of a triad—that is, it is composed of the three mother-energies (*mātṛśakti*) beginning with Vāmā;

it consists of the three points (*bindu*), having the form of the syllable *kāmakalā*. From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that from which something has emanated is its ultimate reality, and it is of that same nature. Just as clay is the [material cause] of a jar, and the jar is of the nature of clay, so too are the threads [the cause of the cloth].

Just as a cloth consists of the form of its threads, so too, for the Śrīcakra that has emanated from the syllable Kāmakalā, the syllable Kāmakalā is the ultimate reality; the meaning is that the Bindu-cakra is of that very nature. || 24 ||

Furthermore, he describes another mode of impression (*vāsanā*) for this very wheel by means of the passage beginning with "In Akula and that which is called Viṣu" and ending with "reeling with supreme bliss" (verses 25–35):
"In Akula, in that which is called Viṣu, in the Śākta, and likewise again in Vahni..."
It is not attained without purification through meditative cultivation, [but rather] at the tip of the uvula or between the eyebrows. || 25 ||
In the Moon, in its half, in Rodhinī, in Nāda, and in Nādānta;
furthermore, in Śakti, in Vyāpikā, and within the sphere of Samanā and Unmanā.
In the Great Bindu, there is Akula;
that which is other than Kula is Akula. The red lotus with a thousand petals situated at the root of the Suṣumṇā is named Akula.
Above that is the six-petaled Kula-lotus, located above the eight-petaled lotus. As it has been said:
In the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Below and above the Suṣumṇā is [the lotus] endowed with a thousand petals;
it is red and white, situated upon those thousand petals, and joined with the Śaktis."
O Īśānī, facing upward and downward, endowed with pericarp and filaments,
it is the form of Śakti, O Mahādevī, auspiciously consisting of both Kula and Akula.
O Īśānī, there are two lotuses situated eternally and imperishably;
between them, within the Suṣumṇā, is the triṃśat-ādhāra-paṅkaja.
The form of Śakti is the very nature of Śiva and is the abode of the presence of Śarvāṇī;
I shall now describe their forms and activities in due order—listen.
O Goddess, the space between the anus and the penis is five finger-breadths in height;
the *kanda* is one finger-breadth in the middle and two finger-breadths in width.
In its center is the Great Yoni, having the form of a triangle;
O Maheśvarī, Suṣumnā is situated in the middle of that Yoni, at its root.
Below is a thousand-petaled lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments;
it is radiant with light, blazing with jewels, and its petals are occupied by the Śaktis.
O beloved, she is surrounded by powers (śaktis) arranged like the filaments of a lotus;
O Goddess, the Kuladevī resides in the center of the pericarp (karṇikā).
Above that lotus, in the center of the Suṣumnā, one finger-breadth higher,
there is a lotus endowed with eight petals and possessed of eight knots.
It is red, endowed with beautiful pericarps, and adorned with red filaments;
it has three prongs at the tip of its knot, and is surrounded by the eight Bhairavas beginning with Brahmāṇī.
It is surrounded by the powers (śaktis), beginning with Vāmā, who reside in the knots situated upon the eight petals,
as well as by other powers stationed on the prongs.
"Then one should meditate upon that which is served by the Kaula power in its center;
above it, at a measure of one finger-breadth, is the six-petaled lotus of Kula.
Now, if the meaning is that "Akula is other than Kula," then would not the eight-petaled lotus situated in the space between them also be Akula?

To address the question "Why should it not be so?", he says: "And [it is] called *viṣuva*. The root *viṣḷ* means "to pervade" (Dhātupāṭha 1095, juhoty-ādi). That which pervades the *suṣumnā* as well as the thirty lotuses situated within it is the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasradalakamala*), and it is called *viṣuva* because it is the support of all. Therefore, the eight-petaled lotus is not *akula*; this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "in the Śākta fire": here, it should be read as "the Śākta [fire] in the fire" (*vahnau śāktaḥ*), by way of transposition.
The "fire" is the *mūlādhāra*, because it is the support for the form of the fire. As it is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"The lotus of the support is yellow, with four petals and beautiful filaments."
And in the center of that, the supreme goddess Kuṇḍalinī is facing downwards.
The inconceivable [goddess] resides in the center of the Svayambhū, surrounded by Varada and the others;
this is indeed the earthen lotus, and above it is the supreme lotus.
O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate upon the fiery [form] and the powers situated within it as being partless (niṣkalā), O Supreme Goddess, resembling a mass of lightning.
"Above that, in the center of the pericarp, is the orb of fire;
above that is the Pūrṇa-pīṭha, and in its center, O Śivā, resides Śākinī.
Thus, in the Śākta [system], *śakti* is *hṛllekhā*; because it is situated above that, the Svādhiṣṭhāna is "Śākta."
A six-petaled lotus.
This is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Above the foundational lotus, at a distance of two and a half finger-breadths..."
The Taijasa [mandala] has eight petals and is joined with a yellow pericarp.
In the center of the pericarp of the Hṛllekhā [cakra], which is served by Anaṅga and others,
two finger-breadths above this is the six-cornered Svādhiṣṭhāna.
"And having meditated upon Kākinī, who is watery and surrounded by powers preceded by Bandinīśakti—[filling the space]—thus [it is said].
In the navel, in the ten-petalled lotus called Maṇipūraka. This has been stated in that very same place:
Three and a half finger-breadths above the navel is that lotus,
the Maṇipūra, which is very beautiful and possesses ten petals.
"And that [lotus] situated in the midst of Lākinī is surrounded by Ḍāmārī and the others. Thus it is said.
In the Anāhata [cakra], located at the heart, there is a twelve-petaled lotus. Regarding this, it is stated in that very same place:
"Above fourteen finger-breadths from the lotus called Maṇipūra..."
The lotus in the center of Rākinī is the twelve-spoked Anāhata.
"And it is surrounded there by the Śaktis such as Kālarātri;
the solar orb situated there, however, is the seat (pīṭha) called Nādoḍyāna.
Thus it is said regarding the pure sixteen-petalled lotus situated in the throat. That very point is stated in that same [text]:
Therefore, one finger-breadth above that is the pure sixteen-spoked [cakra];
O Supreme Goddess, the Ḍākinīs reside in the center, while the Putras are on the outside.
"Situated from the syllable *Amṛta* up to the end of the vowels is the lunar disc above that.
This refers to the eight-petaled lotus at the tip of the *lambikā*. As it is said in that very same place:
"O Supreme Goddess, four finger-breadths above the throat is the *lambikā*."
"In that [lotus] is an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by Vaśinī and the others. Thus it is said.
Within the two eyebrows, in the Ājñā [cakra], is a two-petaled lotus. Regarding this, it is stated in that very same place:
"The support of Ājñā is a two-petaled lotus, joined with the two petals of *ha* and *kṣa*."
"Haṃsavatī is by the side of the Earth (Kṣamā), while Hākinī is between the two of them.
Here, the singular number in "bhravaḥ" (of the eyebrow) is an indication for the pair of eyebrows;
the meaning is "between the two eyebrows. "Indau" means in the *bindu*. [The sequence is] *bindu*, its half (*tadardha*), *rodhinī*, and *nāda*— [End of excerpt]
He will describe the forms and the times of pronunciation for Nāda, Antaśakti, Vyāpikā, Samanā, and Unmanā, each situated one above the other.

In the Great Bindu, known as Paramāda, which is devoid of the forms of space and time, the divisions beginning with Bindu and ending with Unmanā are progressively more subtle; they are common to the cakras of one's own body and to the vidyās. What is the meaning? Here:

The meaning is that one should contemplate the portions of the wheels—ranging from Trailokyamohana to Bindu—as gross, subtle, and subtler, within the portions that are gross, subtle, and subtler, starting from Akula and ending with Unmanī, and also within the Great Bindu (mahābindu). || 25–26 ||
He speaks again of its threefold nature:

"Furthermore, one should meditate on the wheel in this way as threefold. That is to say, one should again meditate on the wheel—already visualized in the manner described—once more as being threefold.
He states the threefold nature: "Up to the level of Ājñā it is called Sakala; beyond that is Sakalaniṣkala. (27)

One should contemplate the gross eight-fold wheel (cakrāṣṭaka), which extends from Ājñā up to Akula—that is, from the beginning of Ājñā to the end of Ājñā, and from the square (caturasra) to the triangle (trikoṇa)—as existing in three ways as partless (niṣkala) in the supreme state up to Unmanī. That contemplation is "with parts" (sakala). Then, starting from the Bindu up to Unmanī...

One should contemplate the increasingly subtle portions of the *cakras*. That contemplation is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*). In the supreme place, the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*), one should contemplate the consciousness of pure emptiness; that contemplation is without parts (*niṣkala*). Thus it exists in three ways. These [stages] beginning from *akula* and ending with the Command (*ājñā*) have been explained in detail in other tantras, and therefore they are not mentioned here. || 27 ||

He describes the essential nature, the time of utterance, and the location of [the powers] beginning with Baindava and ending with Manonmanī, starting from the verse "In the form of a lamp" (dīpākāraḥ) up to "Manonmanī" (ślokas 28–34):
"In the form of a lamp, consisting of half a mora, it is held to be circular in the forehead. (28)
It has the form of a lamp; the meaning is that its illumination is like that of a lamp. It consists of half a *mātrā*.
The time required for the pronunciation of a short vowel is called a *mātrā*. That whose duration of pronunciation is half a *mātrā* is "half-a-mātrā" (*ardhamātra*).
It is intended to be circular on the forehead. Its circular configuration is on the forehead, in the upper portion above the two eyebrows.
The "lamp-shaped" (*dīpākāra*) means the duration of the pronunciation of half a *mātrā*, and its arrangement is that of a circle; this is the meaning of the *bindu*.
The detailed exposition of the *bindu* and the others, however, has been elaborated upon in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*. Regarding the *bindu* therein, it says: "The enclosure of the *bindu* is above."
Resembling ten million suns, it is exceedingly radiant and possesses great qualities.
In the center of that is a lotus measuring ten billion yojanas;
upon its pericarp sits the Lord, the Sovereign Beyond Peace (Śāntyatīteśvara).
Five-faced and ten-armed, his form resembles a mass of lightning;
he is Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti, in due order.
O beautiful one, these stand surrounding Śāntyatītā;
Manonmanī is seated on the left side of Śāntyatītā.
"All [the goddesses] bear five faces and have ten arms adorned with the moon;
the principle of the Bindu (Bindutattva) is thus described as being surrounded by hundreds of billions. (28)
The form above that is the half-moon, measuring one foot;
the Jyotsnā is one-eighth of that, and the Rodhinī has the shape of a triangle.

The half-moon (*ardhacandra*) is the half-portion of the drop (*bindu*); its form is precisely that of a lamp-flame. "A quarter-measure" (*pādamātra*) means the duration of pronunciation equal to one-fourth of the time of a *mātrā*. "Above that" (*tadūrdhvake*) means in the upper portion of the drop; the meaning is that the half-moon, shaped like a lamp-flame, has a duration of pronunciation of one quarter-measure in the region above the drop. It has the appearance of moonlight (*jyotsnākārā*).

Rodhinī has a luster equal to moonlight; its measure consists of one-eighth of that [unit], and the duration of its pronunciation is one-eighth of a mātrā; its form is triangular (tryasra). The detailed explanation for both is as found in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*: "Above that is the Half-moon (ardhacandra), and above that is Rodhinī."
Jyotsnā, Jyotsnāvatī, Kānti, Suprabhā, and Vimalā as well.
These five digits (kalās) situated in the half-moon are proclaimed as:
Rundhinī, Rodhinī, Rodhā, Jñānarodhā, and Tamopahā.
O beautiful one, the five *nirodhikā-kalās* have been described to you,
because they obstruct the attainment of the supreme state by Brahmā and the other supreme lords.
She is called "the destroyer" (nirodhikā); from her differentiation, O fair-faced one, comes the attainment known as "supreme grace" (parasāda). Thus [it is said]. || 29 ||
Between the two *bindus* is the staff (*daṇḍa*), shaped like a phallus and radiant as a jewel;
it consists of one part and two parts, ending with the *nāda*, blazing like lightning. (30)

The *halākāra*, however, shines forth joined with a dot (*bindu*) situated on its left. Having the form of a straight line situated between two dots, it is of the nature of the *śeva*; the vessel situated between the two testicles is called the *śeva*, and it has a form similar to that. It possesses the luster of a gem, with a color like that of a ruby (*padmarāga*). It is a portion of the *kalā*s; [it consists of] the *kalā*s.

"Sixteen mātrās" means the duration of pronunciation consisting of sixteen parts. Furthermore, that portion of a *kalā* is called *nāda* in the *Tantra*. According to Amara: "The word *kala* refers to a deep sound, while *nāda* refers to a sweet yet indistinct sound. Thus, *nāda* is a sweet and indistinct resonance.
The elaboration of Sound (*nāda*) is as described in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*:
"That which was called by you 'Rodhinī'— Sound is situated above it,
resembling the filaments of a lotus, with a radiance equal to ten million suns."
Surrounded by innumerable cities, he is encompassed in the center by five kalās:
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and likewise Mocikā.
Among those [channels], the one going upwards and situated in the middle is the fifth, the supreme digit (kalā);
in its center is a space of eighty million yojanas, possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons.
One should meditate on the Lord seated in the center of a lotus, rising upwards,
resembling ten thousand moons, with five faces and three eyes.
The god, who holds a trident and wears matted locks, was surrounded by Indhikā and others;
and upon his lap sat the supreme Śivā, who ascends upwards.
One should meditate—[on the syllable] *dhyāyet*—thus:
"blazing like lightning," meaning possessing a splendor similar to lightning; "shaped like a plow," meaning having a form resembling a plow;
"joined with a dot situated on the left," meaning joined with a dot located in the right portion between two dots.

"Double portion" (*dviguṇāṃśa*) means the thirty-second part, which is double the sixteen parts mentioned previously. What is its purpose? It means that the end of the resonance (*nādānta*), characterized by specific features such as the shape of a plow (*halākāra*) and so forth, is the duration for the pronunciation of the thirty-second part of a *mātrā*. The "end" (*anta*) of the resonance is its dissolution (*laya*). The expansion (*prapañca*) of that [dissolution] occurs in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
As it is stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*:
"The plow-shaped [vowel] ending in Nāda,
having pierced through this entire universe and having burst forth by means of the downward power (adhaḥśakti), terminates at the upward power (ūrdhvaśakti)."
Dissolved in the channel at the aperture of Brahma (brahmabila), it is characterized by unmanifest sound;
therefore, the aperture of Brahma should be known as being joined by millions and billions of Rudras.
There, Brahmaśiva is to be known as resembling a hundred moons;
he has ten arms, three eyes, five faces, and the moon as his crest-ornament.
"But there is another power, Brahmāṇī, who rests upon the lap of Brahmā;
she stands having blocked the gateway to the path of liberation. (30)
Furthermore, Śakti is of a steady form, arising from the bindu situated on the left. || 31 ||
Pervasive, it has assumed the form of a triangle shining as a *bindu*.
By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), a distinction from the preceding [elements] is illuminated.
For the preceding parts, such as the *bindu* and so forth, their own essential nature, phoneme, measure, and temporal portion were merely conceptualized.

The meaning is that the nature, phonemes, measures, and durations of the constituent parts beginning with Śakti and ending with Samanā will be described later. Śakti is the form of the stable [letter] arising from the bindu situated on the left side between the two bindus. The expansion of Śakti is as follows in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
The great Śaktitattva has been fully described as being enveloped by worlds;
now I shall briefly explain the support of those worlds.
Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, Amṛtā, and Mṛtā are situated in the four directions; Vyāpinī is known to be situated in their midst.
"Five-faced, three-eyed, and possessing great splendor is the fifth;
this is declared to be the Śakti-tattva, which bestows the fruit of liberation through meditation.
This means that by the play of the Bindu, Vyāpikā—consisting of the three powers beginning with Vāmā—has assumed the form of a triangle.

This, however, has been explained by the very discourse on the principle of Śakti (śaktitattva) in the Svacchanda-saṃgraha, as previously stated in the passage beginning with "And [the powers] subtle" and ending with "are situated. || 31 ||
Furthermore, it consists of a straight line situated between two points (bindus). || 32 ||
Samanā is the straight line shining with the *bindu*, and likewise Unmanā.
This is clear. Regarding the expansion (*prapañca*) of Samanā, it is stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*:
"But the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), whose nature is consciousness and bliss, is above that."
That power is indeed called Sāmanā, the cause of all causes.
Presided over by Śiva, she sustains all eggs;
mounted upon her is the Blessed Lord Śiva, the supreme cause.
Śiva, the cause of all causes, constantly performs creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace.
Śiva is the agent of all; this Śakti is held to be the cause.
From the single Bindu alone, she emerges in the form of a radiant straight line as Unmanā.
Regarding the manifestation of Unmanā, it is as stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*:
That power which exists as the cause is known as Unmanā above that;
because the mind transcends [all states] there, it is therefore called Unmanā.
Herein there is no division of time, no principle (tattva), and no deity;
it is called the supreme, pure face of Rudra, which is perfect nirvāṇa.
"It is known as the power of Śiva, free from conceptual construction and untainted. (1.32)
He describes the color, the measure, and the temporal portion of [the principles] beginning with Śakti and ending with Samanā:
"The body of those beginning with Śakti is radiant like twelve suns. (1.33)
Sixty-four [mātrās] above that, and then doubling it again and again;
such is the measure of the parts for Śakti and the others, up to Manonmanī and Unmanī. (1.34)
From Manonmanī up to the limit of Manonmanī. That which is called Manonmanī is Samanā because it is accompanied by the mind (*manaḥ*);

because it is devoid of that [mind], it is called Unmanī. The body, the essential nature, of the parts beginning with Śakti and ending with Manonmanī, is like the twelve blazing suns; its color is the same as twelve suns risen simultaneously in one place.

The "sixty-fourth part of a *mātrā*" means that the time of a sixty-fourth part of a *mātrā*. Beyond that, however, the pronunciation of the *mātrā*-part of the Pervasive (*vyāpikā*) is double; that is, the time for a portion of the *mātrā* of the Pervasive is one hundred and twenty-eighth part [of a *mātrā*]. After that—
The meaning is that the duration of its constituent parts is equal to one two hundred and fifty-sixth part of the time of a single [vocal] utterance.

Unmanī, as has just been described by these specific attributes, is likewise formless and beyond utterance, according to the manner stated in the Upaniṣad: "From which speech turns back, along with the mind, not having attained it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4).

Because its sphere transcends speech and mind, it is called *unmanī*. In the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*), there is no time for the utterance of forms or phonemes; therefore, they are not mentioned here, because that [state] transcends the universe. As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"O fair lady, it transcends the principles (*tattva*) and is the sphere beyond speech and mind."
"Partless, undivided, formless, free from conceptual construction, beyond dualities—the supreme reality known as Śiva, the highest state. Thus [it is said].
The duration for the pronunciation of the gross phonemes, beginning with the letter *ha* and ending with the *bindu*, is one *mātrā*.
The duration from the *bindu* up to the *samanā* is one half-mora (*ardhamātrā*). The time of utterance proceeds from half of that [half-mora] in descending order down to a *lava*.
A *lava* is defined as the time required to pierce a stack of lotus petals with a fine needle.
"Because of the statement: 'But that time which exists in each *dala* is what is designated as a *lava*. Beyond that, there is only emptiness, because there is no time more subtle than that.
The meaning is that through such contemplation (*bhāvanā*), one should become Śiva himself. This has been stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava Bhaṭṭārakas:"

"By means of the gross sequence of phonemes of the mantra in its condensed form, through the utterance of the half-moon, the point, the end of sound, and the void, one becomes Śiva. (Vi.bhai., śloka 42).
Here, although it should have been stated as "the point and the half-moon," the inversion [of the order] is for the sake of metrical requirements.
"Through the utterance of the Void (śūnya), which concludes with Nādānta, Bindu, and Ardhendu, one becomes Śiva"—this is the grasping according to the method of *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).

This is because Rodhinī and Nāda exist above Ardhendu, and Śakti, Vyāpikā, and Samanā exist above Nādānta. By the word "Void" (*śūnya*), Unmanā is expressed. Therefore, it is through the utterance of the Void that concludes with Nādānta, Bindu, and Ardhendu [that this occurs].
"May there be Śiva"—this is the statement in summary form regarding the mantra consisting of the *piṇḍa*. (1.33–34)
Unconditioned by space and time, it is supreme and great beyond that;
it is naturally beautiful and reeling with supreme bliss. (1.35)

Above that, and above all three—the *sakala*, *sakalaniṣkala*, and *kevalaniṣkala*—consisting of the letters beginning with *ha* and ending with the *mahābindu*, is the Supreme Great (*paramaṃ mahat*). Greatness exists even in objects such as pots relative to smaller dimensions; therefore, it is called "Supreme" (*paramam*), because there is no greatness beyond it.
It is supremely great. For this very reason, it is unconditioned by space and time.
That which is indeed unconditioned by space, time, and form is called "supremely great. Therefore, it is naturally beautiful.
In the world, even an object that is not beautiful appears as if it were beautiful through superimposed ornaments such as garments; but this [reality] is—
Beautiful by its very nature (*svabhāvasundara*), because it is desirable as one's own self to all; "reeling with supreme bliss" (*parānandavighūrṇita*).
While there is also a momentary bliss (*ānanda*) even in the experience of objects such as sound and so forth, it is therefore called "reeling with supreme bliss.
What is the meaning? [It is] that which is more ancient than the things established in the three forms, and which is not limited by space or time.

The meaning is: she is the power of reflective awareness (vimarśaśakti), whose form is supremely great, who is beautiful by her very nature, who possesses supreme bliss fulfilled through the state of identity (sāmarasya) with Supreme Śiva whose essence is self-luminous, and who is the venerable Mahātripurasundarī. || 1/35 ||

Now he explains the latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of the *mātṛkā*, which was indicated in the verse: "The expansion, the abode of the waves of the universe, consisting of the three Mothers" (1.11):
"When one perceives the vibration of the Self, that is the supreme *kalā*."
Having assumed the form of Ambikā, the supreme speech (parā vāk) was uttered. || 1.36 ||
She is the supreme [power], whose nature is the non-dual awareness (*vimarśa*) of all phonemes and so forth; *kalā* is the power of awareness.

She should "behold"—that is, she should desire to behold—the "vibration" (*sphuraṇa*), which is the process of awareness proceeding from the levels of *paśyantī* and so on up to *vaikharī*, of the Self who is Paraśiva.
Then, having become supremely tranquil in essence, she assumes the form of Ambikā, becoming a constituent part of the aspect of Light (*prakāśa*).

Having attained a state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) with Ambikā, the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*) is uttered; she is called the Supreme Mātṛkā. As it is stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*: "The fusion of these two is clearly manifest in the supreme light. (1.36)
When Vāmā becomes intent on manifesting the universe that exists in the state of a seed, she assumes the form of a goad (aṅkuśa) because of her emission of the universe. (1.37)
Then this very power of will (icchā-śakti) abides in the form of Paśyantī;

the universe exists in the state of being a seed. Just as a tree resides within a seed, so the universe, consisting of the thirty-six principles (tattvas), remains in the Supreme (parā) as mere causality; she becomes oriented toward manifesting it when she is intent upon making it clear.
She is intent upon making manifest—that is, bringing forth. Here, "bringing forth" (utpādana) means the manifestation of an effect that already exists within the cause.

For this very reason, she is called *Vāmā* because she makes the effect manifest; she is *Vāmā* because she emits (*vamana*) the universe, that is, because she brings forth from the cause what is already present there.
"Emitting" (*vamana*) means the external ejection of food and so forth that was contained within the stomach; "bringing forth" (*utpādana*) is exactly the same.

For this very reason, she is *Vāmā* because she vomits out the universe—which exists within her own belly—in the form of a womb (*garbha*). Furthermore, having assumed the shape of a hook (*aṅkuśa*) due to her curvature, she became the left line of the *śṛṅgāṭa*, whose nature is emission (*sṛṣṭi*). The meaning is that then the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), having attained a state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) with the power of *Vāmā*, abides in the form of *Paśyantī*. || 1/37 ||
Likewise, Jyeṣṭhā is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and she is proclaimed as the intermediate speech (madhyamā-vāk). || 1.38 ||
In the maintenance of the universe, she whose form is celebrated as consisting of straight lines is likewise the Jyeṣṭhā-śakti,

the power of knowledge; and likewise the Vāmā-śakti, having attained a state of equilibrium with the power of will (icchā-śakti), was the left line of the triangle (śṛṅgāṭa) consisting of emanation, and so too is the Jyeṣṭhā-śakti.

She has attained a state of equilibrium with the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). Her form is renowned for the maintenance of the universe, because she is the cause for the stability of the created universe. She consists of straight lines; here, she takes the form of the line at the tip of the *śṛṅgāṭa* (triangle). She is uttered as the *madhyamā* speech, having attained the nature of the *madhyamā-mātṛkā*. (1/38)
But at the time of its withdrawal, she assumes the form of the Bindu.

In this very order of reversal, she who is intensely radiant with the form of a crossroads (śṛṅgāṭa) is this Raudrī, the power of action (kriyāśakti), who is Vaikharī and whose body is the universe. (1.40)
At the time of the withdrawal of the created and established universe, Ambikā,

abiding in the form of the *bindu* (the point) and consisting of the state of tranquil non-duality (*sāmarasya*), having manifested from the central *bindu* and accomplished both creation and maintenance,
becomes intent upon its withdrawal and enters back into that very *bindu*. Thus, by way of this process of return, she is Raudrī.

Through the state of equilibrium with the power of action (kriyāśakti), she herself takes the form of a triangle (śṛṅgāṭa); becoming the southern line of that triangle, she shines brilliantly in the form of a triangle. A "triangle" (śṛṅgāṭa) is a three-cornered figure. The meaning is that Vaikharī, whose body is the universe, has arisen in the form of Vaikharī, which consists of the expansion of the nature of speech. (1/39–40)

Having described the triangular (śṛṅgāṭa) form of Ambikā and the others, who consist of the aspects of light (prakāśa) and reflective awareness (vimarśa), as well as the four powers beginning with Śāntā, he now states the meditative impression (vāsanā) consisting of the fourfold state of the phonemes and the liṅgas in the form of the seats (pīṭhas) situated within the triangle.

From the passage beginning with "Because of the manifestation of the universal form" up to the end of verse 1.49—"These four powers, moreover, are [the letters] Ka, Pa, Jā, and O, respectively"—it is stated:
"Because of the manifestation of the universal form, both within one's own nature and externally, these are the four powers, namely Ka, Pa, Jā, and O, in that order. (1.41)

He states the reason for the fourfold [powers] to be described in the second half [of the verse]: "because of manifestation" (*bhāsanāt*). The universe, consisting of name and form from Śiva down to the level of Earth (*bhūmi*), manifests within His own nature as a seed-potency (*bījabhāva*) and externally as the nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭyātman*);
thus, these four powers derive their designation from the verbal root *śakl* in the sense of pervasion (*vyāptau*, Dhatupatha 1262).

The four [energies] beginning with Ambikā and the four beginning with Śāntā have attained mutual state of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya) in sequence; they reside respectively as Kā, Pū, Jā, and O. Kā is the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Kāmarūpa, Pū is the sacred seat of Pūrṇagiri, Jā is the sacred seat of Jālandhara, and O is the sacred seat of Oḍyāṇa. By virtue of their nature as illumination (prakāśa) and reflective awareness (vimarśa),...

The meaning is that the four previously mentioned powers, having become one in essence (*samarasībhūtāḥ*), have transformed into the form of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) of Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, and Oḍḍiyāṇa. || 1/41 ||
He describes the meditative absorption (*vāsanā*) regarding the nature of the four seats (*pīṭha*) as consisting of the *piṇḍa* and so forth:
"The seats are situated respectively in the *kanda*, the *pada*, the *rūpa*, and the *rūpātīta*.
The *kanda* is the root of the *suṣumnā*. By the word *kanda*, the *kuṇḍalinī* known as the *piṇḍa* located there is indicated.
As it is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Having led that wind from below the Suṣumnā to the location of the kanda,
[one should contemplate] the Supreme Goddess Kuṇḍalinī, whose forms are will, knowledge, and action."

"Śivā, who has the form of the Mātṛkā and the appearance of a sleeping serpent. Here, "pada" means *haṃsa*; "rūpa" means the *bindu*; and "rūpātīta" (beyond form) means the stainless (*nirañjana*) reality (*tattva*).
This is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"The *piṇḍa* is proclaimed to be the power Kuṇḍalinī; the *pada* is celebrated as the *haṃsa*;
the *rūpa* is known as the *bindu*; and that which transcends form (*rūpātīta*) is the pure consciousness (*cinmaya*). Thus [it is said].
There are four seats (*pīṭhas*), designated by the terms *piṇḍa*, *pada*, *rūpa*, and *rūpātīta*.

The respective locations indicated are the foundation (ādhāra), the heart, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). By this, the meaning is that they abide in those places in sequence and consist of their respective natures.
Indicating that these [elements] take the form of earth, air, water, and fire, he states the distinction of their essential nature (tattva):
Likewise, there is a square, one joined with six dots (bindus), and a circle. || 1.42 ||

Their forms are, respectively, a half-moon and a triangle. The seat of Kāmarūpa is square in form; this means it is the element of earth (*bhūtattva*), because the terrestrial mandala is square in shape. And the seat of Pūrṇagiri is circular, joined with six dots (*bindu*).
It has the form of a circle endowed with six dots; this means it is the wind element (*vāyutattva*), because the wind-maṇḍala has the form of a circle with six swirls.

The half-moon is the Jālandhara-pīṭha, which has the form of a half-moon and consists of the water element (*aptattva*), because the water-maṇḍala has the form of a half-moon. The triangle is the Oḍyāṇa-pīṭha, which has the form of a triangle and consists of the fire element (*tejastattva*).

Because the mandala of fire is triangular in form, the meaning is that these are the forms of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) beginning with Kāmarūpa in their respective order. Here, the element of space (gaganatattva) is not mentioned because it is formless and partless. || 1/42 ||
He states the colors of the seats (pīṭhas) in their respective order:
yellow, smoky-grey, white, and red; such is the color declared. (1.43)

The meaning is that because earth, air, water, and fire are respectively yellow, smoky-grey, white, and red in color, the *pīṭhas* (sacred seats) possess those very same colors. The meaning of the individual components is clear. Here, the sequence of the elements follows the order of the *pīṭhas*; however, regarding the *pīṭhas*, the sequence is fixed according to the specific tradition (*āmnāya*). || 1/43 ||
Regarding the lingas on the pedestals, he says:
"The self-manifested (svayambhū), the Bāṇa-liṅga, and the other supreme one—O fair-faced lady, these lingas are established upon the pedestals. (1.44)
They are called *liṅgas* because they lead one to understand the object that is the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), which is withdrawn and beyond the range of the external senses.

The mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and thought (*citta*), as well as the realms of desire and form (*kāmarūpādi*), are *pīṭhas* because they serve as the substrata for the vibration of consciousness (*citsphurattā*).
Within these forms of the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there reside the *liṅgas* such as the *svayambhū*, which consist of their respective fourfold functions.
The meaning is that they reside [there]. All of this has been explained in detail in the *Saubhāgyasudhodaya*, as follows:

"Once again, in the Kāma-pīṭha, which is situated in the front corner and consists of the form of the mind (manas), that light reflected there is declared by the wise to be the Svayambhū-liṅga. (1.5.6)
In the southern corner, within the form of egoity (ahaṅkāra), it has transmigrated into Jālandhara;
by virtue of the distinction of the limiting adjuncts of transmigration, the supreme abode has become the Bāṇaliṅga. (1.5.4)
In the left corner of the central triangle is the venerable Pūrṇapīṭha;
within this, the supreme splendor, reflected in the intellect, has assumed the state of the other Liṅga. || 1/5/2 ||

That which is reflected from the supreme abode (paradhāman) when it has been transferred to the luminous point (jyotirbindu) within the glorious seat consisting of consciousness (cittamaya śrīpīṭha), is proclaimed by the wise as the supreme sign (paraliṅga). Thus [ends verse 1.4]. 1.44.

Having distinguished between the nature of the *liṅgas*—those of yellow and other colors—and the phonemes of *vaikharī* speech, he says: "The self-manifested Great Liṅga consists of three peaks enveloped by vowels, resembling gold, the bandhūka flower, and the autumnal moon. (1.45)
The Bāṇaliṅga is surrounded by the letters from *ka* to *ta*, is triangular in shape,
has the form of a *kadamba* bud, and is encircled by the letters from *tha* to *sa*.
The subtle form, encompassed by all the vowels, is the supreme liṅga;
it is the form of the bindu, the root of supreme bliss, arisen from the eternal state. (1.47)

The *svayambhū-liṅga* is like a jasmine flower, yellow in color, having three peaks in the form of the three *bindus*, and surrounded by the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*. The *bāṇa-liṅga* is like the *bandhūka* flower, red in color, triangular in shape, and surrounded by the consonants from *ka* to *ta*. [The *icchā-liṅga*] is like the autumn moon, white in color.

The other *liṅga* has the shape of a *kadamba* bud and the form of a *kadamba* flower-cluster, surrounded by the letters from *tha* to *sa*. Because the supreme *liṅga* consists of supreme light, it is devoid of phonemes (*avarṇatva*). Therefore, it is of a subtle nature beyond the reach of the senses. For this very reason, the supreme *liṅga* is of the nature of the *bindu*, surrounded by all the phonemes—that is, encircled by the fifty letters from *a* to *kṣa*.

The bulbous root of supreme bliss (*parānandakanda*): the bulbous root consisting of bliss belonging to the Supreme (*parā*), who is of the nature of the imperishable (*akṣara*) and possesses branches such as *paśyantī* and the rest; it is arisen from the eternal state (*nityapadodita*). And its eternity is due to the fact that Mātṛkā is devoid of origination and destruction. "Arisen from the state" (*padād uditaṃ*): from the state that is to be reached by the minds of those seeking liberation from the universe, it has arisen in the form of the first vibration (*spanda*). (1/45–47)
He states that all of these are the forms expressed by the fourth Vidyā, which is joined with the three seed-syllables:
"Furthermore, these forms expressed by the entire mantra joined with the three seed-syllables are indeed composed of Kula and Kaula. (1.48)
These— the four powers, the four *mātṛkās*, the four central corners,
