the four seats (*pīṭhas*), and the four *liṅgas*— all these belong to the fourth Vidyā, which is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of that entire mantra joined with the three seed-syllables, namely the *vāgbhava*, *kāmarāja*, and *śakti* seeds.

These are the forms of the denotable (*vācya*). Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the denoter (*vācikā*), and all these are the denotables. Therefore, the meaning is that this knowledge consists of that tetrad, because of the non-difference between the denoted and the denoter. "Kula" is characterized by the object of knowledge (*meyam*), the means of knowledge (*mānam*), and the knower (*mātṛ*); "kaula" is their aggregate.
The meaning is that they consist of that. || 1/48 ||
He states that all these aforementioned [states] consist of four natures and are composed of waking and the others:
"These, however, have the forms of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth.
Here, waking (*jāgrat*) is the activity of the body and the senses; dreaming (*svapna*) is the functioning of the internal organ alone.
Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the cessation of all the senses and the perception of mere bliss; the fourth state (*turīya*) is the functioning of pure consciousness alone.
Regarding this very point, he will say later: "O Goddess, the Great Waking state (*mahājāgrat*) [occurs] in the fire by means of the two pairs of senses" (3.177), and so forth.
Having previously described the fourfold nature of the wheel (*cakra*), [he now speaks] of her who dwells in the *bindu* within its center.
He describes the nature of self-awareness as transcending that [object] in the following verse:
"But the supreme light, which is the very essence of the arising of self-awareness, is transcendent. (1.49)

It is "transcendent" (*atīta*), meaning it transcends the four states beginning with waking. For this very reason, it is "supreme" (*para*), as it stands beyond the universe (*viśvottīrṇa*) because it is superior to the universe. Furthermore, it is the supreme, unsurpassed (*anuttara*) form of light. Regarding this, scripture says: "That indeed is the light of lights" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 2.2.9). It consists of the arising of one's own consciousness and abides as the Self within all living beings. As it has been said:
In the Navaśatīśāstra: "The infinite, supreme light resides in the heart of all living beings. (1/49)

Furthermore, in order to explain another latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding the Wheel, [the author], having described the reality that transcends the universe, states the impression to be expressed:
"The form of the universe is inlaid with the delineation of the universe consisting of one's own will."

The "sketching of the universe" (*viśvamayollekha*): the universe consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*); that which consists of this is the sketching. It is called a "sketch" (*ullekha*) because it is sketched out; it is a painting. By means of that sketching of the universe consisting of His own will, He is "inlaid" or pervaded—meaning He sketches the painting of *māyā* upon the wall of His own self by means of the brush of His own will. As it is said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"—He unfolds the universe upon his own wall by his own will" (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 2). And regarding this, there is the following authoritative statement:
"Having painted the variegated world within himself with the brush of his own will, the Lord Śiva beholds it himself and finds delight. (1)

It is the universal form (*viśvarūpaka*). Therefore, the meaning is that it has transformed into the forms ranging from Śiva down to the earth. Just as milk transforms into the form of curd, so too does the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) itself transform into the form of the universe.
As it is said in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāhṛdaya*: "Consciousness is autonomous, the cause of the manifestation of the universe" (Sūtra 1).
To the question, "What follows from this for Paramaśiva?", he says:
"Consciousness is the nature of the Self, beautiful with innate bliss. (1.50)
Consciousness (*caitanya*) is the power of self-reflection (*cid-vimarśa-śakti*); it is the nature of the Supreme Śiva, who is the Self whose essence is light, beautiful with innate bliss.
Through its state of equilibrium with that [light], it is desirable to all because of the manifestation of innate joy.
The power of reflection creates the universe through its equilibrium with the Supreme Śiva, whose essence is light, and not in isolation.

Just as a sprout is not produced by the husk alone, nor by the grain alone, but rather by both when they possess an inseparable relationship (*ayutasiddha-sambandha*), so it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"The supreme power (*parā-śakti*) is non-different from Śiva and embodies all sequential processes. (1.50)
He says that very thing:

"Having its radiance contracted by the expansions of the object, the subject, the means of knowledge, and the act of knowing, it assumes the form of a triangle (śṛṅgāṭa), consisting of will, knowledge, and action. (1.51)

This is the object of knowledge (*meyam*); this is the knowable (*prameyam*). Valid cognition (*pramā*) is a correct experience that is the objective domain of valid cognition. One who possesses that [cognition] is the knower (*pramātā*).

The instrument of valid cognition is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇam*). As it has been stated in another treatise: "Valid cognition (*mitiḥ*) is correct determination; and the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtā*) is the possession of that [cognition]."

"Thus, in the system of Gautama, validity consists in the exclusion of non-connection. (Kāvyālaṅkāra 4.5). The very expansion of self-awareness, which is non-conceptual in nature, into the form of concepts consisting of the knower, the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the act of knowing, is itself its contraction. The power of Śiva, whose nature is light like a lamp, is indeed the radiance known as *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).

She, whose nature is non-conceptual (nirvikalpa), assumes the form of the universe through the distinctions of the object of knowledge, the knower, the act of knowing, and the means of knowledge; thus appearing in a contracted form, Śiva too becomes contracted at that time. Both of these consist of will, knowledge, and action;
differentiated by the divisions of the aspects of the powers such as Will, Jyeṣṭhā, and Vāmā, they take on the form of a triangle (śṛṅgāṭa) and are transformed into the shape of a triangle.

The meaning is as follows: having previously, in the verse beginning with "pūrvaṃ bījatritayayuktasya sakalasya manoḥ" (1/48), explained that the Vidyā—consisting of the *kāmakalā* and so forth—is fourfold, being composed of the *pīṭhas* such as the triangle which is the cause of the Śrīcakra; he now explains the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that the Deity likewise consists of those same elements. He elucidates this very point in the passage beginning with "viśvākāraprathādhāraḥ" and so on.
With the words ending in "surrounded by waves flashing from the mass of her powers" (verses 52–55):

[He is] resting upon the lap of Kāmeśvara, seated on his throne, exceedingly beautiful, and taking refuge in Śiva, whose own form is the substratum for the manifestation of the universe in all its forms. (1.52)

The power of self-reflection (*vimarśa-śakti*) is the manifestation of the universe in all its forms, transformed into the nature of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*). Its support is its own innate form, which is its true ontological form; Śiva is that whose essence is light (*prakāśa*). That supreme radiance has as its locus and support Śiva, who is the innate form that serves as the foundation for the manifestation of the universe in all its forms. Thus, it is "that which has as its support Śiva, the innate form that is the foundation for the manifestation of the universe in all its forms."

Seated upon the lap-couch of Kāmeśvara—Kāmeśvara is Śiva, whose nature is light (*prakāśa*); seated upon his lap-couch is she whose form is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*). She is exceedingly beautiful and supremely auspicious, for she is desired by all as their own very self. (1.52)
He bears the noose consisting of the power of will (icchā-śakti) and the goad whose form is knowledge (jñāna-rūpin),
while holding the resplendent bow and arrow consisting of the power of action (kriyā-śakti).

The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) alone is the noose, because it is the cause of bondage. The power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) alone is the goad, because it acts as the restrainer of the elephant consisting of the mind. The arrow and bow consist of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); for according to the statement, "Sound, touch, and so forth became its arrows, and the mind became its bow," the arrows such as sound are coupled with the mind as the bow.

The act of binding (*saṃyojana*) is the very operation of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). In this context, he bears a fourfold array of weapons—namely, the noose consisting of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), the goad consisting of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and the arrow and bow consisting of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)—shining brightly as they are held by his four arms, which assume a form composed of the aesthetic essence of desire (*kāmakalā*) through His own will, because He is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-ātmaka*). (1.53)
It possesses eightfold differentiated weapons by way of the distinction between the substratum (*āśraya*) and that which rests upon it (*āśrayin*).
The substratum is Kāmeśvara; that which rests upon it is the supreme radiance known as Kāmeśvarī.
Thus, it possesses eightfold differentiated weapons by way of the distinction between the substratum and that which rests upon it. "Weapon" (*heti*) refers to an armament belonging to the substratum.

The eightfold cause consists of four weapons and four supports. What is the meaning? Paraśiva himself, having divided his own two aspects through the nature of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), becomes Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī;
thus, by distinguishing between male and female, He holds the noose, goad, bow, and arrows as eight [attributes], existing in the relationship of support and supported.

The meaning is that [the Supreme] dwells in the supreme *liṅga* consisting of the fourth *bindu*, within the *bindu*-cakra known as Sadāśiva, which is situated in the center of the triangle composed of the vowels.
He is mounted upon an eight-spoked wheel and seated on a throne of nine wheels.

In the manner previously described, that very triangle—which consists of the powers of Vāmā, Icchā, and so forth—becomes divided threefold through the distinction between the two powers and the single Fire (Vahni), thus becoming the eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭāracakra*). Furthermore, that same [triangle], having become the three steps and the form of Fire and Power, became the nine-fold wheel (*navacakra*). Such is the Śrīcakra, which is itself the eight-spoked wheel.
Consciousness (citi), the mind (citta), sentience (caitanya), the dual activity of cognition (cetanā-karma),
the individual soul (jīva), the creative power (kalā), and the body— this is considered the subtle "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
Thus, according to the method stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*, having divided one’s own subtle *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city),

it is established as the eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭāracakra*) in the sequence beginning with Vaśinī; this means that the couple situated upon the seat of the nine wheels (*navacakrāsana*)— of such a nature— is itself the ninefold foundation of one's own self, which is divided into the state of nine wheels, [corresponding to] the ninefold power of one’s own resonance (*nāda*).
Having realized [the self] in the form of the Mistress of the Nine Wheels,

I contemplate the great triangle— the triad of powers beginning with Will (icchā), known as the qualities of the bound soul (paśu) such as Sattva and the rest— proceeding from the unsurpassed mouth of the Guru. (1.18)
This region of the eight spokes and the eighth part [is present] in the exits of consciousness, beginning with the *sādi*;
this is the subtle *puryaṣṭaka* of the Goddess, for such is the venerable doctrine. (1.17)
I meditate thus upon the inner ten spokes of the lotus as the row of the organs of knowledge and action belonging to Mahātripurasundarī. 1/16.
This external portion, consisting of ten parts, is the domain of the organs of cognition and action. || 1.15 ||
The fourteen spokes and the earth are the fourteen instruments. 1/4.

I determine that the Lord who resides in the wheel, whose region is marked by the lotus and the covering of wealth (the earth), is the source of the primordial natures beginning with the Unmanifest and ending with the gross elements. (1.13)

I honor that region marked by a sixteen-petaled lotus, which consists of the elements, the senses, and the mind, and has fallen into the state of being subject to transformation, together with the Goddess. (1.12)

Thus, according to the method stated in the *Subhagodayavāsanā*, the meaning is that [the deity] resides in the form of the senses and so forth within the nine cakras—beginning with the *baindava* and ending with the square (*caturasra*)—which serve as the seats. || 1/54 ||
"Such is the supreme splendor abiding in the form of the Śrīcakra.

This means that it exists in the form of the Śrīcakra, which— according to the manner described— consists of parts beginning with the triangle and ending with the square, comprising the sixteen transformations starting from one's own will (*nija-icchā*).

Thus, when that couple has been transformed into the form of the Śrīcakra, he states that the very powers (śakti) which constitute its limbs abide in the form of the deities of the enclosures (āvaraṇadevatā):
"It is completely surrounded by the surging waves of the multitude of its powers" (1.55).

The limbs of those two, Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, are their very members; their powers (*śakti*) are the multitudes or groups thereof, and these are the throbbing waves or ripples. By these it is encompassed.
What is the meaning? [It means] within the limbs of the forms assumed by the will of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, who consist of Light (*prakāśa*) and Reflection (*vimarśa*).

The meaning is that when [the powers] have attained the state of being limbs of the Wheel (*cakra*), even the powers of those limbs remain surrounding [it] in the form of the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*), such as Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and so forth. By the word "wave" (*ūrmi*), this is illuminated:
the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), whose nature is Light (*prakāśa*), is the ocean; Kāmeśvarī, whose form is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is the water.

Its constituent parts are the multitudes of powers (*śakti*) and the waves; just as billows arise in the ocean and dissolve back into it, so too this wheel (*cakra*), consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) together with its powers, arises and sets within that very same [reality]—this is the intended meaning. Regarding this, there is a statement by an authoritative teacher:
One should contemplate that the wheel of power (śakticakra), which has arisen from the root and attained identity with it,
is dissolved into that very same imperishable reality (tattva).
"One should worship that which is the root within one's own self, whose nature is consciousness; for that alone is [the root].

(1.55) Having explained the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of all the wheels (*cakra*), he describes the non-difference between them and the Self, together with those impressions, by means of the passage beginning with "In the expansion of the conscious Self" and ending with "thus consisting of the wheel" (verses 56–71).
When, endowed with the full desire to create, she performs by her own will the manifestation and withdrawal of the universe upon the wall of the conscious Self. (1.56)

The power of action (*kriyāśakti*), however, is called *mudrā* because it gladdens and dissolves the universe; it is the power of consciousness (*cit*) consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). "Upon the wall of the Self" (*ātmabhittau*) means that the Self itself is the wall—the "wall of the Self"—and upon that, [it rests] as its own essential nature.

The meaning is "the wall. Of the universe, from Śiva down to the earth. Illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*amarśana*): illumination is the making manifest of that which was unmanifest; reflective awareness is precisely the state of being brought into the heart as "this-ness" (*idantā*). When such illumination and reflective awareness exist at the time of emission, endowed with a full desire to create—a specific desire to act—[it constitutes the wall].

The desire to transform (*vicikīrṣā*). A transformation also exists for things such as milk through the process of curdling and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "endowed with the full desire to transform. In that case, however, the transformation of milk and the like consists only of curds and so forth; here, however, the transformation takes the form of the *tattvas* beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth. For this very reason, she is "endowed with the full desire to transform. As for the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), however—
Having become the very power of action (*kriyāśakti*)—the particle *tu* being used for emphasis—[she acts] because of the gladdening (*modana*) and the melting (*drāvaṇa*) of such a universe.

Here, "gladdening" refers specifically to a favorable activity; "melting" means becoming of one essence with that [power]. Consciousness (*saṃvit*) thus receives the name "mudrā. The meaning is this: when the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*) desires to sport in the form of the universe, then...

The meaning is that, having become the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), she has attained the name "Mudrā" through her delight (*modana*)— characterized by supreme consciousness and bliss— in the universe which is her own transformation, and through her melting (*drāvaṇa*)— characterized by oneness with that [consciousness]. (1/56–57) In that regard, he first describes the pervasive *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā*:
When that Mother of Consciousness consists of the three kalās, || 1.57 ||
Having assumed a three-part form, she is always present;
she is proclaimed to be the pervader of the entire sovereign wheel (cakrarāja). (1.58)

That consciousness, whose nature is discernment (*vimarśa*), having become Ambikā—the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three *kalās* consisting of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī, and comprising the three *kalās*; and having also become Śāntātmikā—the collective totality of the three *kalās* consisting of the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*)—the mention of "Ambikā" here is intended to include Śāntā as well. This is the meaning.

She has assumed a three-part form (*trikhaṇḍārūpa*). The fingers of the right hand, beginning with the index finger, are the aspect of light (*prakāśāṃśa*); the fingers of the left hand, beginning with the index finger, are the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśāṃśa*). The meaning is that the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā arises as possessing three parts characterized by the binding nature of the union of those two. She is always present; for this very reason, she is the deity of consciousness (*saṃviddevatā*).

She brings about the presence of Tripurā; she is the one who effects her [Tripurā’s] immediate proximity. Because she is the most excellent among all the kings of wheels (*cakrarāja*), all wheels, and all yantras for worship, she pervades the *cakrarāja*.
Furthermore, because she constitutes the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the nine mudrās situated within the nine wheels. (1/57–58)
He speaks of the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā:
"Furthermore, this very Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī exists due to the abundance of the yoni;
she, in whom the power of Vāmā is predominant, resides in the Wheel of the Gate. (1.59)

This very [power] is three-fold (trikhaṇḍā), having released itself into three parts due to the abundance of the *yoni*. One [part] arises from the union of the two middle fingers; another from the union of the two ring fingers; and yet another from the union of the two little fingers. Thus, due to the abundance of the *yoni*, she is the "All-Agitating" (*sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī*).
This *Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī Mudrā* causes the inclination toward supreme bliss; it is dominated by the power of Vāmā (*vāmāśakti*).

Because it is dominated by the power of Vāmā, it is emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). Emanation itself is agitation (*kṣobha*). It resides in the Trailokyamohana Cakra, which consists of three squares and possesses four gates within the Wheel of the Gate (*dvāracakra*). (1/59)
He describes the Drāviṇī Mudrā:
It agitates the entire universe, relies upon the abundance of Jyeṣṭhā, takes the form of gross sound and its subtle parts (kalā), and bestows grace upon all. (1.60)

In the [kalpa] called Sarvāśāpūraṇa (Fulfiller of All Hopes), she is this very one whose form is throbbing; she is the stabilizer of the agitated universe, establishing it in her own pure state of consciousness alone. Therefore, she relies primarily upon the Jyeṣṭhā [power], because the Jyeṣṭhā-śakti is the cause of stability. She is of the nature of the gross *nāda* and *kalā*.

She is *sthūlanāda* (gross sound), because she is within the range of hearing. The *nādakalās* are the sixteen vowels, which are born from *nāda*. Regarding this, there is the statement of an authority: "Therefore, they call the *kalās* those born of *nāda*" (*Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya* 7.18), and so forth.
She has that form because she fills the wheel that fulfills all desires—the abode of [deities] such as Kāmākarṣiṇī.

Because she is the support for the *kalā* that attracts desires (*kāmākarṣiṇī*) in that which is called "the Fulfilled of All Hopes" (*sarvāśāpūraṇa*), she is therefore the one who bestows grace upon all. Indeed, the attraction of desire itself is the grace toward all. By the word "she" (*saiṣā*), the *mudrā* called "The All-Enthraller" (*sarvavidrāviṇī*), as taught in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra* (3.6–7), is referred to. She has a throbbing form because her nature is consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*). What is the meaning?

She is of the nature of *sthiti* (maintenance) because she is the support for the abundance of *jyeṣṭhā*; for this very reason, she consists of the union of the middle and index fingers with the little and ring fingers, which are of the nature of *ṛju*. Because she takes the form of *Kāmākarṣiṇī* and others, she bestows grace upon all; and because she is their support, she manifests her form within the wheel called *Sarvāśāparipūraṇa*, being of the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvit*).
The meaning is that this very mudrā, which causes all things to dissolve, exists as it has been explained in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra*. || 1/60-61 ||
He describes the mudrā that attracts all:
"By the equality of the right and left hands, she relies on the primacy of emanation. (1.61)
This mudrā is known as the Attractress (Ākarṣiṇī) and the All-Agitating (Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī).

It consists of the essential identity of Jyeṣṭhā and Vāmā, being the state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya) between the two powers of Jyeṣṭhā and Vāmā. It relies primarily upon emanation (sṛṣṭi); for Vāmā is the form of emanation, while Jyeṣṭhā is the form of maintenance (sthiti). This is due to the equality of both.

The meaning is that this [mudrā] is common to both creation and maintenance: by its left portion, it consists of the two fingers—the ring finger and the middle finger—bent; by its right portion, it consists of the two fingers—the ring finger and the little finger—joined straight. Precisely because it consists of two bent fingers, this *ākarṣiṇī* (attracting) mudrā is remembered as belonging to the *sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī* (all-agitating) wheel, which causes the agitation of all things. This is the traditional teaching (*smṛti*).

Knowledge produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience. The meaning is that the mudrā previously experienced in the *Catuḥśatī* scripture (3/7–8) is now remembered; it is said to be accompanied by its residual traces (*savāsanā*). 1/61–62.
He describes the mudrā that effects universal penetration:
"O Maheśvarī, it has the form of a bindu situated in the space between the two voids. (1.62)
Through the union known as Śiva and Śakti, she is remembered as the one who brings about divine possession;
she resides in the fourteen-spoked wheel, her form being consciousness and bliss. (1.63)
There are five voids (*vyoma*) within the intervals of the six cakras from the *ādhāra* to the *ājñā*.
Between each pair of these, there is one *bindu*; thus, there are five *bindus* composed of the five elements. As it has been stated by the learned:
"The differentiation consists of the five *bindus*, which are the cage of the five *praṇavas*. Such is its form.

She is in the form of the *bindu* situated in the space between the two voids (*vyoma*). Due to the mutual union of Śiva and Śakti: the fingers of the right hand are of the nature of Śiva, and the fingers of the left hand are of the nature of Śakti. Having been rotated by way of Śiva and Śakti, they are inserted into the intervals between one another's fingers.

Due to the intense mutual pressure of all [the deities], this mudrā, which effects divine possession (*divyāveśakarī*), arises; it is the effectuator of possession—that is, the effectuator of the state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*)—with respect to the Divine (*divya*), who is Śiva whose nature is luminosity. Abiding in the fourteen-spoked wheel (*caturdaśāracakra*), specifically in the wheel named "Bestower of All Good Fortune" (*sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka*), she is the power of consciousness (*saṃvicchakti*), whose very form is bliss (*ānandavigrahā*).
She is of the nature of the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) with Paramaśiva. What is the meaning?

This *mudrā* consists of the act of binding characterized by the description of the essential identity between the two—the Śiva and Śakti—which are composed of five points (*bindu*), each represented by a single finger situated between the fingers of both hands; it is filled with the bliss of the singular flavor of consciousness (*saṃvid*).
The meaning is that she resides in the fourteen-spoked wheel. || 1/62–63 ||
He describes the Unmādinī-mudrā: "Consisting of a crest of subtle form shimmering within the Bindu, it is primarily the power Jyeṣṭhā and causes the intoxication of all. (1.64)
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, you stand established upon the ten-spoked wheel (*daśāracakra*).

From the interval of the *bindu*—that is, from the space between the two self-existent (*svayambhū*) and supreme (*parā*) liṅgas known as the Great Bindus of the Yoni, which reside within the channel starting from the *ādhāra* and ending at the *brahmarandhra*—you shine forth, consisting of a radiant, subtle form of flame. You are shining forth from that interval.

In its subtle form, she has the appearance of a lotus fiber; like a crest, she is the crest of Ambikā and Śānti, consisting of them and having the nature of their single essence (*ekarasya*). She is preeminent in the power of Jyeṣṭhā and abounds in the power of Jyeṣṭhā. She causes universal intoxication (*unmādana*);
"intoxication" (*unmāda*) is a delusion of the mind (*cittavibhrama*). [She makes] all those who are averse to all worldly activities appear as if they were intoxicated.

The meaning is that she causes [the practitioners] to be intent upon the contemplation of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti. "Abiding on the ten-spoked wheel" (*daśāracakramāsthāya*) refers to the external ten-spoked wheel (*bahirdaśāracakra*). "O you who are saluted by heroes" (*vīravandite*): heroes are those intent upon bringing about the dissolution of the enemy of "this-ness" (*idantāripoḥ*) on the battlefield; they are saluted by those who have cultivated the sense of "I-am-ness" (*ahambhāvanā*) through the self. As it has been said:
In the *Parāpañcāśikā*:

"Bringing about the dissolution of the 'I' which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the 'this' (*idam*), he who is intent on supreme valor enjoys his own nature, which removes all inauspiciousness. (Verse 50).

What is the meaning? It is the form of the two bindus (points) resulting from the union of the two thumbs with the two hands called Śakti and Śiva— which resemble the two crests of the *kuṇḍalinīs* of fire and nectar known as Ambikā and Śāntā, shimmering within the interval between the two bindus of *kula* and *akula*.

The mudrā called Sarvonmādinī— consisting of the two little fingers placed within two circles, having the form of the joining of the tips of the two index fingers in a straight configuration due to the predominance of the Jyeṣṭhā-śakti, and characterized by the bond of contemplating the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti— is established upon the external ten-spoked wheel.
The meaning is "established. || 1/64–65 ||
He speaks of the Mahāṅkuśa mudrā:
"Furthermore, the Mahāṅkuśa consists primarily of the left Śakti. (1.65)
In the same way, vomiting forth the universe, she resides in the second decade, intent on delight and having assumed the form of a mudrā. (1.66)

First, there is that [mudrā] which consists of a subtle flame-like form shimmering within the space between the fingers, having the form of a straight union of the index and ring fingers, and is dominated by the power Jyeṣṭhā. Now, it is dominated by the power Vāmā; for, according to the previously stated method, "Vāmā has assumed the shape of a goad because she vomits forth the universe" (1.37), it is therefore dominated by the power Vāmā.
She has the form of binding the index fingers in a curved shape, vomiting forth the universe because she is of the nature of emanation; thus, she is like Paramaśiva.

In the second [wheel], however, the ten-spoked inner ten-spoked [wheel], she is intent on delighting—consisting of the supreme contemplation characterized by the state of essential identity with Paraśiva—and for this very reason, she has assumed the form of a *mudrā*.

The meaning is this: the very power of consciousness (cicchakti), consisting of the reflective awareness of the previously described characteristics of the mudrās, which has become the Vāmā-śakti and takes the form of being inclined toward the supreme bliss of union with Paraśiva through the two index fingers (tarjanī), is the Mahāṅkuśa-mudrā situated within the inner ten-spoked wheel. || 1/65–66 ||
He describes the Khecarīmudrā:
Arising from the friction of dharma and adharma, she has the form of consciousness;
she destroys the defects consisting of the omission of actions arising from conceptual construction. (1.67)
The supreme Khecarī, who removes the diseases of the form of conceptual construction,
abides as pure consciousness within the wheel known as Sarvarogahara.
From the union of *dharma* and *adharma*. *Dharma* is Śakti, because she is the supreme state of all attributes such as creation and so forth.

*Adharma* is Śiva, because he is devoid of all those respective attributes. Their union is their state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*); from that [union] she has arisen. She is "consisting of consciousness" (*vittirūpiṇī*). Consciousness (*vitti*) is perfect awareness (*saṃvitti*). She is the destroyer of the defect consisting of the loss of action arising from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the apprehension of two alternatives, a state of doubt such as "it is thus" or "it is not so. Actions arising from conceptual construction take the form of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites; through their omission, transgression generally arises, and [this [state] is its destroyer. It is the remover of the diseases whose nature is conceptual construction. Regarding the perfect being Śiva, [the thought] "I must do this" or "I must not do this"— *Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be an incomplete thought regarding the cessation of dualistic deliberation concerning one's duty.*

Diseases are of the nature of conceptual construction; mental anxieties themselves are physical ailments. As it has been said by the learned: "The disease of thinking oneself incomplete is the sole source of wretchedness; it brings about affliction and is exceedingly painful. The *khecarī* (the sky-farer) is that which removes these [ailments]—she who moves within the consciousness (*citi*) where all sequences of activity have been cast out, and whose arising is eternal.
"She is the one who brings about the attainment of the state of Śiva, the Khecarī who removes all exhaustion" (Ci.

38). According to this method stated by me, consciousness (*citi*), which moves upon the plane of non-conceptual awakening—the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) whose nature is identity with Paramaśiva—resides as consisting of pure awareness (*saṃvinmayī*) within the wheel called "the remover of all diseases" (*sarvarogahara*), because it is presided over by Him.

What is the meaning? It is the form of a *bandha* (hand-gesture) characterized by the joining of the tips of the two thumbs upon the pair of middle fingers situated above the pair of ring fingers and little fingers, which are held by the two hands with their index fingers extended, while the right and left arms— consisting of Śiva and Śakti— are crossed.

Arisen from the union of the two powers of Śiva and Śakti, she moves upon the ground of supreme, non-conceptual awareness; for this very reason, she destroys the defects consisting of the omission of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites produced by conceptual thought, and consequently,
she removes the diseases of conceptualization characterized by the sense of incompleteness within the wheel known as Sarvarogahara.
The meaning is that the khecarī mudrā is established. 1/67–68.
He speaks of the seed-gesture (bījamudrā):
Furthermore, within the interior of the sky that flashes forth from the close embrace of Śiva and Śakti, she always manifests the universe which exists in a subtle form. (1.69)
The Mahāmudrā, whose form is the seed-syllable, abides within that which consists of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).

It is the union of Śiva and Śakti, their state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), flashing forth in the midst of the space between them—in the exceedingly subtle interior of the sky, which is the nature of light (*prakāśa*) and awareness (*vimarśa*). It exists there in a subtle form.

Abiding as the mere state of being the cause, she constantly and at all times illumines the universe; for this very reason, she is the Mahāmudrā in the form of the seed (bīja), because she is the cause for the future arising of the universe in its forms of moving and non-moving beings. Since she is the support for the Bījamudrā—which is the cause for the arising of the universe and consists of all accomplishments (*siddhi*)—there is the accomplishment, that is, the arising, of everything from Śiva down to the Earth.

This has been stated in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāhṛdaya*: "Consciousness is autonomous, the cause of the manifestation of the universe" (Sūtra 1). She resides within the wheel (*cakra*) composed of that [consciousness]. What is the meaning?
It refers to the two curved hands, known as Śiva and Śakti, with their two little fingers crossed at their tips and held [in that position].

The Seed Gesture (*bījamudrā*), which manifests the universe as existing solely as its causal state within the space perceived in the interval between the tips of the two index fingers and thumbs— joined at their tips and extended from both sides of the face, with their curved forms positioned above the two middle fingers— is designated as "consisting of all accomplishments" (*sarvasiddhimayā*).
The meaning is that she is situated upon the wheel. || 1/69–70 ||
He speaks of the *yonimudrā*:
"Furthermore, this is the ground for attaining the fully perfected light. (1.70)
The Yonimudrā, whose form is the *kalā*, abides in that which consists of all bliss.

It is the ground of attainment, the place of reaching Paraśiva—the light of lights who is the full radiance. For this very reason, it is called Yonimudrā; it is a *mudrā* whose form is the *yoni*. The *yoni* is a triangle.
She is the one whose form is the interior space of the inner triangle, which consists of the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) among the triad of powers beginning with *Vāmā* and *Īcchā*.

She is of the nature of *Kalā*, and her form is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) consisting of the half-*kalā* of the Heart. Therefore, she resides in the wheel named Sarvānandamaya, which is composed of all bliss, characterized by supreme bliss arising from the aesthetic identity of Śiva and Śakti, and whose form is the Supreme Bindu.

She stands. What is the meaning? [It refers to the gesture] wherein the tips of the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*) are grasped by the tips of the two index fingers (*tarjanī*)—which are curved in the form of the left *icchā* (will) [finger]—and which are surrounded by the tips of the two middle fingers (*madhyamā*) joined straightly and consisting of the *jyeṣṭhā* (eldest) [finger] and *jñāna* (knowledge); and the tips of the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikā*), which consist of the *raudrī* (fierce) and *kriyā* (action) [powers], are joined together in their entirety.

The meaning is that the *yonimudrā*— which consists of the form of the two tips of the thumbs as the nature of illumination (*prakāśa*) and which is composed of the digit of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—

abides in the wheel (*cakra*) consisting of the supreme point (*parabindu*), which is characterized by the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) between illumination and reflective awareness and is filled with all-bliss.
(1/70) He concludes:
Because its nature consists of both action and consciousness, it exists thus as the wheel.
"Action, for the power of action consists in the gladdening and the melting of the universe" (1.57)—thus was the power of action introduced.
That very power of action, through its differentiation, consists of creative arrangement (*viracanā*) due to the predominance of the powers such as Vāmā;
it takes the form of various *mudrās* beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Yonimudrā, and because its nature is consciousness, it is composed of the *cakras*.
The meaning is that it exists as consisting of the nine wheels (cakras), beginning with Trailokyamohana and ending with Sarvānandamaya. || 1/71 ||

Now, one might object: "Since it was introduced with the words, 'That supreme power, by her own will, takes the form of the universe' (1.9), how can it be concluded later with the statement, 'Thus, because its nature is both action and consciousness, it exists as consisting of the wheel' (1.71)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that case, this is a grand summary of the subject at hand."
The wise person should always contemplate the supreme light in the form of will (*icchārūpa*).

The "supreme light" is the light consisting of the Supreme (*parāmaya*), which is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti. It is "in the form of will," meaning it consists of the manifold expansion (*prapañca*) of names and forms assumed through its own will. "Always" means throughout the three periods of time. The wise person should contemplate [it].
By the falling glance of one's own Guru, who is the manifest form of Supreme Śiva, [the bonds are severed].
Compassion, doubt, fear, shame, and fifthly, disgust;
as well as family, conduct, and caste—these eight are proclaimed to be the fetters (pāśas).

The meaning is that one should always contemplate the supreme light (*parāmayaṃ tejaḥ*), which consists of the manifestation of various names and forms fashioned by one's own will, transformed into the form of the *Śrīcakra*, and in which the state of "I am the Supreme Śiva" (*paraśivāhaṃbhāva*) shines forth through the eightfold bond (*pāśāṣṭaka*) as described in the words of the authoritative masters.
Furthermore, he describes another mode of impression for this very wheel: "The convention of the wheel is again threefold and ninefold. (1.72)
This is clear. 1/72 ||
In that regard, he first describes the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the three realms:
"One [is formed] by one fire and two powers; another, again, by those [same] and also by the triad of fires and the triad of powers. (1.73)
Another [mandala] consists of two lotuses and three earth-houses;
it comprises five powers, four fires, two lotuses, and three earths. (1.74)

The great wheel is complete with one fire and two powers; this is one mode. Furthermore, by means of those three triangles—which consist of one fire and two powers—there is another [mode] consisting of three fires and a triad of powers.

This is the method. The meaning is as follows: this first method arises from three fires and three powers (śaktis) arranged in ascending order above the very same triangles. Another method consists of two lotuses and three earth-pavilions (bhūgṛhas).
These two lotuses—the eight-petaled and the sixteen-petaled—are located within the space between the three circles, while the three earth-pavilions [are situated] there.
Three squares. When this has been done, the complete Mahācakra in its collective form consists of five Śaktis, four Vahnis, two Padmas, and three Mahīs. || 1/73–75 ||
He explains those three modes by analyzing them in detail: "That mode is now demonstrated.
Among them, the first would be the nine-fold womb (navayoni), joined with the twelve. (1.75)
One should know that the human womb is the third [stage] immediately following that;
it is endowed with eight, two, and eight petals, and is possessed of three squares. (1.76)
The singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jātāvekavacanam*); the meaning is that its various types are being demonstrated. "Therein" means among those types.
"The first is the nine-fold source" (*navayoni*) is an explanation of [the phrase] "by one fire and two powers.
When there is a conjunction of one fire and two powers, the wheel of the nine sources (*navayonicakra*) arises through the bindu, the triangle, and the octagon.

The meaning is that it "comes into being. By that [means], one should know the supreme *manuyoni* (the fourteen-petaled lotus) as being joined with the "twice-ten" (twenty). By that nine-petaled wheel (*navayonicakra*), joined with the twice-ten—that is, joined with two ten-spoked wheels—one should understand the supreme, the second [wheel], which is the fourteen-spoked wheel (*caturdaśakoṇa*). Thus, when the three fires and the three powers (*śakti*) have been established, there arise the two ten-spoked wheels and the fourteen-spoked wheel.

The meaning is that the second wheel consists of three circles. Immediately after that, it is endowed with eight and two sets of eight petals and is accompanied by three squares. By this, it means that [the third wheel] stands immediately thereafter, without any interval, being extremely close;
the third wheel consists of three squares and is endowed with an eight-petalled lotus and a sixteen-petalled lotus—this is the meaning.
Now, one might ask: how is it that each of the three wheels possesses a single modality? It is said:

according to the method stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*, namely "by means of the sequence of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal through the differentiation of parts for each [wheel]," there is an inclusion [of all aspects] because each triad of wheel-components is distinguished by emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). For example: [The text continues with specific examples.]

The three squares are emission-emission (*sṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*); the sixteen-petaled lotus is emission-stasis (*sṛṣṭisthiti*); the eight-petaled lotus is emission-absorption (*sṛṣṭisaṃhāra*). Thus, this triad of wheels is one because it consists of emission. Likewise, the fourteen-spoked wheel is stasis-emission; the outer ten-spoked wheel is stasis-stasis; the inner ten-spoked wheel is stasis-absorption. Thus...

The three wheels are one because they consist of *sthiti* (maintenance). Thus, the eight-spoked wheel is *saṃhāra-sṛṣṭi* (dissolution-creation), the triangle is *saṃhāra-sthiti* (dissolution-maintenance), and the bindu is *saṃhāra-saṃhāra* (dissolution-dissolution). In this way, the three wheels are one because they consist of *saṃhāra*.
Keeping all of this in mind, he says:
The threefold nature of the wheel has been declared, O Supreme Goddess;
this is clear.
Now, if the threefoldness of the wheel has been stated, then does this wheel begin from the central wheel?
To the question "What cannot be produced?", he says:
"Creation would extend from the nine wombs (yoni) up to the earth; reabsorption, however, [proceeds in the reverse order]. (1.77)

The definitive conclusion of the scripture is that [the sequence] begins with Earth and ends with the Nine Yoginīs. Here, by the term "Nine Yoginīs," the Bindu-cakra situated within the Nine Yoginīs is indicated.
Emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) is the extraction starting from that Bindu-cakra and ending with the square (*caturasra*). Resorption (*saṃhṛti*), on the other hand, is as follows:

"From Earth up to the nine sources (yonis)" means that the extraction (*uddhāra*) and dissolution (*saṃhāra*) begin from the three squares and extend up to the *bindu*; this is the definitive conclusion of the *Catuḥśatī* scripture. Therefore, the intended meaning is that one does not extract the wheels (*cakras*) beginning with the middle one. This is just as in the case of Devadatta, Viṣṇumitra, and Yajñadatta.
Just as when it is said, "Fruits are to be given to Devadatta and Yajñadatta" regarding those who are present, it is understood that they are not to be given to Viṣṇumitra; so it is here. 1/77–78.
Having previously explained the visualization (*vāsanā*) by dividing the Śrīcakra part by part, he now states the visualization of the collective (*samaṣṭi*) cakra:
"This, moreover, which is the form of the collective, is called the Tripurā-cakra. (1.78)
This triad of creation and the other two, taken as a collective whole, is called the "aggregate" (*samaṣṭi*). However, the "whole" (*avayavī*) is not like that;

it is not designated by the term "creation," nor by the term "maintenance," nor even by the term "dissolution. Rather, it is called the "Wheel of Tripurā" (*tripurācakra*), because it exists prior to creation and the others, being the primordial and beginningless reality denoted by the word "Tripurā."

One's own consciousness is called the ground of the manifestation of the wheel (*cakra*). This has been stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati* with the passage beginning, "The eight Vaśinīs together with the intermediate spaces," and ending, "Then the Inexplicable (*anākhyā*), which is all-pervading. (1.78)

Now, one might object: "Let that very Tripurā, whose nature is self-consciousness, be known; what is the use of this laborious effort to catch a crane by means of a circle characterized by mental impressions (*vāsanā*)?
To this, he says: "By the mere knowledge of which, one becomes a knower of Tripurā."

By the mere cognition of which, and when that alone is known, one becomes a knower possessing the knowledge of Tripurā through the mere knowledge of the Tripurā-cakra. What is the meaning? It is that the knowledge of the pure, formless form of Tripurā is impossible. Therefore, by the method already stated, she is embraced within the Baindava-cakra in the midst of this [Tripurā-]cakra through its latent impression (vāsanā).
The meaning is that it is possible to know it. As it has been said by the learned:
"I make the sky of consciousness take form within the Great Yoni (mahāyoni), like the wheel [of fire] or the solidity of ghee, and like the solidification of molten gold" (Suvā. 36).
Having previously indicated the ninefold nature of the wheel, he now promises to explain it:
"And I shall tell you, O beloved, the ninefold nature of the wheel. (1.79)
The meaning is: "Since you are my most beloved, therefore I shall tell you even a secret. || 1/79 ||
Now he describes the ninefold nature itself:
"The first [mandala] shall consist of three earths; the second has sixteen spokes;
the other is said to have eight petals; and immediately thereafter is the human-cornered [triangle]. (1.80)
The fifth should be ten-cornered, and the sixth also ten-spoked;
the seventh should be eight-cornered, and the eighth is a triangle in the center.
The ninth [mandala] should have a triangle in the center; by means of three earths (bhūs), it consists of three squares. The "manu-cornered" is fourteen-spoked; the "vasu-cornered" is eight-cornered.
The rest is clear. (1.80–82)
He states the names of the nine cakras that have been mentioned:
"Listen now to their names:
the Trailokyamohana Cakra, which fulfills all hopes. (1.82)
O Gaurī, this supreme wheel agitates all, bestows all good fortune, accomplishes all aims, and provides all protection. (1.83)
O Goddess, it removes all diseases and likewise consists of all perfections;
it is also composed of all bliss—listen, O beautiful one, to this ninth [chapter]. (1.84)

*Trailokyamohana* (the Deluder of the Three Worlds). "World" (*loka*) is so called because it is perceived (*lokyate*), that by which it is perceived (*lokyate 'nena*), or that which perceives (*lokayati*). Thus, through the etymological derivation as object, instrument, and agent, the "three worlds" (*trailokya*) consists of the object of knowledge (*meyam*), the means of knowledge (*mānam*), and the knower (*mātṛ*). Its "deluder" (*mohana*) is that which conceals [duality] by producing the realization of non-duality (*advaita-pratīti*). *Sarvāśāparipūraka* (the Fulfilled of All Hopes). "Hope" (*āśā*) refers to the desire of one who is unsatisfied.

It is the "desire for other objects," and it is the "fulfiller of all that desire" by means of establishing the state of identity with Supreme Śiva, which is characterized by eternal, perfect satisfaction. It is the "agitation of all," meaning the agitation of everything from the earth up to Śiva according to the sequence of the levels of reality (*tattva*); it is the cause of that [agitation] which is characterized by withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

Because its nature consists in the dissolution of the manifold of duality (*bhedaprapañca*), it bestows all auspiciousness (*sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka*). "All auspiciousness" refers to being desirable by all; it bestows this by establishing identity with Supreme Śiva, who is the object of supreme love and desired by all.
It accomplishes all goals (*sarvārthasādhaka*). The "goal" (*artha*) is the purpose of all Vedic and Tantric rites.
The attainment of Paraśiva; as it has been said by the great poets:
"For the paths that lead to perfection, though divided in many ways by the scriptures, fall into you alone, like the torrents of the Ganges into the ocean" (Raghuvamśa 10.26).
It establishes this: it is the "creator of all protection. Protection (*rakṣā*) means the avoidance of injury caused by adverse objects.

Since everything consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) is indeed an adverse object, [this practice] effects protection from all of them, characterized by the cultivation of the state of Śiva-egoity (*śivāhaṃbhāva*). This has been stated in the *Parāpañcāśikā*:

"I, bringing about the dissolution of this [world] which stands in opposition to the 'I'-consciousness, intent upon my own prowess, enjoy my own nature which removes all inauspiciousness. (Śloka 50). Thus, it removes all diseases. That which is characterized by differentiation—the entire system consisting of the thirty-six principles—is itself disease; of that...

It is *hara* because it is the cause of the realization of non-duality (*abhedapratīti*). It has been stated in this very [text]: "The supreme *khecarī* is the remover of the diseases that take the form of conceptual construction" (1.86).
It consists of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhimaya*). All accomplishment means its origination, maintenance, and withdrawal;
it consists of these, because the triangle is the cause of all creation, maintenance, and withdrawal. As it is said in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāhṛdaya*: "Consciousness..."

"Independent, it is the cause of the manifestation of the universe" (Sūtra 1). It consists of all-bliss, because its nature is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which are characterized as Śiva and Śakti. Here, throughout all this, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is precisely the repose in non-duality (*advaita*), due to the difference in the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). || 1/82–84 ||
He states the purpose of the previously mentioned wheel of latent impressions (*vāsanācakra*):
"In this [wheel], the Great Goddess Mahātripurasundarī is to be worshipped.
She is the Great Goddess (*mahādevī*) because she is great (*mahatī*) due to being unconditioned by space, time, and form, and because she is the goddess (*devī*) due to her luminosity (*dyotanāt*).

The Goddess, whose name is Devīpadā, is of the nature of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). Here, as stated previously in the *Vāsanācakra*, she is threefold and ninefold. She is Mahātripurasundarī: "Great" (*mahatī*) because she is the unconditioned form of consciousness;
"Tripura" because her nature is the fourth state (*turya*); and "Sundarī" because she is desirable to all as their own very self. Such is the Vidyā.
The deity of one's own consciousness is to be worshipped; she is to be meditated upon through the threefold worship to be described [in verses 3.2–4], beginning with the *parā* form.

Having stated the fruits characterized by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the meanings corresponding to the respective names of the nine wheels, such as the *Trailokyamohana*, the author now states the fruit of the collective wheel (*samaṣṭicakra*).
The complete Great Wheel brings about freedom from old age and death. || 1/85 ||

The Great Wheel is complete, consisting of the collective form of the nine wheels; it is composed of the mass of supreme light, which is the state of equilibrium between the radiating Light and the reflective Awareness within the Great Bindu-wheel at the center of the Great Yoni; it consists of all-bliss and encompasses all coverings. This is because it is both identical with the universe and transcends the universe, being of the nature of the Supreme.

It is that which effects the state of being ageless and immortal. "Ageless" (ajara) because it transcends the three periods of time; for this very reason, it is "immortal" (amara) because it is devoid of arising and destruction. Thus, "ageless and immortal" refers to Paramaśiva. "Effecting" (kāraka) means that it brings about liberation (mokṣa) for its own worshiper, characterized by the attainment of the eternal state of Supreme Śiva, which transcends the three times and is free from arising and destruction. (1/85)
He concludes the convention of the wheels:
"Thus, O Supreme Goddess, this great convention of the wheels has been declared by the goddess Tripurā; it is that which brings about liberation while living. (1.86)

In the manner thus described, the *mahācakrasaṃketa* (the convention of the Great Wheel) of the Goddess Tripurā—whose characteristics were previously stated—is called the "Great Wheel" (*mahācakra*) because it consists of the wheel of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*). *Jīvanmukti* (liberation while living) is liberation [attained] while one is alive.
For liberation is indeed the release from bondage—that is, from the eightfold noose consisting of passion (*ghṛṇā*) and the rest. What is the meaning?

The meaning is that the one who possesses the secret conventions of the *cakras*—having realized the supreme reality through his own guru, beginning with Paraśiva and ending with the Supreme Deity—by means of his own self-reflection, forcibly brings about the contemplation of the state of "I am Śiva" through the destruction of all fetters. || 1/86 ||

Thus ends the first chapter, the Convention of the Wheels (*cakrasaṃketa*), in the *Yoginīhṛdayadīpikā* composed by the eminent Yogin Amṛtānanda, a Paramahaṃsa disciple of the venerable Paramayogīndra Paramahaṃsa Puṇyānanda.
The second is the convention of mantras.
Now, he promises to explain the second convention of mantras, preceded by a presentation of its fruit, for the sake of engaging the audience:
Now I shall tell you the divine secret convention of the mantras, by knowing which one becomes the Lord of the Circle of Heroes (vīracakreśvara), whose form is Tripura. (2.1)

It is divine because it is dedicated to the exposition of Paraśiva and Parāśakti, whose nature consists of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). It is the "Convention of Mantras" (*mantra-saṃketaka*). Mantras are rays of consciousness (*cin-marīcayah*), so called because they protect the practitioner through contemplation (*manana*). Because they express those [rays], the Saubhāgyavidyā and other such mantras—which are manifestations of the phonemes of the *vaikharī* level of speech—possess the power of protecting through contemplation. As it has been said:

In the *Saṃketapaddhati*: "Because it protects through reflection (*manana*), this is proclaimed as 'mantra'. The convention (*saṃketaka*) is the definition previously stated (1.6). Now I shall speak; that is, I shall tell you, who are of the nature of light (*prakāśātmaka*), [I who am] of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśarūpin*), I shall bring [this] to the heart, meaning I shall make it penetrate the heart. That which is the knower of which...

The knower—that is, the one who understands—the secret convention (*saṃketa*) of the mantra; the venerable Lord Paraśiva, who manifests as the form of Tripura and shines forth through the act of cognition;

he shall become the Lord of the *vīracakra*. The *vīras* are those possessing the characteristics previously described (1.65); their *cakra* is their assembly, and its Lord is Paraśiva. What is the meaning? This mantra—

The meaning is that one becomes none other than Paraśiva, the web of illusion having been destroyed by the supreme contemplation (*parabhāvanā*) which is the secret of mantras such as Śrīvidyā, as established through convention (*saṃketa*). || 2/1 ||
Having introduced the nine mantra-lords of the wheels, beginning with Trailokyamohana as previously mentioned, he begins the exposition of the secret conventions of the mantras:
"The first [mantra] is the purifier of the hands; the second is the protector of the self;
the goddess seated on the seat of the self is the third, immediately following that. (2.2)
Next is she seated on the wheel-throne, then she established upon the throne of all mantras;
the sixth is the supreme one, consisting of the illusory Lakṣmī, whose throne is both that of the goal to be accomplished and of accomplishment.
And that goddess Mūrtividyā is proclaimed as the seventh;
the eighth is the Āvāhinī Vidyā, and the ninth is the supreme Bhairavī.
*Karaśuddhikarī*—
the purification of the two impurities residing in the self-principle (*ātmatattva*), namely those pertaining to action (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*),
is considered the supreme purification of the self and its instruments, consisting of the contemplation of their dissolution into the pure principle (*śuddhatattva*). (Cidgaganacandrikā 11)

According to the method we have explained, the purification of the two hands—which fall within the category of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), are included among the impure principles (*aśuddhatattva*), and are themselves impure—is the contemplation of their dissolution into the pure principle (*śuddhatattva*). This is the *vidyā* (knowledge) that effects such purification, because it is intent upon establishing the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*). On this very point, he will state later: "due to the stainlessness (*vaimalya*) of the organs of action."

"It is known as the purifier of the hands" (3/125). This means that the first [mantra] is the Vidyā of the Mistress of the Wheel of the Deluder of the Three Worlds. Now, one might ask: why does [the author] here merely state the number of mantras such as the Karaśuddhi and others, rather than extracting them?
It is said in reply: their extraction is found in the Vāmakeśvara Śāstra itself; however, this [present work], being devoted to explaining matters not previously understood, [does not do so].

Regarding the phrase "of the scripture," it means that no extraction of mantras is being performed here. Furthermore, the second [verse] concerns self-protection (*ātmarakṣikā*). According to our stated method—that "the supreme self-protection here consists in crossing over the peril of the opposing side characterized by duality" (Cf. *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa* 7)—there is protection from the peril consisting in the defeat of the adversary characterized by the phenomenal expansion of duality; [this protection takes the form of] the non-perception of duality.

By means of establishing the supreme *ahantā*, she acts for the sake of the self; thus, the second Vidyā, the Mistress of the second Cakra named "Fulfiller of All Hopes" (*sarvāśāparipūraka*), is the "Self-protectress" (*ātmarakṣikā*). The third Goddess is "Seated upon the Self-throne" (*ātmāsanagatā*).
According to our stated method: "The throne of the deities who follow the Self-cakra is the manifestation of the state of being composed of Śiva" (Cidgaganacandrikā 45).

The third Vidyā, which resides in the Ātmāsana, is the first of the four Vidyās characterized by the contemplation of the practitioner’s circle (sādhakacakra), mantras, and deities as being of the nature of one's own consciousness (svasaṃvidrūpa). Its meaning is that it is the Vidyā of the Mistress of the Third Cakra, characterized as "the agitator of all" (sarvasaṃkṣobhakarī). Following that is the [Vidyā] residing in the Cakrāsana; following that is the [Vidyā] residing in the Cakrāsana mentioned immediately before.

The fourth Vidyā means the Vidyā who is the Mistress of the Fourth Cakra, characterized by the bestowing of all auspiciousness. Subsequently, she is "seated upon the throne of all mantras. This means she is seated upon the thrones of the mantras of all the deities of the coverings (*āvaraṇa*), through the radiance of the rays of consciousness characterized by the previously mentioned [second] Vāsanā (2/1) and the characteristic of protection through reflection (*manana*).

The fifth Vidyā refers to the Vidyā of the Mistress of the Fifth Cakra, whose characteristic is the name "Accomplisher of All Aims" (Sarvārthasādhakā). The sixth is Sādhyasiddhāsanā. [They are] the rays of consciousness residing in all sacred seats (pīṭhas) and pervading everywhere.
May the Bhairavīs, whose forms are full and complete, protect the mothers of the Kula.

Thus, according to the method stated in the words of the authoritative texts (*pramāṇika-vacana*), the deities of the enclosures who have evolved from the rays of consciousness (*cinmarīci*) are to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

These deities—those situated in the wheels (*cakra*) beginning with the seven-pointed triangle and ending with the sixteen-petalled lotus, as well as those situated in the positions of the three squares—are to be accomplished because they consist of the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*). As it has been said in this very [text]:

"Creation consists of [the sequence] from the nine-yoni up to the earth" (1.77). Those very same [powers] are the *sādhya*s; at the time of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), they are the *siddha*s, withdrawn in the order from the square (*caturasra*) up to the bindu. It is said in this very [text]: "Withdrawal, moreover, is from the earth up to the nine-yoni" (1.77–78). Here, *siddhi* means withdrawal. Thus it has been stated.

In the *Śrīpratyabhijñāhṛdaya*: "Consciousness is autonomous, the cause of the manifestation of the universe" (Sūtra 1). Thus, the sixth [Vidyā], whose name is Sādhyasiddhāsanā, resides upon the seat of the presiding deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*) who are being contemplated through the sequence of emanation and withdrawal; she is the Mistress of the sixth wheel, known by the name Sarvarakṣākara.

The meaning is "Vidyā. That goddess, who consists of Māyā and Lakṣmī, is the supreme form (parā mūrti) and is proclaimed as the seventh Vidyā. Since this Vidyā has not been extracted in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra*, its extraction is performed here. Māyā is the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī; Lakṣmī is the seed-syllable of Śrī. She consists of these, meaning she is abundant with them. The supreme [form] situated above those two—
"O blessed one, the fourteenth [vowel] joined with the end of the lunar day (the letter *m*), and the third Brahman, O fair-hipped one—this is the Heart of the Bhairava-self. (Verse 9).
Thus, the seed-syllable mentioned in the *Śrī Parātriṃśikā* is *Parā*, because she is the designator (*vācaka*) of *Parā*. She consists of these three seed-syllables.
And because she consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, that Vidyā is employed in the conceptualization of the form of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī.

The seventh is the Vidyā known as Sarvarogaharā (the Dispeller of All Diseases), the Mistress of the Seventh Cakra; this is the meaning. The eighth is the Āvāhinī Vidyā, which, by means of the path of the senses, brings forth from within the Mother, who is one's own self of consciousness, to the outside.
"Offering into the consciousness of the 'Me' (the subject) is the invocation, characterized by the state of being of one flavor (*samarasatva*). (Cidgaganacandrikā 20).

According to this method stated by us, the Self (*ātman*) is conjoined with the mind (*manas*), the mind with the sense organ (*indriya*), and the sense organ with the object (*artha*)—as stated in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* (1.1.4)—within the center of the pericarp of the lotus of one's own heart, where the digit of consciousness (*saṃvit-kalā*) is vibrating.

The meaning is that the Vidyā, which flows with the characteristic of the outward expansion of external objects according to the sequence taught in other Tantras, is the bestower of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*) and is the Mistress of the Eighth Wheel (*aṣṭamacakreśvarī*). The ninth is Bhairavī, the Supreme (*parā*). She is called Bhairavī because she sustains the universe as the cause of its maintenance (*sthiti*), and because she protects it as the cause of its withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), which is characterized by its final resolution into pure supreme consciousness.
And because [the Self] is the cause of emission through the act of vomiting. (2.2.4)
Now, one might ask: "Since Bhairavī is not mentioned in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra*, why has she not been extracted here, while the Vidyā of the seventh Cakreśvarī has been extracted? To this he replies:
"The Root-Vidyā is likewise declared to be the subduer of the three worlds."

She is called Mūlavidyā because she makes known the supreme light (*paraṃ tejaḥ*), which consists of the equilibrium of illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and is the root of the universe comprising the thirty-six principles from Śiva down to Earth; thus she is declared to be Bhairavī and none other. Since she has been extracted in that very [text], she is not extracted here. Otherwise...

One should extract [the mantra] here as for the Mistress of the Seventh Wheel. As he will say: "O Supreme Goddess, the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) should be performed with the root-mantra" (2.7).

Although it is appropriate to state the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras of the Nine Mistresses of the Wheels—which will be mentioned in the upcoming ritual convention (*pūjāsaṃketa*)—[he does so now] because it exerts control over the characteristics of the "Liberated from the Three Worlds" (1.82), bringing both creation and withdrawal under one's own power.
In this context, following the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), he says:
"Thus, at the time of worship, these nine types [of offerings] should be diligently performed. (2.5)

O Mistress of the Kula, these [vidyās] should be installed in sequence by the practitioner (sādhaka) according to the manner described. These ninefold vidyās of the Cakreśvarīs are for the practitioner who desires to achieve liberation for himself; O Mistress of the Kula, "kula" [refers to...]

It consists of the forms of the object of knowledge (*meyam*), the means of knowledge (*mānam*), and the knower (*mātṛ*). As it is said in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*: "The *Kula*, characterized by the object, the knower, and the act of knowing, finally comes to rest where [it finds its source]" (verse 72). She is the Sovereign (*Īśvarī*) over its creation and withdrawal. On this point, the Śruti says:
"Just as a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7). It is also stated in the *Ājñāvatāra*: "By her own will alone..."

"The entire universe devours and also emits. At the time of worship—that is, during the occasion of the ritual service (*saparyā*) described by the terminology to be mentioned later—one should install [the deities] in sequence with faith and absorption, according to the method stated in another Tantra: "Effort (*prayatna*) is the activity accompanied by extreme haste for the attainment of that [state]" (Dakṣiṇāmūrti-stotra 1.20). || 2/5-6 ||
He states their locations:
"And in the tips of the feet, the calves, the knees, the thighs, the anus, and the tip of the penis. (2.6)
This is clear. || 2/6 ||
One should place the Mūrti-mantra upon the support (ādhāra), and within that, one should place the Āvāhinī-mantra;
O Supreme Goddess, the Vyāpaka-nyāsa should be performed with the Mūla-mantra. (2.7)

One should place the *mūrti* upon the *ādhāra*. The separate mention of the *ādhāra* and the *mūrti* is for the purpose of indicating their internal nature, since the tips of the feet and so forth are well known as being external. One should place the *mūrti*—that is, the seventh *vidyā*, the *mūrtividyā*—upon the previously mentioned (*1.25*) four-petalled lotus, which is the *ādhāra*. Upon that very *mūrti*, one should place the *āvāhinī*.

O Supreme Goddess, the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) should be performed with the Root Mantra—that is, with the mantra of the Mistress of the Ninth Cakra, which is the Saubhāgyavidyā. The rest is clear. (2.7)

Having explained the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras of the Nine Sovereigns of the Wheels (*navacakreśvarī*), he now describes the internal placement (*āntaranyāsa*), which consists of the visualization of the nine wheels that serve as their support:
"One should contemplate [the deities] within Akula and the other aforementioned locations."
The nine wheels previously mentioned are conjoined with Cakreśvarī. || 2/8 ||
"In Akula and the others" refers to the previously mentioned locations, including Akula and that which is designated as Viṣu (1/25).
By the word "and the others" (*ādi*), the eight [centers]—Vahni, Śākta, Nābhi, Anāhata, Viśuddha, Lambikāgra, Bhruvorantara, and Indu—are included.

This refers to the nine wheels (*navacakra*) previously described in the *Cakrasaṃketa*, which are conjoined with the Mistress of the Wheels (*cakreśvarī*) and presided over by the nine Mistresses of the Wheels (*navacakreśvarī*).

One should reflect: what is the meaning? In *Akula*, at the root of the *suṣumṇā* in the thousand-petaled lotus, is the *trailokyamohana-cakra* presided over by Tripurā; in *Vahni*, at the *ādhāra* in the four-petaled lotus, is the *sarvāśāparipūraṇa-cakra* presided over by Tripureśī; and in *Śākta*, in the six-petaled lotus situated at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
The wheel that agitates all, presided over by Tripurasundarī, is at the navel in the ten-petalled lotus;
the wheel that bestows all good fortune, presided over by Tripuravāsinī, is in the heart at the *anāhata* center in the twelve-petalled lotus;
and [the wheel] that accomplishes all aims, presided over by Tripurāśrī, is in the *viśuddha* center in the sixteen-petalled lotus.
The wheel presided over by Tripuramālinī, which bestows all protection, is located at the tip of the uvula in the eight-petaled lotus at the base of the palate;
the wheel that removes all diseases, presided over by Tripurāsiddhi, is located in the two-petaled lotus between the eyebrows;
and [the wheel] presided over by Tripurāmbikā, which grants all accomplishments, is located in the moon, the forehead, and the point (bindu).
The meaning is that one should contemplate the wheel (cakra) as being presided over by Mahātripurasundarī and consisting entirely of universal bliss. || 2/8 ||
He states the names of the previously mentioned Vidyās, the mistresses of the nine wheels: "I shall declare their names according to their sequential order:
among them, the first is the goddess Tripurā, and the second is Tripureśvarī. (2.9)
The third is likewise declared to be the goddess Tripurasundarī;
and the fourth, O Great Goddess, is the goddess Tripuravāsinī. (2.10)
The fifth is Tripurāśrī, the sixth is Tripuramālinī;
the seventh is Tripurāsiddhi, and the eighth is Tripurāmbikā. (2.11)
The ninth, however, is the Great Goddess Mahātripurasundarī.
This is clear. (2.9–12)

But surely, these Vidyās, who are the sovereigns of the nine wheels, must be installed in sequence through the process of visualization in the locations beginning with the tips of the feet and ending with Akula; why is this so? He says: "No;
one should worship them in sequence in the nine wheels previously mentioned. (2.12)

These aforementioned Vidyās, Tripurā and the others, are the sovereigns of the nine wheels (*navacakreśvarī*). This refers to what was previously stated in the passage beginning with "The wheel that fascinates the three worlds" (1.82–84). The use of the singular number in the term *navacakre* is intended to express their mutual inseparability; the meaning is: in the nine wheels which are to be meditated upon as being joined together within the nine locations beginning with Akula. [This applies] in due order.
And one should worship the wheel that fascinates the three worlds; the meaning is that one should worship each individual wheel in sequence, beginning from the first.
Now, is this ninefold nature of theirs inherent? No, he says:
"O Pārvatī, although the primordial Śakti, who brings about freedom from old age and death, is of a single form, she appears in these nine ways at the time of worship. (2.13)

She is "primordial" (*ādyā*) because she is the cause of the universe, from Śiva down to the earth. She is the "primordial power" (*ādyā-śakti*). She is the power of Paraśiva—the primordial being who consists of all phonemes and whose nature is light—whose form is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). She is of a single form and has attained constant identity-in-difference (*sāmarasya*) with Him during the time of the supreme worship (*parā-pūjā*); however, this is not the case during the time of the lower worship (*aparā-pūjā*).

It exists. In the manner thus described, it is divided into nine types, that is, ninefold. For such a worshipper, it brings about the state of being ageless and immortal. "Ageless and immortal" refers to Śiva, whose characteristics have been previously stated; it makes him attain that reality (*tattva*).
On this very point, the author will say later: "Your eternally arisen worship is established through three divisions" (3.2). || 2/13 ||
Having concluded the incidental discussion, he points toward the primary subject at hand, the secret convention of mantra: "The secret convention of that [Goddess] is established in various forms;
it is obtained through the lineage solely by means of the sequence of various mantras. (2.14)

The "convention" (*saṃketa*) is the revelation of the hidden meaning of that supreme mantra, which consists of the *Saubhāgyavidyā* and takes the form of union with Paraśiva. It is "of manifold forms," meaning it possesses the sixfold nature that will be described immediately hereafter.
This occurs precisely through the sequence of various mantras and the very series of manifold elaborations previously mentioned, such as the purification of the hands.

"It is obtained through lineage" means it is obtained by way of descending the steps, following the sequence of instruction in the tradition starting from Śiva down to one's own guru; not otherwise. For those devoid of lineage and lacking the oral transmission (asampradāya), who merely terminate in the recitation of syllables acquired through theft via the "magnet-like" mode of operation, it leads only to misfortune—this is the meaning. He will state this very point later.

"Those who are devoid of the lineage and are arrogant merely on account of their knowledge—for them, through the violation of their commitments (*samaya*), the rays [of consciousness] undergo transformation. (2/81). Thus ends [the commentary on] 2/14.
He promises to explain the division of the indicated secret terminology of the mantra:
"O Goddess, O sinless one, I shall tell you that which is sixfold.
It is sixfold by way of the six types of meanings, such as the *bhāvārtha*, which will be described immediately hereafter. O sinless one!

Free from defects such as being the disciple of another, [I speak] of you, the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti) who are a portion of myself. I, whose nature is Light (prakāśa), shall describe that [reflective awareness] which is sixfold.
He states its divisions:
"The meaning of existence (bhāvārtha), the meaning of tradition (sampradāyārtha), the innermost meaning (nigarbhārtha), and the Kaula meaning. (2.15)
Likewise, the meaning of all secrets and the very meaning of the Great Reality is the explicit meaning, because its characteristics will be explained [hereafter]. (2/15–16)
Intending to explain the characteristics in six ways, he first states the meaning of the term *bhāva*:
"O Supreme Goddess, the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) is indeed the exclusive meaning of *bhāva*. (2.16)

They are called "syllables" (*akṣara*) because they do not perish, as they denote the eternal Supreme Śiva. Furthermore, the movement of the palate and lips is their manifestor; for this very reason, they are truly "syllables.
Their meaning is that which is to be expressed. The meaning of the fifteen syllables that constitute the limbs of the Śrī Saubhāgyavidyā is as follows:
The meaning of the state [of being]. || 2/16 ||
He states the literal meaning [of the verse]:
"O Dear One, by the Yoginīs, as well as by the Vīras and the lords of Vīras, the King of Mantras is always generated through the union of Śiva and Śakti. (2.17)
The Yoginīs: Yoga is the eternal connection with Śiva; those who possess this are the Yoginīs.

They are Bhāratī, Pṛthvī, and Rudrāṇī, whose nature consists of will, knowledge, and action, and who are portions of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). The Vīras have been explained [previously] (1.65);
they are those who possess an eternal connection with those Yoginīs and are portions of the aspect of luminosity (*prakāśa*).

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, whose natures are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī, are the agents of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
