The Lords of Heroes (Vīrendras), who have transcended the states of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, are the authorities over the Ineffable (Anākhyā); they are of the nature of the peaceful Ambikā, the unified totality of the triad of the Śiva-Śakti couples, and are designated by the three Kāmakalās residing at the summit of the three seed-syllables.

By these four pairs, which consist of the meanings expressed by the syllables of the Vidyā, the King of Mantras—whose form is the Saubhāgyavidyā—is generated (janitaḥ), meaning it has arisen. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an initial action (*ādikarmaṇi*), signifying that it has been brought into being or contemplated, because its essential nature is eternal. This generation occurs through the union (*samāyoga*) of Śiva and Śakti; "union" refers to their conjunction or contact. It is the King of Mantras because it is the most excellent among all mantras.
This very same meaning has been elaborated by me in the *Saubhāgyasudhodaya*:
"She alone, whose essence is the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*), is the Mother who is the sole resting place of the four lineages;
she is born as the progenitor of the four-faced Brahmā and others, bestowing the fruits of the group of the fourfold self."
Having abandoned her own two parts consisting of *asvara* (the unvocalized) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), she herself, possessing four *kalās*,
created these four pairs consisting of Vāmā and the others, as well as Icchā and the others.
The portion of Vāmā would be Brahmā, and Icchā herself is his power, Bhāratī.
This couple of these two is the creation; prior to their union, it is the seed-syllable of speech (vāgbīja).
Viṣṇu is the eldest portion (jyeṣṭhāṃśa), and Viśvambharā is knowledge; these two form a couple.
This very pair, in the form of a lineage of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇānvaya), resides within the Śrī-kāmarāja.
Rudra is of the nature of fury (raudra), while his power (śakti) is Rudrāṇī, consisting of action (kriyā).
This couple is the third seed-syllable (bīja), which protects the western tradition (paścimāmnāya).
Śambhu may be of the nature of Ambikā, and his Śakti may be of the nature of Śāntā;
this couple of Śiva and Śakti, being the essence of the subsequent stage (uttarasamaya), presides over the Fourth State (turya).
Thus, from the two supreme powers, the Supreme (Parā) has arisen, whose form consists of four pairs of parts;
this Vidyā, consisting of Mātṛkā, is Paśyantī, whose nature is the fourfold lineage.
Creation is the primordial tradition (*pūrvāmnāya*), consisting of the seed-syllable *bāgbhava*; it is threefold according to its nature.
Through the processes of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, this creation becomes the embodiment of the three forms (*trimūrti*).
In this context of the creation of the universe, Brahmā is the presiding lord, and Bhāratī is his power (śakti).
This may be the meaning of the laugh; indeed, he alone is the designator of both Śiva and Śakti.
In this context, the purpose would be for amusement (*hāsya*), due to the conjunction of the letters of the name of one who possesses the form of his own power;
however, Viṣṇu is the agent of creation and maintenance, while Viśvambharā (the Earth) would be his power (*śakti*).
Viṣṇu is the object of *kalpi*; his power (*śakti*) would be the object of *lalipi*.
Rudra is the presiding lord (*adhipati*); his power would be *raudrī* therein, in the context of creation and dissolution.
The pair of syllables *ha* and *ra* is the designator (*vācaka*) of these two;
here, the meaning of *ra* is Rudra, and due to its contact with the syllable *ru*, *raudrī* is the power (*śakti*) associated with it—this is the meaning of *ha*.
In this context, however, the Śaktyarṇa (the letter of power) holds primacy because it is the seed of power;
as Śiva and Śakti reside therein, their state is called Saṃjñāna, which consists of a triad.
The Kāmakalā is the one who impels, consisting of the fourth state (turya), with a body that is a mixture of red and white;
the red is the Bindu (Śakti) and the white is Śambhu, while beyond that is their essential unity (aikātmya).
Thus, the second seed-syllable, whose nature is stability, belongs to the lineage of the South;
those very deities abide therein through the distinctions of stability, emanation, and so forth.
Here, the letter *ha*, situated in the middle of the vowels and consonants, reveals its nature as the state of maintenance (*sthiti*);
it manifests the supreme form of maintenance, which is the Mother (*Ambikā*) of Consciousness (*saṃvit*).
In the same way, within the third [moment] consisting of the final samaya which is of the nature of withdrawal,
those very deities reside there by virtue of the processes of withdrawal, emanation, and so forth.
Because Śakti is the primary cause in the process of emanation and because He is the seed of that power,
Śakti shines forth within Her own self by internalizing Śiva during both withdrawal and emanation.
In the third [state], which is the seed-syllable of the fourth (*turīya*) and whose nature is the subsequent sequence of the inexpressible (*anākhyā*),
Śakti and Śiva dwell together incessantly, having attained a state of perfect equilibrium (*sāmarasya*).
She who consists of the nine pairs of syllables of the Śrīvidyā, divided by the distinctions of emanation and the rest;
she whose form is the group of nine nādas—that Mother, known as the "Middle One," is all-pervasive.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma).
Due to the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, there are fifteen [categories] in sequence, numbering accordingly.

The lunar days (tithis) and the digits (kalās) are eternal and consist of that very essence; likewise, through the phonemes (varṇas) numbering the same as those, this Vidyā, as a collective whole, pervades them all.
Through these parts of its own self, expanded in the form of the collective totality at the beginning of creation,
and through the thirty-six components of itself consisting of the letters of the alphabet starting with 'ka', [it manifests].
Furthermore, that Mother indeed pervades those parts of the syllables, which are divided by the distinctions of vowels, consonants, and bindus,
numbering thirty-six and consisting of the principles (tattvas).
"Through the divisions of individual and collective aspects, she is fourfold in nature, consisting of the seat of the seed-syllables of reality;
and by way of the four lineages, she is the Mother, the Vidyā consisting of the eight Mātṛkās. Thus [ends] 2/17.
(2/1–25) He states the meaning of the fourth mantra:
Having realized the Goddess—who is composed of that [reality], whose nature is vibration, who consists of supreme bliss, and who is beautiful by her very nature—they worship her freely. (2.18)
Consisting of that [consciousness], she is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) denoting the triad of couples beginning with Bhāratī and Brahmā;

she is the one expressed by the fourth mantra (*turīya-mantra*). She is gladdened by supreme bliss, filled with the supreme bliss vibrating through the state of identity (*sāmarasya*) with Paramaśiva. She is the embodiment of vibration (*spanda*), [comprising] the thirty-six principles from Śiva down to Earth.

Having realized the Supreme Goddess Mahātripurasundarī— who is by nature beautiful, who has manifested her own glory through the form of the vibration of reality (*tattvaspanda*), who dwells as the Self within all living beings and is the object of supreme love, and whose nature is the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Light (*prakāśa*) and Reflexive Awareness (*vimarśa*)— as their very own Self, they worship Her freely; that is, they sport with autonomy, intent upon their own spontaneous conduct (*svairācāra*).

The meaning is that they come into being. On this very point, he will state later: "By means of one's own natural conduct, she is to be fully worshipped when 'I-ness' and 'this-ness' have become equal" (3.164).
He states the meaning of the word *mantra*:

"In the eternal Brahman, which consists of the union known as Śiva and Śakti, and in that ground characterized by Indra, which is the locus of the embrace resulting from the expansion of its manifestation. (2.19)
She is the form of the mantra consisting of the mental reflection upon the forms of the knower and knowledge.

In that which consists of the union of Śiva and Śakti— that is, in Brahman whose nature is the union and aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) of the light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Śiva and Śakti— from the root *bṛh* meaning "to grow" (*bhvādi*, 735).

According to the method stated by the Grammarians—that because the verbal root *br̥h* means "to expand," the Self (*ātman*) itself is Brahman—[this refers] to the Self within all living beings; [the Self] which is eternal, characterized by past and future time, and the ground for the expansion and attachment of the manifestation of that [Brahman]. By the word "that" (*tat*), the Light-Self (*prakāśātman*) is referred to. As stated in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā: "Oṃ, Tat, Sat—thus the designation of Brahman is remembered as threefold."

(17/23) Thus: the manifestation (*prathā*) of that Śiva, who consists of light, is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), just as radiance is to a lamp. Its expansion (*prasara*) is the transformation into the nature of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*). Its attachment (*āśleṣa*) is its culmination within Śiva as being nothing other than that. Its rest (*viśrānti*) is in the ground (*bhuvi*), which is the place of repose. On this point, there is a scriptural citation (*śruti*): "All..."
"This, indeed, is Brahman; as *tajjalān*, one should worship it with a tranquil mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).

It is "characterized by Aindra," where *idi* means supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*) [from the root *id* in the *bhvādi* class]; Indra is the possessor of supreme sovereignty. Regarding this, the Śruti says: "Indra moves in many forms through his *māyās*" (Ṛgveda 4.7.33). That which pertains to him is *aindra* action; [the object] is characterized by that. It is like the term *kākavat*.

Just as in the expression "Devadatta’s house," the conventional usage of terms such as "the creation of the universe" is merely figurative (*upalakṣaṇa*), and not an essential attribute (*svarūpadharma*) [of the subject]. This refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is eternal, consisting of the equilibrium of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), the witness (*sākṣin*) who effects the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, and who is touched by the great sovereignty (*mahadaiśvarya*) that is its very nature; and regarding this object, [there arise] states consisting of the knower and the knowledge.

She is of the nature of mantra because she is the protection (*trāṇa*) characterized by the cultivation of a mental form identical with that [reality], arising from the contemplation (*manana*)—which consists of the excellence of that [contemplation] through the presence of its practice, its proficiency, its continuity, and the practitioner’s devotion. What is the meaning?

It means that, through the contemplation whose object is the supreme illumination as qualified by the aforementioned attributes, she brings about for her own practitioner the realization of a form identical with that [reality].
By the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) "she protects" (*trāyate*), the meaning is that she is of the nature of the Great Mantra characterized as the Fourth (*turīya*). || 2/19-20 ||
Now, one might ask: what are the characteristics of this [Goddess], who is characterized by the aforementioned attributes and consists of the form of the *turya-mantra*?
To this, he says: "But Mātṛkā is the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*) in the form of their collective totality (*samaṣṭi*). (2.20)

The term *tanmayīm* (2/18) refers to what was stated previously. The Supreme Power (*parāśakti*) is characterized by being the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the creation and other functions of those [deities] beginning with Brahmā and [the goddesses] beginning with Bhāratī. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. It is the Supreme Power alone;
"of Him there is neither effect nor instrument, and no one equal to Him or superior to Him is seen."
"The supreme power of this [Being] is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).
Thus, the Mātṛkā taught by this Śruti is indeed the Supreme;
she crosses over, her form transcending all while possessing the unstruck (*anāhata*) body of the entire universe.
"The Goddess Mātṛkā manifests in the form of various names and conceptual proliferations" (Saubhāgyasudhodaya 1.6).
According to our stated method, the supreme Mātṛkā is active in the forms of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī. On this point, there is a Vedic revelation:
"Speech has four measured quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in the cave of the heart, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what humans speak.

(Ṛgveda 1.164.45). The meaning of this is as follows: [the levels of speech] are Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, characterized by their nature as the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the energies beginning with Brahmā and Bhāratī.
The denotable meaning of the fourth mantra is the nature of the equilibrium between expansion, illumination, and reflective awareness. || 2/20 ||

Now, it has been stated that this [Parā], which consists of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of the letters *a* and *ha*, is indeed the Supreme (*parā*) herself, qualified by the specific mantra of the Fourth State (*turīya*), and is denoted by the word "Fourth" (*turīya*). If one asks, "Where do those two letters reside within the mantra?
and "What is the relationship between this mantra and the Supreme who is denoted by those two letters?", he says:
Within the supreme state consisting of the abiding of the central point and the visarga,
there is the form of Kuṭilā, which is her counterpart and a portion of the ether.

Of that supreme [power], which consists of the abiding within the emission (*visarga*) at the end of the central point (*madhyabindu*): the central point is the upper point, whose nature is the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) between the vowels *a* and *ha*, and it is called *kāma*. As it is said in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"The *bindu* is the nature of the *ahaṅkāra*, and the sun is the form of the union of this couple;
Kāma [is so called] because of his desirability" (verse 7).
The *visarga* is of the nature of its emission, consisting of two *bindus*, the syllable *aḥ*, the sixteenth vowel. As it has been said:

In that very [text]: "The *kalā* and the two points (*bindu*) whose forms are fire and the moon" (verse 7). Between those two—in the middle of both Kāma and Kalā—is the state of abiding, which consists of a dwelling place, in the supreme *ah* syllable. Because it is the beginning and end of the phonemes, the initial *a* is "subsequent" in relation to the final [phoneme], and the final [phoneme] is [subsequent] in relation to the initial.

The letter *ha* is subsequent. By that [subsequence], the two letters at the beginning and end of the phonemes—the letters *a* and *ha*—are spoken of as being in the subsequent syllable. In the metaphor of the "crooked" (*kuṭila*), the two crooked ones are *Akula* and *Kulakuṇḍalinī*, because they possess a crooked form. Those two whose forms are these very [letters] are the two *viyatkale* (space-fragments), which are of the nature of reflections. By the word *viyat*, the void (*śūnya*) is indicated; by that, *viyat* refers to the *bindu*.
The syllable *ha* consists of two *kalās*, each possessing two *bindus*. What is the meaning?

The letter *a*, whose form is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti, dwells within the *mātrā* situated inside the two *bindus* that constitute the parts of the syllable *ha*. Indeed, there are two [bindus] in *aha*.

Furthermore, it is within the syllable that consists of the form of the *kuṇḍalinī* of both the non-family (*akula*) and the family (*kula*), which is the form of the Supreme (*parā*); because it is a part of that, it exists within the syllable *aha*, which is the form of the reflection of those two forms of the Supreme, since the letters *a* and *ha* are manifested therein. (2.21)

Having explained the presence of the letters *a* and *ha* within the art of desire (*kāmakalā*), which constitutes the causal ground of mantra, he now describes the presence of those two letters within the mantra itself:
"Furthermore, it resides in the space of vibration, whose form is the expansion of the central vital breath."
In the middle mantra-cluster, and again in the third cluster, || 2.22 ||

She abides again in the space of vibration (*spanda*), which is the manifestation of the central vital breath (*madhyaprāṇa*), within the six-syllable cluster known as the Kāmarāja-bīja, situated between the Vāgbhava and Śakti seeds in the central mantra-cluster that flashes forth as the non-dual Rāhu-peak. Furthermore, she resides in the sky of vibration, whose form is the expansion of the central vital breath. The central vital breath...

The letter *ha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) situated between the two drops (*bindu*) located at the base of the *kāmakalā*. Its "expansion" (*prathā*) is its perception as something broad, because it has become an object of hearing; thus, the letter *ha* is the space of vibration (*spandavyoma*). Furthermore, [the Goddess] is established within that space, because the letter *ha* consists of the manifestation of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*). As it is said in the *Saṃketapaddhati*: "The final letter *ha* is the form of the *kalā*."
"It is proclaimed as being called *vimarśa*.

This refers to the third *piṇḍaka*, known as the seed-syllable of *Śakti*, which consists of four syllables. Furthermore, in the sense of "again," it does not manifest through a clear appearance like the second seed-syllable; rather, it flashes forth as the non-dual *rāhukūṭa*. *Rāhukūṭa* refers to [the group of letters] *śa-ṣa-sa-ha*.
The "group-peak" (*vargakūṭa*) of the letters is a collection of letters, such as the "five-peaked" or the "six-peaked.
In the *rāhukūṭa*, there are two letters; the second is other than [the first], and the third is the letter *sa*, because it is the third letter of that group.

In the sixfold arrangement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* constitute the *rāhuvarga*. He will state this very point later: "accompanied by the four letters beginning with *śa* in the mouth..."

"And *rāhum eva* (3/25)" means: "Furthermore, [it is] the radiantly manifesting non-duality of *rāhu-kūṭa*. Upon the third *sa* in *rāhu-kūṭa*, it shines forth as indivisible—the supreme, imperishable syllable (*akṣara*) that is the source of all phonemes.
This is stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*: "The letter *a* is the foremost of all phonemes; it is the light, the supreme Śiva. What is the meaning?

The meaning is that the two letters *a* and *ha*, which constitute its subordinate parts, abide respectively in the upper *bindu* of the *kāmakalā* and in the *mātrā*; then, having again assumed a gross form, they become distinct and reside within the *ha* situated between the *ka* and *la* in the *kāmarāja-bīja*, and within the *a* situated above the *sa* in the *śakti-bīja*. (2/22–23)

Now, one might ask: even though the first *piṇḍa* exists, how is it stated that the letters *a* and *ha*, which constitute the final components, reside within the middle *piṇḍa* and the third *piṇḍa*? Why is this not stated regarding the first *bīja*?
It is said in reply: [This is because] Parā, the Goddess of Good Fortune (*saubhāgyadevatā*), favors the right-hand stream (*dakṣiṇasrotas*).

Because the state of persistence (*sthiti*) is characterized primarily by the supreme and inferior powers (*parāpara-śakti*), and because the central seed-syllable (*madhyabīja*) is presided over by these supreme and inferior powers and consists of the nature of persistence, it is said that the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) abides therein. Because Śiva is of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and the seed-syllable of Śakti is essentially withdrawal, it is stated specifically that the power of manifestation (*prakāśa*) abides therein. However, in a general sense:
In the *vāgbhava* [bīja]: for this very reason, because of its connection with those two syllables, it is said that the Supreme (*parā*) consists of the entire universe; thus he says:
"But of that which is established in the state of movement—the object of speech consisting of merit and demerit, and composed of poison and nectar... (2.23).
Through the union of the expressive letters, she is said to be the one whose form is the universe; yet, as the collective totality of them, she is the Supreme Power, Mātṛkā. (2.24)

Meditating upon the primordial Śakti, who consists of the three peaks (kūṭas) and embodies both the totality and its individual manifestations, they consider this to be the true meaning of existence. (2.25)

"Movement" (*cala*) is the state of moving; it belongs to that which is situated therein. Here, "mobility" (*calatva*) means perishability. In this context, it refers to the two—Śiva and Śakti—which are denoted by the term *dharma-adharma* as previously defined (1.67), and which abide within the entire phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), including specific actions, the *vidyācakra*, the *tattvas*, and so forth. Furthermore, they consist of both poison and nectar. As for "poison":
It is *saṃsāra* because it is the cause of delusion (*moha*). It is *amṛta*, death, because liberation is free from that [delusion]. Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage (*śruti*):
"One who knows Him thus becomes immortal here" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.1.3). Because it is composed of that, it is the cause of both.
Through the conjunction of the syllables that express those two—the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*abhidheya*)—it consists of both Śiva and Śakti.

Through the union of the forms of *māyā*, the signified (*vācya*), and the signifier (*vācaka*), she is the one whose form consists of the *vidyā-cakra* and the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *Ādi*.

For this very reason, she is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi-rūpa*) of all those [elements] composed of the triad of triads; she is Parā-Śakti, the Mātṛkā of Paraśiva—who transcends the universe—as described in the definition at 2.20, consisting of the three *kūṭas*.

One should contemplate the Primordial Power (*ādyāṃ śaktim*), whose nature consists of the seed-syllables *vāgbhava*, *kāmarāja*, and *śakti*; who is the Goddess whose form is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between luminosity (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); and who, for that very reason, possesses both the nature of the totality (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*). She is the totality in the form of that equilibrium, and the individual in the form of the three peaks (*kūṭatraya*). One should contemplate her as the Primordial Power by way of being the beginning of the entire universe, according to the sequence previously stated (2.13).
Yogins consider this to be the true nature of existence. (2/23–25)
Having explained the meaning of the term *bhāva*, he now states the meaning of the *sampradāya* (the tradition):
"The *sampradāya* consists of Great Awakening (*mahābodha*) and resides in the mouth of the Guru;
it is that which is the basis for the greatness of the manifestation of the universe in all its forms. (2.26)

*Sampradāya* means that which is handed down (*pradīyate*) correctly (*samyak*), according to reality (*yāthārthyena*), into the ear of the disciple. It is of the nature of great awakening (*mahābodharūpa*); that is, its form (*rūpa*) is the awakening or thorough knowledge of the Great Light (*mahat-prakāśa*), which is unconditioned by space, time, or form. It abides in the mouth of the Guru.
Salutations to the Guru, Śiva, who has made the three worlds his own and proclaims his own true nature, appearing in the form of both the means and the goal.

According to the manner stated in the words of the learned, the Guru is one intent on revealing the ultimate reality of his own self; [the teaching] resides in his mouth alone, and not in the mouth of anyone else who has not mastered the scriptures of the Āgamas, who has not acquired all the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, who has not ascertained the ultimate reality, and who is intent on deceiving others. In this regard—
The authoritative statement:
"For Śiva, the omniscient, knows the deeds of men, both good and evil;
therefore, he does not bestow grace through the words of a teacher who possesses only limited knowledge."

In this context, "of the Guru" means one who is honored as a Guru, because one who possesses only limited knowledge lacks the status of a Guru. Regarding "the manifestation in the form of the universe": the universe consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth; the manifestation in that form is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). On this point, there is a scriptural passage: "He thought, 'Shall I now create the worlds? (Ai. U. 1.1). Its "greatness" consists in its capacity to assume that form.

"What is its basis? What is the meaning? The meaning is that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of the state of being the universe—which takes the form of the essential identity with Paraśiva and is transformed into the form of the three seed-syllables—is obtained only through the mouth of the Guru. (2.26)
Explaining the meaning of the phrase "the greatness that is the locus of the manifestation of all forms," he says—

out of the great importance of the subject matter to be discussed— "O Supreme Goddess, you must listen with the utmost attentiveness [to this] by means of the Root-Vidyā consisting of Śiva, Śakti, and so forth."
The entire world is pervaded by her; listen attentively, O beloved. (2.27)
Śiva is the syllable *a*, and Śakti is the syllable *ha*; she is that [Mūlavidyā] which has those two as its primary causes.
By such a Mūlavidyā, which has become manifest in the manner previously described, the entire world of the aforementioned nature is pervaded.
Listen attentively—listen with extreme care. (2.27)
He declares the universal pervasiveness of the Vidyā itself:
"O sinless one, the universe consists of the five elements, and she (the Vidyā) is always composed of them;
the Root-Vidyā is likewise composed of them, and I shall explain that to you. (2.28)

The universe consists of the five elements; the elements are earth, water, fire, air, and ether, and the universe is said to be composed of them, possessing the characteristics previously described. That supreme Goddess of Good Fortune (*saubhāgyadevatā*) is identical with that [universe], being composed of the five elements. The Root-Vidyā (*mūlavidyā*) is also identical with that, as it denotes her, denotes the deity, and denotes the five elements. Therefore, she is composed of both.
The meaning is: "I shall describe that manner. According to the method stated in the Upaniṣad—"From this very Self, space was produced;
from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1)—the five elements arise from Paramaśiva, whose nature is light.
For it is the established principle that from the Power whose nature is reflective awareness (vimarśa) arises the origin of the letters of the Vidyā which denote it. (2.28)

This being the case, dispelling the doubt as to what is the signified and what is the signifier, he describes her very nature as consisting of the universe, preceded by the exposition of the creation of the phonemes:
"From the letter *ha*, space was produced; from the letter *ka*, however, the wind."
From the letter *ra* arises fire, and from the letter *sa* arises the element of water.
From the letter *la*, the earth was born; therefore, it consists of the universe.
From the letter *ha*, space (*vyoma*) was produced. First, from the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), the letter *ha*—the designator of space—was born.
Subsequent to the letter *ha*, the space denoted by it was produced from Paraśiva, whose nature is light (*prakāśa*).

Afterwards, the letter *ka*, which denotes air (*vāyu*), arose; immediately following the letter *ka*, the wind (*prabhañjana*) denoted by that letter came into being. After that, the letter *ra*, which denotes fire (*agni*), arose; immediately following that, the fire denoted by the letter *ra* came into being.
Then, the letter *sa*, which denotes the water principle (*jalatattva*), arose; immediately after that, the water principle denoted by it [came into being].

Regarding "origination": the meaning is that immediately after that, the letter *la*, which denotes the earth, was born; and immediately after that, the earth denoted by it was born. Therefore, since the five great elements and the syllables denoting them have arisen from the light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the supreme part, which consists of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti, [they are said to be born from that].
Therefore, that Supreme [Consciousness], whose nature is the equilibrium of those two, consists of the phonemes that are Her own limbs; the meaning is that She is composed of the universe.
As it is said in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"From the throbbing, reddish Bindu, the sound of the sprout of the Brahman-Nāda becomes manifest."
Therefore, there is the manifestation of space, air, fire, water, earth, and color. (2.9)
Now, even from a subtle drop, there arises the birth of ether, air, fire, water, and earth;
this entire world, from the atom up to the cosmic egg, is a transformation of these five elements. (2.10)
The Mother, the measure, and the measurable are the forms of the seed-syllables divided by the three points;
they are also conceived through the distinctions of the three abodes, the three seats, and the three powers. (2.13)
"In them, respectively, are the three genders and likewise the three *mātṛkās*.
Thus, this Vidyā consists of the triad and is distinguished by the fourth seat (*pīṭha*) and so forth. (2.14) Thus [ends the section].
(2.29–30) Now, why are the phonemes not situated in the Vidyā according to such an order? It is said:

It is true that such a sequence does not exist; nevertheless, for the purpose of manifesting the previously mentioned creation, maintenance, withdrawal, and the ineffable (anākhyā), the phonemes are recited in the *vidyā* without a fixed order. Therefore, the sequence of the phonemes as they occur in the elements is not able to subvert the sequence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the phonemes, because the phonemes exist for the sake of those impressions. But then, [one might ask]:
"Why are there not as many syllables as there are elements (*bhūta*), since many others are indeed heard? To this he says:
"The qualities (*guṇa*) of the elements are said to be fifteen; Śivā consists of them. (2.30)
Through the relationship of pervaded and pervader among the five elements, there are fifteen qualities.

Therefore, this Vidyā consists of them, is composed of them, and possesses their number of syllables; it is auspicious (śivā), and its ultimate nature is the manifestation of supreme non-duality, which is the true reality that stands as the adversary to all inauspiciousness and is the very form of the world consisting of sorrow and delusion.
Because it is of the nature of the supreme auspiciousness. (2.30)

Now, one might ask: since only as many categories of objects have been enumerated as correspond to the number of syllables in the Vidyā, can it be said that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) consists of those alone? To this, he says:
"Whatever power is proclaimed for whichever object..."
She is that Goddess, the sovereign of all; he is that Maheśvara, the lord of all.

In this world, whatever power—characterized by the capacity to perform some function—exists in any given object, each such power is the Sovereign Goddess, the Supreme Goddess who is the ruler and controller of all things from Śiva down to the earth; and every such object is Maheśvara, the Supreme Śiva, the controller of the entire universe. Thus it is in the world.

Whatever object possesses the capacity for any particular action, it can be said that Parā has transformed herself into the form of that capacity, and Paramaśiva has transformed himself into the form of that very object possessing such capacity. What need is there to say more? Those two themselves [appear] in the form of categories (padārtha) whose number is equal to the phonemes of the *avidyā* mantra.
The meaning is "in transformation. As it has been said by the learned:
"You are the moonlight in the moon, you are the radiance in the sun, you are consciousness in the person, and you are strength in the wind."
"You are sweetness in water; you are heat in fire; O Mother, if everything were devoid of essence without you. (2/31, Ānandalaharī 20).
Now, it has been stated that Śivā consists of the qualities of the elements; why then is their number [of thirty-six] attributed to Śivā? To this, he says:
By pervasion, that Vidyā consists of fifteen syllables and is composed of the qualities of the elements;
likewise, it is formed by five, six, and also four syllables.

That Śivā is indeed the supreme Vidyā, because of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier. [She consists of] five syllables, which are the constituent parts of the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable; six syllables, which are the constituent parts of the *kāmarāja* seed-syllable; and four syllables, which are the constituent parts of the *śakti* seed-syllable. They do not perish (*na kṣaranti*), for they are imperishable (*akṣara*) due to their eternity. [She is thus composed of] her own parts, which are devoid of destruction.
It is pervaded by fifteen phonemes; for this very reason, its nature consists of the qualities of the elements. (2.32)
Having analyzed the three seed-syllables letter by letter and explained the latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of the nature of the elements and their qualities,
he now explains the latent impression consisting of the nature of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) by analyzing the syllables into their constituent parts:
"Through the division into vowels and consonants, it is divided into thirty-seven."
Through thirty-seven divisions, she consists of the nature of the thirty-six principles.
And this Vidyā, whose essential nature transcends all categories (tattva), is constantly meditated upon.
In the first seed-syllable, there are five vowels: the four forms of the letter *a* and the letter *ī*;
the remaining six are consonants. Thus, there are eleven [syllables]. In the second seed-syllable, there are six vowels: the five forms of the letter *a* and the letter *ī*.

The remaining consonants are seven; thus, there are thirteen. In the third seed-syllable, there are four vowels—three *a*s and one *ī*—and five remaining consonants, making nine. Thus, by this division, the constituent parts of the syllables are thirty-three. With the three *bindu*s at the end of the three seed-syllables, they become thirty-six.

The aggregate of those is one. Thus, this Vidyā, consisting of thirty-seven divisions, is of the nature of the aggregate; likewise, through these thirty-seven divisions, this Vidyā consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) and has as its essential nature that which transcends the principles. Through the distinction between the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the aggregate (*samaṣṭi*), she is both composed of the thirty-six principles and transcendent of them.

The thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) are its constituent parts; she is *Rūpavatī* (the Embodiment of Form) through them, yet her essential nature transcends the principles by virtue of being the thirty-seventh division. "Essential nature" (*svabhāva*) means one's own state of being; the meaning is that one should contemplate her as having the very same state of being as Śiva. The definitions of the principles have been set forth by me myself in the *Saubhāgyasudhodaya*.
For example:
"When this Supreme Form, by His own will, vibrated in order to create the entire universe,
that first vibration is called the Śiva-principle (śivatattva) by those who know it."
That very desire, being pure and eternally inherent, is the power (śakti),
the seed of the entire world of moving and non-moving beings that is latent within itself.
Having veiled his own nature as the "I" (ahantā) over the universe projected by his own power of will,
he who dwells thus, ever intent upon bestowing grace upon all, is recognized as Sadāśiva.
The Lord himself, perceiving the entire universe as "this," becomes the individual;
that which is the cognition of non-difference between "this-ness" and "I-ness" is Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā).
The intellect that perceives diversity within all beings, who are but its own parts,
constantly obstructs His unrestrained majesty, just as the shore restrains the ocean.
With his form thus limited and all his powers contracted, this person—
like the sun at twilight, reddened and with its rays withdrawn— is incapable even of illuminating itself.
The many powers belonging to Him, such as complete agency and so forth, become contracted through limitation; in the form of *kalā* and the rest, they cause Him to experience contraction.
That universal agency of His, when contracted and directed toward only a few objects, conceives of Him as a limited agent;
it is thus designated by the name "Kalā."
The power of his omniscience, when its body is limited and directed toward a cognizer who knows only a small amount,
is called "vidyā" by the ancient sages because it brings about knowledge.

His power, which is eternally full and satisfied, becomes limited when it takes delight in objects of enjoyment; thus, constantly coloring him, it attains the state of the principle of passion (rāgatattva).
That power of this [Self], which is eternal, having been extracted by bestowing both destruction and emergence,
is fashioned as the principle of Time (kālatattva), which effects fixed delimitation.
That very power of his known as autonomy, when characterized by contraction,
became Necessity (niyati), which restrains this [soul] helplessly and invariably regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done.
His power (*śakti*), which is the triad of will and the rest in their collective totality, is quiescent (*śāntā*) yet possesses a contracted form;
for while it is essentially the equilibrium of *sattva* and the other qualities, its nature consists of the contraction of will and the rest.
Prakṛti is considered to be of the nature of the mind, consisting of the equilibrium of intellect (buddhi) and the other guṇas;
its desire, which takes the form of rajas, became the ego (ahaṅkāra), which produces the cognition of "I."
The intellect (*buddhi*) is the cause of that knowledge which consists of the nature of *sattva* and is the awakening of certainty;
its activity, whose form is composed of *tamas*, is called the mind (*manas*), which effects conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
That very Lord, whose form was contracted, became fivefold— beginning with Vāmā—
and assumed the nature of various objects due to the predominance of the coloring of knowledge and action.
The ear, eye, skin, tongue, and nose are the instruments of cognition;
those known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and generative organ are the instruments of action.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the subtle elements;
even though he was born as the most lowly among beings, he is the Lord of Beings by virtue of his nature as the Self of all beings.
The sky, air, fire, water, and earth are the five elements;
sound and the others are cognizable by the sense organs such as hearing, while those [elements] are the perceivers of the others.
Speech became the instrument for speaking; the hand became the instrument for grasping;
and the triad beginning with the feet became the instruments for the triad of movement, evacuation, and sexual pleasure.
"The earth possesses smell; water is naturally liquid; fire is hot to the touch; wind is intangible to the touch; and space is sound. (Saubhāgyasudhodaya 1.28–48).
Furthermore, by the maxim of the lion’s glance, [the text] addresses the fifteen qualities of the elements and of the Vidyā.
He explains the state of being composed of that [nature]:
"In the elements, beginning with earth, each subsequent one is all-pervasive. (2.34)

Among the elements beginning with earth, each preceding element is pervaded [by the subsequent one]. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), water, fire, air, and ether are included. Among these, each succeeding element is the pervader (vyāpaka) and has a wider extension; each preceding element is the pervaded (vyāpya) and has a narrower extension. What is the meaning?

Space is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the elements below it, because its occurrence is more extensive (*adhika-vṛttitva*). The other four elements are the pervaded (*vyāpya*), because their occurrence is less extensive (*nyūna-vṛttitva*). Likewise, air is the pervader of the three beginning with fire, while those three are the pervaded. Similarly, fire is the pervader of the two below it, while those two are the pervaded. The same applies to water.
They pervade the earth; the meaning is that the earth is pervaded [by them]. || 2/34–35 ||
Therefore, he says that the pervasive qualities reside in the pervaded:
"O Goddess, those qualities, which have the pervasive as their locus, are situated within the pervaded according to the distinction between the gross and the subtle. (2.35)

The qualities of the pervader (*vyāpakaguṇa*) are those qualities belonging to the pervader; they reside within the pervaded (*vyāpya*), distinguished as gross and subtle. That which has a greater range is the gross pervader, while that which has a lesser range is the subtle pervaded.
The meaning is that, due to the distinction between gross and subtle in the relationship between the pervader and the pervaded, the qualities of the pervader abide within the pervaded.

Now, one might ask: which qualities belong to which elements, and in which elements do they reside? Furthermore, which syllables of the Vidyā characterize the qualities of which elements? To this, he says:
"Therefore, sound, the quality of space (ākāśa), exists pervading the air and the other elements."
One should perceive the fivefold sound by means of the seed-syllables of space situated within the Vidyā.

Therefore, because space is more gross than its own other elements, it is all-pervasive; by means of that, sound, which is the quality of space, remains pervading air and the rest—namely, air, fire, water, and earth. One should characterize the pentad of sounds residing in the five elements by means of the five seed-syllables of space belonging to the Vidyā-mantra, because they denote space.
The meaning is that the fivefold *hakāra*, possessing those qualities, indicates the fivefold sound (*śabda*). || 2/36 ||
Now, one might ask: "Since there are already six *ha*-letters within the Vidyā, what is the purpose of this other *ha*-letter?
To this, he says: "The supreme [Vidyā] consists of sound (*dhvanimaya*) and exists as the cause-form of those [six]."
The sound (*dhvani*) or resonance (*nāda*), which exists as the causal form of those sounds—that is, which exists as their cause—is the cause of all sounds. As it has been said by the learned:
"It is the condensed essence of the vast expanse of expressive words; it is the state of remaining as a residual impression."
"O Goddess Umā, this *nāda* of yours, rising from the crown of your head and transcending the limit of the *samanā*, gradually ceases like the ringing of a bell;
smelling the subtlest of other fragrances and experiencing the state of supreme consciousness (*paracit*), it reaches your ancient form. Thus [it is said].

It is "consisting of that" because it characterizes that. The "Supreme" (para) is the syllable *ha* situated between the letters *ka* and *la* within the *Kāmarāja-bīja*. What is the meaning? The sixth letter *ha*, situated in the middle of the *Kāmarāja-bīja*, is of the nature of *nāda*, the cause of the fivefold sound residing in the five elements beginning with space; it constitutes the state of stability (*sthiti-rūpatā*) of the *Kāmarāja-bīja*.
The meaning is that it perceives.

Now, it has been stated that the phonemes beginning with *ha* denote the elements such as space (*ākāśa*); how then can they be said to denote the qualities (*guṇa*) of the five elements, such as sound? To this, he says:
"May [the seed-syllable] be the seed of those possessing qualities, and also the denoter of the qualities themselves. (2.37)

It is the seed of the five elements—ether and the rest—which possess the five qualities (*guṇa*), namely sound and so forth; the singular number is used here to denote the class. In this context, within the *vidyā*, there are the five consonants that are the letters of the five elements, beginning with the letter *ha*. It has been stated in this very [text]: "From the letter *ha* arises ether" (2.29).
By such statements as these, the seeds (*bīja*) are thus described. The status of the consonants from *ka* to *kṣa* as seeds is stated in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*:

"Excluding the neuter [vowels], those vowels belonging to the one of great splendor, and those pure [consonants] which are devoid of the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the visarga (*sarga*), [are the seeds]."
"All the digits of the moon are indeed the *yoni*s [sources] of Śiva, being vowels that hold the seeds. (Śloka 40).
It is also stated in the *Parāpañcāśikā*: "This Goddess Mātṛkā exists in two ways, by way of the seed (*bīja*) and the womb (*yoni*). (Śloka 40).
These [vowels] are the denoters (*vācaka*) and indicators (*lakṣaka*) of their qualities, such as sound and the rest.

The letters beginning with *ha* are merely indicative (*lakṣaka*) of the qualities such as sound and so forth, because they are conventionally established (*saṃketita*) to denote the elements such as space.
As it has been stated by the learned: "That which denotes the directly designated meaning is the denoter (*vācaka*)" (Kāvyaprakāśa 2.7).
What is the meaning? It refers to those seed-syllables (*bīja*) which are the denoters of the elements such as space, which possess qualities such as sound.
The letters beginning with *ha* signify those qualities such as sound and the rest; this is the meaning. (2.37)
He states the reason for the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*):
"The identity of those two is intended by way of the relationship of cause and effect.

Of those two, namely the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), the possessor of the quality is the cause and the quality is the effect. By way of this relationship of cause and effect, [the identity is intended].
Therefore, oneness is indeed intended by virtue of the desire to express oneness through the relationship of cause and effect, but it is not ontological (*tāttvika*).

The meaning is that, having superimposed oneness upon the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) because of their causal relationship, and taking that connection as the basis, words denoting the possessor of qualities are applied to the qualities themselves through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). As it is said in the *Mahāsvacchandasamgraha*:
Sound possesses the forms characterized by the distinctions of being peaceful or terrible;
sound, moreover, is the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), which is soft, warm, hard, and mobile.
That which is characterized by specific touch is designated as the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra);
likewise, form itself is characterized by blueness, yellowness, and whiteness.
That which is joined with sweetness and so forth is called the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra);
however, that which is distinguished by fragrance and so forth is known as the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra).
Smell is the subtle element of smell; from those [subtle elements] indeed arises the five gross elements. Space is the subtle element of sound; it is eternal, great, and has sound as its quality.
The all-pervading, stainless principle, which provides space,
became the wind— the moving air— arising from the subtle element of touch.

The vital breath (anila) is the life-force of the world; it is light and performs the impulse of the bodily formations. It is declared to have the qualities of sound and touch, and its function is the act of coming and going.
O Śivā, the principle of fire (tejas-tattva) possesses the qualities of sound, touch, and form;
it is luminous, is the effect of the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra), and performs the function of digestion.
The water-element, born from the subtle element of taste, is liquid by nature;
it possesses the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste, and performs the function of cohesion.
The earth element is said to be endowed with the five qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; it is solid and supports all things.

"The pentad beginning with earth and ending with the principle of space (vyoma), each preceding one enveloping [the subsequent], exists in sequence according to the perception of its effects. Thus it is said.

Having previously stated that the five *ha* syllables situated in the *vidyā* indicate the five sounds residing in the five elements, he now indicates the four types of touch located in the four elements beginning with air by means of the seed-syllables that denote air.
Also by Mahāmāyā, Ātreya, and by the cause which is the Bindu. || 2.38 ||
O Goddess, one should meditate upon the fourfold tangibles of air, fire, water, and earth as they have arisen, according to their distinction as gross and subtle. (2.39)

Mahāmāyā is the letter *ī*; their "triad" refers to the triad of *ī*-letters situated at the summit of the three seed-syllables—namely, the three *ī*s consisting of two dots (*bindu*), a half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), and Māyā. And by means of the "instrument," which is the *bindu* that is the cause of those three syllables, [that is], by the *bindu* above known as Kāma, whose nature is the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) between the letters *a* and *ha*.

One should meditate upon the fourfold objects of perception—touch—arising from air, fire, water, and earth, according to their division into gross and subtle. Earth, water, and fire are subtle; air is gross compared to those preceding it. Therefore, by means of these three *ī*-sounds, six drops (*bindu*) are indicated. The drop (*bindu*) is the cause.
For the circle of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) consists of a circle marked with six dots, as is the case with the wind-mandala (*vāyumaṇḍala*). Thus it has been stated by the learned:
"The circle from the throat up to the palate is marked with six dots; it is smoke-colored. [Likewise elsewhere:
"By means of the collective dot (*samaṣṭibindu*), the wind is [designated], according to its gross and subtle divisions. By that which denotes the wind-mandala...

The meaning is that one should perceive the fourfold set of tangibles residing in the four elements beginning with air—distinguished as gross and subtle—by means of the three *ī* vowels together with the collective *bindu*. (2/38–39)

Having indicated the quality of air— the fourfold touch— by means of the words denoting air, he now indicates its quality, the threefold form, by means of syllables denoting fire: "In the same way, the triad of forms is manifested by the three *repha*s."
The triad of forms residing in fire, water, and earth— the triad of forms— is manifested and characterized by the three *repha* (ṛ) sounds.
Now, since form (rūpa) is common to earth, water, and fire, how is it characterized by the seed-syllable *repha*, which belongs to fire? To this he says:
"The primary [form] is that of fire; for it is produced by its seed-syllable. (2.40)

It is true that form exists in all three elements; nevertheless, because it is absent in air and space, form belongs primarily to fire alone. Subsequently, in the other two elements, it is produced and manifested by means of their seed-syllable, the letter *ra*.
"Production" (*janana*) here means manifestation (*prādurbhāva*). (2.40)
Having previously indicated the threefold form of the quality of fire (*tejas*) by means of syllables denoting fire,
he now indicates its two-fold taste (*rasa*) quality by means of syllables denoting water:
"By the seed-syllables of the Moon situated in *vidyā*, the gross and the subtle taste are declared."

[The mantra is formed] by the seed-syllables of the Moon (*candrabīja*) situated within the seed-syllables of Knowledge (*vidyābīja*), namely the letter *sa*. This is merely a designation. As it has been stated by the learned:

"One [syllable] is formed by the sky (*vyoma*), moon (*indu*), fire (*vahni*), and the lower drop (*adhara-bindu*); another by blood-red (*rakta*), clear (*accha*), Indra (*indra*), and fire (*śikhin*), along with the earth (*sara*) and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*); another by the sky (*dyu*), moon (*śītakara*), fire (*pāvaka*), and the anusvāra (*manva*). By these seed-syllables, the Vidyā known as Tripurā is proclaimed. (Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya 9.3)

It is gross and subtle. The gross rasa resides in the *aptattva* (the water element), because it is pervasive. The subtle rasa resides in the *bhūtattva* (the elemental essence), because it is that which is pervaded. "Smṛta" means cultivated (*bhāvita*); for memory is indeed cultivation.
Now, an objection may be raised: "In the *vidyā* there are three *sa*s, whereas in *ap* and *pṛthivī* there are only two *ras*s; what, then, is expressed by the other *sa*? To this he says:
"The connection between *rasa* and *amṛta* is well known in the world. (2.41)

The connection with *amṛta*—the nectar, the essence—is well-known in the world; for it is established by the authority of the Purāṇas that when the ocean was being churned by the gods and demons, the nectar emerged as its very essence. This is what is "known" (*vidita*) in the world, meaning it is thoroughly understood. Here, because it is the essence of the water-element (*aptattva*), its quality, *rasa*, is indicated by the third letter *sa*. What is the meaning? [It is] the water-element.

The gross is the nectar, which is its subtle essence; and the earth, pervading that, is also subtle. Therefore, the meaning is that the *rasa* (taste/flavor) situated threefold within the water, nectar, and earth is indicated by the three *sakāra*s residing in the *vidyā*. || 2/41 ||

Having previously indicated the three tastes, which are the qualities of water, by means of letters that do not denote water, he now indicates smell, the quality of earth, by means of letters denoting earth:
"Smell is the quality of the Earth; its script is the denoter of smell."
The quality (*guṇa*) of Vasundharā, that is, the Earth (*pṛthivī*), is fragrance (*gandha*). Its syllable (*lipi*) is the letter *la*, which denotes the Earth.
[The mantra] "Gandhavācikā" is the one that defines fragrance.
Now, since there are three instances of the letter *la* in the Vidyā, by means of one of those *la*s, the quality of fragrance situated in the Earth [is indicated].
Having been characterized [by the first two *lakāras*], he asks what is done by the remaining two *lakāras*, and therefore says:
"But its threefold nature, O Maheśvarī, arises from its connection with the three worlds. (2.42)

The "three worlds" refers to the three realms (*lokatraya*). Because of its connection with that—meaning because it is the substratum of the three realms—the relationship is one of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). For that reason, as a consequence of this relationship, the earth possesses a threefold nature.
Therefore, the meaning is that the three *la*-syllables symbolize the three types of fragrance residing within the three portions of the earth. (2.42)
Regarding the statement, "From the letter *ha* the ether (*vyoma*) is born, and from the letter *ka* the wind (*prabhañjana*)" (2/29),

since the letter *ka*, which was mentioned there as denoting the element of air, can also be said to denote the subject (*pramātṛ*), [the author] now indicates the three subjects by means of the three occurrences of the letter *ka*, having previously indicated the four types of tangible objects (*sparśa*) by other letters.
The supreme body of cognizing subjects—whether impure, pure, or mixed—is then revealed by the triad of Krodhīśas situated within the Vidyā-tattva. (2.43)

Impure subjects, whose essence consists solely of the cognition of duality and who are devoid of the contemplation of the state of "I am Śiva," are the *sakala* bound souls (*paśu*). As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Bound souls are of three kinds; among them, some are considered to be *sakala*."
O Maheśvarī, some among them are known by the name Pralayākala.
But others are mere consciousness alone; hear their nature in due order:
covered by beginningless impurity, veiled by māyā and karma, and non-omnipresent.
The embodied being is ignorant of the principle of Śiva, delights solely in duality, is insignificant,
always performs actions, and experiences the fruits of his own karma.
"This person is to be understood as always attached to sense objects and is to be purified.

Thus, the pure subjects (*pramātāraḥ*)—those whose impurities have been matured and whose consciousness consists solely of the essence of Śiva-ness—are the *vijñānakevalas*, who are still bound souls (*paśus*). As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
Enveloped by mere impurity, he is a bound soul (paśu) who is consciousness alone;
when his impurity is fully ripened, O Dear One, he is a consciousness-alone (vijñānakevala) by himself.
"By means of an extremely intense descent of power (*sutīvra-śaktipāta*), he renders them pure (*kevala*). Thus,
the "mixed" subjects (*miśrāḥ pramātāraḥ*)— who are bound solely to the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka-sūkṣmaśarīra*)—
having been born in various wombs for the sake of experiencing their *prārabdha* karma, [proceed] through the experience of the fruits of those respective actions.

When there is an equilibrium of the two types of karma, those whose impure karma is fully ripened, who possess the grace of Śiva even without a Guru, and who are common to both ritual action and knowledge, are the *pralayākala* bound souls (*paśus*). As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*: "The *miśra* [souls], which consist of the nature of the subject, are designated as *pralayākala*."
And they possess bodies composed of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), O beloved, by the power of their respective karmas.
Having been born in all wombs for the sake of experiencing their respective karmas,
and having enjoyed those experiences, Śiva himself [manifests] when there is an equilibrium of those karmas.

"And having slightly favored those whose impure karma is well-ripened, the Lords of the Worlds (Lokeśvaras) exist threefold within the midst of the principles (tattvas), beginning with the water-principle.
Thus, the "body" (vapuḥ) refers to the essential nature (svarūpa) of those three kinds of subjects; it is "supreme" (parama) and distinct from the others.

By the triad of Krodhīśas according to the sequence of the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa—Krodhīśa being the letter *ka*—by that triad; [and] by that which resides in the Vidyā, meaning by the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) residing therein, it is revealed, that is, manifested. What is the meaning? By the three instances of the letter *ka* contained within the three seed-syllables, [the threefold nature of the individual soul (*paśu*) consisting of the impure, the pure, and the pure-cum-impure—namely those called Sakala, Vijñānākala, and Pralayākala—is indicated].
The meaning is that the nature of the three mixed subjects is manifested. || 2.43 ||
Having previously indicated the triad of subjects by means of the triad of Krodhīśas situated within Vidyā,
he now indicates the Unmanifest (avyakta) by the first ten among the twelve Śrīkaṇṭhas situated within Vidyā, the vital breath (prāṇa) by the one immediately following, and Īśa by the last.
Likewise, O Goddess, the ten Śrīkaṇṭhas are the designators of the Unmanifest (avyakta); similarly, the supreme eleventh stands in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa). (2.44)

The "ten Śrīkaṇṭhas" refers to the ten vowels (the letters *a*) among those beginning with the letter *ha*—which are twelve syllables excluding the three *hṛllekhās*. The Śrīkaṇṭhas are the vowels (*a*);
their group consists of ten. The unmanifest individual soul (*jīva*), being covered by beginningless impurity (*anādimala*), [is thus described].

He is placed [in this state] by virtue of being included within the category of insentient things, such as the senses, which have their cause in the non-recognition of one's own Śiva-nature. As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Enveloped by beginningless impurity, veiled by Māyā and Karma, he is not all-pervasive."
"The embodied one is ignorant of the Śiva-principle, delighting solely in duality, and is base.

Its designator is the letter *A*, which, according to the method stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*—"The letter *A* is the foremost of all phonemes, the supreme light, the highest Śiva"—is expressed by the letter *A* as Paramaśiva, because it is a portion of Paramaśiva. It is like that.

"Like Paraśiva": the meaning is that just as Paramaśiva is denoted by the letter *A*, so too the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a portion of him, is expressed by the ten *A*-sounds. "Like that," i.e., like the soul: just as the soul, being a portion of Śiva, is indicated by Śrīkaṇṭha who denotes Paramaśiva, so too, like the soul, is Śrīkaṇṭha the eleventh.

It exists in the form of *prāṇa*, which is the support of the individual soul (*jīva*). For *prāṇa* is indeed the support of the soul, since the soul cannot abide without *prāṇa*. The supreme, the twelfth, Śrīkaṇṭha, is the designator of the *puruṣa*; because he fills the universe, Paramaśiva is the *puruṣa*. As it has been said in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*:

"We worship those great seers, headed by Patañjali, who fixed their minds upon the Lord, the Self of Consciousness, the abode of the universe, who has attained the state of Puruṣa through the act of filling [the universe]. (2/9).
Thus it is said. Furthermore, the Śruti also states: "Puruṣa alone is all this" (Ṛg Veda 10.90.2). (2/44)

Now, one might object: "In the *Vidyā* [section], there exists a group of twelve Śrīkaṇṭhas; since Śiva is mentioned by one, the individual soul (*jīva*) by another, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by another, these three alone would suffice—what is the use of the others? To this he replies: "Though being truly one, the Person indeed manifests in many ways."

It is true that Śiva is spoken of as one, and the individual soul (*jīva*) and vital breath (*prāṇa*) as two; nevertheless, being indeed one, he is the "one without a second Brahman" (*tri.ma.nā. 3/3*), for according to the method stated in the Upaniṣads—"He became both *sat* and *tyat*" (*tai.u.
2/6*)—the Puruṣa, who is of the nature of *Sat*, is indeed one and is born in many ways. The word "hi" indicates well-known fact (*prasiddhi*). Moreover...
And the authority for this point is: "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion" (Ṛgveda 6.47.18).
"For the single Self of all beings, though established in every being, is seen as one and as many, like the moon reflected in water" (Brahma-viśeṣa Upaniṣad 11).

In this manner, although Śiva is truly one alone, nevertheless, in order to illuminate the fact that he is divided manifoldly as the individual soul (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa), the meaning is that many Śrīkaṇṭhas reside within the Vidyā.
Having described the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the phonemes (*akṣara*), he now states the latent impressions of the points (*bindu*), the resonance (*nāda*), and so forth:
"The deities known as Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva possess limited forms. (2.45)
By means of the three *bindus*, the infinite and immeasurable forms are described:
Śānti, Śakti, and Śambhu, who are awakened by the triad of *nādas*. (2.46)

Rudra is the lord of the *tattva* of fire (*tejas*). The *tattvas* beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Māyā are included within the *tattva* of fire. As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*: "O Maheśvarī, the *tattva* of fire begins with Puruṣa and ends with Māyā. Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva consist of the *tattva* of air (*vāyu*). As it is said:

In the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*: "Vidyā, Īśvara, and Sadākhya are declared to be the Vāyu-tattva. Therefore, the deities Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Sadākhya possess limited bodies; they are of finite form. As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*: "That which extends up to Sadāśiva is joined with destruction and origination," by means of the three *bindus*.

These have been described. "The triad of points" refers to the three points situated above the Kāmakalā at the summit of the three seed-syllables. "Of immeasurable and infinite forms" refers to Śānti, Śakti, and Śambhu, who are awakened by the triad of Nādas.
Śānti is characterized by the unmanifest sound (nāda); she is that state wherein the entire universe, having been transcended, attains dissolution.
It is the ground culminating in the *brahmarandhra*, because it is the cause for the state of quiescence of the upward-moving powers (*ūrdhvaśakti*). As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Nāda, indeed, is the support of the channels; having pierced through this entire world..."
Having emerged through the downward power (adhaḥśakti), it culminates in the upward power (ūrdhvaśakti).
"Absorbed in the channel at the aperture of Brahmā, characterized by unmanifest sound.
Here, *śakti* refers to the upward-pointing power (*ūrdhvaśakti*), the *śakti-tattva* situated above. As it is said in this very same text:
"The lower *śakti*, however, is Brahmāṇī, who moves upon the lap of Brahmā."
Having blocked the gateway to the path of liberation, she stands firm.
Having pierced that, O lady of excellent hips, one reaches the supreme Śivā, the upward-pointing power (ūrdhvaśakti),
the Goddess whose essence is the principle of power (śaktitattva), who has the form of a slumbering serpent.
"The great Śaktitattva is fully described as being encompassed by worlds. Thus it is said.

Śambhu, who is the Śivatattva, resides above the Śaktitattva. Regarding this, it is stated in the very same [text]: "The Śivatattva is fully described as being above the Śaktitattva. They possess immeasurable and infinite forms; these are infinite.

They possess undifferentiated forms because they are contained within the principle of space (*vyomatattva*). As it is said in this very [text]: "The principle of power (*śaktitattva*), Śiva, and space.

They are the awakeners of the triad of *nāda*s. The triad of *nāda*s situated above the three *bindu*s located above the seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti—namely, those situated above the triad of *rodhinī*s—is their sequential awakener.
"Lakṣaka" means that by which the three Nādas are made known. The meaning is as follows: Śānti is manifested by the Nāda revolving around the Bindu situated above the Vāgbhava seed-syllable;
Śakti is manifested by the Nāda situated at the peak of the Kāmarāja seed-syllable; and Śiva is manifested by the Nāda situated at the peak of the third (Tārtīya) seed-syllable. || 2/45–46 ||
Having previously described the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the *vidyā* as consisting of *bindu* and *nāda*, he now states, with examples, the latent impression consisting of all mantras:
"In the ring at the base of the snare, the threads and so forth are swallowed up."
Likewise, all mantras are established here within this Vidyā. || 2.47 ||

"A *vāgurā* is a snare for binding deer" (*Amarakośa* 2.10.26). In this context, however, by the word *vāgurā*, a net—the means of catching fish—is indicated, because there is a commonality in the act of capturing living beings. Otherwise, the phrase "threads and so forth on the base coil" would be untenable, since a snare for binding deer lacks a base coil, being made of rope.

Because even the threads and so forth do not exist [independently]. "Threads and so forth" means the threads (*sūtra*) are the strands; by the word "and so forth," iron beads strung upon the ends of the net are included. Just as the root of the threads—the parts of the net—is swallowed within an iron ring, so too Vaikharī, which is the root of all mantras, is [absorbed] into this Vidyā.
She is rested; therefore, the meaning is that all mantras abide within this Vidyā. || 2/47 ||
He says that this meaning is attained through the sequence of the guru’s instruction: "The meaning of the tradition is said to be attained through the lineage of gurus.
The lineage of gurus is the sequence of transmission; [it is attained] precisely through the sequence of their instruction.
From the perfect form of Śiva and the others, the cause of all causes,
[emerges] the supreme, subtle, and pure sound-form, which is the essence of all splendors.
The reality that has issued forth in the form of speech is the solitary power Unmanā;
it is the unmanifest appearing in a manifest form, partless, and the cause of sequential manifestation.
Svacchandabhairava, having composed it in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, declared that which is the nature of supreme bliss through its various divisions, such as the *Svacchanda*.
Having reflected upon that, the Lord Anāśrita spoke at length;
all of that has been explained in great detail within the portion concerning the Śāntyatītā level.
This very [reality] is indeed Śiva, who exists by means of his supreme form known as "Being" (Sat),
seated upon the throne of mantras, and whose body consists of the five mantras.
Within the Kaulika and other traditions, there is the entire range of scriptures beginning with the Siddhānta;
therein lies the means for achieving the goals of human existence, including the Kaulika and the Atikaulika.
That knowledge, which is incalculable and immeasurable, was previously proclaimed by Śiva; it was bestowed upon Īśvara by Īśvara through the will of Śiva.
In the beginning, the Vidyā was truly bestowed upon Vidyeśa;
that knowledge was then granted by Vidyeśvara and transmitted in due order.
This was given by Rudra to the Lord of the Guṇatattva, and it was given by Īśvara to Śrīkaṇṭha; after that, it was given by him [Śrīkaṇṭha].
O Ambikā, after Śrīkaṇṭha had initiated them in due order according to the prescribed rite, beginning from Pradhāna and ending with the ten Rudras, he indeed bestowed upon them knowledge.
Having initiated him and then consecrated him by both Śrīkaṇṭha and myself,
I bestowed upon him the entire Śrī-Dakṣiṇa, which is the means for accomplishing all desires and goals.
Thus, according to the method taught by Svacchandabhairava, I have declared the meaning of the tradition precisely through the sequence of instructions from my own guru’s lineage.

The meaning of the tradition, as stated by means of difficult words—verses whose sense is not understood by those ignorant of the oral transmission—is impossible to grasp by the power of mere intellectual analysis alone, like verses from the Purāṇas and similar texts, without the instruction of a guru; this is the intended meaning.
Now, he states the meaning of the *nigarbha*, which follows in sequence:
"O Great Goddess, the *nigarbha* also has as its sphere of experience Śiva, the Guru, and the Self. (2.48)

The *nigarbha* is the innermost meaning. Śiva is beyond the reach of speech and mind, characterized by the distinctions of being with parts (*sakala*), without parts (*niṣkala*), or both with and without parts (*sakalaniṣkala*).

A Guru who has realized the meaning of all the scriptures perceives such [Śiva] as his own self, designating him by all the qualities beginning with "Self" (*ātman*), and whose every fetter has been dissolved by the falling glance of the compassion of such a Guru—[he is pure].
The experience of the nature of consciousness is the Self (ātman) of the disciple. As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"O beautiful lady, it transcends the principles (tattvas), it is beyond the sphere of speech and mind;
it is partless, not composed of parts, formless, and free from conceptual construction."
"The supreme reality, free from dualities, is the highest state known as Śiva. Thus [it is said].

"The teacher, who knows all sciences and is devoted to the dharma of liberation, should unite the bound soul (paśu) with that very [reality] through the application of the Guru's oral instruction. Thus [it is said].
The Guru:
Salutations to the Guru Śiva, who proclaims his own essential nature— which has made the three worlds its own— and who is both the means and the goal.

This is the definition stated [above]. The meaning is that the "innermost secret" (nigarbha) refers to the contemplative realization whose object is the identity of Śiva, the Guru, and the Self as described in this manner. || 2/48 ||
Now, one might ask: in what manner is the identity of Śiva, the Guru, and the Self to be contemplated? To this he says:
"O Goddess, I shall describe that method to you in its broad outlines:
through the contemplation of the identity of Śiva, the Guru, and the Self, one becomes identical with That. (2.49)

That method consists of the contemplation of the identity of Śiva, the Guru, and the Self; I shall describe it only by way of a brief indication, not through an elaborate exposition that sets forth every detail—this is the meaning. (2.49)

He states that method: "Having realized the partless nature (niṣkalatva) in Śiva, and likewise the identity with that form in the Guru, and through the power of beholding Him, [one realizes] the self's own nature as Śiva. (2.50)
One should meditate, being bowed with devotion and unstained by the emergence of doubt;

having understood that "parts" (kalā) mean limbs, and that "partlessness" (niṣkalatva) means the state of being without limbs or parts, in Śiva, who possesses the characteristics previously described.
Salutations to the Guru, Śiva, who has made the three worlds his own and proclaims his own true nature, appearing in the form of both the means and the goal.

According to the method stated in the words of the learned masters, one who perceives Śiva— who is partless and whose nature is partlessness— as one's own self possesses the status of a Guru; having realized that even the Guru is of that same nature,
that is, identical with Śiva, through the power of such perception.
By the power of the Guru’s command, having perceived that which is solely free from conceptual proliferation, one becomes moistened by the nectar of such a non-dual ocean of consciousness.

In accordance with the manner described in such statements as, "Just as even a purified disciple may merge into the solid mass of bliss-consciousness," the gaze of that Guru is capable of severing all fetters (*pāśa*). By virtue of that power, the purified disciple, bowed down in devotion, [becomes] suddenly awakened—

The immersion in the state of "I am Supreme Śiva" (paramaśivāhaṃbhāvanā), through the power of daily, respectful, continuous, and skillful practice, remains unstained by the emergence of doubt (*śaṅkā*). Doubt is contraction, the conceit of being a transmigrating being (*saṃsāritva*);
its emergence is attachment to external objects such as son and wife. Being unstained by that means being free from the conceits of "I" and "mine. And of the Self...

One should contemplate the state of being Śiva. The meaning is that, just as the purity of a crystal emerges from the removal of its proximity to a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*), one whose mass of bonds (*pāśapaṭala*) has been torn asunder by the falling glance of the Guru—himself permeated by the contemplation of the non-duality of the Self—shall become the perfectly full nature. (2/50–51)
Now, he states the Kaulika meaning which follows in sequence: "I shall explain the Kaulika [meaning] of both the wheel and the deity. (2.51)

I shall explain the Kaulika [teaching] regarding the Kaulika goal, which is the identity of the Vidyā, the Guru, and the Self. The meaning is that the contemplation of the identity of the deities of the wheels (cakradevatā), the Guru, the Vidyā, and the practitioner (sādhaka) is the Kaulika goal. The literal meaning is clear. (2/51)
He states its manner:
"Its manner is demonstrated" and so forth; thus, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the Kaulika meaning has been told. (2.68)
[This is] by means of this much [of the text]. (2.52)
First, he states the identity of the Vidyā and the Cakra:
"By means of the letter *la*, [one forms] squares, joined with three circles. (2.52)
O Dear One, the pair of lotuses consists of Śakti and has the nature of Agni and Soma, formed by the nine syllables arising from the three *hṛllekhās*. (2.53)

O Dear One, that which is produced by the three *bindus* consists of nine *yonis*, formed by the letter *la*s situated within the three seed-syllables of the *vidyā*. Since the earth-mandala is square—as stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*: "The squares are the earthly abodes; the earth-mandala is yellow, square, and very beautiful"—it takes the form of a square.

The meaning is that the three squares are produced by the *lakāras* which denote the reality of the elements (*bhūtattva*). By the *śākta* [sounds, i.e., the *sakāras*]. As it is stated in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra*: "Mādana is above, and Śakti is below it" (1.111). It is also stated in the *Haṃsapārameśvara*:
"The letter *ha* is said to be Śiva; the letter *sa* is the imperishable Śakti. [This refers to those situated within the three seed-syllables of Vidyā.]
With circles, it is joined with three circles: one circle within a square;

inside that circle is a sixteen-petaled lotus consisting of the nature of the moon (Soma); inside that is a second circle; inside that is an eight-petaled lotus consisting of the nature of fire (Agni); and inside that is a third circle. Thus.

The meaning is as follows: according to the method stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*— "two lotuses consisting of fire and moon, joined with three circles, and a perfectly round white water-image marked with a lotus"— because the water-image takes the form of a circle marked by a lotus,
the two lotuses joined with three circles are produced by the letter *sa*, which denotes the water-principle (*jalatattva*).

The meaning is that the wheel consisting of nine yonis has arisen from the letters known as *ha*, *ra*, and *e*—which constitute the three components of the three *hṛllekhās* situated at the peak of the three seed-syllables (*bījas*)—and which, joined with the three *bindus*, consist of the number nine. || 2/52–54 ||

Now, one might ask: since it would have been logical to describe the three wheels consisting of two sets of fourteen spokes immediately after the two lotuses, why was the nine-petaled wheel (*navayonicakra*) described instead? It is said in reply:
