when the layout is made above the nine-petaled wheel, there arise three wheels consisting of twelve and fourteen corners [respectively], formed by the three powers (*śakti*) and the three fires (*vahni*).
Since [this] has arisen, these three wheels arise immediately after the wheel of the nine sources; keeping this in mind, he says:
"But the wheel joined with the three mandalas consists of power (śakti) and fire (anala). (2.54)
By means of the three seed-syllables of space alone, it is endowed with the triad of subjects;
it consists of the forms of will, knowledge, and action, and is joined with the three absorptions (ādanas).
O Goddess, the seat of Sadāśiva is supreme and consists of the Great Bindu (mahābindu).
Thus, the wheel is essentially mantra in nature and is joined with three mandalas; it is a wheel consisting of the fire of Śakti situated within three circles.

When the grid is laid out above the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*), because it is produced by the three *Śaktis* and the three fires, the triad of wheels beginning with the fourteen-spoked one is formed by the three void-seeds (*vyomabīja*) alone—that is, by the three *ha*-letters, since the *ha*-letter signifies the void (*vyoman*). Within the three *hṛllekhās*, the three *ha*-letters are already contained; [the remaining structure is formed] by the remaining three *ha*-letters.
The meaning is that the triad of wheels beginning with the fourteen-spoked one has arisen.

The subjects (pramātṛ) are of three kinds, as previously described, consisting of the impure, the pure-impure, and the pure; [the wheel] is endowed with these three. Subsequently, through the grace of Śiva, due to the ripening of impurity and karma, [there arise] the lords of earth, water, fire, and air.
This [world] has been obtained as endowed with those three, both individually and collectively. As it is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"But when impurities and the like have not yet ripened, there occurs a general grace;
the sovereign authority of office arises solely from the grace of Śiva."
O Supreme Goddess, the bound souls (paśus) are of three types;
having bestowed a slight grace upon those whose impurities and karmas have been ripened, they attain [liberation].
"Among the principles (tattvas) beginning with the water-principle, the Lords of the World (lokeśvaras) are threefold.

Thus, the seat of Sadāśiva is conjoined— that is, thoroughly mixed— with the triad of the letter *ka*, which consists of the three intoxicants (*mādana*) representing the three types of subjects (pramātṛ) whose primary natures are the powers of will, knowledge, and action.

The fifth seat, consisting of Sadāśiva, the lord of the fifth element, space, is supported in the form of feet by the four— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara— who are the lords of the four elements beginning with earth and ending with air; it is supreme and consists of the Great Bindu (mahābindu).

As stated in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*: "When the pure mirror of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—which is a mass of rays from the sun that is Paraśiva—is shining forth, the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*) settles upon the wall consisting of consciousness (*citta*), which is exceedingly beautiful. Following this method, [the state] is supreme and most excellent, consisting of the Great Bindu which is the reflection of Paraśiva.

Because Śiva and Śakti are worthy of being consecrated [therein]. As it is stated in the *Jñānadīpavimarśinī*: "In the midst of the Oḍyāṇa seat, within the Kadamba forest, upon the four-legged auspicious throne: *Laṃ*, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the earth;
*Vaṃ*, salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the waters; *Raṃ*, salutation to Rudra, the lord of fire; *Yaṃ*, [salutation] to the lord of wind..."

"Salutation to Īśvara. Having worshipped these [deities] with [the mantra], "Haṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva, the five-faced Great Preta-throne of the Lord of Space," one thus worships Sadāśiva in his glorious form as the letter *Ca*.
In this manner, according to the stated procedure, the wheel consists of mantra; that is to say, it is composed of the Saubhāgyavidyā. (2/54–56)
Now he describes the identity of the deity with the wheel:
"The supreme body of the deity. (2.56)

The *cakra* is another supreme form (*vapuḥ*) of the deity. Thus, in the passage "Then [one should meditate on] the Goddess who resembles a lotus" (*Niśvāsakārikā* 1.130), the form of the deity possessing hands, feet, and so forth is described.

That very same [form] is divided limb by limb into the forms of the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-devatā*) residing within the locations of the *Śrīcakra*, beginning with the triangle and ending with the earth-house (*bhūgṛha*).
The meaning is that the deity of one’s own consciousness, residing in the *bindu*, abides in the form of the *śrīcakra*. As it has been stated in this very [text]:
"Such is the supreme radiance, abiding in the form of the *śrīcakra*, surrounded by the surging waves of the multitude of its powers" (1/55). || 2/56 ||
He establishes this very point:
"Furthermore, by virtue of being the essence of one hundred and eleven deities,
the three goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī reside in the right, left, and apex corners of the triangle of one hundred and eleven deities."

Outside of that, within the space between the eight corners, there are the eight deities who are the weapons of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, arranged in the four directions around the triangle; on the eight corners are the eight [deities] beginning with Vaśinī; within the space between the eight corners are the deities of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga); on the inner ten-spoked wheel are the ten [deities] beginning with Sarvajñā; and on the second ten-spoked wheel are those beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā.
In the fourteen-spoked [wheel], there are the fourteen [deities] beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī; in the eight-petaled [lotus], the eight beginning with Anaṅgakusumā;

in the sixteen-petaled [lotus], the sixteen beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī; within the inner square, the ten mudrā-deities; in the middle square, the eight beginning with Brāhmī; and in the outer square, the ten beginning with Aṇimā.
Thus, the meaning is that the deity in the form of the Śrīcakra is the substratum of those [energies] by virtue of being the essence of one hundred and eleven deities.
Anticipating the objection as to where this Kaulika meaning is indicated in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra, [the author], while dispelling that doubt,

explains the Kaulika meaning indicated in the verse beginning with *gaṇeśa* (Niḥśeṣatantra 1.1) for the very purpose of establishing the identity (*aikya*) of the deity, the mantra, the wheel (*cakra*), the guru, and the disciple:
The state of being Gaṇeśa belongs to the Great Goddess, together with Soma, Ravi, and Pāvaka.

Furthermore, through will, knowledge, and action, conjoined with the three qualities (*guṇas*), that Goddess takes the form of the planets; moreover, by the word "furthermore," she possesses the nature of the Lord of the Multitudes (*gaṇeśatva*) by virtue of being the essence of one hundred and eleven deities. This is her state as the Lord of the Multitudes.
The term "Mahādevī" is also connected [to the preceding] by way of the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*).

The "Gana" (multitude) of Mahādevī consists of the collection of one hundred and eleven deities who reside within the Śrīcakra—from the previously mentioned triangle up to the square—acting as her own self. Of the Goddess, [the forms are] Soma, Ravi, and Pāvaka.
The white [energies] are in the form of the eyes;
Icchā is situated in the region of the head, Jñānā is below that,
and Kriyā is indeed located in her feet.

Thus, according to the method stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*, [the goddess] consists of the nine planets in the form of her own limbs—such as Will (*icchā*) and the rest—as her head and other parts, and the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. In this way, that Goddess is composed of those nine which constitute her own limbs. (2/57–58)
And also by means of the organs of cognition and action. (2.58)

Furthermore, O Goddess of the Gods, by means of those very internal instruments for that purpose, as well as by primordial nature (prakṛti), the qualities (guṇas), and the self through its bondage to masculinity; 2/59.
The constellations became the organs of cognition—

namely, hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell, which are the instruments of perception— and the organs of action— namely, speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ; their objects are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure; the internal instruments—the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*);
primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is the equilibrium of the *guṇas* and the unmanifest (*avyakta*); the *guṇa*, which is the principle of the *guṇas* and the root of pleasure, pain, and delusion;
and the bondage of masculinity—the self, which is the principle of the *puruṣa*. As it is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
O Goddess, just as the bound soul (paśu) is filled with these six— beginning with Māyā— and experiences enjoyments, so too does that which is designated as Puruṣa.
That very Māyā, for the sake of the experience of the bound soul (paśu), is known as the Unmanifest (avyakta),
the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) of the universe, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas).
Within that primordial nature (prakṛti), however, the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva) came into being;
that is the root of suffering, pleasure, and delusion, consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Buddhi, by its very nature as a constituent of the gunas, consists of the determination of objects; it takes the form of a collection of mental operations and is characterized by manifest qualities.
According to the three qualities (guṇas) and according to the three types of karma,
the ego (ahaṅkāra), produced by that intellect (buddhi), is of three kinds.
O Lotus-seated One, in the form of the exertion of all living beings,
his objects and their distinctions are threefold according to their karma.
This very [organ], by its essential nature, consists of the fiery, the transformative, and the elemental;
and the modifications as well as their own subdivisions are contained within the aggregate of the organs of speech and the rest.

O Īśānī, O Daughter of the Mountain, the denotative meanings [of words] become restricted here and there according to the states such as *sāttvika* and the rest. Thus one attains [these meanings], O Daughter of the Mountain.
The mind, which is of the nature of desire and the agent of volition, arises from the Taijasa state;
and through its various modified states, the organs of knowledge and action are produced.
O Supreme Goddess, the elements— earth, water, fire, air, and ether— and the subtle elements— sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— have arisen as the functions of the organs of speech and the rest.
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—these five are the organs of cognition; their respective functions follow in order, one by one.
O Dear One, the perception of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell [is the function of the sense organs];
the organs of action are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ.
Speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure are proclaimed to be, respectively,
the five functions of the organs of action.
"These ten external [elements], followed by the three internal ones— namely, mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and ego (ahaṅkāra)— are designated as the internal organs. Thus,
the Goddess was born with a body composed of the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakṣatra) formed from these constituent parts.
She who assumes a form according to her own will. || 2/58–60 ||
Now, the state of being a Yoginī is described: she [is also] associated with Ḍākinī and the others, who are the mistresses of the elements such as the skin and so forth. (2.60)
Accompanied by yoginīs established in the eight groups (vargas), she who possesses a universal form shines forth, having assumed the form of a yoginī. (2.61)
The *dhātus* are skin and so forth—skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, and semen;

their lords (*nātha*), the presiding deities, are the *Ḍākinīs* and others: *Ḍākinī*, *Rākinī*, *Lākinī*, *Kākinī*, *Sākinī*, and *Hākinī*. The *vargas* are *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*; the *Yoginīs* such as *Brahmāṇī* and the rest are established within these eight groups. As it has been said:
In the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"She who is the root of all speech, encompassed by the eight groups [of consonants], and who,
through the Bhairavas emitted from the eight powers at the end of the sequence of universal manifestation..."
"And joined with the Śaktis, the series of Mātṛkās is unendurable. Thus it is said.

It is also stated in the *Catuḥśatikā*: "In which [the Wheel], by means of the sequential arrangement of the groups (vargas), the eight measures (mātras) reside" (*Niḥśeṣatantra-ṣoḍaśikā* 1.11). [The goddess] is conjoined with these. [She is conjoined] with Ḍākinī and the others in the six ādhāras, because [she] is the gross form of the Mātṛkās.

"Because she pervades the skin and other [constituents], the Yoginīs are to be known as manifest" (3/114). According to the method that will be explained, she—having been attended by Brāhmī and the others within the elements such as the skin—shines, assuming the form of the Yoginīs as the totality of all things, possessing a universal body (*viśvavigraha*), and sporting in the form of each respective Yoginī. On this very point, he will say:
"The eight groups of eight [offerings] should be performed, free from stinginess regarding wealth;
for you alone, O Enchantress of the Universe, sport in their form. (3/194) Thus, [ends] 2/60-61.
Prāṇa, apāna, and samāna, as well as udāna and vyāna; furthermore, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. (2.62)
The individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*):

by these, [the aggregate] consists of ten vital airs (*vāyu*), beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *dhanañjaya*; the individual self is the "bound soul" (*paśu*) as previously defined; and the supreme self is that which is declared in the Upaniṣads: "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.7.3).
She is the inner controller of all beings; by these twelve [deities], she is the embodiment of the zodiac signs. (2.62–63)
He applies the term "Gaṇeśa" and so forth even to the plane of knowledge (vidyāpada):
"By means of the sequence beginning with the third [vowel], which consists of the three rows starting from 'A', 'Ka', and 'Tha'. (2.63)

Gaṇeśa became Mahāvidyā, the supreme speech (*parāvāk*) which consists of the primordial manifestations of speech. "Supreme speech and the others" refers to the four forms of speech—*parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*—of which *parāvāk* is the first. As it has been said:
In the *Saṃketapaddhati*:
"The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, the supreme light, Śiva;
the final letter Ha, whose form is *kalā*, is proclaimed as that which is called reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)."
The perfect integration of these two that is manifest in the supreme splendor is proclaimed as the "syllableless" (avarṇa), which is condensed by means of the vowels beginning with *vā*.
At the beginning, Raudrī is proclaimed as his head; Vāmā is declared to be his face;
Ambikā is said to be his arms; and Jyeṣṭhā resides at the tips of his nails.
These, whose form is the half-moon digit, abide as a fivefold form;
though they are the colorless essence of all colors, they do not appear externally as something separate.
Will resides in the region of the head, knowledge is situated below that,
action is indeed located in the feet, and tranquility should be in the center of the heart.
The Unstruck (anāhata) is said to be eightfold, according to the divisions beginning with the Void (śūnya):
the Void, touch, resonance (nāda), sound (dhvani), and likewise the point (bindu).
The unstruck (anāhata) is traditionally said to be eightfold, including the syllables of the seed-mantra of Śakti;
when multiplied by forty-seven, it is proclaimed as the struck (hata).
That which is called the letter *kṣa* is declared to be a conjunction of two kinds;
thus indeed is the supreme seat of the Mātṛkā known as the sixty-seventh.
"Victorious is that Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha) called Mātṛkā, which stands everywhere through the three divisions—unstruck, struck, and transcendent.

Thus, this [Mātṛkā] consists of speech in its fourfold form beginning with Parā; having set aside its own two parts, which consist of the resonance (vimarśa) of vowels and the absence of vowels (asvara), [it remains].

According to the method set forth in the *Saubhāgyasudhodaya*, "She herself consists of four parts" (2.2), the Vidyā is composed of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī. This occurs through the sequence beginning with the third [letter] of the three rows starting with 'A', 'Ka', and 'Tha'.
In the phrase "beginning with A, Ka, and Tha," the word "beginning" (*ādi*) is connected to all three: 'A', 'Ka', and 'Tha'. The "beginnings" refer to the vowels ending in the visarga.

There are sixteen [consonants], from *ka* to *ta*, sixteen from *tha* to *sa*, and sixteen from *tha* to *ha*. Thus, in the sequence of the third [seed-syllable] beginning with *Ka*, the Kāmarāja beginning with *Tha*, and the Vāgbhava beginning with *A*: the third [syllable] consists of the row of vowels starting with *a*; the Kāmarāja consists of the row of consonants starting with *ka*; and the Vāgbhava consists of the row of consonants starting with *tha*. This is the sequence.

The word *paṅkti* refers to a group (*gaṇa*), because it consists of the fourfold *mātṛkā*, and because it possesses the three groups of letters—beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *ṭa*—and the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) starting with *vaikharyādi*. Thus, the meaning is that this Great Vidyā became Gaṇeśa. (2/63–64)
And she, whose nature is that of the planets, resides within the seed-syllables, the points, and the sounds in the three peaks.
This [Vidyā], which has the form of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra), consists of letters numbering fifteen—produced from the three *hṛllekhās*—as well as twelve other syllables. (2.65)

In this context, the word *kūṭa* refers to a cluster of syllables (*akṣarapiṇḍa*). As it has been stated by the learned: "Among the three *kūṭas*, due to the gravity of the task, the vowel *ī* follows the sequence of the 'peaks' (*śṛṅga*). Within the clusters of syllables of the *saubhāgyavidyā*, there are the seed-syllables (*bīja*), the points (*bindu*), and the resonance (*dhvani*). The "seed" (*bīja*) consists of the group of syllables ending in the vowel *ī*; the "point" (*bindu*) is defined [in verse 1.28].

*dhvani* means *nāda*. The use of the genitive case in *bījabindudhvanīnām* is a Vedic (archaic) usage for the sense of the instrumental (*by means of*). The meaning is that the *vidyā* consists of nine *grahas*: three seed-syllables (*bījas*) of the three *kūṭas*, three *bindus*, and three *nādas*.
Furthermore, it is formed by the syllables arising from the three *hṛllekhās* situated at the top of the three seeds, namely the letters *ha*, *ra*, and *ka*.

The meaning is that she is the embodiment of all the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakṣatras), consisting of all twenty-seven syllables—namely, fifteen syllables consisting of the *bindu* and *nāda* along with the number of lunar days (fifteen), and twelve other syllables devoid of the three *hṛllekhās*, which are the constituent parts of the three *kūṭas*. Thus, [she consists of] fifteen and twelve, totaling twenty-seven syllables. || 2/65 ||

Through the six Śākta syllables, beginning with Śakti and the others which are included within the Vidyā, one attains the state of a Yoginī; and through those same syllables, excluding the last, one attains the state of a Rāśi (the aggregate). || 2.66 ||

The three *hṛllekhās* and the three *la*-letters that precede them are included within the fifteen-syllable *vidyā*. Through these six syllables associated with the *śaktis*, this *vidyā* possesses the nature of a *yoginī*. The *yoginīs* are the six beginning with *ḍākinī*. Within this fifteen-syllable *vidyā*, the final three *hṛllekhās* are...

The meaning is that the state of being a zodiac sign (*rāśitva*) occurs through twelve letters excluding those [previously mentioned]. The signs (*rāśayaḥ*) are the twelve beginning with Aries (*meṣa*).
He extends by analogy the meaning already stated: "In this way, the Great Goddess, who consists of all varieties, is the form of the wheel.
In the manner described, the Great Goddess Tripurasundarī, whose various forms include Gaṇeśa and the rest, is the form of the wheel.
The meaning is that, just as in the case of the *vidyā* aspect, the status of being Gaṇeśa and so forth should also be applied to the *cakra* aspect. As for the method of application:
the status of being Gaṇeśa is established by the line of the central triangle composed of the letters *a*, *ka*, and *tha*; the form of the planets (*graha*) by the nine triangles;
and the form of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) by the three circles, the fourteen triangles, and the ten outer triangles.

The state of being a Yoginī is [attained] through the eight triangles, which correspond to the number of Yoginīs beginning with Brāhmī; the state of being a zodiac sign (rāśi) is [attained] through the two lotuses, the four fires, the five powers, and the earth-dwelling (bhūgṛha). || 2/67 ||
Furthermore, he extends the previously stated definition to the teacher and the disciple as well:
"Just as it was described in the body of the Goddess, so indeed is it in the body of the Guru. (2.67)

And by her grace, even the disciple shines forth as having that same form within the body of the Goddess Tripurasundarī, whose playful form (*līlāvigraha*) is assumed according to her own will, as it has been stated: "Furthermore,
through the nature of being the essence of one hundred and eleven deities, the state of Gaṇeśa belongs to the Great Goddess" (2.57), and so forth.
Salutations to the Guru, Śiva, who has made the three worlds his own, who proclaims his own true nature, and who consists of both the means and the goal.

According to the method stated in the words of the authoritative masters (*abhiyukta*), since the body of the deity itself is the Guru, even within the body of the Guru—just as the nature of Gaṇeśa and so forth was attributed to the body of the Goddess—in the same way, that [nature] should be attributed to the body of the Guru who possesses that very form; this is the meaning.
By his grace...
"The Guru, who is Śiva himself, being of the nature of self-luminous form, bestows his grace upon the summit of the categories of existence.
Having obtained that grace here, which is the purification of the principles (*tattva-śodhana*), the fortunate seeker attains joy.
(Cidgaganacandrikā 31). According to this method stated by us, the disciple who has obtained the grace of the Guru becomes identical with him, indeed the very form of the Deity.

"It is fully revealed. Therefore, the meaning is that just as the state of being Gaṇeśa and so forth was applied to the bodies of the Goddess and the Guru, it should likewise be applied to the body of the disciple. (2/67–68)
He concludes the Kaulika meaning:
"Thus, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the Kaulika meaning has been explained. (2.68)
The word "iti" (thus) indicates the conclusion of the incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*). The word "evaṃ" (in this way) serves as a restatement of what was previously mentioned.
The remainder is clear. (2/68)
Now, he promises to explain the meaning of all the secrets, which has come in due order:
"In that manner, O sinless one, I shall tell you the meaning of all the secrets.
The word *tathā* (in that manner) serves to refer back to the types of meanings previously mentioned. [The phrase] "the meaning of all the secrets" (*sarvarahasyārtham*).
It is the secret among all those previously mentioned, because it consists in the attainment of the Supreme. || 2/69 ||
He speaks precisely on the meaning of all secrets:
"When [the energy] in the form of lightning at the mūlādhāra has assumed the form of the Vāgbhava [syllable]," (2.69).
The Vidyā, whose form consists of fifty phonemes endowed with thirty-eight Kalās, has the nature of Kuṇḍalinī and pierces through the three Maṇḍalas. (2.70)
Resembling the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes, its form like a lotus fiber, it is attached to the lunar orb in the sky and consists of a stream of nectar. (2.71)
O Maheśvarī, the secret meaning is this realization: "This [consciousness], which eternally pervades the entire universe and whose nature is eternal bliss, is my own Self. (2.72)

In the *mūlādhāra*, which possesses the characteristics previously described (1/25), having the form of lightning and the color of lightning, it assumes the shape of the *vāgbhava* [syllable]. That which comes into being through those words—namely *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*—is the *vāgbhava* triangle. This has been stated in this very same work (beginning with 1/36): "The vibration of the Self... and so forth; for this *kriyāśakti* is *raudrī*, who is *vaikharī*.
Up to the point where it says "viśvavigrahā" (1/40), [it means] having attained that form, having been transformed into that nature.
The thirty-eight *kalās* are as follows: ten belonging to Fire, beginning with *Dhūmrārcis*; twelve belonging to the Sun, beginning with *Tāpinī*;
and sixteen belonging to the Moon, beginning with *Amṛtā*. Thus, these are the thirty-eight *kalās*, and [the deities] are joined with them.
The fifty phonemes consist of: the ten consonants from *ya* to *na* joined with the ten digits of Fire (*vahnikalā*);

the twenty-four consonants from *ka* to *ma* joined with the twelve digits of the Sun (*sūryakalā*) in both direct and reverse order; and the sixteen vowels from *a* to *au* joined with the sixteen digits of the Moon (*somakalā*). Thus, these fifty phonemes constitute the body (*vigraha*).
She who possesses that [knowledge] is "tathā" (such). That knowledge is the "vidyā of good fortune" (*saubhāgyavidyā*).

According to the previously mentioned method—"consisting of the thirty-six principles through the distinction of vowels and consonants" (2.33)—she consists of fifty syllables, possesses the limbs of the thirty-six principles, is of the nature of *vaikharī* speech, and takes the form of *kuṇḍalinī*.
In its center, a flame of fire, extremely subtle, is situated facing upward.
"Resplendent like a streak of lightning situated in the midst of dark clouds,

slender like the awn of wild rice, yellow, radiant, and resembling an atom"— according to the manner described in this Śruti passage (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.11.11–12), she is a creeper of light resembling the coils of a serpent, piercing through the three circles.
The "three mandalas" refers to the triad of the fire, sun, and moon mandalas situated at the base, the heart, and between the eyebrows;
she is the "piercer" of these. The meaning is that, having pierced the three mandalas, she is intent on entering the *akula* through the central path.
She is "resplendent like the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes," meaning her radiance is similar to the appearance of ten million streaks of lightning.
Its form resembles a lotus fiber; it is as subtle in form as a lotus fiber. It is attached to the lunar orb in the sky, beginning from above the forehead and ending at the top of the skull.
The supreme ether is proclaimed to be in the region of the head, three finger-breadths above.

According to the method stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*, she is attached to that lunar orb which is the reflection of the moon of consciousness (*ciccandra*) in the supreme ether; she is of the nature of a stream of nectar, consisting of the flow of the nectar trickling from it. She has eternally pervaded the entire universe—meaning that at all times throughout the three periods, she has pervaded the entire universe composed of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).

"Sadānandasvarūpiṇī" means she whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is eternal bliss (*sadānanda*), that supreme Śiva who is eternal bliss. This consciousness-constituted (*cinmayī*) Kuṇḍalinī energy is one's own self (*svātman*); the realization of this and the immersion (*samāveśa*) into that identity is the secret meaning.
As it is said in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra*:
When she, in the form of a crescent moon, shines forth from the seat of the Śṛṅgāṭa.
Having pierced the solar orb of Śiva and melting the lunar orb,
she is delighted by the supreme bliss of the flowing nectar arising therefrom.
A woman of noble family, having abandoned her own family,
goes to another man who is devoid of auspicious marks, lacking virtues, and bereft of noble lineage and beauty.
Then, having taken the Lord of the World according to her own will,
she, being satisfied, returned alone by that same path.
"Tripurā, who is herself unmanifest, delights [in this world] having attained manifestation. (Niśvāsakārikā 4.12–16).
Now, he makes a formal declaration to explain the meaning of the Great Principle (*mahātattvārtha*), which follows in due order:
"O Goddess, I shall tell you that which is called the 'meaning of the Great Principle'."
This is clear. || 73 ||
He speaks precisely of the meaning of the Great Reality (mahātattva):
"In that which is partless, supreme, subtle, beyond characteristics, and devoid of objective existence. (2.73)
The union with one's own self—that supreme reality which transcends the void, whose form is light and bliss, which is beyond the universe yet consists of the universe—[is the goal]. (2.74)

In that which is partless and without limbs—*kalā* meaning limbs; in the supreme, greater even than the great; in the subtle, subtler even than the atom; in the unobservable, beyond the range of the sense organs and other instruments; in that which is devoid of objective existence (*bhāva-varjita*), yet as stated in the *Cidgaganacandrikā* ("That which is said to be observable is beyond thought-constructs, tradition, and the senses," verse 13), it is accessible through contemplation (*bhāvanā-gamya*); in that which transcends space, the space itself.

The previously mentioned definition (2/71) applies to that which transcends [all categories]: in the supreme reality (*para-tattva*), which transcends all *tattvas* and is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It is whose form (*vigraha*) consists of light (*prakāśa*) and bliss (*ānanda*); light is the unsurpassed light of lights, and bliss is the supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) which is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of all worldly pleasures. That which has these two—light and bliss—as its form.

In Him—transcending the universe, yet transcending all that is liberated from the universe; consisting of the universe, whose nature is space, time, and objects—I take refuge in that digit of pure consciousness which shines in whatever form and in whatever manner each and every object appears. (Saubhāgyahṛdaya 4)

Thus, according to the manner of the words spoken by authoritative sources, the "joining" (*yojanam*)— that is, the entry into oneness— with one's own Self, which appears as this or that [limited] self, yet is in reality the Supreme Śiva who bestows the supreme knowledge of the ultimate meaning of the Upaniṣadic statement *tattvam asi* (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), and whose stainless nature has been awakened by one's own Guru— this is the true meaning of the Great Reality (*mahātattvārtha*).
This is the meaning. || 2/73–74 ||
Now, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is such a nature of one's own self-reality (*svātmatattva*) determined? To this he says:
"At that time, luminosity belongs to both lights and darkness;
therefore, the universe is everywhere of the nature of inseparable concomitance. (2.75)

When Śiva vibrates within the minds of all living beings, then— according to the method stated in other systems (*tantrāntara*) as "the self is conjoined with the mind, the mind with the sense organ, and the sense organ with the object" (*Nyāya-bhāṣya* 1.1.4)—

there occurs the manifestation even of insentient things, such as light from the sun and so forth, and darkness from jars and so forth. [This occurs] when [Śiva] is in the *citta*, which is the conscious self (*cidātman*).
Only when Paramaśiva first flashes forth does the flashing forth of various objects occur through the respective doors of the senses.

On this point, the Śruti says: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15). Therefore, for the entire universe characterized as described [in verse 1.41], there exists a state of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

"Non-existence without [something else] is *avinābhāva* (inseparable concomitance). What is the meaning? This entire universe has a cognition that is dependent upon a seer (*draṣṭṛ*), because it is an object of sight (*dṛśyatva*).
Whatever is an object of sight has a cognition dependent upon a seer, just like the commonly accepted pot.
That which does not have a cognition dependent upon a seer is not even an object of sight, just like a rabbit's horn."

The meaning is that this is determined by the means of valid cognition known as inference, which is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), as indicated by the phrase "and so forth. (2.75)

Alternatively, enough with this deliberation on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for even the means of valid cognition possess the status of being valid only through the penetration of consciousness (*cit*).
Therefore, their very nature is also sufficient to establish the existence of this [consciousness], because it is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*). Thus he says:
"The Great Reality shines forth, radiant with the savor of divine play."

The Great Reality (*mahātattva*), which is not delimited by space, time, or form, shines by itself; without it, nothing whatsoever is capable of shining, because everything shines everywhere only through its own light. Regarding this, there are the Śruti and Smṛti: "By its light all this shines" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15), and "The sun does not illuminate it... (Gītā 15.6).

And it is said: "The moon, not fire" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.6). There is also the statement of those who are proficient: "For those whose minds are entirely absorbed in focused attention, the intellect itself is the witness here;
what is the use of those wretched means of knowledge that are themselves animated by consciousness?"

"For the light of the sun does not depend upon the illumination of a lamp" (Pañcāvaraṇastava 11–12). [This is] an address to the Goddess (*devyāḥ saṃbuddhiḥ*). "Divine" (*divya*) refers to Paramaśiva, who exists in heaven (*divi*);

his "play" (*krīḍā*) is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) whose nature consists of the activity of worldly transactions such as the creation of the universe; their "essence" (*rasa*) is their state of aesthetic relish or identity (*sāmarasya*); [the Goddess is] radiant (*ujjvale*) by means of that.
The meaning is: O Goddess, who are eternally perceived as being devoted to the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti. (2.76)

Now, one might ask: "Is the fruit of the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Reality (mahātattva) a cognition that occurs in another body, in another place, or at another time, like the fruits of rituals such as sacrifices? He says, "No"—it is preceded by a state in which all conceptual constructions and mental fluctuations have been eliminated. (2.76)
The secret meaning is greatly concealed and produces immediate conviction.

*Saṃkalpa* is mental action consisting of the thought, "I shall do this"; *vikalpa* is the cognition that relies on two alternatives, such as whether "this should be done by me" or "it should not. However, in the state of Śiva’s absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), both of these are discarded.

From the mere thorough knowledge of that, through the very rejection of both [duality], stability and steadiness of mind arise. Preceded by that, the secret meaning does not become fit for hearing. For this very reason, it is "greatly guarded" (mahāgupta), not told to anyone, and protected with extreme effort. It produces immediate conviction; by hearing this, the conviction arises: "I am Śiva."
The meaning is that it arises immediately. || 2/76-77 ||
"But where does this matter reside? Or where have you seen it? What, moreover, is its fruit? To this he says:
"It is seen in the great ocean of knowledge; O Pārvatī, there is no doubt in that regard. (2.77)
Established in the *vidyāpīṭha-nibandhas*, [the Lord] bestows divine perfection.

"Vidyāpīṭha" means that the *vidyā* itself is the seat (*pīṭha*), because it is the place of rest for Śiva and Śivā. Those [texts] in which this is composed, or those which constitute its limbs—the seed-syllables (*bījas*) known as Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti—in them [He resides].
In the *Vidyāpīṭhanibandha*, according to the method stated in the passage "in Akula and that which is known as Viṣu" (1.25),

when one contemplates [the reality] through the sequence of the Bindu, Half-moon, Rodhinī, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpikā, Samanā, and Unmanā situated at the peak of the three seeds, [one realizes] the supreme reality which is not delimited by space, time, or the state of Unmanā.
The meaning is that the reality of the great principle consisting of consciousness (cidātmaka-mahātattva) is established. As it is stated in the Svacchandasaṃgraha:
"That which is this power of Samanā, above that is Unmanā known [to exist].
Here there is no division of time, no category of existence (tattva), and no deity."
That which is well-extinguished, supreme, and pure is called the face of Rudra;
it is renowned as the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti), free from conceptual construction and untainted.
O lady of excellent hips, it transcends reality, lies beyond the sphere of speech and mind,
is partless and yet not composed of parts, formless, and free from conceptual construction.
"The supreme reality free from duality, the highest state called Śiva.

Thus [it is said]. "The bestower of divine perfection" (*divyasiddhida*): He is "divine" (*divya*) because he exists in the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*), which is the end of the *unmanī* state and in which the entire phenomenal world has been cast out;
this refers to the aforementioned Supreme Śiva (2/76). His "perfection" (*siddhi*) is the thorough realization of him as non-different from oneself; its characteristic is as follows:
He is called "the bestower of divine accomplishments" because he grants the supreme goal; this is seen in the *Mahājñānārṇava*.

Such a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in the state of identity (*sāmarasya*) with Supreme Śiva is itself "great knowledge" (*mahājñāna*), and that alone is the "ocean" (*arṇava*), because it is filled with the supreme nectar that constitutes the waveless expanse of the beyond. It is in that [ocean] that he is seen.

It is cultivated through the contemplation of one's own self as "I. What is the meaning? This supreme Great Reality (mahātattvārtha), characterized by the attainment of the Supreme Śiva, which abides on the ground at the conclusion of Unmanī at the peak of the three seed-syllables of the Saubhāgyavidyā, has been [described] by me as bestowing such a fruit.

The meaning is that [He] is constantly perceived during the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). "O Pārvatī, there is no doubt in that" means you should not entertain any doubt regarding that. Since I am your trustworthy authority (*āpta*), seeing things as they truly are and speaking of the objects exactly as they have been seen, you should place your confidence even in the matter I have spoken. || 2/77-78 ||
Now, it has been stated that this great reality-meaning is "greatly secret"; if so, by what kind of people is it attained? To this he says:
"O Goddess, by those devoted to the Kaula conduct and intent upon the meditation on the Pādukā. (2.78)
By those intent on the union with the Yoginīs, who have received the divine consecration, who are free from the stain of doubt, and whose minds are always joyful; (2.79)

Those for whom the Kula and the body are to be known as being obtained through tradition by those who are experts in the secret meaning— because they serve as the cause for a great purpose— are the Kaulas. As it has been said:
In the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Now I shall explain the knowledge of the Kula for the benefit of the Kaulikas;
by the mere realization of which, the means of yoga [are attained] by yogins."
O beloved, when well-guarded, all the *siddhis* become easily attainable.
It is said that the body is the *kula*... [and so forth].
Listen now to the conduct common to all initiated disciples within the lineage, regardless of their particular state.

Devotion to the Guru, tranquility, worship, faith, forbearance, and fortitude—according to the method stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*, those devoted to the conduct of the *samaya* and intent on the contemplation of the *pādukā* [should realize]:
"The form of Śiva as self-luminous is one, and the body of its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is one; of these two..."
"The Supreme Pādukā is held to be the embodiment of *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium) belonging to the Guru, whose self is Paraśiva" (Cidgaganacandrikā 1).

According to this method stated by us, those who are intent on the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the three Śrī-guru-pādukās as the triad of *prakāśa*, *vimarśa*, and their synthesis; who are engaged in the *melana* (union) with the Yoginīs; [and]...
Wherever the rays of light converge, there the All-pervading Lord alone unfolds Himself.
For the virtuous, this is indeed the foundation of their discipline; meditation, worship, and discourses are but mere imitations.

Thus, according to the manner stated in the words of authoritative teachers, the *yoginīs* are the cognitions of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; their "union" (*melana*) is the resting in the supreme subject through inward-turning. Alternatively, the "union of the *yoginīs*" is the gathering of the circle of conventional powers (*sāmayika-śakticakra*) for the purpose of worshipping the eight [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī; [this union is performed] by those intent upon it who have received divine consecration.

Then, by means of the sprinkling of water from a jar consisting of the essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*), consecrated by the excellent Guru—who is himself one with the supreme Śiva—their bonds consisting of impurity (*mala*) were washed away;
for this very reason, they were freed from the stain of doubt (*śaṅkā-kalaṅka*).

Doubt is the lack of certainty regarding knowledge, such as "this might be so" or "this might not be so"; that itself is the stain because it is the cause of defilement (*mālinya*); [they were] freed from that.
Therefore, by those whose minds are always joyful— the meaning being that just as the true nature of the sun shines forth when the veil of clouds has vanished,
so too does the supreme Śiva-nature, characterized by bliss, manifest eternally in their minds once the bonds of impurity have been removed—
it is attained by those who are experts in the secret meaning known through the lineage.

The meaning is that this great reality is attained by those whose intellects are most proficient in investigating the entire range of secret meanings received through the sequential lineage of gurus, beginning with Śiva and ending with one's own teacher. Regarding the statement "by those devoted to the Kaula conduct" and so forth, he speaks with an oath that this meaning is not attained by those devoid of the aforementioned qualities.
O Goddess, O beautiful one of noble lineage, I do not swear this against you otherwise.
This is clear. || 2/80 ||

Now, one might object: "Let there be no succession of the lineage of gurus; even by means of the power of proficiency gained through reading books and the like, some degree of thorough knowledge can be achieved.
To this he says: "Those who are devoid of the lineage and are arrogant merely on account of their knowledge..."
Through the violation of their commitments, these mirages undergo transformations.

Otherwise, for that practitioner, accomplishment does not occur through mere knowledge—that is, through knowledge produced merely by reading books—apart from the Kaula practice. This refers to those who, being devoid of the oral lineage (*pāramparya*), are arrogant on account of a mere partial understanding gained through the power of etymological analysis; because of their violation of the *samaya*, [the following occurs]: "Mādana" is the Śakti below that. (Ni.)

The rays of consciousness, which reside in all sacred seats (pīṭhas) and pervade everything, undergo transformation by omitting the sequence of pronunciation and so forth, due to a lack of thorough knowledge of the conventions of all the syllables of mantra prescribed in the scriptures such as the *Ṣoḍaśikā* (Ṣo. 1/111).
May the Bhairavīs, whose forms are full and complete, protect the mothers of the Kula.

Thus, according to the manner stated in the words of authoritative sources, the goddesses of the *dhātus* (constituent elements) such as Brāhmī and the others, as well as Ḍākinī and the others, "undergo transformation" (*vikurvanti*), meaning they produce a modification; by generating a modification in the form of an increase in their respective *dhātus*, they destroy their [the practitioners'] body—this is the meaning. (2.81) 2.
Now, one might ask: on which day, under which lunar mansion, or on which day of the week should the gathering of Yoginīs be performed according to the Kaula tradition? To this, he says:
"He whose contemplation rejoices in the tasting of the divine essence..."
On the day of the deity, the guest-star, the lunar mansion, and also on the day of the Sun. || 2.82 ||
Reeling with the bliss of wine, he indeed delights the rays [of consciousness];
and especially at all times,
the yogi who is devoted to the Kaula practice, whose reflective awareness rejoices in the tasting of the divine essence, [does so] in heaven, that is, in the supreme void.
He is the divine Supreme Śiva; by him, "rasa" means the state of aesthetic relish (*sāmarasya*); its "tasting" is the direct experience (*anubhava*).

He is one whose mental activity is the act of reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) rejoicing through that [experience]. First, he is solely the unartificial bliss flashing forth from the contemplation of identity with Supreme Śiva; subsequently, he is reeling with the intoxication of the bliss of wine.

Having performed the purification of the *arghya* as will be described [in verses 3.98–103], the yogi, having attained bliss through the wine that has become supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*), [should worship] the deity, the guest, and the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). The fourteenth and eighth lunar days are the "deity-guests," and the Puṣya asterism is the "deity-asterism. On this very point, he will state later:
O Supreme Goddess, on a Wednesday and on a Saturday, during the Puṣya asterism.

"On the Guru’s day, on one's own natal asterism, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, one should especially perform the worship of the Cakra and the Yoginīs" (3/191–192). Thus, [the practitioner] surely pleases the Marīcis. The word "eva" (surely/only) serves to exclude non-conjunction; [it means that one should do so] at all times during the aforementioned periods.

One should perform that which pleases the Yoginī; otherwise, there will be an obstacle (pratyavāya)—this is the meaning. The mention of a specific time is for the purpose of indicating a special occasional worship (naimittika-pūjā) and so forth. One must indeed perform the pleasing of Marīci at all times and every day; this is the connection with the word "indeed" (eva). The intended sense is that there is an obstacle in failing to perform the daily worship (nityārcanā); regarding the daily worship:

Because, according to the method stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*—"When the teaching has been lost, one should gradually perform the concealment"—the performance of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is mandatory. (2/82–83)
He states that non-performance results in transgression, whereas performance yields a fruit:
"One attains full awakening" (2.83).
Wherein Svātmaśambhu, characterized by objectless consciousness, abides "constantly" (Ci.
10)—the meaning is that, according to the method we have described, he attains the state of Svātmaśambhu, whose nature is unobscured consciousness. || 2/83 ||
Now, one might ask: by whom, in what time, and through what means is the state of perfect awakening attained? To this he says:
"O Goddess of gods, such a state, consisting of great knowledge, O Goddess, is attained immediately by men through the grace of the supreme teacher. (2.84)
Such a state is the condition of full enlightenment. By the grace of the Supreme Teacher—
He who is the Supreme Śiva, the solitary Lord, by whose mere casting of a compassionate glance the net of bonds is severed—
by His grace [this state is attained].
"By his grace,
which consists here in the purification of the principles (*tattva-śodhana*), the fortunate seeker attains joy" (Cidgaganacandrikā 31)—
according to this method stated by us, through the seizing of his feet [one attains this]. He is composed of great knowledge and is the unobscured, pure consciousness (*cinmaya*).

By men distinguished by the aforementioned qualifications, such as "those devoted to the Kaula conduct" (2/78), [the goal] is attained immediately—at the very moment of obtaining the grace of the supreme Guru. (2/84)

He concludes the secret convention of the mantras: "Thus, O Goddess, this knowledge which bestows [liberation], the domain of the arrival of the syllables of the Vidyā, has been explained as a dear secret; O Durgā, it is sixfold."
By the immediate awakening to which one becomes the Lord of the Circle of Heroes (vīracakreśvara)—

in the manner thus described— this is the knowledge that bestows this [state], namely, the supreme reality of Śiva characterized by perfect awakening. It is the domain of the "letters of Vidyā" (vidyārṇa), where the "letters" (arṇāḥ) of Vidyā are the fifteen phonemes, and these themselves are the "scriptures" (āgama).

Because it makes known the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*), its scope has been explained as having that as its object through the network of verses beginning with "He who knows this becomes the Lord of the *Vīracakra*, whose form is Tripurā" (2/1) and ending with "Thus it bestows this" (2/85). O Goddess, it is of six kinds, as established by the passage beginning with "The meaning of the underlying intention (*bhāvārtha*), the meaning of the tradition (*sampradāyārtha*)" (2/15), which sets forth the six modes. O Goddess...

O Durgā, O Durgā, whose nature is unattainable by those devoid of the glance of the supreme Lord of Teachers, You who consist of the state of equilibrium between light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). By whose immediate awakening— through the awakening of the sixfold object—

one becomes the Lord of the Circle of Heroes (*vīracakreśvara*), [I am] the "I" in the battle against the enemy that is "this-ness" (*idantā*), intent upon bringing about dissolution upon the field of combat.
O heroes, their *cakra* is the assembly; its Lord is Paraśiva.
The meaning is that at the very moment of realizing the sixfold reality previously mentioned, one becomes Paraśiva. (2.85)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Convention of Mantras," in the *Yoginīhṛdayadīpikā* composed by the eminent yogi Amṛtānanda, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Puṇyānanda.
The third chapter is "The Convention of Worship."
Now, he promises to explain the convention of worship that follows in sequence:
"O sinless one, I shall now tell you the convention of worship clearly."
He states the fruit [of this work] so that people may be motivated to listen: "By the mere awakening to which, one who is liberated while living rejoices. (3/1)

By the mere awakening—that is, by the simple thorough knowledge—of this *pūjā-saṃketa* (the convention of worship), which possesses the threefold divisions to be described beginning with *parā*, one becomes liberated while still living (*jīvanmukta*). Possessing the realization "I am Śiva," one rejoices; for the very thought of the identity of the supreme Śiva and the self (*ahantā*) is the cause of that joy. (3.1)
He begins the section on the secret convention of worship:

"Your eternally arisen worship is established through three divisions. [This refers to] my own nature as Light, and yours as the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), whose form is that very reflection. Your worship is eternally arisen; it is perpetual.
The worship performed daily at sunrise is established through three distinct divisions.
He states the names of the worship:
"Parā, Arā, O Gaurī, and the third is Parāparā. (3.2)

The first worship is called the supreme and most excellent. Its excellence over other forms of worship lies in its capacity to bring about the manifestation of the non-duality of Paramaśiva. As it is stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*:
"That worship which is not performed constantly with external substances such as flowers..."
"In one's own great, non-dual abode, that worship is the supreme state. Thus it is said.
The other, secondary worship—which consists of the external adoration of wheels (*cakra*) and enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), whose essence is merely the manifestation of duality—is inferior;
for it has been stated previously: "That worship which is performed incessantly with external substances such as flowers is not [true] worship."

The third worship is the Parāparā; it consists of the contemplation of the absorption of consciousness (cillaya) within the non-dual inner abode of the external [deity], and is thus the Madhyamā, because its nature is both Parā and Aparā. || 3/2 ||
He states their characteristics in sequence: "The first is the state of non-duality, the sphere of all outward expansion.
'The self is conjoined with the mind; the mind with the sense organ; the sense organ with the object' (Nyāya-bhāṣya 1.1.4)."
In accordance with the sequence previously stated (2/2–4), they have become the objects of the expansions—that is, the activities—of all the sense organs. What is the meaning?
Wherever the mind goes, whether externally or internally toward what is dear;
In each and every case, the supreme state, being all-pervasive, where could it go?

(Śloka 113) Wherever the consciousness of the Lord is manifested through the path of the senses, because that [consciousness] has that very [sensation] as its sole substrate, the intellect becomes full through absorption into Cit. (Śloka 114)

Thus, according to the method stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava, the meaning is that the manifestation of non-duality, characterized by the dissolution of the external world into consciousness, is the supreme worship (parā pūjā).
And the second, the worship of the wheel, is always performed by me. (3.3)

The second is the *cakrapūjā*, which is the "other worship" (*aparā pūjā*); the meaning is that the "other worship" consists of the worship of the deities of the enclosures within the abode of the *śrīcakra*, beginning with the square and ending with the bindu. It is performed by me always—that is, every day—even by me, the omniscient one; it is performed because it brings about the realization of non-duality. The other worship is for the sake of the realization of non-duality.

The meaning is that this must be practiced by all who possess knowledge. Otherwise, there would be a negation of non-duality (*advaita*) regarding something that was never even suggested; and that is not appropriate. As it has been said in another Tantra:
"Whatever has acquired a form somewhere is negated only as being exactly like that [form]."
"Therefore, without a positive injunction, a prohibition is not possible.
(Brahmasiddhi 2.2) He speaks of the worship of the higher and lower [forms]:
"O Goddess, in this way, the third [form] consists of self-manifestation within that which is composed of knowledge."

Thus, within the abode consisting of knowledge— which is composed of the previously mentioned contemplation of non-duality— the resting of ritual action (karma) within the state of being composed of knowledge is the third, intermediate (*parāpara*) worship, which consists of the self-manifestation of that which is external and characterized by the veil of a separate nature. As it has been said by the learned:

"I cast the expansions of conceptual thought and the like into the abode that is a single mass of light, through the act of worship, just as offerings of clarified butter are cast into a fire. Thus [it is said].
He states the procedure for worship:
That is to be known as the supreme and highest; now listen to the procedure.

That is the supreme worship (*parā-pūjā*). By stating that supreme worship is the highest, it is implied that the other two—the lower (*aparā*) and the intermediate (*parāpara*)—are respectively inferior and middling. It should be known that this [supreme worship] is to be practiced according to knowledge (*jñāna*). The lower worship will be explained later. Because this [supreme worship] is to be known (*jñeya*), it is "supreme" (*parā*); for this very reason, it is the "highest" (*uttamā*).
This is the meaning. Now, listen to the procedure for the worship of that which is to be known. (3.4)
He explains the very procedure:
"Within the Mahāpadma forest, [one should meditate upon] the Guru’s sandals in the Vāgbhava [syllable], which nourish the form of the universe and shower forth the supreme nectar. (3/5)

Having reflected upon the Great Lotus Grove (*mahāpadmavana*), which consists of a thousand white petals with their faces turned downward from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), it is like a forest because of its density of lotus petals; as it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
As far as the upward-tending lotus with a thousand spokes and downward-facing mouth,
it is white, containing the partless power (niṣkalā-śakti) at its center and possessing innumerable powers.
Pervasive, absolute, and eternally raining down floods of nectar is Samanā,
situated above that Great Lotus Forest.
"Within that, in the center of the pericarp, she resides in the form of Vāgbhava.

According to the method previously stated (2.69), the triangle is called *vāgbhava* because from it arise the [four] aspects of speech: Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī. In that [triangle], one should place the Guru’s sandals.
Salutations to the Guru, Śiva, who has made the three worlds his own and proclaims his own true nature, appearing in the form of both the means and the goal.
In accordance with the manner stated in the words of the learned, the *pādukā* of Paramaśiva, the Teacher of the Universe, is as follows:

"The single form of Śiva as self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśa*), and the single body of its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—the supreme *pādukā* is held to be their state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*), belonging to the Guru who is the very self of Paraśiva. (Cidgaganacandrikā 1)

Thus, according to the method we have described, one should contemplate her as possessing three aspects: as she whose form nourishes the world by spreading forth the intense cooling of her own rays, thereby refreshing all that is moving and unmoving; and as she who showers the supreme nectar, raining down a continuous and dense stream of the essence of consciousness. Having contemplated her thus, one should realize her as being one's own self. (3/5-6)
Immediately after the contemplation (*parāmarśa*) of the Guru’s sandals, he speaks of the acceptance of grace:
"Reeling with the intoxication of the contemplation of supreme non-duality.
"Supreme" refers to Paramaśiva; by him, "contemplation of non-duality" consists of the form of immersion (*samāveśa*), namely, "I am He alone."

That very state is called *mada* (intoxication), because it is the cause of intoxication. Reeling with the intoxication produced by that, and being gladdened, the Guru—who is Śiva himself whose nature is self-luminous—becomes gracious toward the summit of all categories (*padārtha*).
Having obtained His grace here, which is the purification of the principles (*tattva*), the fortunate seeker attains joy. (Cidgaganacandrikā 31)

Thus, according to the method we have explained, the meaning is that he is overwhelmed by supreme bliss, which shines forth through the acceptance of the grace of the Guru characterized by the contemplation of the non-duality of Paramaśiva. || 3/6 ||
Immediately after accepting [the disciple's] devotion, he speaks of the internal recitation (japa) itself: "Intent on beholding the Nāda as it spreads within the small space (dahara). (3.6)

"Turning away from discursive thought and verbalization, [one sees] the small, stainless lotus of the heart, which is the dwelling place of the Supreme, situated in the center of the city"—so says the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* (8.16);
and also by the Śruti: "Within this is the small ether" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.1.1).

The space situated in the center of the heart-lotus is called *dahara* (the small). It is "small" (*dahara*) as it were. Moving within that is the *nāda* (the primordial sound); thus, it is "moving within the *dahara*" (*daharāntarasaṃsarpannāda*). One who is intent upon its contemplation—that is, its visualization—is "intent upon that" (*tatpara*). As it has been said by the learned:
"O Sovereign, Your form, characterized by bliss, has transformed into the nature of *nāda* within the region known as the *anāhata*;
the blessed ones declare that this is being perceived by the mind through every limb, face, and so forth, accompanied by tears from the eyes and horripilation.
Thus, having restrained the movement of the senses, one should intensely utter the internal *nāda*.
This alone is declared to be true recitation; external recitation is not recitation at all.

In accordance with the method stated in the words of the learned masters, one should perform the internal recitation (*japa*) characterized by the contemplation of the *nāda*, and not the external recitation characterized by the utterance of various sounds. One should be turned away from the discursive chatter (*saṃjalpa*) consisting of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
"Conceptual constructions" refers to the various forms of syllables; "chatter" is their utterance.
One who is turned away from external recitation characterized by [fixation on] the tall [form].
As it has been said by the venerable Vijñānabhairava: "That meditation which is cultivated again and again upon the supreme reality..."
For one who recites, the internal resonance itself, whose nature is mantra—such is this recitation. (Verse 152) 3/6–7
He says that one should practice meditation in exactly that same way: "Always inward-turned;
with the contraction shattered by the surge of the power of consciousness, it is exceedingly beautiful. (3.7)
In this context, according to the method stated in the Yogaśāstra— "Meditation (*dhyāna*) is the one-pointed continuity of mental impressions" (Yoga Sūtra 3.2)—

the meaning is that, by means of meditation characterized as a stream of homogeneous mental impressions uninterrupted by heterogeneous ones, one should become inward-turned— constantly indicated by the internal sound— and devoted to the contemplation of the non-duality of Paramaśiva.
This has been stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava:
"Meditation is that thought which is partless, formless, and without support;
meditation is not the mental construction of the body's features such as the face and hands" (verse 143).

"Because the contraction [of the limited self] has been shattered by the unfolding of the supreme *citkalā*, one is exceedingly beautiful. According to our stated method, this refers to the state of the imagined, perfect *ahaṃbhāva* (I-consciousness), which has dispelled the distress of contraction through the great wave of the ocean of consciousness; for this very reason, one is "exceedingly beautiful" (*atisundara*).
This is the supreme [state], the locus of the unfolding of the supreme *citkalā* known by the name Mahātripurasundarī.
The meaning is that he is non-different from Supreme Śiva, who is the object of beautiful and supreme love. || 3/7 ||
He says that one should perform worship in this very same manner: "Having performed self-worship with substances that gratify the senses.
The senses are hearing and so forth; the substances that gratify them are specific sounds, touches, and so on.
Possessing form, taste, and smell, he is one by whom the worship of his own self-deity has been performed through those [senses].
This is stated in the *Mukhyāmnāyarahasyavidhi*:
"The self-deity [is worshipped] with scents and other objects perceivable through the doors of the senses."
"This great sacrifice is to be accomplished by the knower through its own inherent nature.

(Śloka 70) "By the expansion of the bliss of aesthetic flavor arising from the exhilaration produced by eating and drinking, one should contemplate the state of fullness; from that, Great Bliss shall arise. (Śloka 71)

Thus, according to the method stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava, the meaning is that the unification in a state of equal flavor (*samarasīkaraṇa*) with the Great Bliss (*mahānanda*) of the joys produced by the experience of objects such as sound through the sense organs, beginning with the ear, is the supreme worship (*parā pūjā*).
Now, in order to explain another form of worship, he describes the external placement (*bāhyanyāsa*) which serves as its constituent part:
"One should perform the placement upon the body, preceded by the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*). (3.8)

The sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) was indicated in the initial aphorism beginning with "O Gaṇeśa" (*Ni. Ṣo. 1/1*). It is performed on the body—of which "one's own" is the understood subject. "Sixfold" means consisting of six modes. (3/8)
He states the enumeration of its types:
"The first arrangement is by the lords of the ganas (gaṇeśas); the second is considered to be by the planets (grahas);
the third is by the lunar mansions (nakṣatras); and the fourth is by the yoginīs. (3.9)

The fifth assignment (*nyāsa*) is by means of the *rāśis* (zodiac signs), and the sixth is said to be by means of the *pīṭhas*. This is easy to understand. "Nyāsam" refers to the collection of assignments; the singular number is used because it denotes a class (*jātāvekavacanam*). The word "should perform" (*nirvartayet*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 3/9-10 || The sixfold (*ṣoḍhā*) is a single assignment of six types; its method, the greatness of the sixfold assignment, and its fruit [are as follows].
And he said:
"This sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa) has been proclaimed as invincible everywhere. (3.10)
Thus, he who has renounced his body is to be honored by all yogis;
for him, there is no one in the worlds worthy of worship, not even his father, mother, or other elders. (3.11)
He alone is worthy of worship by all; he is himself the Supreme Lord.
O Pārvatī, whoever bows down to one who is devoid of the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), [he incurs sin]. 3/12.
He meets death before long and falls into hell.

This sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhā-nyāsa*) has been declared; it is invincible and its power is unimpeded everywhere, even in all the worlds, for one who has thus placed the limbs upon his body according to the sequence to be described.

By virtue of the power of the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), he is himself the Supreme Lord because his bonds have been severed. For this very reason, among the worlds and among people, he alone is to be worshipped by yogis. What need is there for more? He is the worshipful one of all; there is no one at all in the world who is his worshipful object.
If he were to prostrate before another by force, that other would die and go to hell—this is the meaning.
He promises to explain the method of the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa):
"O sinless one, I shall tell you the method of the sixfold deposition. (3/13)
This is clear. 3/13
He states the various forms of that [deity]:
Vighneśa, Vighnarāja, Vināyaka, Śivottama, Vighnakṛt, Vighnahartā, Gaṇarāj, and Gaṇanāyaka. (3.14)
He who has one tusk and two tusks, the elephant-faced one, the stainless one;
he who wears matted hair, the long-faced one, the spike-eared one, and the bull-bannered one. (3.15)
Gaṇanātha, Gajendra, Śūrpakarṇa, Trilocana, Lambodara, Mahānāda, Caturmūrti, and Sadāśiva. (3/16)
Āmoda, Durmukha, Sumukha, and Pramodaka;
Ekapāda, Dvijihva, Śūra, Vīra, and Ṣaṇmukha. (3.17)
The Bestower of Boons, Vāmadeva, Vakratuṇḍa, Dvituṇḍaka, Senānī, Grāmaṇī, Matta, Vimatta, and Mattavāhana. (3.18)
Jaṭī, Muṇḍī, Khaḍgī, Vareṇya, Vṛṣaketana, Bhakṣyapriya, Gaṇeśa, Meghanāda, and Gaṇeśvara. (3.19)
[In another work—
] These are the fifty-one syllables of Gaṇeśa in their proper order:
Śrī, Hrī, Tuṣṭi, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Sarasvatī.
Ramā, Meghā, Kānti, Kāminī, Mohinī, Balā, Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Surasā, and Kāmarūpiṇī.
Ugrā, Jayinī, Satyā, Vighneśānī, Surūpiṇī, Kāmadā, Madajihvā, Vikaṭā, and Ghūrṇitānanā.
Bhūti, Bhūmi, Satī, Ramyā, Mānuṣī, Makaradhvajā, Vikarṇā,
Bhrūkuṭī, Lajjā, Dīrghaghoṇā, and Dhanurdharā.
Likewise, *yāminī* means night; *candrakāntā* means moonlight;
*lolākṣī* means a fickle-eyed woman; *capalā* means lightning; *ṛddhi* means prosperity; *durbhagā* means unfortunate; *subhagā* means fortunate; and *śivā* means a female jackal.
Durgā, Guhapriyā, Kālī, and Lalajjihvā are the Śaktis;
these names need not be explained here. (3.14–19)
He describes their meditative visualization:

resembling the young morning sun, with elephant faces and three eyes, holding in their hands the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and endowed with spears. (3.20)

Resembling the young morning sun, having the complexion of the young morning sun; those whose faces are like the face of an elephant are "Gajavaktras" (Elephant-faced ones)—[one should visualize them] holding a noose and a goad in their upper hands, and the gestures of boon-granting (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*) in their lower hands, accompanied by Puṣṭi and the others. Since the names indicated here are also mentioned in the ritual manuals (*paddhati*) of other Āgamas, [they need not be further elaborated].
He states the places of placement: "O Dear One, one should place these upon the body just like the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
"These" refers to the Gaṇeśas. "Just like the Mātṛkā-nyāsa" means that they should be placed in the same locations as the *vaikharī* (manifest) Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
He states the placement of the *graha*s:
"One should place the Sun, accompanied by the vowels, below the heart. (3.21)

O Dear One, one should place the source of nectar (the letter *ya*) in the location of the Bindu, the son of the Earth (the letter *ra*) in the two eyes, and the lord of the *ka*-group (the letter *kha*) in the [two] ears. (3.22)
One should again place Śukra, the lord of the *ca*-group, in the heart;
one should place Budha, the lord of the *ṭa*-group, above the heart. (3.23)
O beloved, Bṛhaspati, the lord of the ta-series, is in the region of the throat;
and O Sovereign of the Gods, Śanaiścara, the lord of the pa-series, is in the navel.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should place Rāhu together with the four letters beginning with Śa in the mouth, and Ketu together with the letter Kṣa in the anus.

Accompanied by the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the visarga, one should place [the letter] at the beginning of the name, below the *Sūryahṛdaya*. At the location of the *bindu*, on the forehead; as it is stated right here: "The shape of a lamp, consisting of half a measure, is desired as a circle on the forehead" (1.28), and so forth. [One should place] the moon, the source of nectar, with the four letters beginning with *ya*.

The meaning is that one should place [the letters] with the four *yaralava*s. *Bhūputra* is Aṅgāraka (Mars). One should place the presiding lord situated above the *ka*-group in the pair of eyes. In the heart—that is, on the chest—the rest is clear until the end: "O Goddess of Gods, one should place [it] in the anus."
He states the locations of the constellations and their ritual assignment (nyāsa):
"On the forehead, the right eye, the left [eye], and again on the two ears;
on the two nostrils, the nose, the throat, and again on the two shoulders. (3.26)
Thereafter, [one should place them] on the pair of elbows, likewise on the two wrists, on the breasts, at the region of the navel, and then on the waistband. (3.27)
Likewise, upon the pair of thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, and the two feet,
[there are goddesses] resembling the blazing fire of time (kālānala), with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should place these—Aśvinī and the [three] preceding ones—who possess beautiful hands and are adorned with all ornaments—in these respective positions. (3.29)

The term *kaṭibandha* refers to the two waistbands (*kaṭibandhayoḥ*), as it is intended as a copulative compound (*dvandva*); otherwise, the number twenty-seven would not be accounted for. The phrase "the two ears" refers to the right and left, because the sequence established in [verse 3.26], "the right eye and the left," has already been introduced. From the expression "hands granting boons and fearlessness" (*varadābhayapāṇayaḥ*) and "hands in the gesture of salutation" (*natipāṇayaḥ*), the possession of four arms is understood.
The remainder is easy to understand. || 3/26–29 ||
He describes the *nyāsa* of the Yoginīs:

"In the *viśuddhi*, the heart, the navel, the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and the root [cakra], as well as in the *ājñā*, the presiding deities of the elements—the goddesses beginning with *Ḍā*—are to be installed. (3.30)
O Goddess of the Suras, they should be properly meditated upon as being endowed with nectar and other [substances], at the feet, the linga, the belly, the heart, and the two armpits. (3.31)
In the purification [of the elements], there is the sixteen-petaled lotus at the root of the palate; the twelve-petaled lotus in the heart, the *anāhata*;

the ten-petaled lotus at the navel, the *maṇipūraka*; the six-petaled lotus in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*; the four-petaled lotus at the base (*mūla*); and the two-petaled lotus in the *ājñā*. The bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*) are skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, and semen.
Their protectors and mistresses are the deities beginning with *ḍa*: Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Sākinī, and Hākinī.
They are endowed with Amṛtā and the others as described in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*, as follows:
"Amṛtā is the first goddess; the second is considered to be Ākarṣiṇī."
Indrāṇī shall be the third, while Īśānī is the fourth.
The fifth should be the goddess Umā, and the sixth is indeed Urdhvakeśinī;
the seventh is declared to be Ṛddhidā, and the eighth is considered to be Ṛṣā.
The ninth is said to be *ḷ*, and likewise the tenth is *ḹṣ*.
O Śivā, the eleventh is *yathā* and the twelfth is *ekapādā*.
The thirteenth is Oṃkārī, who delights in sovereignty;
the fourteenth is Auṣadhātmā; and the fifteenth is Ambikā.
The goddess Ṣoḍaśī is said to have sixteen syllables; these sixteen are located in the throat.
Beyond that are Kālarātri, Khātītā, and Gāyatrī.
Ghaṇṭādhārī, she whose essence is the syllable Ṅa, Caṇḍā, Chāyā, and Jayā;
then Jhaṅkārī, who is the form of knowledge, and Ṭaṅkahastā.
One should worship these twelve on the twelve spokes:
Ṭhaṅkārī, Ḍāmarī, Ḍhaṅkārī, Ṇāminī, and likewise Tāmasī.
One should worship Thāntā, Dākṣāyaṇī, Dhātrī, Nandā, Pārvatī,
and Phaṭkārī on the ten petals, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
O Dear One, one should worship Bandhinī, Bhadrakālī, the illustrious Mahāmāyā, Raktā, and Lamboṣṭhikā in their proper sequence.
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, one should worship Varadā and Śrī on the four petals, and likewise Ṣaṇḍhā and Sarasvatī in due order.
One should worship Kṣamā and Haṃsavatī on two leaves;

endowed with these Śaktis, O Sovereign of the Gods, they should be meditated upon. (Thus) one should perform the Nyāsa. This is the internal Nyāsa. [The meditation: (3/8) Thus ends the internal Nyāsa. [Now] the meditation:
This is to be understood from another scriptural source. || 3/30–31 ||
He describes the placement of the zodiac signs (rāśinyāsa):
"O Pārvatī, beginning from the right foot and ending with the left foot, the zodiac signs starting with Aries are to be placed along with the phonemes. (3.32)
In the locations beginning with the feet, starting from the right and ending at the left, the zodiac signs— Aries, Taurus,
Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces—
are to be installed together with the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet. The letters corresponding to the zodiac signs are [found] in other Āgamas.
I shall state it according to the oral tradition: Aries is situated at the right foot with the first four syllables;
Taurus is at the right side of the *liṅga* with the three letters beginning with *u*.
The sign of Gemini is formed by the three letters beginning with *ṛ* in the right side of the belly;
the sign of Cancer is joined with *e* and *ai* on the right side of the chest.
The Lion is accompanied by O and Au at the base of the right arm;
Kanyā is on the right side of the head, accompanied by Aṃ, Aḥ, and the Śa-group of consonants.
The sign of Libra is on the head with the *ka*-group;
Scorpio is on the left armpit with the *ca*-group; and Sagittarius is on the heart with the *ṭa*-group.

On the left, the Makara is joined with the *tavarga*; on the left side of the belly is the Kumbha with the *pavarga*. Furthermore, on the region to the left of the linga is the Kumbha with the *pavarga*.
The class of *ya* joined with the letter *kṣa* is called *mīna*, located in the left foot. Thus [ends verse 3/32].
He describes the placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*): "O Goddess, one should again place the seats in the locations of the *mātṛkā*s.
The term "locations of the *mātṛkā*s" is used in the singular to denote the class; it means "in the locations of the phonemes of *vaikharī* speech. Now, [an objection]:
To the question "What are those seats?", he says:
"Their names are being told; listen attentively, O beloved. (3/33)
The meaning is: because the seats (*pīṭha*) and the names of the seats are so numerous that they cannot be fully enumerated, you must remain extremely attentive. (3/33)
He states their names: Kāmarūpa, Vārāṇasī, Nepāla, Pauṇḍravardhana, Purasthira, Kānyakubja, Pūrṇaśaila, and likewise Arbuda. (3.34)
Āmrātakeśvara, Ekāmra, Trisrotas, Kāmakoṭaka, Kailāsa, Bhṛgunagara, Kedāra, and Pūrṇacandraka. (3.35)
The Śrīpīṭha, Oṃkārapīṭha, Jālandhra, Mālava, Utkala, Kulānta, Devikoṭṭa, Gokarṇa, and Māruteśvara. (3.36)
Aṭṭahāsa, Viraja, Rājagṛha, Mahāpatha, Kolāpura, Melāpura, Kāleśa, and Jayantikā. (3/37)
Ujjayinī, Vicitra, Kṣīraka, Hastināpura, Oḍḍīśa, the one called Prayāga, and the sixth is Māyāpurī. (3.38)
