Jaleśa, the Malaya mountain, Meru, the best of mountains,
as well as Māhendra, Vāmana, and Hiraṇyapura.
Mahālakṣmī, Puruṣottama, and thereafter Chāyāchatra—these are declared to be the sacred seats (pīṭhas) that exist in the form of the Mother-letters (mātṛkā). 3/40.

These are declared to be the *pīṭhas*, the *pīṭhas* whose names have been taken up. "Having the form of the *mātṛkā*" means those whose form is the *mātṛkā*. The meaning is that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *pīṭhas* in their respective locations by uttering each letter from *a* to *kṣa* in sequence at the beginning of each [letter], [placing them] in the positions corresponding to those respective letters.
[The statement that the *pīṭhas* consist of the *mātṛkās* is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for Gaṇeśa and the others;

the meaning is that the letters of the *vaikharī* speech should be applied by dividing them at the beginning of each group of phonemes (*vargavarṇa*), in accordance with the testimony of other scriptures.]
Since the placement of the Śrīcakra necessarily follows the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), he now describes that placement of the Śrīcakra:
"Having first performed the sixfold placement in this manner, one should perform the placement of the Śrīcakra."
The meaning is that having first performed the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) in the manner thus described, one should subsequently perform the placement of the *śrīcakra*. || 3/41 ||

Because the installation of the Śrīcakra (śrīcakranyāsa) is of great purpose, he says: "O beloved, listen now to the installation of the wheels (cakranyāsa) of the venerable Tripurasundarī," even though it has not been told elsewhere. (3/41)
That which has not been told to anyone, which brings about supreme purity of the body,
and by means of which one wanders incessantly through the hamlet of sound, touch, and so forth for the sake of begging for a mere morsel of bliss— the wise know that to be poverty.

According to the manner stated in the words of the learned, that which destroys the poverty characterized by contraction and consists of the nature of perfect supreme bliss is called *Śrī* (Prosperity). Tripurasundarī is the possessor of that [prosperity]. She is *Tripurā* because her form is the fourth state (*turīya*), and she is *Sundarī* because she is the supreme [reality] synonymous with the dissolution of the phenomenal world characterized by duality.

She has ascended to the state of supreme non-dual auspiciousness (*paramādvaita-saubhāgya*), which is the obstacle to misfortune; she has become the object of supreme love for all living beings by virtue of being their very self (*ātmatayā*); she is a portion of the Supreme Consciousness (*paracit-kalā*). Her wheel (*cakra*) consists of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth.
O Dear One, hear now the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of that [wheel], which is the ground of its manifestation. To the Beloved.
I shall tell it to you, who are longing for the sake of Madaikara; for it has not been told to anyone else due to its extreme secrecy.
The meaning is: because the installation of the Śrīcakra (Śrīcakranyāsa) serves a great purpose, I tell it to you, my beloved, even though it has not been told to anyone else.
It is supreme for purifying the body—purifying the body which consists of the thirty-six principles (tattvas).

It brings about the characteristic of culminating in the knowledge of others' minds; for this very reason, it is supreme (*param*), being more excellent than other types of renunciation (*nyāsa*). (3/41–42)
He states the method for the placement (nyāsa) of the Śrīcakra:
"One should perform the placement starting with 'Obeisance to the first line of the square' (caturasrādyarekhāyai namaḥ)," and so forth. (3.42)
Then, on the right shoulder, the back, the tips of the hands, the buttocks, and the toes of the feet;
and on the toes of the left foot, the buttocks, the tip of the hand, and the shoulder and back. (3.43)

O beautiful one, with the mantra "Salutation to the square and other lines for pervasion," one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) at the ten locations— beginning from the back of the right shoulder and ending at the back of the crest (*cūlī*)— by way of pervasion across the back of the head, the crest, and the back [of the body]. Regarding the right shoulder:

The back is the posterior part. "Along with the root of the crest" (*sacūlīmūla*): the "root" (*mūla*) is the front part of the head; the "back" (*pṛṣṭha*) is the rear part of the head. The "sphig" is the same as "sphikka," which is the hip joint. The rest is clear. (3/42–44)
Regarding these locations where the Śaktis are to be placed, he says:
"In this very same set of ten locations, one should place the ten [powers] beginning with Aṇimā. (3.44)

The supernatural powers (siddhis) are known as atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), magnification (mahimā), lordship (īśitā), mastery (vaśitva), irresistible will (prākāmya), attainment of objects at will (bhuktīcchā), reaching anywhere (prāpti), and the fulfillment of all desires (sarvakāma);
these are the ten siddhis beginning with aṇimā. (3/44–45)
He describes the pervasive [mantra] on the middle line of the square:
"And within that, O beautiful one, by virtue of its subtle pervasiveness;
'Salutation to the middle line of the square,' O beloved," thus he says. (3.45)

The syntactical connection is as follows: one should place [the mantra] within that, in the inner region of the places of accomplishment (*siddhisthāna*), with the mantra "Salutation to the central line of the square," by means of a pervasive placement upon the body (*tanuvyāpakatvena*). (3/45–46)
Regarding the powers (śaktis) to be placed upon the central line of the square, he says:

"In its [the square's] locations, likewise in eight places, [one should place] Brahmāṇī and the others. "In its" means in the central line of that square. "In eight places" means in the eight locations. [One should place] Brahmāṇī and the others.
One should place Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī; such is the syntactical connection. (3.46)
He states their eight locations:
on the two big toes, on the right side, and on the other side of the head. (3.46)
And likewise on the left and right knees, as well as on the two shoulders outside;
this is clear. (3/46–47)
Regarding the pervasive [mantra] for the final line of the square, he says:
"The lines of the final square should also be placed with the words 'namaḥ'. (3/47)

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) by way of pervasion within the body, ending with what was previously mentioned, using the mantra: "Obeisance to the final line of the square. "Within the body" means in the internal locations of the previously mentioned sites, such as those of Brāhmī and the others; they are to be placed by way of pervasion in the interior regions suitable for placement.
One should place [them]. || 3/47-48 ||
Regarding the powers (śaktis) to be placed upon that final square line, he says:
"In its ten locations, one should place the ten mudrās. (3.48)
Upon the four outer lines of that [square], one should place the ten mudrās beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī, together with the Trikhaṇḍā mudrā, in ten locations. (3.48)
He states their locations:
"Then one should place eight of them within the eight locations beginning with Brahmāṇī;
the remaining two should be placed at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta) and on the big toe. (3.49)

Among those mudrās, one should place eight mudrās within the eight intermediate directions of the eight locations beginning with Brahmāṇī. One should place the remaining two mudrās at the dvādaśānta and on the big toe. The dvādaśānta is the location of the solar maṇḍala situated below the lunar maṇḍala at the ṣoḍaśānta; as it has been said:
In the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*: "That which is known as the 'End of the Sixteen' is the lunar orb situated in the station of space (*vyoma*).
Below that station is the solar disc, possessing twelve powers."
That which is known as the "twelve-finger limit" (dvādaśānta) is situated in the region of space;
by that [term], both the principle of the Bindu and the four-petalled lotus are designated.
"From a distance of one and a half finger-breadths below and above the solar disc"—

according to this method, the location of the solar mandala situated above the point (bindu) of the principle (tattva) located at the forehead is indicated by the term "the end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta) above the forehead. || 3/49 ||
He speaks of that which pervades the sixteen-petaled lotus:
"Having also placed [the mantra] 'Obeisance to the sixteen-petaled lotus within that'..."

Regarding those squares, the meaning is that one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-vinyāsa) by touching the locations starting from the back of the right ear with the mantra: "Obeisance to the sixteen-petaled lotus in the intermediate space. (3/50)
He states that the Śaktis are to be placed upon those petals:
"And one should place Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others on those petals. (3.50)

"On those petals"—the singular is used for the class (*jātāvekavacanam*), meaning "on those petals. One should place Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others, who attract desire, intellect, ego, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, mind, fortitude, memory, name, seed-syllable, self, nectar, and body. (3.50)
He states the locations for those petals:
"The petals are the back of the right ear, the shoulder, the elbow, the back of the hand, as well as the thigh, the knee, the ankle, and the sole of the foot. (3.51)
"Starting from the sole of the left foot"—thus this very group of eight is intended.

From "dalani" up to "tathā" is clear. In this manner, according to the stated method, starting from the sole of the left foot and ending at the back of the left ear, this very group of eight is intended. This constitutes the two groups of eight locations.
The meaning is "sixteen petals. (3/51–52)
He states that which pervades the eight petals:
"And within that, [one should say] 'Obeisance to the eight-petaled lotus' (aṣṭadalapadmāya namaḥ). (3/52)

The meaning is that, having placed [the seed-syllables] within that—in the interior of the sixteen-petaled lotus—one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) by touching the locations beginning with the right temple (the *dakṣa-śaṅkha*) with the mantra: "Obeisance to the eight-petaled lotus" (*aṣṭadala-padma-āya namaḥ*). || 3/52–53 ||
He states those petals:
"On these petals, on the right temple and the clavicle;
and on the left, within the thigh, at the ankle, the thigh, the clavicle, and the temple. (3/53)

The understanding [of these terms] arises because words such as *śaṅkha* (conch), *jaṭru* (collarbone), and so forth, when denoting parts of the body, are well-known in the *nighaṇṭus* (lexicons). (3.53)
He states that the eight Śaktis beginning with Anaṅgakusumā are to be placed upon those respective petals: "One should place the eight Śaktis beginning with Anaṅgakusumā"—
namely, Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgamadanā, and so forth.
"Anaṅgamadanāturā," "Anaṅgarekhā," "Anaṅgaveginī," "Anaṅgāṅkuśā," and "Anaṅgamālinī. The remainder is easy to understand. 3/54.
He states that which pervades the fourteen-spoked wheel:
"Also, [the mantra] 'Obeisance to the fourteen-spoked wheel within that'. (3.54)
Having performed the placement (vinyāsa) within that—

that is, inside the eight-petaled lotus— one should touch the locations of the fourteen corners, beginning with the forehead, with the mantra "Salutation to the fourteen-spoked wheel" (*caturdaśāracakrāya namaḥ*), and perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-vinyāsa*). || 3/54–55 ||
He states that the powers (śaktis) are to be placed in the fourteen corners:
"One should place the fourteen powers, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, in its corners."
Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and the others: Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, Sarvavidrāviṇī, Sarvākarṣiṇī, Sarvāhlādinī, Sarvasaṃmohinī, Sarvastambhinī, Sarvajṛmbhiṇī,
Sarvavaśaṅkarī, Sarvarañjanī, Sarvonmādinī, Sarvārthasādhinī, and Sarvasampattipūraṇī.
She consists of all mantras and effects the destruction of all dualities; the rest is clear. 3/55.
He states its corners by way of a formal proposition:
"I shall describe its corners. (3/55)
On the forehead, on the right side, between the right cheek and shoulder,
on the other side [of the chest], between the thighs and the shanks, and beginning with the left shank, O Pārvatī— (3.56)
On the left thigh, on the left side, on the left shoulder, on the left cheek, on the left part of the forehead, and likewise on the back. (3.57)

"On the right side of the forehead" means, since "forehead" (*lalāṭa*) is the subject under discussion, it refers to the space between the right cheek and the right shoulder. The word "right" (*dakṣa*) is applied to all three: the sides, the thighs, and the shanks. In the phrase "left shank, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) indicates the commencement of the remaining parts. In the case of "left shoulder" (*vāmāṃsa*), the word "middle" (*madhya*) should also be supplied.
"Back" (pṛṣṭha) should be understood as the back of the head itself, because the forehead is mentioned first for both the right and left [sides].
The forehead is the front part of the head. (3/55–57)
He speaks of that which pervades the outer ten-spoked wheel:
"Then, O Pārvatī, [one should say] 'Salutation to the ten-spoked wheel' (*daśāracakrāya namaḥ*).
That is, immediately after the placement of the corners of the fourteen-spoked wheel, one should [worship] with the mantra: "Salutation to the ten-spoked wheel."

Having touched the ten corners, beginning with the right eye, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*); the word "also" (*api*) should be construed as implying that one should also perform the placement (*vinyaset*).
He states the corners of the ten-spoked wheel: "Its corners are in the right eye, the root of the nose, and the eyes. (3/58)
In the corners of the belly, the wind (northwest), and the anus,
as well as in the corners known as the belly, the southwest (nairṛti), and the southeast (vahni)—
these are the ten corners of that ten-spoked wheel; [they correspond] to the ten locations beginning with the right eye.

The word "to be meditated upon" (*bhāvanīyāni*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. [They are located] in the belly, the two arms, and the corners. Due to Vedic usage, the plural is used for the dual.

By the term "belly" (*kukṣi*), the area from the two arms up to the two thighs is indicated. Thus, the upper part of the belly is the East, the lower part is the West, the right and left sides are the South and North respectively, and by the word "corners" (*koṇa*), the two arms are meant.

The two thighs are also observed. By that [calculation], the base of the left arm is the northeast corner (īśakoṇa), the base of the left thigh is the northwest corner (vāyukoṇa), the base of the right thigh is the southwest corner (nairṛtikoṇa), and the base of the right arm is the southeast corner (agnikoṇa). The rest is easy to understand. || 3/58–59 ||
He states that the Śaktis are to be placed in the ten corners:
"One should place them again. (3.59)
O Dear One, there is a group of ten powers beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā.

The [goddesses] beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā, namely: Sarvasiddhipradā, Sarvasampatpradā, Sarvapriyaṅkarī, Sarvamaṅgalakāriṇī, Sarvakāmapradā, Sarvaduḥkhavimocanī, Sarvamṛtyupraśamanī, Sarvavighnanivāriṇī, Sarvāṅgasundarī, and Sarvasaubhāgyadāyinī. The remainder is clear. 3/59–60.
He states that which pervades the inner ten-spoked wheel:
"And within that, 'Salutation to the wheel beginning with the ten-spoked one' as well. (3.60)

Having placed [the mantra] within that, inside the outer ten-spoked [lotus], one should touch the ten corners starting from the right nostril with the mantra "Obeisance to the inner ten-spoked wheel" (antardaśāracakrāya namaḥ) and perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-vinyāsa). || 3/60-61 ||
He states that the powers (śaktis) are to be placed in the ten corners:
"One should place the [powers] beginning with Sarvajñā in its corners.
These are: Sarvajñā, Sarvaśakti, Sarvaiśvaryapradā, and Sarvajñānamayī.

She is the destroyer of all diseases, the essential nature of all supports, the remover of all sins, composed of all bliss, the embodiment of all protection, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires. The rest is clear. 3/60.
He states its corners: the right nostril, the corner of the mouth, the breast, and the testicle. (3.61)
The perineum, the left testicle, the breast, the corners of the mouth, the two nostrils, and the tip of the nose—these are to be known as the ten corners (koṇas). (3.62)
This is clear. 3/61–62.
He states [the mantra] that pervades the eight-spoked wheel:
"Having performed the placement, one should also say, 'Obeisance to the wheel beginning with the eight spokes within that.'"

"Within that" means within the ten-spoked [lotus]. Having touched the eight corners starting from the chin with the mantra "Obeisance to the wheel beginning with the eight-cornered one" (*aṣṭakoṇādicakrāya namaḥ*), one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-vinyāsa*). The eight-cornered wheel is designated as "beginning" because it arose prior to the other wheels, such as the triangle. (3/63)
Regarding the powers to be placed in the eight corners, he says:
"In its corners, one should place the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī. (3.63)
In the corners of that eight-spoked wheel are the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī: Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśvarī, and Kaulinī. (3/63)
He describes its eight corners:
"The right [sides] of the throat, heart, and navel, as well as the four sides beginning with Maṇipūra, should be known as the left. (3.64)
And this is the group of four sides; furthermore, there are eight corners.

The four sides beginning with the chin are on the right, starting from Maṇipūra—Maṇipūraka being the location of the navel—and continuing through the navel, heart, throat, and chin. The four sides on the left are likewise [from the chin upwards].
And this is the group of eight corners. (3/64–65)
Immediately following, he describes the placement of the weapons and the armor:
"One should place [the weapons] outside, in the four directions of the triangle situated at the heart. (3.65)

The bow and arrow, as well as the noose and goad, reside in the heart; thus, that triangular shape situated between the two breasts, which is depressed at the center, is called the "triangle residing in the heart" (*hṛdayasthatrikoṇa*). Outside of it, in the four directions starting from the east, [reside] Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara.

One should place the four weapons combined: the arrow and bow, and the noose and goad. Since "arrow and bow" and "noose and goad" each form a pair according to the distinction between male and female, there are eight [deities]. On this very point, he will state later: "One should place the arrows in the eyes, the two bows on the eyebrows, and the two nooses in the ears."
"And one should place the two prongs at the tip of the nose, with the right prong pointing forward. (3/70–71). Thus [ends] 3/65–66.
Then, he speaks of that which pervades the triangular wheel:
"Salutation likewise to the Triangle.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*).
Having touched the three lines with the mantra "Trikoṇāya namaḥ," one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa).
He states that the goddesses are to be placed in the triangle:
"In its corners and in the spaces between the front and the right" (3.66).
One should place the Goddess in the midst of the goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī.

Within that triangle, [one places] Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī in the front, right, and left [corners], respectively. One should place the Goddess in the midst of those goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī—in the center, within the Śrīcakra at the point of the Bindu (baindava). The Goddess.

The meaning is that one should also install Tripurasundarī, whose nature is the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). || 3/66–67 ||
He concludes the installation of the Śrīcakra:
"O Goddess, thus has this sequential installation been taught by me; let it be grasped. (3.67)
This is clear. 3/67
Therefore, He says that even you must keep this collection of consignments secret: "O Goddess worshipped by heroes, this task is indeed most secret;
it is clear."
Now, one might ask: "Why should this not be told to anyone at all? To this he replies:

"It should be given to one who abides by the *samaya*; it should be given to a follower of the *kaula* path who is established in the practice of the *samaya*. [It is not for one following] the *samaya*-practice of the fettered (*paśu*)."
The meaning is that it should not be given once the completion has been reached.
But should it not be given to everyone, even to one who abides by the Kaulika observance? No; he says: "Never to one who is not a disciple. (3.68)
It should not be given even to one who abides by the samaya if they are not a disciple. || 3/68 ||
He says, "I too have not previously revealed this to anyone other than you":
"And this has been revealed to you today, more secret than the secret.
More secret than the secret because it is an absolute mystery even among mysteries. This [has been revealed] to you.

The intended meaning is that since I have today revealed [this] even to my beloved, who is of the nature of the reflective awareness (vimarśa) that constitutes a portion of myself, whereas previously it was not revealed to anyone else. (3/69)
He states another method for this very nyāsa:
"One should again perform the nyāsa beginning with the Root Goddess and ending with Aṇimā" (3.69).

Having first performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities of the Śrīcakra’s enclosures starting from *aṇimā* and ending with the Root Goddess, one should now perform the placement of the deities of the Śrīcakra’s enclosures again, starting from the Root Goddess and ending with *aṇimā*; this is the meaning.
He explains the method of the placement (*nyāsa*) of Mūladevī and the others:
"One should place Kāmeśvarī and the others, starting from the east, within the triangle on the head.
By the phrase "starting with Mūladevī," it is indicated that the first placement of Mūladevī is in the center of the triangle on the head.

It should be known that subsequently, within the triangle of the head, in the middle of the skull, there is a depression in the shape of a triangle; this appears very soft in childhood. Therein, starting from the east—the word "etc.
(ādi) including the south and north corners—are Kāmeśvarī and the others; by the word "etc.," Vajreśvarī and Bhagamālinī are included.
The meaning is that one should place Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī on the right and left corners of the triangle at the head [of the yantra]. || 3/70 ||
He describes the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the weapons and armor:
one should place the arrows in the eyes, the two bows on the eyebrows, and the two nooses in the ears. (3.70)
One should place the two goads with their tips pointing southward at the tip of the nose;
the arrows on Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī; the eyes on the two eyes; the two bows on the eyebrows;
the two nooses on the ear and both ears; and the two goads on both sides of the tip of the nose. [The remaining weapons are placed] on the eyes and the ear.

The use of the singular form "at the tip of the nose" (*nāsāgre*) is an indication for the dual, because of the subsequent mention of "the right tip" (*dakṣiṇāgram*). The meaning is that one should place the weapons of Kāmeśvara on the right side and those of Kāmeśvarī on the left side in these locations.
He describes the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the enclosure beginning with Vaśinī:
"One should place the eight goddesses of speech according to the sequence of the *Muṇḍamūla*. (3.71)

The head is shaven; upon it, following the sequence of the roots, one should install the group of eight deities—Vaśinī and the others—who are the presiding goddesses of the eight groups of consonants and who dwell in the eight directions surrounding [the head]. (3.61)

Now, one might ask: why has the placement (*nyāsa*) of the subtle constituents beginning with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and ending with the *unmanī*, which are above the *baindava* wheel, not been mentioned? To this he says:
"The wheels beginning with the *baindava* are to be placed, O fair-faced one."
The nine wheels, beginning with the Baindava and ending with the Quadrangle (Caturasra), are to be installed because they are gross;

the meaning is that [the wheels] beginning with the Half-moon and ending with Unmanā are to be meditated upon. Therefore, in the context of the gross installation, the installation of only the gross [wheels] is being described; this is the intended sense. || 3/72 ||
He states the placement of the obscurations beginning with that of omniscience:
"At the base of the eyes, at the outer corners, and again at the front and upper parts of the ears. (3.72)

One should place [the marks] on the crest-lock (cūḍā) and so forth, which is half-sunken; the remaining half on the back of the ear; and on the front of the ear, at the outer corner of the eye (apāṅga), and at its base. (3.73)

*Karṇottaram* means the region behind the ear. *Cūḍādike* refers to the forehead, which is the beginning of the *cūḍā* (the crown-lock). According to the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*), one should place [the marks] in a slightly depressed area immediately following the *karṇottara*. *Nimnam* refers to the depressed part at the back of the head; it is indeed the *avaṭu*. What is the meaning? [The marks of] Sarvajña and the others are to be placed on the forehead, the root of the eye, the outer corner of the eye, and the front and back of the ear, starting from the *cūḍā*.

One should place half of the ten [deities]. Now, the meaning is that one should place half of those very same [deities] at the base of the ears, the inner corners of the eyes, the back of the head, the front, and the outer corners of the eyes. An objection is raised:
"The names of Sarvajñā and the others were not mentioned; how then can it be said that they alone are to be placed here? It is replied:

The [deities] beginning with Vaśinī were stated to be installed in the previous wheel; now those beginning with Sarvasiddhi are stated to be installed in the subsequent upper wheel. Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is understood that those beginning with Sarvajñā are to be installed in the ten intermediate positions of both [wheels]. (3/72–73)
He states the placement of the enclosures beginning with *sarvasiddhi*: "One should place *sarvasiddhi* and the others around the throat in a clockwise direction.
This is clear. (3/74)
He describes the placement of the enclosures beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī: "In the heart, the Śaktis residing in the eight-petaled lotus are also as before. (3.74)

"In the heart" means on the chest. "As before" means in a clockwise direction. "The powers residing in the fourteen corners"—namely, those beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī who dwell in the fourteen corners—should be installed; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. (3/74)
He describes the placement of the protective coverings (āvaraṇanyāsa) beginning with Anaṅgakusumā:
"One should place that eight-petaled [lotus] at the navel;
then one should place the first four [syllables] on the left side of the backbone, on the abdomen, and on the right side. (3.75)
One should install another tetrad in the spaces between the bamboo-veins and so forth;

[this is] the eight-petaled lotus at the navel, in the region of the navel. The word "tat" (that) refers to the previously mentioned group of eight beginning with Anaṅgakusumā; [the phrase] "that and the other four" refers to that tetrad.
There are four [deities]: Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgamadanā, and Anaṅgamadanāturā.

The *vaṃśa* is the backbone. The left side and the right side [are specified]. The phrase "the space between the backbone and the left side," etc., refers to the interval between the backbone and the left flank; by the word "etc.," the interval between the left flank and the front part is included.
The space between the front and right sides, as well as the space between the right side and the spine, is taken [as the locations].
Furthermore, there is another set of four: the quartet of Anaṅgarekhā, Anaṅgaveginī, Anaṅgāṅkuśā, and Anaṅgamālinī.
From the region of the navel toward the right side starting from the west, there is the quartet beginning with Anaṅgakusumā.
The meaning is that one should place the four [deities] beginning with Anaṅgarekhā in the directions starting from Vāyu (the northwest) and ending with Nairṛta (the southwest). || 3/75–76 ||
He describes the placement of the first enclosure, beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī:
"One should place [the deities] in one's own Svādhiṣṭhāna, starting from the east and ending at the south. (3/76)
One should place four [syllables] each, in sequence, in the four directions.
In the region of one's own *svādhiṣṭhāna* lotus, starting from the east— the eastern direction—
and continuing until the end of the south— the southern direction— one should place four [syllables] in each of the four directions.

The Śaktis, beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others, are to be installed in their proper sequence. Now, one might ask: "How are Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others inferred? To this it is replied: Just as before, because the names of the Śaktis of the preceding and succeeding wheels are mentioned, the names of the Śaktis of the middle wheel are determined by the principle of elimination (pāriśeṣya), even though they have not been explicitly stated.
He describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the enclosure of the powers (*śakti*) of the mudrās, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī:
"The best of practitioners should place the ten mudrās at the *mūlādhāra*. (3.77)
"In the *mūlādhāra*, that is, in the region of the *mūlādhāra*. The rest is clear. (3/77)
Now, one might ask: "Should the ten mudrās be installed through meditation in the mūlādhāra?
In response to this doubt, he says:
"Furthermore, in the backbone, on the right, on the left, and in the intermediate space."

The ten mudrās are [placed] above and below; by the word "again" (*punaḥ*), the locations for the placement of the eight petals are stated, beginning with "the eight-petaled [lotus] at the navel" (3/75). "In the backbone" means on the spinal column. "And on the left side"—by the word "and" (*ca*), [it includes] the north and south as well.

The term "pārśvayoḥ" (of the two sides) refers to the left side and the intermediate space—that is, the space between the backbone and the left side. By the use of the word "ca" (and), the intermediate spaces starting from the left side are included.

What is the meaning? One should place ten mudrās in the directions of the backbone and so forth, as well as in the intermediate directions such as Vāyavya, and above and below. Now, regarding the phrase "above and below":
What is the interval between these two positions? He says "no," for there is no interval between the upper and lower;
another position is proclaimed to be between the directions of Indra and Īśāna.
Another location is proclaimed to be in the middle between the southwest and the western directions.

Thus, according to our stated method in the *Tattvavimarśinī*, the two remaining locations for the two remaining mudrās should be conceived in the same manner as the procedure for the worship of the ten world-protectors (lokapālas). || 3/78 ||
He states the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the enclosures beginning with Brahmāṇī:
"Furthermore, excluding the upper and lower [directions]. (3.78)
One should place the eight Brahmā-mantras on the right calf; this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*). The remainder is clear. (3/78–79)
Now, it was stated that one should place [the goddesses] on the right shank; regarding that, as to what their locations are, he says:
"They, however, as before. "They" refers to Brahmāṇī and the others. "As before" means in the locations previously mentioned in [verse 3.78]: "Again on the backbone and on the left [side]."

Here, by the term "backbone" (*pṛṣṭhavaṃśa*), the posterior part is indicated. The meaning is that those [deities] beginning with Brahmāṇī are to be installed in the four directions starting from the west of the right shank, as well as in the intermediate directions starting from the northwest (*vāyavya*). || 3/79 ||
He describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the coverings beginning with *aṇimā*:
"Starting from the left calf, and also proceeding in the sequence beginning with the left [limb]. (3.79)
One should place the eight Siddhis upon them; two should be placed on the soles of the feet.

Starting from the left calf—specifically beginning from the rear part of the left calf—and proceeding in order from the left and through the intervals between the left, [they are to be placed] upon those aforementioned locations. The eight Siddhis.
One should place [the remaining two]. The meaning is that one should place the remaining pair on the soles of the feet; that is, one should place them on both soles of the feet. (3/79–80)
Demonstrating the excellence of the aforementioned Nyāsa, he concludes by prescribing the latent impression (vāsanā) which is its fruit:
"The Nyāsa has issued forth from its cause, like one lamp lit from another. (3.80)
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), O Goddess of Gods, one should contemplate [the deity] as non-different from oneself.

From the Cause—which consists of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Light (*prakāśa*) and Reflection (*vimarśa*), and which is the form of the entire universe—a Great Radiance issues forth, conforming to its cause, like a lamp [emerging] from a lamp. In this manner, as described; it has been declared.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate [the deities] as non-different from oneself. The meaning is that, having visualized the constituent parts of the Śrīcakra together with their Śaktis as being inseparable from the parts of one's own body, one should contemplate the non-difference between oneself and the Supreme Goddess who presides over them. (3/80–81)

Having contemplated the characteristic of supreme consciousness and bliss through the three aforementioned sixfold installations (*nyāsa*), one whose heart is matured should perform the installation beginning with the purification of the hands (*kara-śuddhi*) for the sake of fitness for the ritual of external worship; thus it is said:
"And thereafter, being composed, one should perform the installation beginning with the purification of the hands. (3.81)

Then, following the threefold nyāsa, one performs the nyāsa for the purification of the hands and so forth: "I perform a pure, conscious purification of the two hands, which purifies through touch, residing in the fingers whose form is the effect touched by the causal Self" (Su. Vā. 24).

According to the method stated in the words of the learned masters, this refers to the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of which *karaśuddhi* (purification of the hands) is the first; the singular number is used here to denote the class.
"Samāhitaḥ" means attentive. The *nyāsa* beginning with *karaśuddhi* is as taught in the *Catuḥśatī-śāstra* (verses 1/126–129).
Therefore, it is not described here, but is mentioned by name alone. (3/81)
In that regard, he states the placement of knowledge (*vidyānyāsa*) which was not previously mentioned:
"O Goddess, [one should place it] on the head, the secret place, the heart, and the three eyes; likewise on the pair of ears, the mouth, and the two arms. (3.82)
One should perform the *vidyā-nyāsa* on the back, the two knees, and the navel.

*Vidyā-nyāsa* is the ritual placement [of mantras] by means of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the *vidyā*. One places the *vāgbhava-bīja* on the head, the *kāmarāja-bīja* in the secret place, and the *śakti-bīja* at the heart. Thus, one recites the three seed-syllables in all three locations.
The meaning is that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). The remainder is clear. (3/82–83)
He states the names of the purification of the hands and so forth:
"The purification of the hands, and likewise the seats, and the six-limbed [practice]. (3.83)

And [the placement of] Śrīkaṇṭha and the others, as well as the goddesses of speech (vāgdevyaḥ), namely Vaśinī and the rest. The ritual placement (nyāsa) of Śrīkaṇṭha and the others is as stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*;
it is not mentioned here because it is well-known from other tantras. The remainder is clear. || 3/83–84 ||
He states the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī:
"In the foundation (*ādhāra*), in the heart, again in the crest (*śikhā*), and in the station of the *bindu*, one should place those beginning with the Fire-wheel (*agnicakra*). (3.84)
The sequence should be understood as reversed, namely: "at the *bindu*-place" and "at the crest.
The previously mentioned forehead is the *bindu*-place, which is desired to be circular in shape, like a lamp, and measuring half a mora (1/28).
The "crest" (*śikhā*) refers to the tip of the *kuṇḍalinī*, the place of rest for Śiva. Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage: "In the middle of that crest..."

"The Supreme Self is established" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.12.1). By that word "crest-lock" (*śikhā*), the Brahma-aperture (*brahmarandhra*), which is the locus of its pervasion, is indicated. Regarding the fire-wheel (*agnicakra*) and others: in the fire-wheel, at the abode of Kāmagiri, which consists of Mitrīśanātha, I worship the Śrī-pādukā of the goddess Śrī-Kāmeśvarī, who is the Rudra-natured power; in the sun-wheel (*sūryacakra*), at the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) of Jālandhara...
I worship the venerable sandals of the goddess Vajreśvarī, whose nature is Ṣaṣṭhīśanātha and whose power is Viṣṇu (p. 271).

In the lunar wheel (*somacakra*), at the seat of Pūrṇagiri, I worship the venerable sandals of the goddess Bhagamālinī, whose nature is Oḍḍīśanātha and whose power is Brahmā. In the Brahma-wheel (*brahmacakra*), at the seat of Oḍyāṇa...

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantras: "I worship the Śrīpādukā of the Supreme Brahman-essence, the Goddess Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, who is the very self of the *caryānātha*. The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) consist of the wheels (*cakras*) of Fire, Sun, Moon, and Brahman. What is the meaning?
[They reside] in the wheels of Fire, Sun, Moon, and Brahman, located respectively in the Foundation (*ādhāra*), the Heart, the Center of the Brows, and the Cavity of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

The meaning is that one should assign the powers consisting of Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the Supreme Brahman to the sacred seats (pīṭhas) of Kāma, Giri, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and Oḍyāṇa—namely, Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Mahātripurasundarī. This very same meaning has been elaborated in the ritual manuals (paddhatīs) by the preeminent teachers who know the tradition. (3/84)
He describes the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa):

"The three principles in their entirety, conjoined with the three seed-syllables of Vidyā, [should be deposited] from the feet up to the navel, then from the navel up to the throat, and likewise from the throat up to the head. (3.85)
And having placed the pervasive [deity],

namely the triad of principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva— the three principles collectively in the form of the totality of the triad of principles— and the fourth principle which is the aggregate of those three principles; as it has been stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
The principles beginning with Earth and ending with Māyā are remembered as being contained within the principle of Ātman;
while Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva reside within the principle called Vidyā.
The dual Śiva and Śakti are proclaimed as the Śiva-tattva;
it consists of these three aspects: the knower, the known, and the act of knowing.

"This is the reality, the auspicious Śiva-reality (śivatattva), which consists of all realities. Thus [it is said]. It is endowed with the three seed-syllables of Vidyā. The seed-syllables of Vidyā are the Bāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti seeds;
the fourth seed-syllable is the form of this collection of seeds. It is endowed with these four seed-syllables, from the feet up to the navel.
By the force of the final word, the throat (*galam*) is not indicated; rather, by the force of the ablative case in "from the head" (*śirasaḥ*), it is understood as "from the throat" (*galāt*).

What is the meaning? Having uttered the four principles of Ātman, Vidyā, Śiva, and Turīya, along with the four seed-syllables of Mūlavidyā—namely Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, Śakti, and Turīya—ending in the dative case and followed by *namaḥ*.

The meaning is that, having touched the body from the feet up to the navel, from the navel up to the throat, and from the throat up to the head, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*). || 3/85–86 ||
He speaks again of the meditation on supreme egoity (*parāhaṃtā*): "Having again made the other one one's own.
The "other" is the light transcending the universe; having again made that one's own. This occurs after the previously mentioned installation of the *śrīcakra*.

The phrase "one should contemplate as non-different from oneself" (3/81) expresses unity with the Supreme; now, even after the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) such as *karaśuddhi* and so forth, one should again contemplate that which—due to the power of *māyā*—appears as if different from oneself, as non-different from oneself.
Having thus assimilated the Supreme, when *māyā* has departed through the efficacy of the ritual placements such as *karaśuddhi*, [the state of unity is realized].
The meaning is: having contemplated Śrī Mahātripurasundarī as one's own self. || 3/86 ||
He speaks of the immersion in nectar:
"Furthermore, one should satisfy the Goddess with the gentle and fiery liquid essences of nectar. (3.86)

The "gentle" (saumya) is that which consists of the supreme vowel-less (anacka) and unsurpassed (anuttara) essence, the nature of the half-moon (ardhakalā), situated within a triangle located in the center of the full moon-maṇḍala, which resides in the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus facing downward at the *brahmarandhra*.
The [next] is that which resides in the center of the pericarp of the four-petaled lotus at the *mūlādhāra*, which is full—

The fiery [element] consists of the form of the supreme digit (*kalā*), which is the nature of the Unstruck (*anacka*) and the Absolute (*anuttara*), situated within the triangle located in the center of the circle of fire.

Through the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the two forms of the Nectar and Fire Kuṇḍalinīs, which flow respectively downward and upward in the shape of the Yoni and the Liṅga, one should satisfy and drench [the deity] with the downpour of the flowing nectar-fluid. This very [process] has been taught by the teachers who know the tradition.
In the paddhatis, this is called the supreme placement (parānyāsa). || 3/86 ||
He concludes the previously mentioned fourfold nyāsa by way of restatement:
"O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the fourfold nyāsa should be performed in this manner;
as well as the sixfold nyāsa beginning with aṇimā, O Dear One, and that beginning with the Root Goddess. (3.87)

And for the sake of complete accomplishment, the practitioner should perform the purification of the hands and so forth, according to the manner described above. The sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) and the rest are for the sake of "complete accomplishment" (*susiddhi*), meaning for the attainment of supreme liberation through the power of the depositions, by which obstacles are easily dispelled. By the practitioner.

This must be performed by one who desires liberation (mumukṣu), but not by one who has already attained perfection (siddha), because the latter is already liberated. As it was said by the venerable Vijñānabhairava Bhaṭṭāraka: "By whatever substances one worships or satisfies the Supreme-Non-Supreme (parāpara)..."
"And whoever is the worshipper, he alone is everything; where then is there any separate act of worship? (Vi.bhai., ślo. 150).
He states the application of the fourfold nyāsa according to the difference in time:
"At the time of morning, likewise at the time of worship, and during the rite of fire-offering (homa). (3/88)
At the time of recitation, their application is performed separately;
however, at the time of worship, the best of practitioners may perform them all together. (3.89)

One should perform the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) at dawn, the placement of *aṇimā* and the other powers (*aṇimādinyāsa*) at the time of worship, the placement of the root goddess and others (*mūladevyādinyāsa*) at the time of the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the placement beginning with the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhyādinyāsa*) at the time of recitation (*japa*). This is the specific application for each occasion. Alternatively, the preeminent practitioner may perform all four types of placement together at the time of worship.

The most excellent practitioner, by virtue of his capacity to perform the fourfold nyāsa, because the web of his bonds is being shattered, and because liberation is near, has indeed accomplished all that was to be done. (3/88–89)
Having prepared the seat extending up to the thirty-six principles (tattvas),
one should then offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) with the mantra of the Guptā and other Yoginīs.

Having conceptualized the seat as the aggregate of principles (tattva) beginning with earth and ending with Śiva, extending up to the thirty-six principles; and having conceptualized the Śrīcakra as the seat because it is the substratum for the rays of consciousness—this is stated in the *Śrīparākrama*:
"Meditating within the lotus of the heart upon that which begins with earth and ends with Śiva..."
"One should bring [the goddess] to the state of being seated by casting flowers that have been heated [and empowered] starting from the Guptā [level].

Regarding the phrase "of the Guptā and other Yoginīs," the term *samasta-prakaṭa* (all-manifest) is to be supplied at the beginning. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), the Yoginīs of the Guptatara, Sampradāya, Kulakaula, Nigarbha, Rahasya, Atirahasya, and Parāpararahasya are included. This is the *bali*.

Worship (*pūjā*). Regarding this, the *Nighaṇṭu* states: "The word *bali* is used for an offering in worship as well. Great poets have also said: "Having gathered flowers for the offering" (*Kuṭṭanīmata* 1.60). What is the meaning? One whose self is purified should first perform, internally, whatever external [offering] is to be described later, rather than performing it externally.
Thus, according to the method we have described, having meditated upon one’s own body as the Śrīcakra— the form of the aggregate of all principles— for the sake of the internal sacrifice,

[one should offer salutation] with the words: "Obeisance to the Śrīpādukās of all the Yoginīs of the Manifest, the Secret, the More Secret, the Tradition, the Kula, the Kaula, the Nigarbha, the Secret, the Ultra-Secret, and the Supreme-Ultra-Secret."
The meaning is that one should perform worship upon one's own head with the root-mantra of the Yoginī. By this, it is indicated that all external worship should first be performed internally. (3/90)
He speaks of the removal of internal obstacles:

"By piercing the knots of the body, form, and word, there is the destruction of obstacles through the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Vidyā upon the secret place, heart, mouth, and head, O beautiful one. (3.91)
On the secret place, the heart, the mouth, and the head. By the word "secret" (*guhya*), the area between the anus and the genitals is indicated.

By the word "mouth" (*mukha*), the forehead, which is a part of the face, is indicated. On these four locations—the secret place, the heart, the mouth, and the head—there is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *vidyā*, that is, the ritual placement of the four seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the *Saubhāgyavidyā*. [The term] *piṇḍa*...
Kuṇḍalinī. By the word *piṇḍa*, the location of Kuṇḍalinī—the *kanda* situated between the anus and the genitals—is indicated.

One should understand that there is an inversion [of order] in the phrase "rūpa-pada. *Pada* refers to the *haṃsa*; by the word *pada*, the location of the *haṃsa*, the heart, is indicated. *Rūpa* refers to the *bindu*; by the word *rūpa*, the location of the *bindu*, the forehead, is indicated. By the word *granthi*...

That which is the root of the universe, the Brahma-aperture (*brahmarandhra*), consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*), is perceived as that in which the entire universe is strung together like a gem on a thread.

By piercing these four [centers], there is the piercing of obstacles. What is the meaning? By the placement (*nyāsa*) of the four seed-syllables of Vidyā in the four locations beginning with the secret place (*guhya*), those obstacles characterized by obstruction that exist in the worlds beginning with Pātāla are destroyed. (Suvā. 23)

According to the method stated in the words of the learned masters, the meaning is as follows: having pierced the locations of the knots (*granthi*)—which consist of the *piṇḍa* and *pada* and take the form of the netherworlds (*pātāla*) and so forth—namely the anus, heart, forehead, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), which are characterized by piercing, one comes to rest in the state beyond them, which is consciousness (*cinmaya*) and non-dual; this is the internal removal of obstacles. By this, everything [is explained].
It is indicated that one should perform the internal [worship] after the conclusion of the external worship. || 3/91 ||

Since the body itself is the sacrificial hall in the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), one should first dispel the obstacles within it and then proceed to drive away the obstacles located in the external sacrificial temple; thus he says:
"The knower of mantras, having driven away the obstacles residing in the sacrificial temple..."
May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
The practitioner who knows the mantra, using the mantra "HŪṂ astrāya PHAṬ," should expel the departing obstacles by giving them passage through the contraction of his own left side.
"One should dispel the obstacles that have gone to the earth, those that have gone to the sky, and those that are divine," he says:
"By a blow with the heel one should dispel those on the earth, and by a clap of the hands those in the sky. (3.92)
One should dispel divine obstacles by means of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) and by one's gaze;
terrestrial obstacles, those situated on the ground, by a kick or by three kicks;
and obstacles gone to the sky, those moving in the intermediate space, by a clap or by three claps of the hands. The phrase "by the weapon-mantra" applies throughout all these cases.
One should dispel—that is, expel—the obstacles, including even divine obstacles, by means of the gaze, that is, by looking with the eyes. || 3/92-93 ||
To ensure that the obstacles which have departed do not enter again, he describes the meditation on the enclosure of fire:
"One should meditate upon a great enclosure of fire in all directions, above, and below. (3.93)

"In the fire of consciousness, which is the great essence and whose sole body is reflective awareness (vimarśa), I offer this appearance of duality as an oblation so that it shall not arise again" (Suvā. 64). According to the method stated in this verse of the learned masters, the great fire is precisely the supreme consciousness itself, manifesting everywhere; that alone is...

The "enclosure" (*prākāra*) is so called because it is difficult to cross. The meaning is that by means of the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of imagining a great enclosure of fire whose nature is non-dual supreme consciousness vibrating in all directions, there is no entry of obstacles characterized by the perception of duality. (3/93)
He describes the worship of the Sun:
"O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship Mārtaṇḍa with the general *arghya* offering,
accompanied by the Power of Radiance (*prakāśaśakti*)."

The general *arghya* and the special *arghya* will now be explained (3.98–103). Supreme Śiva is Light accompanied by the power of manifestation (*prakāśa-śakti*); that power is called "reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*), and He is eternally conjoined with it.
Śiva himself, as self-luminous light, is the sun, and the rays are the glory of that reflective awareness.
"By those [rays] he illumines the circle of the knowable; the mind [should perform] its worship with the greatness of that [Self]. (Cidgaganacandrikā 5).

According to the method stated by us, the meaning is that one should contemplate everything through the general *arghya*—that is, through the worship characterized by the contemplation of the "I-ness" (*ahambhāvanā*) of one's own Self. As for the external meaning, it is quite clear. (3/94)
He describes the preeminence of its qualities:
"Blazing like the dawn. (3/94)
And her retinue consists of the planets and other celestial bodies, illuminating with universal splendor.

According to the method stated in authoritative scriptures, "The Goddess Tripurā is one's own consciousness, and the crimson [light] is its reflective awareness (*vimarśana*)," she is resplendent, adorned with the reddish ornaments that constitute the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), because she is devoid of rising and setting. Her retinue consists of the planets and other celestial bodies.

And: the senses (*indriya*) are called *graha* because they seize their objects; of these, the "first" (*ādi*) is the mind (*manas*), which, along with its retinue, sets in motion the stream of conceptual cognitions (*saṃkalpa-pratyaya*) characterized by the grasping of various objects. Regarding this, the Upanishadic mantra says: "May He impel our intellects" (*Ṛgveda* 3.4.10). It is the illuminator of all splendors; it is indeed "the light of lights" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*).
(2/2/9) According to the manner stated in the Upaniṣad, this is one's own radiance which is the cause for the perception of the external multitude of lights. As for the external objects:
here, "the planets" (grahāḥ) refers to Soma and the others; because the Sun is the primary one, the word "etcetera" (ādi) includes the six limbs [of the ritual]. The rest is clear. (3/94–95)
He states the extraction of the outer wheel:
"O Goddess, with yellow orpiment, agallochum, and saffron joined with [the substances of] the north and southeast... (3.95).
While reciting the root mantra, one should correctly contemplate the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*).

The "gentle" (*saumya*) is camphor, because it is designated by the name *soma*. The "fiery" (*āgneya*) is saffron, because it is known as *agniśikhā*. As Amarasimha states: "Saffron is born in Kāśmīra and is called *agniśikhā*" (2.6.124). *Rocanā* is *gorocanā* (cow-gallstone).

Having made a paste from agallochum (*agaru*), black agallochum (*kālāguru*), and saffron (*kuṅkuma*) mixed with lime (*sudhā*), one should inscribe it upon a plate made of gold or other materials using a golden needle. While reciting the root *saubhāgyavidyā*, if another person causes the wheel (*cakra*) to be drawn, [the practitioner] should do so while reciting; if he draws it himself, he should likewise recite. This is because the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*) consists of the four traditions (*āmnāya*).

It is superior even to all other wheels of worship (*pūjācakra*). According to the method stated by the learned authorities: "One should meditate upon or draw [it], or have it drawn, as being perfectly equilateral with its three corners meeting at the point of power (*śakti*), with straight lines, and beautiful"—as it is said:
"One should draw the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*) with musk, saffron, camphor, sandalwood, and nectar. (3/95–96)
Then, one should cast a handful of flowers with the root mantra of the Yoginī.

Then, one should cast a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) there, upon that *śrīcakra*, with the root mantra previously mentioned, beginning with "the entire manifest [group] of yoginīs" (*samastaprakaṭa*). (3.96)
He taught that even in the absence of flowers,
one should always ensure that [the vessel] is not empty by filling it with gems, pearls, or corals, using the root-vidyā in reverse order.

*Viloma* means in reverse order. By means of the recited root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) or the *saubhāgyavidyā*; the word "or" (*vā*) connects to both [cases], like the eye of a crow. It should be made "not empty," that is, not devoid [of flowers]. At all times, by whatever means possible;
in the absence of flowers, one may use gems and so forth, or with the root-mantra of the Yoginī.
Or, by means of the *saubhāgyavidyā*, one should always keep the wheel from being empty; that is to say, one should worship it. (3.97)
He states that if one does not act accordingly, there is fruitlessness:
"In the void, however, obstacles are manifold. (3.97)
If the Śrīcakra is devoid of gems and other such items, many—indeed, numerous—obstacles that interfere with the worship may arise. (3/97)
He states the procedure for the general *arghya* offering: "One should establish the *arghya* between the Śrīcakra and oneself.
That is, between the Śrīcakra—which has been raised up according to the method previously described—and the practitioner (*sādhaka*). The *arghya* [is to be placed] there.
One should establish or cause [it] to be established according to the method that will be described. (3.97)
He describes the method for the installation of the *arghya* offering:
"O Goddess of the Gods, within the square [area], there are eight corners located in the intermediate spaces. (3/98)
Having worshipped the six seats, one should again worship the four sacred seats within the triangle, O Goddess, in the sequence beginning with Kāpūjā. (3.99)

Having performed worship with the *arghya* and *pādya*, one should worship the ten digits (*kalā*) of Fire. First, having drawn a square within the intermediate space, then a circle inside that, then a hexagon within that, and finally a triangle in its center— one should thus draw the mandala on a ground smeared with cow dung using the *matsyamudrā*.
This is obtained through the power of implication. As it is stated in the *Śrīparākrama*:
"Then, on a square area of ground smeared with cow dung, [one should perform the rite] by means of the 'fish-seal' (*matsyamudrā*) formed with the hand of the flowing breath."
"One should draw the *arghya* mandala, endowed with divine fragrance, within a square, a circle, a hexagon, and a triangle, one inside the other. Thus,
having worshipped the six seats in the six corners within the space between the square and the circle, [one proceeds].
Having worshipped the pot-born lotus in the ocean of nectar, the self-manifest wheel, and the seats for accomplishing all mantras,
one should worship the four pīṭhas— Kāmagiri-pīṭha (kā), Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha (pū),
Jālandhara-pīṭha (jā), and Oḍyāṇa-pīṭha (o)— respectively in the three corners of the triangle situated within the hexagon, and the third in the center.

And having worshipped one [deity], having established the vessel there upon the support—the *arghya-pāda*—and having worshipped it, one should worship the form of fire (*vahnibimba*) in its center and worship the *kalās* surrounding it. As it is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Within the hexagon, however, is the triangular form of fire, endowed with the *kalās*."
"O Goddess, having invoked [the fire] from its support, the best of mantra-knowers should worship it.
Thus, one should worship the ten kalās of that fire, beginning with Dhūmrārcis and preceded by the ten syllables from *ya* to *kṣa*, in their proper order.
This has been stated in the Svacchandasaṃgraha:
O Maheśvarī, these are the phonemes from *ya* to *kṣa*, which are the digits (*kalā*) of Fire;
having worshipped these digits according to the rule with their respective colors.
The mantras of the fire-energies (vahnikalā) are said to begin with their own seed-syllables, have names ending in the dative case, and conclude with "namaḥ. Now, listen to the names.
Dhūmrārcis, Nīlaraktā, Kapilā, Visphuliṅginī,
Jvālāmālinī, Arciṣmatī, and above those, Havyavāhinī.
"The eighth is Kavyavāhā, and then Raudrī and Saṃhāriṇī. [And:
"Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, Havyavāhā, Kavyavāhā, and Īśvarī" (Śāradātilaka 2.15).
Thus [it is said] in another tantra. (3/98–110)
Having established the vessel for the *arghya* offering, one should worship the digits of the Sun (*sūryakalā*) therein.
One should worship the twelve digits of the Sun, beginning with *ka*, within the vessel;
that is, having worshipped the solar disc within the vessel, namely the middle of the *arghya* vessel. This is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Having placed a conch shell washed with the *astra-mantra* upon it [the vessel]..."
"Having invoked the solar disc from the heart by means of one's own mantra," it is said.
Herein, one should worship the digits of the Sun (sūryakalāḥ).
One should worship the collection of phonemes beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*, and those beginning with *bha* and ending with *ḍha*, in both direct and reverse order.
Two by two they should be employed, and immediately thereafter, the *kalās*.

Thus, according to the method we have described, one should worship the twelve solar digits (kalās), beginning with Tāpinī and so forth, which are sequentially joined with pairs of letters starting from *ka* and *bha*—that is, from *ka* and *bh*. As it is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"O Goddess, the letters from *ka* to *ṭha* are proclaimed by the names of the [twelve] forms (*mūrti*)."
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Śodhanī, and likewise Śoṣaṇī.
Bhrāmaṇī, Kledinī, Vareṇyā, Ākarṣaṇī, Suṣumnā, Vṛṣṭivāhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Hiraṇyadā.
"These are the solar digits (saurakalā), beginning with *bhā* and ending with *ḍā*, arranged in their proper sequence.

From this statement that they begin with *ka* and *bhā*, it is understood that the ten consonants beginning with *ya* are the fire-digits (*vahnikalā*), and the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* are the lunar digits (*somakalā*). Therein, the vessel is perfumed with cloves and other fragrant flowers.
Having filled it with water and worshipped the lunar disc therein, one should cast into that water the substances mentioned in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*:
"One should throw into that water cardamom, cloves, kaṅkola, well-combined nutmeg, fragrant flowers, and other aromatic ingredients."
Having drawn the ninefold womb-diagram as before in the midst of water,
one should invoke [the deity] from the state of purity and worship the lunar mandala.
Thus (it is said). || 3/100 – 101 ||
But when the substance has been separated again, one should worship the sixteen digits of the moon.
When that substance has been held, the liquid substance is the special *arghya*. For wine (*madya*) is indeed composed entirely of liquid. As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Therefore, the means for accomplishing the special *arghya* is now being proclaimed."
And one should perform the worship of Fire and the Sun upon those two, the support and the vessel.

"In the vessel for which the worship has been performed and the object of worship honored according to the path described for the general *arghya*, one should fill it with *āsava* as before with the *Śiras-mantra*.
[These are] the sixteen lunar digits (*kalā*) in sequence, beginning with the sixteen vowels starting from 'A', namely the sixteen digits beginning with Amṛtā."
One should sacrifice. This has been stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"The sixteen gentle digits (*kalā*) residing at the beginning and end of the vowels have been proclaimed.
I shall state their names; listen, O beautiful one in every limb."
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Puṣṭi, Prīti, O Maheśvarī;
Revatī, Hrīmatī, Śrī, Kānti, and then Sudhā.
"Jyotsnā, Haimavatī, Chāyā, Sampūrṇī, Vāmā, and Rāmā—these are the names of the digits (kalās), O Beloved," thus [it is said]. (3/101)
And one should meditate upon Amṛteśī in the center of that by means of the Navātman mantra;
then, O Goddess, one should satisfy the deities of the bodily constituents with the Navātman mantra.
One should satisfy Ānandabhairava with the syllable *vauṣaṭ* at the end.
Having raised up Lakulīśa, as well as Bhṛgu, Saṃvartaka,
Pinākin, Khaḍgīśa, Bhujaṅga, and likewise Bālin.
Having joined them in due order up to the summit of cause and effect, one should finally join Arghīśa; thus this Navātman is extracted.

Thus, having extracted the Navātman from the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*, [he says]: "In the midst of that, with that mantra, I meditate upon you, O Bhavānī, the Amṛteśvarī, who has spread forth to satisfy all moving and non-moving beings with a flood of nectar-rays, for the sake of the pacification of worldly existence. (Sau.hṛ. 7)

One should meditate upon [the deity] as flowing with nectar, according to the method stated in the words of the masters. Then, O Goddess, the deities of the elements, such as Ḍākinī and the others, arise in their new forms. It is said in this very [text]:
"In the Viśuddha, the heart, the navel, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, and the Mūla."
"The lords of the elements and the deities beginning with *ḍa* should be placed within the command (*ājñā*). (3/30).

Thus, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the previously mentioned *navātman*. By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "and indeed Ānandabhairava," it is meant that one should satisfy Ānandabhairava with the *navātman* alone. Having uttered the *navātman*, [one says] "to Ānandabhairava, *vauṣaṭ*."
The meaning is that one should satisfy [them]. || 3/102 – 103 ||
He extends the procedure for the general *arghya* to the special *arghya* as well:
"In the same way, the best of practitioners should prepare the *arghya* specifically. (3.103)
This is clear. 3/103
Having thus performed the purification of the *arghya*, he says that one should thereafter worship the Gurus:

"Having worshipped the line of the Gurus' feet, one should offer it again to Bhairava. This refers to the lineage of the sandals (*pādukā-paramparā*) of the Gurus, beginning from Paramaśiva and ending with one's own Guru.

Having worshipped [the lineage] consisting of the three currents—the divine, the perfected, and the human—and having honored it upon one's own head with arghya water, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and flowers; and having thrice lifted the purified arghya up to the forehead, one should offer or present it to Bhairava, who possesses the form of the Guru, whose definition was stated previously (1/1), and who dwells within the *śṛṅgāṭa* at the center of the great lotus forest. 3/104.
Furthermore, impelled by that command, he should present it before the lineage of gurus. (3.104)
That substance, impelled and authorized by the command of that Bhairava who is in the form of the Guru, one should then offer again in the lineage of gurus (gurupaṅkti). || 3/104 ||
Regarding the taking of the prasāda, he says:

"Having taken the remainder of that [offering], one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) while reciting the root-vidyā and the pādukā-mantra over the sacrificial fire, which blazes with light on all sides. (3.105)

Taking the remaining substance— that which has been offered to the Guru and the Deity— one should, according to the method we have described, namely "Kāma is God because He is desired" (*Saubhāgyasudhodaya* 4.3), perform the purification of the four principles (*tattva*) with the corresponding mantras into the fire of the Self, which is called Kāmeśvara, the devourer of the universe within the web of *kalās*, and which shines forth on all sides in all living beings.

"Then, according to the method taught in the *Ājñāvatāra*, [one should worship] that form which consists of light and is by nature the devourer of the universe, within the web of the digits (*kalā*) that consume the universe. Reciting the *pādukā*—the venerable *pādukā* of one's own Guru—and the Root-Vidya as well as the Saubhāgya-Vidya, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), characterized by the casting of the fuel of duality. This is stated in the *Śrīparākrama*:
Having offered the arghya to the Guru residing upon his head, by his command,
[he offers it] into the fire of consciousness, which is capable of enduring the fire at the end of an aeon and consumes the entire universe.

"Offering the oblation consisting of the measureable aggregate (meyarāśi), with the latent impressions (vāsanā) as the condiment, he should recite the mantra while offering it through their mutual interpenetration, contemplating the Self. (3.105)
Now, what is the fire of desire? Where does it reside? And what is its oblation? To this he says:
"In the great light, which is intent upon vomiting forth the universe, one should offer the circles of rays with the mind into the mouth of Kuṇḍalī. (3.106)

[The term] "at the mouth of Kuṇḍalī" is to be understood as "situated. Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage: "In the center of that crest-lock, the Supreme Self is situated" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.11.12). [It is] in the Great Light, in the fire of the subject which is ignited without fuel and devoid of extinction; it is intent upon the emission and withdrawal of the universe. Of the universe, from Śiva down to the level of the Earth.

In the context of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), it refers to abiding as that alone which is its own cause; in the context of vomiting (*vamana*) and emission (*sarjana*), it is impelled. Power (*śakti*) is indeed the primordial source of the universe. As it is said in the *Ājñāvatāra*: "By her own will alone, she swallows and also emits the entire universe. One should offer the functions of the rays together with the mind (*manas*). The rays of the internal fire of consciousness (*cidanala*) are the senses (*akṣāṇi*); their movement is toward external objects.

The functions [of consciousness]. This has been stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava Bhaṭṭāraka: "Wherever, through the path of the senses, the consciousness of the Lord is manifested" (verse 114). What is the meaning? When the crest of Kuṇḍalinī is established in the Great Void, the Self becomes united with the mind within the fire of desire, which is characterized by light, residing in the Self of all living beings.

The meaning is that one should offer as an oblation—characterized by the activity of the senses whose rays of consciousness have extended toward external objects—the mind, together with the internalizing mind, through that very same path, according to the method stated in other systems: "by means of the mind-sense, [one offers] the sense-organ to the object" (Nyāya-bhāṣya 1.1.4). This has been stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava:

"In the fire that is the abode of the Great Void, the elements, the senses, the objects, and so forth, are offered together with the mind; this is the oblation performed with the ladle of consciousness. (Verse 146).
This indeed is the internal oblation (*antarahoma*). As it is stated in the *Paddhatis*:
"In the fire of the Self, kindled by the oblation of dharma and adharma, I constantly offer the functions of the senses with the mind as the ladle, by way of the path of Suṣumṇā. (3.106)
He speaks of the *pūrṇāhuti* (the final oblation) as being internal:
"The identity of 'I' and 'this' is conceived in the *sruc* (ladle) of *unmanī*;
the great sacrificial offering (*mahāhavi*) is the essential reality produced from the intensity of churning. (3.107)

Having repeatedly offered oblations in this manner, one who is himself the embodiment of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) should, through perfectly pure offerings and libations consisting of the nature of nectar, transform this entire universe—which bears the form of the sacrificial oblation—into the state of Great Egoity (*mahāhaṃtī*). (Suvā. 39)

According to the method stated in the words of the learned masters, there is the identity of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*); "I-ness" is the subject (*pramātṛ*), "this-ness" is the object (*prameya*), and their identity is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), consisting of the equilibrium of these three.
[One should contemplate] the Brahmic [power] within the Mahāvāgbhava [syllable], which is beautiful with the objects of knowledge that are the scattered words of the universe.

I churn the fire-drill of mantra, which is filled with the mass of reality kindled by the sun of consciousness; it possesses the body of the great light transcending the universe, its innate power, and is inlaid with the three powers inclined toward valid cognition, wherein the fourteenth day resides in the midst.

In accordance with the manner stated in the words of the learned masters, [the offering] is produced from the intensity of the friction of the fire-drill of mantra; it is the form of the *vastu*, that is, the substance (*dravya*), which is the unified totality (*samaṣṭi*) of those three. As it is said in the sequence of the primary tradition (*mukhyāmnāya*): "One should constantly take hold of that *vastu* which becomes the bliss of *ānanda*. It is the "great oblation" (*mahāhavis*). When this oblation, characterized by one's own object of knowledge (*svaprameya-lakṣaṇa*), has been offered...

The light characterized as the subject blazes incessantly; that is the great oblation (*mahāhavis*). This is offered as a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the *sruc* ladle conceived as *unmanī*. *Unmanī* is that which has been previously defined [in 1.34]; she is the *sruc*, from whom [the oblation] flows.
Having filled that *sruc* with the nectar consisting of her own nature, one should offer the full oblation. Having thus offered the oblation of this form:
Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that is established within the body;
the substance that manifests it is drunk by the yogis.
Thus, according to the manner stated in the words of authoritative teachers, the sense of the repetition (*vīpsā*) is: "for as long as the manifestation of bliss continues.

And he himself becomes the very embodiment of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); through the experience of wine and other such things, because of the blossoming of artificial bliss, and through the contemplation of Great Bliss (*mahānanda*), he should become absorbed in that. As it has been said:
By the venerable Vijñānabhairava:

"Through the expansion of the bliss of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arising from the joy produced by eating and drinking, one should contemplate the state of fullness; from that, Great Bliss (*mahānanda*) arises. (Vi.bhai. śloka 71)

What is the meaning? Having repeatedly offered as oblations the clarified butter consisting of the reality of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between "this-ness" (*idantā*) and "I-ness" (*ahantā*), which arises from the friction of the fire-drill of mantra, one becomes the manifest supreme bliss; this is the internal full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). || 3/107-108 ||
Therefore:
"When the essence of *sīdhu*— which consists in the removal of duality— has entered within,
the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) attains stability even without the association with external objects."
Thus, according to the method described in the *Kramodaya*, once [the reality] has become stabilized in the mind, one should perform the worship of the external wheel; thus he says:
"The wise person should worship the Śrīcakra, which takes the form of the expansion of his own self-manifestation. (3/108)

The wise one, through drinking the essence of *sīdhu*, becomes unattached to other objects and his mind becomes steady in self-awareness alone. When the mind is steady, concentration (*dhāraṇā*) becomes steady; when that is steady, meditation (*dhyāna*)—defined as "the one-pointed flow of cognition toward that [object]" (*pratyayaikatānatā*) according to the method taught in the *Yoga-pātañjala-śāstra* (3.2)—comes to be. Without...

Meditation and worship become fruitless. Therefore, having first consecrated the liquor (*āsava*) as nectar (*amṛta*), one should offer it to the gurus beginning with Śiva, and by offering it into the fire of one's own self, one should become one whose intellect is steady in the blazing supreme bliss. This is the meaning.

"The form of the expansion of one's own manifestation" (*svaprathā-prasara-ākāra*): *svaprathā* is one's own consciousness; its "expansion" (*prasara*) refers to its outward movement toward external objects by means of the senses.

Activity (*vyāpāra*) is its manifestation as that very essence. Therefore, one should worship the Śrīcakra, which has that form. The so-called Śrīcakra is nothing else at all; rather, it is the form of the expansion of the deity of one’s own consciousness (*svasaṃvid-devatā*), consisting of the four internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa-catuṣṭaya*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great principle (*mahat*), and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*).

This entire manifold expansion of the sixteen transformations—the five subtle elements, the ten sense organs, their functions, their objects, and the puryaṣṭaka—is what vibrates as the essence of the Śrīcakra. // 3/108 //
He describes the worship of the Śrīcakra with the passage beginning with "Gaṇeśa" and ending with "having performed the worship of the cakra" (3/168):
"O Goddess, one should worship Gaṇeśa and his messenger, as well as Kṣetreśa and his messenger, at the outer door; and one should worship the goddesses, such as Svastikā and the others. (3/109)
One should worship Gaṇeśa and his Śakti Dūtī at the two door-panels of the Śrīcakra, as well as Kṣetreśa known as Baṭuka and his Śakti Dūtikā. This has been stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*:
"He who is capable of dispelling the night of the great delusion of duality and non-duality..."
Like the radiant sun, the one Gaṇeśa, accompanied by his messenger, is victorious.
"The supreme radiance of intuition, like another moon,
that young ascetic (baṭuka) accompanied by his messenger and engaged in the tāṇḍava dance is victorious.
Thus, at the outer gate— that is, in the area outside the entrance of the Śrīcakra— one should worship the goddesses beginning with Svastika.

The four goddesses Sarasvatī, Śrī, Durgā, and Bhadrakālī; the compound meaning is "those of whom Svastikā is the first. Furthermore, there are five: Svāhā, Śubhaṅkarī, Gaurī, Lokadhātrī, and Vāgīśvarī. One should worship these goddesses as singers;
this is well-established in the ritual manuals (paddhatīs). || 3/109 ||
Then, within the inner triangle as well, [one should contemplate] the lineage of gurus situated in three ways.

That is to say, within that Śrīcakra, one should contemplate the lineage of gurus situated in three ways—the triple current consisting of the Divine (divya), the Siddha (siddha), and the Human (mānava)—which is the succession of gurus from Śiva down to one's own guru. By the use of the word "also" (api),...
