The word "should worship" (*yajet*) is to be supplied [from the previous verse]. The lineage of gurus (*guruparamparā*) must be known only from the mouth of the guru, not from common worldly sources; nor is it written in books, because of its extreme secrecy.
And at its end, having invoked that Great Goddess, one should worship her again.
[He saw] the Goddess, who dwells within the Great Lotus Grove, whose form is the bliss of the cause, who rests upon my lap, and who bestows the fruits of desire and will. (3.111)

[We worship] you within that, in the center of the Śrīcakra, in the wheel known as Binda; her whose form was established in the passage: "In the Mahāpadmavana, [we worship] the Guru-pādukā in the Vāgbhava [wheel] situated within the Mahāpadmavana" (3/5).

The thousand-petaled lotus of Akula, facing downwards, is a great forest of lotuses. It rests upon my lap—that is, it dwells in the lap of me, the self-luminous Anāśrita (the Unsupported), who takes refuge in my own body. She is the embodiment of the Bliss of the Cause (*kāraṇānandavigrahā*).
"Cause" (*kāraṇa*) here refers to the causal substance. As he will state in this very context: "One should offer an oblation to me, the Lord of the Fields (*kṣetrāṇāṃ pati*), by means of the Cause."
(3/199) Thus: she whose form (*vigraha*)—her very appearance—is that bliss which arises from drinking that substance. What is the meaning?

It means she whose body consists solely of the supreme bliss flashing forth from drinking the purified substance that has become nectar (*amṛta*). You, the Unattached One (*anāśritā*), my Goddess, whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), who bestows the fruits of desire according to one's wish—that which is desired by will.
O Giver of the fruit of all that [is performed],
O Mother who dwells within the Great Lotus Forest, whose form is the bliss of the cause,
who is devoted to the welfare of all beings— come, come, O Supreme Goddess!
Having invoked with this mantra, one should worship.

Now, if it is asked: "How is it determined that, by the phrase 'residing within the Great Lotus Grove' alone, the Lord Anāśrita and the Goddess Anāśritā are to be invoked here into the wheel and worshipped in the form of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī?"—it is replied as follows:
Even the Lord, who resides within the Mahāpadma forest and is the speaker of all the Āgamas and Śāstras, is indeed Anāśrita (the Unsupported);

his Śakti is likewise Anāśritā for that very reason. Otherwise, how could the statement "O You who reside within the Mahāpadma forest and take refuge in my lap" be logically consistent? As for Sadāśiva and the others...

Although he possesses the status of being a speaker of the scriptures of the Āgamas, nevertheless, he does not reside within the interior of the Mahāpadma forest. As it is stated in the Svacchandasaṃgraha:
"In the center of Anāśrita is the vast sky-lotus."
There, seated upon a lion throne, he was [visible] for an extent of incalculable yojanas.
Resplendent like ten million billion suns, with the moon as his crest-ornament,
the Lord has five faces, ten arms, and fifteen eyes.
Complete in all his limbs, he is the eternal form of Brahman;
omniscient and the creator of all, he is ever intent upon bestowing grace upon everyone.
Studded with all kinds of jewels and adorned on every limb,
the Goddess Anāśritakalā always remains seated upon his lap.
She has five faces, three eyes, ten arms, and the moon as her crest;
the group of four beginning with Vyāpinī is proclaimed to be of that same nature.
Śiva was accompanied by his attendants stationed in the directions from the east to the north,
as well as by hosts of crores and billions of Rudras who were identical in form to him and possessed their own powers.
Served by those Lords of the World, he performs the acts of creation and so forth;
this Blessed One is without support, possessing five faces and likewise three eyes.
Having ten arms, four arms, two arms, and one face, this Sadāśiva, the God of gods, is the speaker of the Kaula Āgamas and other scriptures.
"He proclaimed the innumerable Āgamas through the division of the higher and the lower.
Thus it is said; and in the *Uttarapada* it is also stated:
"In the thousand-petaled lotus of the sky, crowded with white filaments..."
There, the mistress of the family questioned Mahādeva as he sat [there]. (1/1) || 3/110–112 ||
One should worship You with offerings such as food (naivedya) that consist of nothing but You;

the word "You" (bhavatīm) applies here as well. You are she whose characteristic is one's own self-awareness (svasaṃvit). Since the universe consists of the five elements and those elements consist of You, O sinless one, she [the Goddess] is always identical with them.
"And the root-vidyā is composed of that; I shall explain it to you accordingly.
(2/28) Thus, according to the manner previously stated, the five elements are the manifestations of Your will and are Your own forms;
[I worship] the Self, who possesses these five forms, with the five divine offerings.
One should offer the earth together with fragrance, and the sky with a flower.

One should worship with those very offerings, such as the *naivedya* (food offering) and so forth, according to the method stated in the words of authoritative sources: "By incense one worships the air, by the lamp the fire, and again by food the taste. By the phrase "with the *naivedya* and so forth," the perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings are included. [This is done] through the experience of fragrant substances.

Resting in the subject by turning inward (*pratyaṅmukhatayā*) is the offering of fragrance. Resting in the subject by turning inward through the experience of an object possessing beauty, like a beautiful sound, is the offering of the flower. Resting in the subject by turning inward through the experience of an object possessing beauty of touch is the offering of incense. [The same applies] through the experience of an object possessing beauty of form...

The offering of the lamp is resting within the subject by turning inward (*pratyagmukhatayā*). The meaning is that the offering of the food (*naivedya*) is resting within the subject by turning inward through the experience of objects as having a sweet taste. This has been stated in the *Mukhyāmnāyarahasya*:

"One's own deity is to be propitiated by means of fragrances and other objects perceivable through the doors of the senses, according to their true nature; this is the great sacrifice for the knower. Thus it is said. Furthermore, externally, one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings with the meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*) of them as earth, space, air, fire, and water.
One should offer it to the Goddess; such is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the ritual services (upacāra). || 3/112 ||
Furthermore, within the triangle, there are the forms of reflections of its own radiance. (3.112)
These are the eternal goddesses (nityās) consisting of their respective lunar days (tithis), corresponding to the essential points of one's desired aims.

"In the triangle of the Śrīcakra," that is, within the three lines of the triangle; "the reflections of its radiance" are the fifteen qualities said to belong to the elements. This is because, according to the method previously stated in the verse, "Śivā is composed of those [qualities] of the elements" (2.30), the Śrīvidyā—whose body consists of fifteen syllables and whose nature is the qualities of the elements—manifests there.

They consist of fifteen reflected forms, each embodying a specific lunar day (*tithi*)—that is, having the nature of the lunar days beginning with the first (*pratipad*) and numbering fifteen—which correspond to optional rites (*kāmyakarma*). According to the method stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*, "the worship of the external wheel (*bāhyacakra*), which bestows the accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as great subjugation (*mahāvaśya*) and so forth, is the optional rite"; thus, they assume forms possessing hands, feet, and other limbs that are appropriate to those rites.
Because they are devoid of arising and destruction, they are eternal; therefore, Kāmeśvarī is eternal, as is Bhagamālinī,
Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and Vahnivāsinī.
Mahāvidyeśvarī, Dūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī,
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā.
Jvālāmālinī and Citrā—thus are the sixteen Nityās.
(1/26–28) These are as stated in the *Catuḥśatika* scripture. Furthermore, from the word "again," the phrase "one should worship" is to be supplied. (3/112–113)
There, in the wheel that deludes the three worlds, are the manifest Yoginīs. (3.113)

There, in the *śrīcakra*, within the *trailokyamohana* wheel—which, according to the previously stated etymology (1/82), is characterized by three squares—the *prakaṭayoginīs* [are to be worshipped]; this connects with the phrase "they are to be sacrificed to" (*yaṣṭavyāḥ*) which occurs later (1/116). || 3/113 ||
He states the etymological definition of the term *prakaṭa* (manifest):

"Because they possess the gross form of the *mātṛkā*s and because they pervade the skin and other [sheaths], the Yoginīs should be known as *prakaṭā*s within the self that is the primary cause of the gross universe. (3/114)

The *mātṛkās* are *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*. Among these, the gross form consisting of the fifty phonemes from *a* to *kṣa* is the nature of *vaikharī*. As it is stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*: "The gross [form] consists of fifty aspects. Because it has that nature—that is, because it consists of the eight groups of phonemes which are the gross forms of the *mātṛkā*s and the *vaikharī*—[it is so described].
And [it refers] to the *siddhis*, such as the *brāhmya* and others. As it is said in the *Catuḥśatikā*:
"I praise her, the Mistress of the eight great *siddhis* arising from the eight groups, in whom the eight measures (*mātrā*) reside according to the sequence of the classes of letters" (1.11).

"Because of their pervasiveness over the skin and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and *ojas* are included. Because they pervade these, the [energies] beginning with Brāhmī reside in the *cakras* of the skin, the base of the eyebrows, blood, the buttocks, flesh, the navel, fat, the heart, bone, the throat, marrow, the mouth, semen, the nostrils, *ojas*, and the forehead.

The statement "in the self that sustains the gross universe" (*sthūlaviśvapradhātmani*) is an explanation of its gross nature. For this very reason, it is called *viśvapradhā*—the "sustainer of the universe"—because it is the *viśvambharā* (the earth). It resides within the *trailokyamohana* cakra, which consists of the three levels of the earth-abode (*bhūgṛha*).

Furthermore, because it is the gross form of the *mātṛkā* and is a constituent part of *vaikharī*, it is [associated] with the skin and other bodily constituents (*dhātu*), as these are parts of the gross body.

The meaning is that because the Trailokyamohana-cakra is all-pervasive and consists of the gross material world (sthūla-viśvambharā), the accomplishments (siddhis) contained within it, such as Brāhmī and the others, are to be understood as manifest. || 3/114 ||
He describes the meditation preceded by the utterance of the names of those who dwell in the final earth-dwelling:
"O Great Goddess, the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* are established there;
they are exceedingly red in color and likewise hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (3.115)
Holding the great jewel of contemplation, they bestow the fruits of one's desires;
these are the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, as described in the *Catuḥśatī-śāstra* starting from "Aṇimā at the western gate" (1.153), namely:
*laghimā*, *mahimā*, *īśitā*, *vaśitā*, *prākāmya*, *bhukti*, *icchā*, *prāpti*, and that which is called *sarvakāma*.
The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the *siddhis*. The eight established *siddhis* are those well-known from the lexicons (*nighaṇṭu*).
However, the intended meaning here is that there are ten: beginning with the left calf, they proceed in order starting from the left.

Because it has been stated in that very place [at 3/79–80]: "One should place the eight siddhis upon them, and two should be placed on the soles of the feet. *Mahāratna* is the *cintāmaṇi*. The rest is clear. (3/115–116)
O Dear One, the deities beginning with Brāhmī should also be worshipped there in their proper sequence. (3.116)
The [deities] beginning with Brāhmī—namely Brahmāṇī at the western gate—are those mentioned in the *Catuḥśatī-śāstra*.
In that very same [mandala], they are to be worshipped within the central square (*madhyacaturasra*) in successive order. || 3/116 ||
He describes the meditation on each of them individually:
"Brahmāṇī is yellow in color and adorned with four faces;
she grants boons and fearlessness with her hands, and is radiant with a water-pot, a rosary, and a garland. (3.117)
The word "with hands" (*karaiḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The remainder is clear. || 3/117 ||
Māheśvarī is white in color, three-eyed, and holds a trident; she carries a skull, a deer, and an axe in her hands, O Dear One. (3.118)
Holding a trident in one hand and bearing a skull, a deer, and an axe with three others,
the supreme goddess Kaumārī— yellow in color, holding a spear and a javelin, and with hands granting boons and fearlessness— should be meditated upon. (3.118–119)
This is clear. ||119 ||
Vaiṣṇavī is dark-complexioned, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus in her lotus-like hands, and she is adorned with divine ornaments. (3.120)
Vārāhī has a dark complexion and is radiant with the face of a boar;
she holds a plow, a mace, a sword, and a shield in her arms. (3.121)
This is clear. 3/120–121.
Aindrī is dark green in color, and her hands shine with a vajra and an utpala;
this is clear. 3/122.
Cāmuṇḍā is black in color, and she likewise holds a trident and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka).
Holding a sword and a vetālaka with her right hands, she holds a snake, a shield, and a bell with others, and a skull-cup [with yet another]. (3.123)

A *vetāla* is a specific kind of *piśāca*. The meaning is that he holds a trident, a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), a sword, and a *vetāla* in his right hands, and a snake, a shield, a bell, and a skull-cup in his left hands. (3/122–123)
Mahālakṣmī, however, is yellowish in luster; the Supreme Goddess holds two lotuses, a mirror, and a mātuluṅga fruit. (3.124)
This is clear. Now, one might ask: why are the ten mudrās not mentioned as objects of worship within the inner square? True;

because they are not mentioned in the *Catuḥśatī-śāstra*, they have not been described here as primary [objects of worship]. However, they are indicated by the statement: "The best of practitioners should place the ten mudrās at the *mūlādhāra* during the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Śrīcakra" (3.77). Therefore, regarding the inner square...
One should also worship the ten mudrās. || 3/124 ||
Having meditated in this manner, one should then worship these [goddesses] and Tripurā, the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśī).

"In this manner" means according to the method described. Having meditated upon these manifest yoginīs, one should worship Tripurā, the Mistress of the Wheel of the Enchanter of the Three Worlds (trailokyamohana-cakreśī). || 3/125 ||
And, with the intention of expressing the non-difference between the Vidyā and the deity, he states the etymological definition of the Vidyā of the Trailokyamohana-cakreśvarī:
"She is remembered as the purifier of the hands because of the stainlessness of the organs of action. (3/125)

"Regarding the two—the impure *ātmatattva* and the *karma-karaṇa*—the supreme purification of these two is considered to consist of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of their dissolution into the pure reality (*śuddhatattva*). (Cidgaganacandrikā, Stanza 11). According to this statement of ours, because the *ātmatattva* is impure, [so too are] the organs of action (*karmendriya*).

Because the two hands fall within the [categories of the] principles (*tattva*), and because they are organs of action (*karmendriya*)—being impure and consisting of effect and instrument—the purification of the hands, which are effects, consists in the contemplation of their dissolution into non-duality with Śiva within the pure principle that is their own cause; this is what is taught here.
This has been declared and explained in the *Smṛti*. (3/125)
The perfection arising from the purification of the task, namely *aṇimā*, is established here.
I perform a pure, conscious purification of the two hands—which take the form of the body touched by the causal Self—residing in the fingers, which purifies through touch. (Su. Vā. 24)

According to the method stated in the words of the learned, "purity of the effect" (*kārya-śuddhi*) means its resolution into being nothing more than its causal state. Since the self (*ātman*), which exists within the most subtle cause described in the Śruti as "smaller than the smallest" (*aṇoḥ aṇīyān*, Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.20), achieves subtlety (*aṇimā*), this is the accomplishment of *aṇimā*. And that [accomplishment] resides here in the wheel of the Deluder of the Three Worlds (*trailokya-mohana-cakra*).
The intended meaning. || 3/126 ||
Regarding the worship in the second wheel along with its latent impressions (*savāsana*), he says:
"In the mass of sixteen vibrations, the digits (*kalā*) consist of wonder. (3.126)

Of the sixteen winds beginning with prāṇa, those whose nature is vitalizing (prāṇana) are the seeds; because they are of the nature of vowels, they take the form of seeds through their creative differentiation (kalanā). (3.127)
O Dear One, because they are internal and secret, the Yoginīs—beginning with Kāmākarṣaṇī and Rūpā—are established as preeminent within the process of emanation. (3.128)
One should worship on the left at the wheel named Sarvāśāpūraṇa. Spanda is the expansion of Parā in the form of the *tattva* (principle). This has been stated in the *Parāpañcāśikā*:
"The first vibration (*spanda*) of the Lord desiring to emanate is known as the Śiva-tattva" (verse 18). By that [wheel], there are sixteen.

The "vibrations" (*spandāḥ*) are the sixteen transformations consisting of the elements, the senses, and the mind; their "conglomeration" (*sandohaḥ*) is that [totality]. What is called "wonder" (*camatkāraḥ*) is the emergence of a pre-eminence of consciousness within that [conglomeration]. As it is said in the *Kramodaya*: "Wonder attains stability even without contact with sense objects. The sixteen *kalās*, which are composed of that [consciousness] and have entered into the elements, senses, and mind, flash forth as being of its very nature.

This is the meaning. The *kalās* are sixteen in number and are designated as such. Those whose first is *prāṇa* are the ten well-known vital airs (*vāyu*), namely apāna, udāna, samāna, vyāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. The other six are to be sought in other scriptural traditions (*āgama*). Of all these, they consist of the nature of *prāṇa*.

For the vital breaths and so forth consist of the act of breathing; indeed, the meaning is that these [energies] also consist of the act of breathing for those very vital breaths and so on. They are the seeds because they are conjoined with the *bindu*. They are the sixteen vowels, beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga*, because they consist of those [vowels]. This follows from the process of differentiation (*kalana*), since they have attained the state of being vowels conjoined with the *bindu*.

Due to their activity (*kalanā*), they possess the form of seeds—that is, their own respective seed-natures. Because the sixteen transformations exist within them in a latent state, like the layers of bark and other tissues, these Yoginīs are composed of that [inner essence] and remain hidden. By virtue of being "internal" (*antaraṅga*), the internal organ is the intellect (*buddhi*); since these [Yoginīs] consist of its wondrous manifestation, they too are internal.

For this very reason, they are "protected" (*guptāḥ*). In the wheel called *Sarvāśāpūraṇa*, however, regarding the term "yoginīs," the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). [The goddesses] beginning with Kāmākarṣaṇarūpā and Kāmākarṣaṇarūpā are those mentioned in the *Catuḥśatī* scripture. Because of the predominance of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), the left wheel alone is primary in the process of emanation; therefore, of this very [wheel]...
Because the wheel has the nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), one should therefore worship those Yoginīs with the left hand—that is, one should worship them in a counter-clockwise sequence.

The sixteen modifications (*vikāra*) are of the nature of playful manifestations. Each of them is conjoined with the sixteen vowels together with the *bindu*, representing the sixteen vital winds (*vāyu*) beginning with *prāṇa*, whose essence consists of the power that animates the world.

The meaning is that one should worship, by way of the left path (*vāmamārga*), all the *kalās*—Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others—which are hidden within the inner consciousness as being composed of the sixteen transformations, in the wheel that fulfills all desires. (3/126–129)
He describes their meditation:
"These indeed hold nooses and hooks; they are red, clothed in red garments. (3.129)
This is clear. 3/129 ||
He states the perfection attained through the worship of the deities of that wheel:
"The perfection consisting of the purification of the vital breath is the power of lightness (*laghimā*) for the experiencing self."

According to the manner stated in the Śruti, "That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power" (Ṛgveda 10.129.2), the dissolution of the vital airs, such as prāṇa and the rest, into their own cause— that which breathes as a single essence together with *svadhā* in the form of the universal animation— is what is called their purification. Here, the word *prāṇa* is intended to indicate the vital air (*vāyu*) in general.
Through that, when there is purity characterized by the dissolution of the vital breath (vāyu), there arises a meditative absorption (samādhi) characterized by the dissolution of the mind.
Then, for the living self (jīva)—the experiencer who has become one in essence with that [purity]—there arises the supernatural power (siddhi) of levity (laghimā), which is a quality of that [state].
Tripureśī, the mistress of the wheel (cakreśī), is to be worshipped with all ritual offerings.

The meaning is that just as the Root Goddess was worshipped with all the ritual offerings such as perfumes and so forth, in the same manner the Mistress of the Wheel, Tripureśī, is to be worshipped in the Sarvāśāparipūraṇacakra. || 3/130 ||
He describes the worship along with its latent impressions (*savāsana*) in the third wheel:

"Residing in the eightfold city of enjoyment (*bhogapuryaṣṭaka*) permeated by the experience of the Kaulas, they are connected with the eightfold *vāgbhava* and are subtle by virtue of their nature as the [phonetic] classes (*varga*). (3.131)
But all those [energies], beginning with Anaṅgakusumā, are more secret, consisting in the agitation of all things;
"Kula" is the body composed of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), and the experience of its objects is "I am emaciated."

"I am fat," and so forth; the individual soul (*jīva*) is permeated by that [ego] because it is dependent upon it. Its "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*), which is the locus of its experience, is considered to consist of:

consciousness (*citi*), the mind (*citta*), sentience (*caitanya*), cognition (*cetana*), the two types of karma, the individual soul (*jīva*), limited agency (*kalā*), and the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*). This is known as the "city of eight."

Thus, according to the method stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*, there is the subtle *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body), and those [energies] resting upon it are connected with the eight *vāgbhava* vowels (*ai* sounds) by virtue of being composed of them. The "subtle group" refers to the group of eight letters of the *vaikhari* speech-level. As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*: "The gross [level] consists of fifty forms..."

"The subtle [group] is remembered as the eight octads. This is because they have that as their essential nature and consist of that. They are "more secret" because they are composed of the eight groups of letters of the subtle *vaikhārī* speech; thus, the meaning is that these too are subtle, and being most internal, they are even more secret. All of them, beginning with Anaṅgakusumā and so forth—Anaṅgakusumā is first (1/163).
It should be understood that those [deities] mentioned in the *Catuḥśatī* scripture are to be worshipped in the third wheel, called Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa, which is an eight-petalled lotus. (3/131–132)
He describes their meditation:
"Adorned with red jackets. (3.132)
With their beautiful hair tied in braids, bearing bows and arrows, they were auspicious;
this is clear. 3/132–133.
Of the sovereign lord who is the enjoyer, whose nature consists of cognitions possessing various forms, and who is the object of enjoyment.

The Supreme Goddess is the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī), whose form is the purification of the intellect, endowed with the quality of beauty that rests upon the words *piṇḍa* and the rest. (3.134)
She, whose form is the perfection of greatness, is to be worshipped with all ritual offerings.

Having gone out through the doors of the senses, the intellect—which is a transformation of the internal organ—assumes various forms, taking on the shapes of the respective objects of those senses. Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the objects of enjoyment, having that [intellect] as their essence; he is the enjoyer of them.
The knower (*pramātā*)—that very lord of the earth, the sovereign, which is to say the *kṣetrajña*—[possesses] the repose of the "bodies" and so forth;

that is, the repose of the states consisting of the body, word, form, and that which transcends form. Liberation is [attained] in the fourth state (*turyapada*), which transcends form. On this point, there is the authoritative statement:

"O Six-faced One, those who are liberated in the aggregate, liberated in the word, and liberated in form—those who are liberated in that which transcends form are truly liberated; of this there is no doubt. (Jñānakārikā 1.4–5).
That very [beauty] is [actually] ugliness, characterized by the supreme misfortune of the impermanent and impure cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Beauty is precisely the manifestation of the nature of Supreme Śiva—who is the source of all, the object of eternal purity, the locus of supreme love, and desired by all; that alone is the quality (*guṇa*), and she is endowed with it. By virtue of having that as her sole essence, she is the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*) known as Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī (the All-Agitating), the Mistress of the third wheel. What is the meaning? [It is] of the subject who perceives objects such as sound, which consist of consciousness.

The meaning is that Tripurasundarī—the Mistress of the Third Cakra—is the primordial one characterized by the repose of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) beyond the forms of the body and words; she is endowed with the beauty of oneness with those three. She is of the nature of the purification of the intellect (buddhiśuddhi);
"purification of the intellect" means the dissolution into the non-conceptual Self of Consciousness after abandoning contact with sense objects, and she is of that form. For this very reason—

She is the form of the accomplishment of greatness (*mahimā-siddhi*). Because of the coloring (*uparāga*) of the intellect by that which is beyond its object, the greatness—the state of being great—of the conscious self (*cidātman*) is accomplished.
Cakreśvarī, whose nature is that accomplishment, is to be worshipped with all the previously mentioned offerings, such as fragrance and the rest. (3/133–135)
Regarding the fourth wheel, he describes worship together with its latent impressions:
"For one whose consciousness has blossomed through the piercing of the twelve knots. (3.135)
Preceded by the experience of Śakti through the immersion in the state ending in the Visarga, there are twelve knots—two knots each for the six cakras, one above and one below.
On this very point, he will say later: "O Dear One, by the piercing of the twelve knots, [one attains] the phonemes within the channels" (3.184). When it shines forth...

According to the method taught in the *Catuḥśatī* scripture—“from the seat of the Śṛṅgāṭa, she whose form is crooked” (4/12)—there is the penetration of the state ending in *visarga* by means of the piercing of the twelve knots of the *kuṇḍalinī*, which is consciousness (*saṃvit*) shining forth and arising.
*Visarga* is the sixteenth vowel; thus, by the word *visarga*, the number sixteen is understood. Therefore...
That which ends with the visarga, which is the end of the sixteen,
which has the form of the sixteen digits, which is the end of the elements and resides in space—
that is known as the "end of the sixteen," the lunar orb situated in the station of space.
Thus, according to the method stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*, that very [state] is the "descent of the ten" (*daśāveśa*), because it is the form of the awakening of consciousness;
its "descent" (*tadāveśa*) is attachment (*āsakti*) to that. As it is said in this very [text]: "Attached to the lunar orb in the sky, she whose nature is a stream of nectar" (2.71).
This occurs preceded by the experience of Śakti, [arising] from Kuṇḍalinī who has risen from the root.

The experience of Śakti consists precisely in the conceptualization of the attachment to the lunar orb in the void (*vyomendumaṇḍala*), through the process of piercing the accumulation of knots in the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakragranthi*).
This [experience] is preceded by that [piercing]. The phrase "the arising of the future phonemes" is an adverbial modifier of the action. (3/135–136)

Having described the latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of the manifest speech (*vaikharī*) within the three wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana, he now describes the latent impression consisting of the intermediate speech (*madhyamā*) in the form of the *būta* syllables within the three wheels beginning with Sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka:
"By means of the expansions of the power of unfolding (*unmeṣaśakti*), which are primarily characterized by the power of will (*icchāśakti*). (3.136)

In the same way, [the phonemes] are also to be understood through the four groups of letters (*varṇacatuṣṭaya*) which consist of agitated combinations, as well as through the letters *va*, *e*, *dya*, *rṇa*, and so forth, when they are mixed and permeated by the Will (*icchā*). (3/137)

[The mantras] are endowed with two syllables consisting of the form of the immersion into the *kula-śakti*, which take the form of the union (*saṃghaṭṭa*) with *akula*. *Akula* is the white thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head (*brahmarandhra*) facing downward; the letter *a* situated there is the foremost of all letters, the Light, the Supreme Śiva. Thus it is said: "The letter *a* is the foremost of all letters, the Light, the Supreme Śiva."

The letter *A*, as described in the *Saṃketapaddhati*, which is of the nature of Paramaśiva, is indicated by the word *akula*. By that [word], "union" (*saṃghaṭṭa*) means connection; [the letters] are of that form. They are primarily characterized by the power of will (*icchāśakti*). The letter *I* is the power of will. They are the expansions of the power of unfolding (*unmeṣaśakti*). The letter *U* is the power of unfolding. This has been stated in the *Parāpañcāśikā*:
"In the supreme will, there is unfolding, bliss, and non-deficiency;
and the existence and swelling of the powers of action, will, and knowledge—these are the six" (verse 32).
What is the meaning? It refers to the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), which is the *Kulakuṇḍalinī* arising from the Root, [united] with the letter 'A' situated in the *Akula*.
When there is a conjunction (*saṃghaṭṭa*) of those two, the letter *e* arises. When there is a conjunction of their very power of unfolding (*unmeṣa-śakti*), the letter *o* arises.
The meaning is that when there is a conjunction of those two with *A* (the Absolute, *akula*), the letters *ai* and *au* arise.
As it is said in the *Parāpañcāśikā*:
"When the powers of Anuttara and Ānanda are joined within the power of Will,
the triangle and the hexagon become established within that Will" (verse 24). By means of the union with Unmeṣa, these two indeed manifest the clear form of the power of Action.
It has been said: "The trident of the triple union of powers devours duality" (verses 35–36). And:
"Even those conditioned by mixed desires have ascended to the inner state of Will and Power; they consist of the world, both manifest and unmanifest."

"Four letters from the other [tradition] are of neuter nature when combined. (Śloka 33). According to this method stated in the *Parāpañcāśikā*, the gross letters are those of neuter nature, produced by the mixture of the Lord of Akula (*akuleśa*) and the Navel (*nābhi*); by these as well. In that context, only the two short vowels are to be taken. For this very reason, there is one letter in Akula.

The second [vowel] consists of *icchā* (will), the other is *unmeṣa* (expansion), and there is the supreme neuter (*ṣaṇḍha*) along with the two short vowels; thus, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*—these nine are the vowels in the *cit*. In the seed-syllable (*bīja*) denoting existence (*sattā*), which consists of the knowable (*vedya*), the *ūṣman* letters, and the letters beginning with *sa*, the world begins with *sa* and ends with *māyā*.
"Only this remains, its form as a causal condition having been dissolved" (Śloka 44).

According to the method stated in the *Parāpañcāśikā*, the sibilants (*ūṣman*) consist of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) that constitute the object of knowledge (*vedya*), because another Tantric text states: "The sibilants are *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*. Such [principles] are that which constitutes the beginning of this [series].

The letter *ha* itself is to be known as the *vedya-uṣman* (the audible breath-sound) beginning with *ha*; [this is indicated] by the letters beginning with that. Here, one word "beginning" (*ādi*) is to be supplied. It is accompanied by two letters whose nature is the immersion (*samāveśa*) of *kula-śakti*. *Kula-śakti* is Kuṇḍalinī;
her "immersion" consists of the two places of arising and resting, namely the *ādhāra* and the *brahmarandhra*. That is their form.

The two syllables consist of *la* and *va*. According to the method stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*, beginning with "the foundational lotus is yellow, four-petaled, and well-filamented" and ending with "for this is the earthly lotus," the syllable *la* represents the foundational lotus because it is of the nature of earth (*pārthiva*).
O Maheśvarī, at the Brahmarandhra, four finger-breadths above, is the Kula-lotus, white,
endowed with beautiful filaments, possessing a thousand petals, and facing downwards.

By this and other passages ending with "the all-pervading, absolute Śakti, raining down a flood of nectar," according to the method stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*, the letter *va* consists of nectar. [The [mantra] is] endowed with these two letters.

What is the meaning? From the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of the Kuṇḍalinī, who is the Will-nature of Kula-śakti, there arises the group of fourteen phonemes—*a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, ai, o, au, ha, ya, ra, va, la*—through the penetration of the *Akula* state by means of piercing the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) and the twelve knots (*dvādaśagranthi*) of the five voids (*pañcagagana*). This has been stated in another scripture (*āgama*) in the context of the extraction of the *bhūtalipi*: [The text continues with the extraction of the phonemes.]
"The five short vowels are the phonemes of conjunction: ether, air, fire, water, and earth" (Śā.
Ti. 7.2). This means that the fourteen-spoked wheel consists of those [elements]. (3/136–138)
He states the latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding the two words "bestower of good fortune" (*saubhāgyadāyaka*) which have come down through the lineage of tradition:
"O Maheśvarī, because it has issued forth as being composed of the essence of Śakti. (3/138)

These [phonemes], which have come down through the lineage of oral tradition within the wheel that bestows good fortune (*saubhāgyadāyaka-cakra*), are the essence and expansion of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*)—that is, of Kuṇḍalinī. According to the method previously described, they arise from being identical with and produced by the union of the Absolute Śiva (*anuttara-śiva*) residing in the station of *Akula*; such is the case for these phonemes.
Because these phonemes have issued forth, the powers beginning with *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* possess a lineage succession (*sampradāya-krama*) that has been transmitted;

for, according to the previously stated method, the emergence of the phonemes is attained from the mouth of the Guru, as it is said: "The lineage, which consists of Great Awakening, resides in the mouth of the Guru" (2.36). Furthermore, these [powers] are identical with those [phonemes]. Therefore, they...
The meaning is that they have come down through the sequence of oral tradition. || 3/138–139 ||
Due to the power of the excellence of its form, which consists of uninterrupted expansion. (3.139)
O Goddess, these auspicious [powers] named according to their meaning, beginning with Aṇimā and starting with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, bestow purity upon the body, the senses, and so forth. (3.140)
Furthermore, the accomplishment of lordship (īśitvasiddhi) resides within the three cities of the aforementioned form;
Tripuravāsinī is established through the various afflictions such as yoga and the like. (3.141)
"O Goddess, one should worship all these with every type of offering;

they resemble the *aṇimā* [siddhi] and are exceedingly red in color. (3/115). Thus, as previously stated, they possess forms similar to the *aṇimā* perfection (*siddhi*). "Beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī"—that is, the power (*śakti*) Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī (1/165).

These are stated in the *Catuḥśatī* treatise and other works. Uninterrupted manifestation is the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the non-duality of Śiva; that alone is "good fortune" (*saubhāgya*), because its object is the non-difference from Paraśiva, who is the supreme object of love and the most fortunate. That alone is "strength" (*bala*) or power (*śakti*); through union with that, [one transcends] everything that is impermanent, impure, and supremely unfortunate—

Due to the union with Śakti, which establishes the auspiciousness characterized by the *ahantā* (I-consciousness) that is supremely beautiful, supremely desirable, the supreme object of love that opposes the cycle of transmigration marked by the characteristic of aversion, and [is] the supreme Śiva— [this occurs] in the wheel (*cakra*) which possesses a name whose meaning is true to its sense,
which is endowed with syllables of favorable meaning, which bears a designation, and which bestows auspicious fortune.
The word "should worship" (*sampūjayet*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The "body" (*deha*) is characterized as a collection of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the subject (*pramātṛ*) who identifies with that ego-sense (*ahaṃtābhimānin*) is indicated. The "senses" (*akṣāṇi*) are the organs of perception, which are the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) in the form of sense-objects are included.
They are grasped. Their purification is their resting solely in consciousness (*cid-eka-viśrānti*); [the text] bestows that.

In that purification, the sacrificer’s sovereignty—that is, his freedom—is accomplished. And this [purification] resides here in the "three cities" (*pura-traya*)—characterized as subject, means of knowledge, and object—as it is the dwelling place of consciousness. Regarding this very point, he will say later:

"...the nourisher of the ancient [distinctions] of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge" (3/150). This refers to the distinctions such as those between yoga and other afflictions (*kleśa*).

According to the method stated in other systems (*tantrāntara*), the self (*ātman*) is conjoined with the mind (*manas*), the mind with the sense organ (*indriya*), and the sense organ with the object (*artha*), because of the rule that sense organs function by reaching their objects;
thus, it proceeds from the sense organ which is in contact with the object, according to its respective form among the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
The expansion of the rays of consciousness and their conjunction constitute *yoga*; that itself is the primordial affliction (*ādikleśa*).

For the affliction, or the state of being afflicted, consists precisely in the external coloring of the Self—which is non-attached, non-dual, and undivided consciousness—by way of the mind, the senses, and their objects; it is through the distinction from that [state] that, by turning inward and attaining identity with that [Self], [affliction ceases].
Difference (*bheda*) is the resting within another subject. As it is said in the *Parāpañcāśikā*:
"Salutation to the ocean of Śiva-consciousness, whose body is the subject, and who is the ground of rest for all the various rivers of consciousness divided by difference."
Also in the *Stotrāvalī*:
"Wherever the rays converge, there the All-pervasive Lord (*vibhu*) alone unfolds. Thus, Tripuravāsinī is established;

she is the Mistress of the Fourth Wheel (*caturthacakreśvarī*), whose nature is the repose within the three cities previously mentioned. These are the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*) who are to be worshipped.
Accompanied by the Mistress of the Wheel of Siddhis, one should worship all of them with all the ritual offerings, beginning with perfumes and so forth. (3/139–142)
He describes the worship of the fifth wheel along with its latent impressions: "Of the eternal sounds whose nature resides in the nine apertures... (3.142).
In the form of the great universal (mahāsāmānya), she consists of the nature of excluded sounds;
through the ten vowels, which are like shadows of both unstable and stable objects of cognition, [she manifests]. (3.143)

The Kula and Kaulika Yoginīs are the bestowers of all accomplishments (siddhis). They belong to those eternal ones who have cultivated [the practice] as long as the body exists; they are known by the names of Nāda, Avikṛta, Śūnya, Sparśana, Ādhvan, Bindu, Śakti, Bīja, and Akṣara; and they reside within the nine apertures of the self.
The nine apertures are the nine supports (*ādhāra*), which consist of the portions of space located within the *suṣumnā*.
They are known as the *ādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūra*, *anāhata*, the *vajrapadma* above that, *kaṇṭha*, *lambikā*, *viśuddha*, and *ājñā*. As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:

The Foundation (ādhāra), the Self-Consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna), the Jewel-Abode (maṇipūra), the Unstruck (anāhata), the Central (madhyama), the Vajra-Throat (vajrakaṇṭha), the Hanging Tongue (lambikā), and the Purification (viśuddhikā).
"Know that the Command (ājñā) is ninefold and the six chakras are reduced by three.

Thus, for those whose selves abide in these [chakras], [it exists] in the form of the Great Universal (mahāsāmānya). The "Great" is the universal totality (samaṣṭi), characterized by sound devoid of distinctions and lacking beginning or end; it exists in that form. [The other] consists of the form of differentiated sounds (vyāvṛttadhvani). In this way...

The sound (*dhvani*) is differentiated and divided tenfold; it has that as its form, meaning it consists of the subtle and intermediate forms beginning with the unmodified *ādināda*. [This pertains] to objects of cognition, whether unstable or stable. Unstable objects of cognition are those consisting of action, falling within the domain of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), known as speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure; stable objects of cognition are...
The objects of the sense organs—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—are those which are perceived as either unstable or stable.

By means of their shadow-forms, that is, their reflected counterparts, they are manifested through the ten syllables of the two *ṭa* and *ta* classes; this is the understood remainder. These are the Yoginīs of the Kula and Kaulika traditions. For this very reason, the ten sense organs are the constituent parts of the *kula*, which is the body.
They are not denoted by the word *kula*; rather, because of their connection with that [Kula], the ten external objects are called *kaulikāḥ*.
Those who possess a union (*yoga*)—that is, a relationship characterized by the nature of cause and effect—with those [objects] are the *kulakaulikayoginīs*.
Now, according to the procedure for extracting the *bhūtalipi*, the *kavarga* and *cavarga* should follow in sequence; why then are the *ṭavarga* and *tavarga* [used]?

Regarding that ten-spoked [wheel], how are they described in reverse order? It is said: because the two wheels of the fourteen-spoked and ten-spoked [wheels] are of the nature of *sthiti* (stasis), and because the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) is a constituent part of the *madhyamā*, and because the *madhyamā* itself is of the nature of *sthiti*, this sequence of stasis involves a transposition of the classes (*varga*). For this very reason, by way of its subtle *madhyamā* self which is the cause of that [manifestation]:
This is the description of this wheel as being composed of sound (*nāda*).

"Bestowers of all accomplishments" means they bestow accomplishment—defined as the realization and the resting of the subject—upon everything previously mentioned, namely the entire range of objects of the cognitive and active senses. (3/142–144)
He describes their meditation:
"They are white, wearing white garments, and adorned with white ornaments. (3.144)
This is clear. 3/144 ||
He states the systematic presentation of the wheel that accomplishes all aims:

"Because of the application of the mantras' own manifestation as their form, [the deities] beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā reside in the wheel called 'Accomplisher of All Aims' (Sarvārthasādhaka), which is so named according to its literal meaning. (3.145)
The goddesses beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā and ending with Sarvasiddhipradā are those mentioned in the *Catuḥśatī* scripture (1/161).

Regarding mantras—defined as previously stated (2/1) as possessing "reflection" (*manana*) and "protection" (*trāṇa*)—because they consist of the manifestation of one's own nature, the "manifestation" (*prathā*) of the practitioner whose self is Śiva is the cultivation of the state of "I am Śiva" (*śivāhambhāva*). That itself constitutes reflection and protection.

Because of its connection with that: in the *Sarvārthasādhaka-cakra*, which possesses a name according to its meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñaka*) and is endowed with a designation consistent with the purpose of accomplishing all goals, one accomplishes the goal—the supreme aim, which is liberation—for all practitioners through the meditation (*manana*) characterized by the contemplation of the identity of Śiva and the self (*ahambhāva*); thus, due to this distinction, they are said to be "established" in the *Sarvārthasādhaka-cakra*.
The remainder. 3/145.

Having first provided an etymological derivation of the meaning of her own name, he speaks thus to Cakreśvarī: "O Maheśānī, you are the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakranāyikā) because you are the cause of the prosperity of the three worlds; furthermore, O Tripurāśrī, you arise from the purity of mantra. (3/146)
The attainment of mastery has been explained; one should worship all of these.

According to the etymologies "the world (*loka*) is that which observes," "the world is the act of observing," and "the world is that which is observed," [these goddesses] are the cause of the prosperities of the three worlds—characterized by the subject, the means of knowledge, and the object—which consist in their complete repose within the perfect knower.

The meaning is that Tripurāśrī, the sovereign of the fifth wheel, is to be worshipped. The purification of mantras consists of the cultivation of their consciousness-nature (*cinmayatā*) through the recitation characterized by dissolution at the time of *unmanī*, according to the previously mentioned method beginning with "In Akula and that which is called Viṣu" (1.25). Through such purification of the mantra, the practitioner attains mastery (*vaśitva*) in the creation of the entire universe.

The attainment of such supreme Śiva-hood consists in the realization of sovereignty over both protection and withdrawal; and that, within this wheel, is the accomplishment of mastery (*vaśitva-siddhi*). One should worship all these deities of the enclosure together with the accomplishments of the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*).
He describes the worship of the sixth cakra along with its latent impressions (vāsanā):
"O Goddess, [the deities] are manifested by Kuṇḍalinī, who is turned upward and downward. (3/147)

Because they have emerged externally by the will of the Kula, consisting of the manifestation of the letters beginning with *ka*, they are to be expressed as the Nigarbha Yoginīs in the form of immersion into one's own essential nature. (3.148)
"In the wheel that effects all possession (*sarvāveśakara*) and the wheel that effects all protection (*sarvarakṣākara*), the supreme [deities] beginning with Sarvajñā are situated;
when she flashes forth with faces upward and downward... (4/12)—thus it is stated in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra*.

By means of the upward-facing [Kuṇḍalinī], she attains the Supreme Being who resides in the *kula*; then, by the downward-facing Kuṇḍalinī entering the *mūlādhāra* for the sake of the creation of the universe—
being manifested (i.e., made manifest) because of its existence in the causal state—

and by the will of *kula* (*kulecchayā*), that is, by the will to create that *kula* characterized as described above, which consists of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

Due to its external manifestation, [the energy] consists of the unfolding of the phonemes beginning with *ka* and so forth; by the will to create the *kula*— characterized by the subject, the means of knowledge, and the object, which consists of the three principles (*tattva*) that comprise the totality of the thirty-six principles—
it issues forth externally from Paraśiva, who resides in *akula*, as the Kuṇḍalinī who contains within her all the principles and phonemes.
The meaning is that she is manifested as the expansion of the ten phonemes beginning with *ka*. They are called "nigarbha-yoginīs" because they are to be expressed by the term *nigarbha-yoginī*;

for, according to the previously stated method, "O Great Goddess, *nigarbha* is the sphere of Śiva, the Guru, and the Self," those who possess the yoga of the supreme subject—characterized by the expansion of non-duality—are the *yoginīs*.
The ten functions of the senses, characterized by the contact between objects and the sense organs, are the rays of consciousness (*cinmarīcayaḥ*) and are the *nigarbhayoginīs*.
"Consisting of the immersion into one's own nature" (*svarūpāveśarūpake*): immersion (*āveśaḥ*) is the realization of the self as the cognizer and practitioner that "I am the Supreme Śiva.

For in the world, immersion is the manifestation of supreme subjectivity (*parāhaṃtā*), just as in the expression "I am a Brahma-rākṣasa"; thus, it is that which defines or characterizes such [realization].

Therefore, it is "the maker of universal immersion" (*sarvāveśakara*). According to the method stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava—"Wherever the mind goes" (verse 113), and "Wherever consciousness is manifested through the path of the senses, O Lord" (verse 114)—it causes that immersion and its non-differentiation to flash forth everywhere. Thus, it is the sixth wheel, the "maker of all protection" (*sarvarakṣākara*), within the wheel that effects universal immersion.
Just as in the expression "protect the curd from crows," protection (*rakṣā*) consists in warding off harm from an adverse object;

here, protection from all adversaries characterized by the phenomenal expansion of duality (*bheda-prapañca*) takes the form of the realization of non-difference from Supreme Śiva (*para-śivābheda*). The [verses] beginning with *sarvajñā* are supreme (*parāḥ*) because they are intent on establishing the non-duality of Supreme Śiva; they are "all-knowing" (*sarvajñā*) because they possess omniscience and other such qualities.
And [the powers] beginning with "possessing all powers" (1.173), as taught in the *Catuḥśatikāśāstra*, are established [therein]. (3.147–149)
He describes their meditation:
"These [goddesses] hold a book and a rosary. (3.149)
"Pusta" means a book. The remainder is clear. || 3/149 ||
Following an etymological derivation of her name, he speaks of the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī):
"The Mistress of the Wheel, known as Tripuramālinī, who completely nourishes the Mothers, the Means of Knowledge, and the Objects of Knowledge—the three cities—and who deludes all. (3.150)

Because they consist of the vibration of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit*), the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the object of knowledge (*meyā*) are themselves the "cities" (*purāṇi*). That which nourishes and primarily expands these cities is therefore known and designated as Tripurāmālinī, the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśī*), the Mistress of the Six Wheels, and the All-Enchantress (*sarvamohinī*). Indeed, it is solely through the power of the delusion produced by her that there arises the manifestation in the form of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
As it has been said in the *Parāpañcāśikā*: "The principle of *māyā* is the cognition of differentiation regarding entities that are in fact one's own limbs" (verse 21). (3/150)
One should worship these deities in sequence with all ritual offerings: Vidyāśakti, Viśuddhi, and the Siddhi known as Prākāmya. (3.151)

Mantras are presided over by that which is denoted as male, while Vidyās are presided over by that which is denoted in female form. Therefore, the purification of the power of Vidyā—which is expressed by the syllables of the *saubhāgyavidyā* and consists of the thirty-six *tattvas*—is characterized by the supreme consciousness (*paracit*) that transcends time; [the goddess] is of that nature. [She bestows] the accomplishment (*siddhi*) known as *prākāmya*.
Its characteristic is that it conforms to one's desire; as it has been said by the great poets:
"You are fluid, solid, hard, gross, subtle, light, and heavy; you are manifest and other than manifest; your sovereign will prevails over all your manifestations. (Kumārasambhava 2.11)

These deities—in order, first the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*), then the Mistress of the Mandala (*cakreśī*), and thereafter Siddhi—should be worshipped with all ritual offerings (*sarvopacāra*). The singular form *jātā* is used for the sake of the collective; the meaning is that one should worship them with all the ritual offerings.
He describes the worship along with its latent impressions (*savāsanā*) in the seventh wheel:

"From the root of the knots burst open by the impact of the restrained breath, [the worship is performed] through the void of inner consciousness in the heart, which has the *puryaṣṭaka* as its essence. (3.152)

In accordance with the sequence of the seed-syllables, forms, vowels, and kalās that touch the [phonetic] classes, [one should worship] the goddesses who are secret yoginīs, radiant in their destruction of saṃsāra. (3/153)
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, you are established in the wheel that removes all diseases;
[you arise] from the friction of the two winds— prāṇa and apāna— which are restrained and have abandoned their independent movements, beginning with Vaiśinī and the others.

Having repeatedly contracted the anus and restrained both the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths, through their union—according to the method stated in the words of the masters—the knot is burst open; [the breath], moving as far as the *mūlādhāra*-lotus situated within the *suṣumnā*, reaches such a root, namely the *mūlādhāra*. From there...

"By means of the *puryaṣṭaka* which is empty of internal consciousness within the heart, one should meditate on the form of a serpent—the light agitated by the *huṃ* sound—and, through the expulsion of breath and the mind, cause it to ascend. Following this method stated in the words of the masters, when [the power] has arisen from the base in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, one should contemplate that digit of consciousness (*sāṃvidī kalā*) flashing within the lotus of the heart. (Sūtra 34)

According to the manner stated in the words of the learned authorities, within the heart there vibrates consciousness (*saṃvitti*), which is the conscious self (*cidātman*). Consciousness (*citi*), mind (*citta*), sentience (*caitanya*), awareness (*cetanā*), the dual action,
the individual soul (*jīva*), limited power (*kalā*), and the body— these are considered the subtle "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*).

Thus, according to the method stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*, because the subtle *puryaṣṭakas* are difficult to perceive due to their subtlety, they are [called] "void" (*śūnya*). According to the method stated in the scripture, "The lotus of the heart is situated in the middle of the city" (*Mālinīvijayottara* 8.16), the "city" is the body; the "void-body" (*śūnya-śarīra*) is the void *puryaṣṭaka*, which consists of the eightfold consciousness.

"By that self" means "by that form"; the word "are situated" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. According to the method stated in the *Parāpañcāśikā*—namely, "this Goddess Mātṛkā exists in a twofold way, by way of being the seed (*bīja*) and the womb (*yoni*)"—the vowels from *a* to the visarga are the sixteen digits (*kalā*) in the form of seeds. Touched by these, the consonant groups (*vargas*) are joined with the guttural group (*avarga*).
Following the sequence of *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa-ya-śa*, O Goddess, the first group (*avarga*) is situated therein as *Vaśinī*;

according to the respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) extracted from the *Catuḥśatī* scripture— beginning with "One should extract the letter *ra* first" (*uddharet prathamaṃ rephaṃ*) and so forth— one should utter each respective seed-syllable at the end of its own group in due order.
The meaning is that one should worship [them]. Now, it was stated regarding the deities in the previous cakras— such as those with four corners—
that they consist of the letters of the *bhūtalipi* and *mātṛkā*, the vowels, the five groups beginning with *navaka*, and the five groups beginning with *ṭa*, *ta*, *ka*, and *ca*.
If it is asked why the remaining consonants *pa*, *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* have not been stated as belonging to the deities of the eight corners and so forth, the answer is true:

although the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the deities of the eight corners have not been explicitly mentioned, they are to be understood [from context]. The statement regarding the sequence of vowels, phonemes (*kalā*), and consonant groups (*varga*) according to their seed-forms, however, is an exposition of the mantras for the worship of the deities beginning with Vaśinī. [This refers to] the secret Yoginīs; [it is] the secret of the subtle mantra.

The "puryaṣṭaka" is the subtle body; those Yoginīs, such as Vaśinī and the others, whose connection with it—characterized by the relationship of cause and effect—is their association, are to be concealed because they consist of the puryaṣṭaka, which is difficult to perceive due to its subtlety.
They are "resplendent in the destruction of saṃsāra": *saṃsāra* consists of the nature of impermanence, impurity, and affliction; in its "destruction," that is, its removal, they are "resplendent."

In that which consists merely of being illuminated by another; for this very reason, in the wheel (*cakra*) that removes all diseases—wherein "all" refers to the disease that is *saṃsāra* in the form of impermanence, impurity, and affliction—in the seventh wheel characterized by powerful efficacy, reside Vaśinī and the others. As it is said: "O Goddess, the first group is the *a*-varga; there resides Vaśinī" (1.77).
Those mentioned in the *Catuḥśatī* treatise [should be worshipped]; the word "one should worship" (*pūjayet*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. || 3/153–154 ||
He describes their meditative visualization:
"They are red in color and sealed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (3.154)
Holding a book and a rosary, they are the perfected Yoginīs.

"Siddha" refers to Paramaśiva; "yoga" is the connection with him, characterized by the induction of his state as a living soul (jīva) through the nature of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body); they possess that [connection]. The rest is clear. 3/154–155.
And the purification of pure knowledge, as well as the accomplishment of enjoyment, O Maheśvarī. (3.155)

"One should worship the Sovereign Goddess, the accomplishment of the triple seat, with libations at the *bindu*; the realization of the identity between 'I' and 'this' is called *Vidyā*" (verse 21). According to this method stated in the *Parāpañcāśikā*, there is the purification of *Śuddhavidyā*—which is characterized by the manifestation of non-duality with Śiva—by means of knowledge, having perceived the object of knowledge through that knowledge.
In accordance with the method established by the statement, "One should subsequently abandon even knowledge" (Tattvārthadhigamasūtra 3.41),
there is immersion (*samāveśa*) into Paraśiva, whose characteristic is non-conceptual awareness devoid of the division between knower, knowing, and known; [the state] which possesses that very form,
and for this reason, the accomplishment of enjoyment (*bhukti-siddhi*).

In accordance with the statement of the learned masters, "I offer unto Maheśa, the Great Enjoyer, the entire universe— from Śiva down to the Earth— which is the locus of the aesthetic flavor of wonder," [the text] accomplishes for its own practitioner the great enjoyment (*mahābhukti*) pertaining to the entire universe.

One should worship that Cakreśvarī, the sovereign of the seventh wheel, who is Tripurasiddhi— the perfection characterized by the state of supreme Śiva transcending the triad of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge— by means of libations of *bindu*, through the union of the ring finger and thumb (*anāmā-aṅguṣṭha-yoga*) in the mudrā of the meeting of Śiva and Śakti, and with offerings of substances, *bindu*-libations, and flowers accompanied by raw rice grains (*sākṣata*).
"One should worship," [thus it is said] in verses 3.155–157.
He describes the worship of the eighth wheel along with its latent impressions (vāsana):
"O Goddess, [the rays] consisting of the three powers are the auspicious expansions of the abode of consciousness. (3/156)

O Goddess of the Gods, those whose forms are like the fire of universal destruction at the end of an aeon, and who possess the supreme secret, are the cause of accomplishment (siddhi) for her whose nature is both full and incomplete. (3.157)
In the wheel known as Sarvasiddhimaya, which is adorned with weapons, reside the four deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha), beginning with Kāmeśvarī. (3.158)

They consist of the three powers— desire, knowledge, and action; they are the expansions of the abode of consciousness, the rays of the light of *citi*, of the Mother known as *saṃvid*, namely the powers whose nature is Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī.

The emanations known as Oḍḍīśa, Ṣaṣṭhīśa, and Mitreśa are of the nature of vibration (*spanda*), because they constitute the primary state of all-encompassing obscuration (*sarvāvaraṇa*). They take the form of the digit (*kalā*) of the Saṃvartāgni;
Saṃvartāgni is the devourer of the universe, the supreme Śiva who is without sound (*asvara*), and these [emanations] are his digit.
The letter *ha*; they have that form, they consist of that essence, because they are constituent parts of the power of peace (*śāntāśakti*).

They are supremely secret; "supremely secret" means more secret than all the deities of the veils (*āvaraṇa*), shining forth as the supreme [reality] through the three limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṃkāra*).

Because they consist of the substratum of consciousness (*cidādhāra*), they are to be kept strictly secret. Of that perfection (*siddhi*) which possesses both a full and an incomplete nature—the full nature because it consists of absorption into Paraśiva, and the incomplete nature because its object is the universe—that perfection is of a dual character. Of everything...
Because it is the cause of *siddhi*— characterized by resting in Paraśiva— which begins with Earth (*kṣiti*) and ends with Śiva,
[it is] in that which is called "consisting of all *siddhis*" (*sarvasiddhimaya*), as described in [verse 1.84], and which is adorned with weapons, [the seat] of Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara.
Adorned with the eight weapons— the sword, arrow, bow, noose, and goad— paired together in the sequence of west, north, east, and south,
according to the method taught in the *Catuḥśatī* scripture beginning with [verse] 1.179; by that, of the weapons...
It is established that they fall within the enclosure of Kāmeśvarī, according to the method stated in the *Catuḥśatī-śāstra*: "They abide in the eighth wheel, beginning with Kāmeśvarī;
[place] Kāmeśvarī in the eastern petal" (1.182). Thus, there are four deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭha-devatās*). As for the sacred seats, what is their worship? It is "O" (*o*).

Regarding the phrase "in sequence" (kramāt) [1/41], this refers to the previously mentioned characteristics of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*); the deities presiding over them are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Ambikā, Maya, Mitrā, and Śarva, who constitute the limbs of the supreme light.
Aṣṭhīśa, Oḍḍīśa, Caryānātha, and Śiva seated upon his lap, [along with] Will, which is a portion of the power of their reflective awareness (vimarśa), and Ignorance—

Kriyāśāntā, Mayakāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Mahātripurasundarī—these four, together with the deity of the ninth wheel, constitute the total. However, in the eighth wheel, there are only three, namely Kāmeśvarī and the others, along with their weapons. (3.156–158)
He describes the meditation on the weapon-deities:
"The weapons, however, possess an intensely red luster, with their heads blazing with their own respective weapons;
they have hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and should be worshipped as bestowers of fruits upon the meditator. (3.159)

And yours and mine are the weapons that bring men and women under control; they are the deities of the weapons—the use of the masculine gender is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Their heads are blazing with their own weapons, meaning their heads are adorned by the weapons upon which they themselves preside.
[He meditated on] the Goddess, who dwells within the Great Lotus Grove, whose form is the bliss of the cause,
who rests upon my lap, and who bestows the fruits of desire and will.

Regarding the phrase "bhavatīm" (you): according to the manner previously stated, [it refers to] you, who belong to me— the Lord residing within the Mahāpadma forest, the teacher of the universe— and who abide upon my lap as the digit Anāśrita (the Unsupported).

The arrows, bow, noose, and goad are the means for subjugating men; however, for one such as I, these same arrows, bow, noose, and goad serve to bring women under control. As it is said in the *Catuḥśatī-śāstra*:
Becoming Madana through his intoxicating powers, he should agitate the women of the heavens, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld with his noose, goad, bow, and arrows.
In the same way, O Goddess of the Gods, one whose body has been made into the triple-city by means of the Śaktis may agitate even the gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas.
The rest is clear. (3/159–160)
Since they have not been extracted in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra*, he extracts the seed-syllables consisting of the arrows of Śakti:
"O Sovereign of the Gods, [the syllables] ending with the letters for skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. (3/160)
These arrows of yours are conjoined with the second vowel;

according to the sequence of the Śrīkaṇṭha and other nyāsas, the five letters beginning with *ya* correspond to the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) starting with the skin. These [letters] conjoined with the second vowel are the arrows. The letter *ā*...

The second vowel; by implication, the *bindu* (dot) is also indicated. Your arrows—meaning the seed-syllables of the arrows belonging to you—consist therein of the letter *ya*, which is of the nature of the skin;
the letter *ra*, which is of the nature of blood; the letter *la*, which is of the nature of flesh; and the letter *va*, which is of the nature of fat.

The term "ending with the sound of bone (asthi), marrow (majjā), and ocean (arṇa)" indicates the syllable *sa*, which consists of semen (*śukra*) and resides above the bone and marrow. Furthermore, regarding the seed-syllables of the arrows of Kāmeśvara that are not mentioned in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra*: first, [one should place] the one called Pādāvareṇyā...
Regarding the phrase "in the sequence of Nalaraka" (*saṃyujen-nalarakrame*),
since it has been extracted from the *Svacchandasaṃgraha* and is well-known in other scriptures (*āgama*),
no further extraction [of its source] is made here. (3/160–161)
Tripurāmbikā is the mother of the ancient cities beginning with Vāma;
O Maheśvarī, because her nature is supreme autonomy, she is the perfection of will. One should worship these [goddesses] with all ritual offerings, O infinite one, bestower of boons. (3/162)
Of Vāmā and the others— namely those called Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—
who take the forms of Mitreśa and so forth,
and who are presided over by Kāmeśvarī and the rest, they are portions of the power of self-reflection (*vimarśa*) consisting of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).

Because she is bowed to (*ānata*), she is denoted by the word *pura* (city); Ambikā, the power who is the mother of those three cities (*tripura*) because she is their collective totality (*samaṣṭi-rūpa*), is indeed Tripurāmbikā—she is, as the remainder of the definition implies, the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*). By her own will alone, she swallows and also emits the entire universe.

According to the method taught in the *Ājñāvatāra*, the accomplishment of the will—characterized by the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of Paraśiva consisting in the creation and withdrawal of the universe—is achieved for the worshiper of this wheel;
the meaning is that this very accomplishment of will resides in this wheel. These are the deities of the weapons.

One should worship Kāmeśvarī and the other goddesses of the wheels (cakreśvarīs), together with their supernatural powers (siddhis), using all the ritual offerings (upacāras), such as perfumes and the rest. || 3/161-162 ||

He describes the worship of the ninth wheel along with its latent impressions (*savāsana*): "O Goddess, within the supreme wheel which consists of the Supreme Brahman and is composed of universal bliss, resides Mahātripurasundarī, whose nature is pure consciousness. (3/163)
She is to be worshipped through spontaneous conduct as the equality of "I" and "this-ness";
she is the form of the Great Kāmakalā, and one realizes that bliss is Brahman (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.6).

Because it consists of the supreme bliss that is the aggregate of all bliss, according to the scriptural statement, "All other beings live subsisting upon a fraction of this very bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32), it is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman; for this very reason, it is the Supreme.

In the ninth wheel, which transcends the universe, consciousness takes the form of the Goddess Tripurā— the self-awareness— consisting of the vibration (spanda) of Paramaśiva. According to the statement of the learned masters, "Lauhitya is that [self-awareness] and its reflective awareness (vimarśana)," there is a state of equality between the knower and the known, or between the "I" and the "this."

The intermediate consciousness is Mahātripurasundarī, whose etymology was stated previously (1.85). She is the form of the Great Kāmakalā; the Great Kāmakalā consists of the three great points (*mahābindu*) which are the state of equilibrium between light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and she is the half-syllable (*ardhakalā*). Having conceived that form as a point (*bindu*), [one should meditate].
According to the method taught in the *Catuḥśatī* scripture beginning with "The face," she is to be worshipped according to one's own inclination;
wherever the mind finds satisfaction, there alone one should fix the mind.
"In each and every instance, the nature of supreme bliss shines forth" (verse 73).
According to this method stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava,
[one should worship] with substances that gratify the senses in accordance with one's own desire.
The meaning is that one's own consciousness as the deity is to be realized through free conduct characterized by the contemplation of the vibrating supreme atom (paramāṇu). || 3/163-164 ||
He states the attainment of success:
"It bestows the success of the *pīṭhas*, the *vidyās*, and so forth. (3.164)
"The goddess consisting of Mahāmudrā is to be worshipped; what is the worship? It is 'o' and so forth in sequence" (1/41). Thus, the four seats previously mentioned are the *vidyās*.
Consisting of the seed-syllables Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, Śakti, and Turīya, and by the word "etcetera" (ādi),
the four deities beginning with Kāmeśvarī are included;
it bestows upon them the perfection characterized by dissolution and repose in Paraśiva, who transcends the fourth state (turīyātīta).

"Attainment" (prāpti) means "it causes one to reach" (prāpayati). "Consisting of Mahāmudrā" means that Mahāmudrā is the womb-seal (yonimudrā) because she is the synthesis of all seals; the meaning is that she, being composed of that, is the object of worship.
Consisting of fifteen aspects, the eternal ninth goddess Bhairavī, who is composed of each respective lunar day, is supreme. (3.165)
In each wheel (cakra), there are mudrās proclaimed in the *Cakrasaṃketaka*.
The fifteen-fold [mudrā] is the expressed meaning of the fifteen-syllable vidyā,
consisting of the qualities of the fifteen elements, and is composed of their respective lunar days (tithis).

She consists of the fifteen lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad); she is the eternal one (*nityā*), whose nature is eternally incomparable and composed of her own bliss; she is the ninth, the supreme Bhairavī;
and she is likewise declared to be the Root-Vidyā (*mūlavidyā*)—according to the manner previously described. (2/5)

The meaning is that the Root Vidyā, who is the Mistress of the Ninth Cakra, the Root Goddess who consists of the sixteen digits (kalās) and is the Mistress of the Ninth Cakra, is to be worshipped. In each individual cakra, such as the Trailokyamohana and others, those [deities] mentioned in the *Cakrasaṃketaka*— the Yonis— [are to be worshipped].
By the passage beginning with "Because of its abundance, this [power] is again the All-Agitating One" (1.59), it is established in the *Cakrasaṃketanirṇaya* that all mudrās,
such as the All-Agitating One (*sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī*) and others, are the specific mudrās of their respective wheels and are to be worshipped within those respective wheels.
It should be applied. || 3/165 – 166 ||
And likewise, the Nityaklinnā and others [should be worshipped] according to the requirements of the rites for desired results. || 3/166 ||
The wise practitioner should worship either within a square or within a triangle.

Because Māmeśvarī and Bhagamālinī fall within the interior of the [triangle] facing Āra, their placement is said to be in the middle and the left corner of the triangle's apex. As for the remaining [deities]:
Likewise, Nityaklinnā, Nityā, Bheruṇḍā, and Vahnivāsinī.
Mahāvidyeśvarī, Dūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī,
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā.
Jvālāmālinī and Citrā—
these thirteen Nityās mentioned in the *Catuḥśatī* scripture [should be worshipped] either in a triangle,
or in the central triangle of the Śrīcakra, or within the intermediate space of the square.

Or, within the sixteen-petaled square, the wise one— who knows the subject matter of the procedures for those various rites of desire— should perform worship according to the specific rite of desire, such as subjugation (*vaśya*), using colors, meditations, flowers, and so forth that correspond to the desired rite. (3/166–167)
Concluding the worship of the wheel (*cakrapūjā*), he speaks of the offering that illuminates the family (*kuladīpanivedana*):
"Having propitiated the deities with wine, meats, perfumes, and incense... (3.167).
Having thus performed the worship of the wheel, one should offer the family lamp (kuladīpa), O Dear One, which shines both internally and externally, radiant with its own self-luminosity. (3.168)
By means of the syllable *ali* as the cause; the terms *piśita*, *gandha*, *dhūpa*, and *śabda* have their meanings clear.
The deities are those residing in the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana and ending with Baindava;
having propitiated them with *ali*, *piśita*, *gandha*, and *dhūpa*, one should perform the worship of the wheels (*cakrapūjā*) in this manner, according to the previously stated method.

Having established the lamp of the lineage (*kuladīpa*); "lineage" refers to the body, which consists of the aggregate of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*). The "lamp" is that which exists therein. Thus, according to the method stated in the words of the learned masters, "the digit of consciousness (*sāṃvidī kalā*) throbbing within the heart-lotus" (*Su. 34*), [one should contemplate] within the heart—

One should offer the Kula-lamp, which is the manifest form of the digit of consciousness (*saṃvitkalā*), appearing externally toward objects through the doors of the senses in that very form; for this reason, it is radiant with self-luminosity, its perception independent of external means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and devoid of extinction.
Furthermore, the repose of consciousness within by turning back toward the interior through that very same door is what is called "offering" (nivedana). 3/167–168.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should perform recitation with a concentrated mind;
restraining the movement of the senses, one should utter the internal sound.
This alone is declared to be true recitation, for external recitation is not recitation.
