Thus, composed and with senses restrained according to the method stated in the words of authoritative persons, one should perform *japa*, characterized by the recitation of mantras in the form of resonance (*nāda*). The remainder is clear.
He now describes the manner of *japa*:
O Great Goddess, [this occurs] in the three peaks and also in the triad of Kuṇḍalinīs.
The joining of each preceding group of wheels (cakras) in the form of sound occurs within the triad of peak-syllables—
namely, the triad known as the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti seeds— and likewise within the triad of Kuṇḍalinīs.

The "triad of Kuṇḍalinīs" refers to the triad of Kuṇḍalinīs; these are situated at the base (ādhāra), the heart, and the station of the Bindu, as stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*: "The base, the heart, and the station of the Bindu are proclaimed [as their locations].
Thus, they reside in the base, the heart, and the middle of the eyebrows.

In the triad of fire, sun, and moon-kuṇḍalinīs— which consist of the form of the supreme half-kalā contained within the desire-portion (*kāmakalā*) situated at the peak of the three seeds— and in the locations beginning with Akula and ending with Bindu, as stated in the verse "in Akula and that known as Viṣu" (1.25), [the worship of] the preceding cakras [is performed].
The application in the form of sound (*nāda*) consists of dividing the nine cakras— beginning with the Trailokyamohana— which have been cultivated within the nine [lotuses],
thirty times each, and joining them to each individual seed-syllable (*bīja*) and to the Kuṇḍalinī. [The word] *trailokya-*...

The heart [of consciousness] arises through the upward movement of the Fire-Kuṇḍalinī, which takes the form of the half-moon digit (ardhakalā) situated within the Kāmakalā— the wick at the peak of the Vāgbhava syllable located in the fire-maṇḍala that serves as the support for the triad beginning with Mohanā situated in the nine-spoked wheel.

The recitation of the Vāgbhava seed-syllable consists of the meditation on its nature as consisting of resonance (nāda), which extends as far as the Kāmarāja seed-syllable; [this pertains to] the three wheels beginning with Sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka,
wherein the Kāmarāja [seed-syllable] resides within the solar orb situated at the heart.

The recitation of the *kāmarāja* seed-syllable consists of the contemplation of its nature as the pervasive *nāda*, which extends from the rising of the solar *kuṇḍalinī*— which has the form of the half-moon (*ardhakalā*) contained within the digit of desire (*kāmakalā*) residing on the peak— to the seed-syllable of power (*śaktibīja*) located in the station of the awakened drop (*uditabindu*). [This applies] to the triad of wheels beginning with the "remover of all diseases" (*sarvarogahara*).

By that which pervades as far as the moon of *samanā*, which transcends the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) and is situated above the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), having arisen from the upward movement of the lunar Kuṇḍalinī— whose form is the half-moon digit residing within the digit of desire (*kāmakalā*) at the tip of the seed-syllable of Power (*śaktibīja*) located within the lunar orb of the station of the Bindu.
The meaning is that the recitation of the seed-syllable of Śakti consists of contemplating its dissolution into Unmanī along with the Nāda.
As it has been stated by the learned:
"The Piṇḍa is the state of the vast expansion of the expressive [mantra] remaining as a residual impression."
O Goddess Umā, this *nāda* of yours, having transcended the limit of the *samanā* at the crown of your head,
gradually subsides like the ringing of a bell; smelling the subtlest of other [energies], it experiences the state of supreme consciousness (*paracit*), the primordial form.
Thus [ends the section]. 3/169–170.

Now, one might ask: why has the pronunciation up to the state of *unmanī* not been mentioned for all three seed-syllables, given that [it is stated] "the form of a lamp, consisting of half a mora, is desired as a circle on the forehead" (1.28), and so forth? [The answer is:
because the twelve parts of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which culminate in *unmanī*, are present everywhere.
Because it is possible to speak of them collectively, he says:
"Among those [levels], there are Prāṇa, Agni, Māyā, Arṇa, Kalā, Bindu, and Ardhacandra. (3.170)
Rodhinī, Nāda, and Nādānta, along with Śakti joined by Vyāpikā, as well as Samanā and Unmanā— these, O Dear One, are situated at the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta).
Then again, O Maheśvarī, she resides in the form of the root-kuṇḍalinī within the central channel,
and in the form of the sustainer of the universe when it is oriented toward emanation.
O Goddess, in the third [state], which has a variegated form, there is the twelfth digit (kalā) consisting solely of sound (nāda), joined with each subsequent [element]. (3/173)
Among those three seeds, the letter *ha* is *prāṇa*, the letter *ra* is *agni*, and the letter *ī* is *māyārṇa*; that itself is *kalā*. As it is said in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"The *bindu* is the essence of *ahaṅkāra*, and the sun (*ravi*)—this is the form of the union and integration of this couple."
"Kāma and Kalā are the forms of the Fire and the Moon, [and] the two Bindus. (Verse 7).
The [principles] beginning with Bindu and ending with Unmanī have the characteristics previously stated (1.28–34).
These [principles], from Prāṇa up to Unmanī, reside at the *dvādaśānta* (the "twelve-finger space" beyond the head), within the form of the Mūla-kuṇḍalinī.
O Goddess, we ever meditate upon that measure which resides in your first seed-syllable, Vāgbhava— the measure which rivals the rising of the extremely fine fibers of the trapusī creeper.
Having known that Śakti, known as Kuṇḍalinī, is intent upon the exertion of creating the universe, men shall no longer experience childhood again within the womb of a mother.

(Verse 2) Thus, according to the method stated in the *Laghustotra*, when the universe is oriented toward emanation, it resides within the central *Kāmarāja* seed-syllable, which constitutes the state of the universe's persistence, because it stands between dissolution and emanation.

"Merely in the form of sound" means solely in the form of *nāda*, excluding the utterance of constituent parts such as *nāda* and so forth. "Successive conjunction" is an adverbial modifier for the act of utterance. [One should contemplate] the *nāda* residing at the peak of the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable, [and] the *kāmarāja* seed-syllable located in the heart...

One should utter [the mantra] up to the limit; the meaning is that one should utter [it] from the peak of the Kāmarāja-bīja down to the Śakti-bīja situated in the place of the Bindu. In this third Śakti-bīja, which is of a variegated form due to the mixture resulting from the union of these two bījas and the two Nādas, it is the twelfth.

The phrase "the *kalā* Unmanā is situated" is to be supplied [to each]. By this, it is understood that the twelve *kalās*, beginning with Prāṇa, are also to be recited as being situated at the summit of the third seed-syllable (*bīja*). What is the meaning?
Although [these *kalās*] are at the end of all three—the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti seeds—[the instruction applies specifically here].

Although the twelve kalās— known as prāṇa, agni, māyā, bindu, ardhacandra, rodhinī, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpikā, samanā, and unmanā— can be described, such is not the case for the two seed-syllables, vāgbhava and kāmarāja.
Because its nature consists of both emanation and maintenance, the upward movement (*uccāra*) does not extend beyond the Transmental (*unmanā*), which transcends the universe.
Therefore, there is no contradiction; this is the meaning. (3/170–173)
Regarding what should be meditated upon at the time of recitation, he says:
"O Goddess, one should recite while mentally contemplating the six voids, as well as the five states, and the equinox consisting of seven forms. (3.174)
At the time of recitation, these should be meditated upon as parts of the Vidyā-mantra:
the five voids [are represented] by mandalas with the variegated colors of a peacock's feathers.
For one who meditates on the supreme void, he becomes one whose body is the ultimate ether. (Verse 32)
Thus, according to the method stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava, the nature of the six voids (śūnya-ṣaṭka) is to be known.
The five states consist of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turya), and that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta). Of these, beginning with waking—
He will describe its essential nature (3.176–181) and will describe the equinox and the seven forms;
he now states the locations and essential natures of the voids (*śūnya*) and so forth in sequence:
"O fair-faced one, having omitted three each among the twelve [places] beginning with Fire and ending with the End (Ādhāra)," etc.
O Dear One, one should understand the three voids as being separated by single intervals. (3.175)

One should meditate upon the Great Void (mahāśūnya) in the position beyond the three voids; this means between each pair [of voids]. Having omitted six—namely, three sets of three beginning with fire (agni), where "fire" refers to the syllable *repha*—the "three voids" refers to the six voids.
One should understand this. What is the meaning? One should place the letter *ra* between the letter *ha* and *māyā*;
the *bindu* between *māyā* and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*); *rodhinī* between the half-moon and *nāda*; *nādānta* between *nāda* and *śakti*; and [the letter *sa*] between *śakti* and *samanā*.
Having abandoned the six [levels]— the Pervasive (vyāpikā), and above that, the Unmanā— one proceeds there,
in the five locations of Repha, Bindu, Rodhinī, Nādānta, and Vyāpikā,
according to the previously mentioned method beginning with "by means of the variegated forms of the peacock's feathers" (verse 32).

The meaning is that one should meditate upon the five voids (*pañca-śūnyāni*), whose forms resemble the moonbeams situated within the peacock feathers (*barhibarha*). Regarding the "body of the void" (*vyomatanu*) in the sixth station of *unmanā*, it is according to the method stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava: "In the sixth station of *unmanā*, however, one becomes the body of the void" (verse 32). Thus, it is the "body of the void."

Furthermore, another distinction is that the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is empty. The meaning is that one should contemplate the formless Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnya*) in the state beyond the three emptinesses. (3/175–176)
Now, desiring to explain the cultivation of the five states in their proper sequence, he first describes the cultivation of the waking state:
"Then, the cultivation of the instrument of awakening as being the waking state. (3/176)
O Goddess, in the fire [of the heart] is the state of great waking (mahājāgradavasthā) by means of the two pairs of faculties— that is,
by means of the ten faculties consisting of the two pairs of knowledge and action faculties.
The worldly transaction (vyavahāra) of the knower is called waking, awakening, or the waking state.

The contemplation of that instrument, the Light, as being the waking state, occurs within the inner illuminating fire situated at the peak of the third seed-syllable, the letter *ra*; this is the state of Great Waking (*mahājāgradavasthā*),
characterized by the perpetual destruction of sleep and the stage of supreme awakening.
The meaning is that it is to be cultivated. || 3/176–177 ||
He states the nature of dream-experience:
"Dream is the awakening to illusion by means of the internal organs alone. (3/177)
In the region of the throat,
the activity of the knower occurs solely through the internal instruments— namely, mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and consciousness (citta)— which are devoid of external senses.
Dream: by means of the fourth vowel situated within the third seed-syllable through *māyā*, its awakening is understood;
the meaning is that it is denoted by that [seed-syllable]. The location of the dream is in the region of the throat.

He states the contemplation of deep sleep: "Deep sleep, however, is the perception of that which was previously dissolved, due to the dissolution of the functions of the internal organs as well as of the object. (3/178)
The vowels of the first half [of the alphabet], situated as the *bindu* between the eyebrows in reverse order, [are present there].

Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is characterized by the cessation of all the senses due to the dissolution of the functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that exist during dreaming; therefore, it belongs to one for whom [the former] has dissolved.

The perception—that is, the manifestation—of one's own Self occurs precisely as it remains dissolved, embraced within the body, senses, and so forth. For subsequently, one reflects upon the nature of one's own Self as consisting of bliss, thinking, "I slept happily. This is deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
As for the object (*viṣaya*): the object is the third seed-syllable (*tārtīya-bīja*), because it is the locus of the pervasion of the universe (*viśvavyāpti*).
Regarding its preceding syllables—those syllables situated before the *bindu*—in reverse order:
"O Maheśānī, the Māyā-seed joined with the Madana and Śakra."

From the passage beginning with "The seed-syllable of the Moon alone" (1/116–117) and ending with "one should extract the seed-syllable of Śakti by means of the process of withdrawal" (1/118), [it refers to] the seed-syllables of Śakti extracted according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra*, arranged here in reverse order.
In due order, she is situated as a point (*bindu*) between the eyebrows;
the meaning is that she is to be meditated upon as residing in the upper *bindu* of the *hṛllekhā* located at the station between the eyebrows. (3/178–179)
He states the contemplation of the fourth state (*turya*):
"The form of the fourth, and here its inclusion of half-verse and so forth. (3/179)

"But there is no perception of that which has the form of sound (*nāda*) as the cause for the manifestation of consciousness. That is to say, there is no manifestation— meaning the making manifest— of that which has the form of *nāda*, characterized as previously stated (1.33), as the cause for the manifestation of consciousness, which is to say, of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

The form of the Fourth (turyarūpa). Of that form of the Fourth: here, in the third seed-syllable, there is the collection of the half-circle and so forth—where "half-circle" means the crescent moon (*ardhacandra*), and by the word "etcetera," the *rodhinī* and *nāda* are included—in the crescent moon, *rodhinī*, and *nāda* residing at the peak of the third seed-syllable.

The meaning is that the fourth state (*turya*), which consists of the subtle resonance (*nāda*) that is the cause for the manifestation of the consciousness of one's own self, is to be meditated upon as the *turīya*. || 3/179–180 ||
He describes the contemplation of that which transcends the fourth state:
"O Dear One, the state beyond the fourth is the abode of bliss, situated at the end of the resonance (nādānta) and so forth. (3.180)
At this very time of recitation, the wise one should contemplate the five states, according to the method stated in the Upaniṣad:
"The bliss of Brahman, from which words turn back along with the mind, failing to reach it—knowing that [bliss]... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4). This refers to the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).

The meaning is that one should meditate upon the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), whose essential nature is supreme bliss transcending mind and speech, which is the abode of happiness, situated at the end of *nāda* and so forth, and which resides within *nādānta*, *śakti*, *vyāpikā*, *samanā*, and *unmanā*. It is right here, in this very seed of power (*śaktibīja*), [that the five...]

The wise one, skilled in the focused application of the recitation of the Vidyā, should, at the time of recitation, remember the previously mentioned states beginning with waking, preceded by the continuous contemplation of these five states.
Now, desiring to explain the cultivation of the seven equinoxes (*viṣuva*), he first states the cultivation of the vital-breath equinox (*prāṇa-viṣuva*):
"The union of the vital breath, the self, and the mind is the equinox known as *prāṇa*. (3.181)

The conjunction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of the letter *ha*, with the wind, the self (*ātman*) who is the sacrificer, and the mind, is called the "equinox of the breath" (*prāṇaviṣuva*). As it is stated in the Śaiva Tantra:
"They know the conjunction of the disciple's self, breath, and mind as the 'breath-equinox' (*prāṇaka*)."

He describes the meditation on the equinox of mantra (mantraviṣuvabhāvanā): "O Maheśvarī, having perceived the form of the Self dissolved in the resonance (nāda) arisen from the foundation (ādhāra), [one should meditate] through the conjunction and disjunction of the letters of the mantra. (3/182)

The contemplation of the nature of *nāda*, from the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) up to the end of the support (*ādhāra*); "equinox" (*viṣuva*) refers to that which arises from the support, namely from the *mūlādhāra*, by means of the upward-rising breath when the *nāda* has come into being.
Residing at the pinnacle of knowledge (*vidyā*), the "form of the self" (*ātmarūpaka*) is that form of one's own which consists of consciousness,

having become a single essence of bliss; [it exists] through the separation— that is, the dispersed state— of the syllables of the *vidyā-mantra*, namely the seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti.
By means of the conjunction, that is, by way of the collective form of the fourth seed-syllable (*turīyabīja*), [the breath] reaches from the *anāhata* to the end of the *ādhāra*:

the *anāhata* is the location in the heart; the *ādhāra* is the location at the end of all [the centers], namely the *brahmarandhra*. Here, the word "end" (*anta*) is uttered with a double meaning (*tantra*).

"From the Unstruck (anāhata) up to the Foundation (ādhāra)" means as far as that point. "Contemplation on the nature of Nāda" refers to the visualization of Nāda as the form of the sacrificer; "named Mantra" is the ellipsis.
What is the meaning? [It is] the Nāda residing at the peak of the Vāgbhava [cakra] situated in the Mūlādhāra.

The meaning is that having recited [the mantra] up to the heart, one becomes absorbed therein and contemplates the identity of one's own self with that; this is called the "equinox of the mantra" (*mantraviṣuva*). As it is said in the Śaiva Tantra:
Having truly brought about the dissolution of the self into the midst of the *nāda*,
through the conjunction and subsequent separation of the phonemes beginning with *a* and *u*.
"And from the heart to the end of the aperture, it is the equinox known as mantra. (3/182) Thus [it is said].
He states the contemplation of the channel-equinox: "From the contact with the resonance (nāda), it is called the channel-equinox. (3/183)
O Dear One, by piercing the twelve knots from the phoneme into the interior of the channels—
from the phoneme that is the syllable of the digit of desire (*kāmakalā*) situated at the peak of the three seed-syllables—
one pierces the twelve knots of the six root cakras beginning with the *mūlādhāra*.
Therefore, within the central channel (suṣumnā) along the middle path, by virtue of the contact with *nāda*— that is,

through the contact of the *nāda* residing at the peak of the three seed-syllables (*tribīja*) as it is articulated from the base up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)— it is called the "equinox of the channels" (*nāḍīviṣuva*). This has been stated in the Śaiva Tantra:

"Having pierced the knots in succession with the trident of the root mantra, through the union of the *nāda* and the *nāḍī*, one performs the meditation on the equinox of the channels (*nāḍī-viṣuva*). (3.183–184)
He speaks of the meditation on the tranquil equinox:
"The yoga of sound is indeed tranquil, with the range of the senses stilled. (3.184)
One should contemplate fire, *māyā*, *kalā*, consciousness, and the half-moon, as well as *rodhinī*, *nāda*, and *nādānta*, all dissolved into *śakti*. (3.185)

*Vahni* is the letter *ra*; *māyā* is the vowel *ī*; *kalā* is the line (*rekhā*) situated in the middle of that, representing the supreme half-measure (*saparārdhakalā*); and *cetanā* is the *bindu*.
The *bindu* is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of consciousness (*caitanya*), because it has the nature of pure sensation (*vedana*). As it has been said:

In the *Parāpañcāśikā*: "The refinement of the one who knows the center is this emission, which is creation" (verse 37). One should contemplate the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the obstructress (*rodhinī*), the sound (*nāda*), and the end of sound (*nādānta*) as dissolved within the power (*śakti*) whose characteristics were previously described (1.31); for this [is so].

The *nāda* is characterized by the power that transcends the sacrificer; therefore, it is the sphere of the pacified senses, having as its object that which is beyond all the senses—this is to be understood as "the peaceful equinox" (*praśāntaviṣuva*).
Thus it is said in the Śaiva Tantra:
Having sequentially abandoned the vowels *ā* and *ū*, the letter *m*, the *bindu*, and those known as *nāda* and *nādānta*, by means of Brahmā and the others;

"In the seventh [cakra], in the midst of the power (śakti), one should contemplate the self of the disciple; one should know that [state] to be profoundly tranquil, with the range of the senses stilled. (3.184–185)
He describes the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the *śakti*-equinox and the *kāla*-equinox:
"The equinox is indeed named *śakti*, and above that is the meditation on *nāda*.
Above that, O Maheśvarī, is the *kāla*-equinox, which extends to the end of *unmanā*. (3.186)
Above that, from the top of Śakti up to the end of Samanā, is the contemplation of Nāda,
which is the Viṣuva of Śakti. Above that, even above Samanā, there is no measurement of time or kalā, according to the method stated in the Svacchandasaṃgraha.
The contemplation of Nāda, extending from Kālātīta up to Unmanā, is the Equinox of Time (kāla-viṣuva). As it is stated in the Śaiva Tantra:
"Nāda, situated in the center of Śakti, flows forth as far as Samanā."
"That is declared to be the equinox of power (śakti-viṣuva), which in Unmanī is designated as Time (kāla). (3.186)

Now, one might ask: "In how much time does the Nāda cause the realization of reality? To this he says: "The realization of Nāda occurs in eighteen *tuṭis* of the Moon of Sages; as long as the eye of a man sitting at ease continues to throb."
The thirtieth part of that is proclaimed as tatpara.
"A hundredth part of that [nimeṣa] is called a *tuṭi*.
According to this method stated in another tantra, a *tuṭi* is one three-thousandth part of a *nimeṣa*.
Seven sages (*muni*), one moon (*candra*), and the well-known numbers eight and ten; by that—

When the utterance of the components of the Vidyā, beginning with the letter *ha* and ending with *unmanī*, is performed through ten thousand eight hundred and seventeen *tuṭis*— according to the method stated in [verse 1.25] as occurring in *akula* and that which is called *viṣu*— then, at the end of the *nāda*, [there is] the *tattva*.
The meaning is "feeling.
He states the meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) of the equinox of the principles (tattva):
"And the equinox, known as the principle (tattva), is the cause for the manifestation of consciousness. (3.187)
The "equinox of reality" (*tattvaviṣuva*) is the cause of the manifestation—that is, the illumination—of consciousness, which is one's own essential nature (*svātmatattva*). What is the meaning?
Above the *unmanā* state, through the dissolution of the *nāda* by means of the aforementioned number of *tuṭi*s, one's own self—
The meaning of *nusandhāna* is the equinox (*viṣuva*) of reality (*tattva*). As it is stated in the Śaiva Tantra:
"In its own domain, within the supreme abode, is the equinox known as reality. (3/187)
O Great Goddess, the supreme state is beautiful with innate bliss;
it is the supreme state that transcends the six voids, the five states, the seven equinoxes, and the tumultuous roar.

Because it is the ground of rest for all things, it is beautiful with innate bliss (*nisargānanda*). This innate bliss is the supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) which constitutes the totality of the bliss derived from all sense objects;
therefore, it is the adversary of the manifold expansion (*prapañca*) of impermanence, impurity, affliction, and misfortune.
Because its nature is that of the supreme cause, it is the form of the supreme Śiva—characterized by supreme bliss, the object of supreme love, and supremely beautiful;
the meaning is that it is naturally beautiful with bliss. || 3/188 ||
He states the fruit of the aforementioned meditation:
"O Pārvatī, for one who reflects in this way during the times of recitation... (3/188).
"By your grace, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) are swiftly attained.

In this manner, according to the previously stated method, during the times of recitation (*japa*); for recitations are said to be "entire" (*sakala*) up to the End of the Command (*ājñānta*), as described by the aforementioned sequence beginning with [verse 1.27–28]. "Entire" (*sakala*)—
There are three forms: the Sakala, the Niṣkala, and the Kevala-niṣkala.

Their durations—the times for the utterance of the previously mentioned components of the Vidyā—are described by the passage beginning with "dīpākāro 'rdhamātraś ca" (1.28–34), and so forth; among these...

For one who contemplates the six voids and so forth, all the previously mentioned accomplishments (*siddhis*), such as *aṇimā* and the rest, are attained through your grace— provided that you, the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) within me whose nature is light, are pleased; [this occurs] there and there by way of the respective sense-faculties.

The meaning is that, according to the method stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava— "Consciousness is manifested by the Lord" (Śloka 114)— when [the state of] being composed of all cognitions is attained through your grace, it becomes dependent upon oneself. || 3/188–189 ||
Having performed the recitation in this manner, one should offer it into the left hand of the Goddess.
Having thus performed the recitation (japa) characterized as previously described, preceded by such meditation,

one should offer it into the left hand— which consists of the state of aesthetic relish (vimarśa) intent upon swallowing the universe and which embodies the state of equilibrium between light (prakāśa) and awareness (vimarśa). || 3/189 ||
Having explained the procedure for worship, he now states the procedure for libation (*tarpaṇa*):
"One should offer libations to the deities of the *cakras* by means of the union of the ring finger and the thumb.
Here, the ring finger (*anāmā*) is Śakti and the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*) is Śiva; their "union" (*yoga*) refers to their meeting.

The meaning is: by means of the *mudrā* known as the union of Śiva and Śakti (*śiva-śakti-melāpana*). One should satisfy (*tarpayet*) the deities of the wheels (*cakradevatāḥ*), who reside in the nine wheels beginning with the square (*caturasra*) and ending with the bindu (*bindu*), and who have attained a state of essential identity (*samarasībhūta*) through light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). This is the meaning.

The meaning is that one should contemplate its dissolution into the Supreme, according to the manner stated in the words of the learned: "By means of perfect offerings and libations, which are pure and of the nature of nectar, I make this universe, which bears the form of the sacrificial oblation, into the Great Ego. (Suvāsinī Tantra 39).
He states the substances for the rite of satiation (tarpaṇa):
"One should offer liquor, meat, and likewise fish to the Goddess. (3/190)
The meaning is that the very offering of all wine, meat, and fish, by means of the *mudrā* of the union of Śiva and Śakti, constitutes the libation (*tarpaṇa*). || 3/190 ||
He says that one should perform worship only together with those who abide by the *samaya*:
"One should worship together with heroes (*vīra*) who are endowed with the Kaula conduct.
Those for whom the characteristics of the *kula* are to be known as things to be abandoned are [the ones excluded].
The Kaulas are those initiated into the currents (srotas) beginning with the Dakṣiṇa; their conduct, devotion to the Guru,

tranquility, worship, faith, forbearance, fortitude, and so forth, are prescribed in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha* and other scriptures, and [this applies] to the heroes (vīras) endowed with those qualities.

"Bringing about the dissolution of this 'this-ness' (*idamaḥ*), which is its opposite (*pratiyogin*), and intent upon supreme power (*parākrama*), he enjoys his own nature (*svābhāva*) which removes all inauspiciousness. (Verse 50).
According to the method stated in the *Parāpañcāśikā*, [this refers to] the means for the perception of duality (*bhedapratīti*).
These heroes here, who are intent on bringing about the dissolution of the enemy on the field of battle—
one should honor them along with those [others],
and not with those who have fallen away from the tantric conduct (*tantrācāra*) and are devoted to the vows of worldly proliferation (*prapañca*).
One should not perform the blending of substances with animals that are engaged in lowly activities.
The meaning is that one should not perform worship together with those established by such statements as these. (3/191)
Now, one might ask: "Under which asterism, on which day of the week, or on which day should this worship be performed? To this, he says:
"O Supreme Goddess, under the asterism Puṣya, on the day of Venus, and on a Saturday... (3.191)
On the day of one's preceptor, on one's own natal asterism, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
One should especially perform the wheel-worship (cakrapūjā) for the sake of the yoginīs. || 3/192 ||
"One should worship the Goddess, along with Her command and Her cycle, perpetually and in due order"— thus,
although daily worship is prescribed in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha* and other scriptures, nevertheless, on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, by means of the Puṣya constellation...

On the day that coincides with the rising of the Guru, on one's own natal asterism (nakṣatra), and on the lunar days (tithis) of the fourteenth and the eighth, one should especially perform the worship of the wheel (cakrapūjā)—the worship of the deities residing within the wheels beginning from the square (caturasra) and ending with the bindu. This is not like the daily worship (nityapūjā); rather, it is as follows:

The meaning is that one should worship by means of occasional rites (*naimittika*), preceded by the propitiation of the host of Yoginīs, such as those of the eight groups of eight (*aṣṭāṣṭaka*) and so forth. (3/191–192)
Dispelling the doubt as to how the worship of eight groups of eight on the wheel is consistent, he explains the specific worship itself:
"Since there are sixty-four crores of Yoginīs of great splendor..."
O you who are praised by heroes, they remain established by relying upon this wheel.
One should perform eight groups of eight [offerings], free from stinginess regarding wealth.
The sixty-four yoginīs, such as Akṣobhyā and others, are the constituent parts of Brāhmī and the other goddesses who reside in the Wheel that Enchants the Three Worlds.

Since this wheel consists of sixty-four million yoginīs who possess great splendor and are endowed with great power, each of whom is a constituent part [of the whole] and possesses the characteristics previously described;
They are situated resting upon this.

Within the middle earth-palace, there is the "eight-times-eight" (aṣṭāṣṭaka)— the group of eight for each of the eight— consisting of Akṣobhya and the others, who are the collective embodiment of the sixty-four million yoginīs.

One should act in such a way as to be free from stinginess regarding wealth and devoid of any deception concerning one's own resources. Here, "action" (kṛti) is intended to mean the application of the ritual of worship.
[3/193] — Now, one might ask: "What concern does this have for me in their worship? To this, he says:
You alone, the enchantress of the universe, sport with them in their very forms.
You alone, whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), are a portion of me, who am the light-natured awakener of the universe;
you reside within the *bindu*-wheel (*baindavacakra*), enchanting the universe and bringing about the state of transmigratory existence for those [energies].

You sport in the forms of Brahmā and others, as well as Akṣobhya and others; though you are but one, O Blessed Lady, you appear in manifold ways even from the perspective of ultimate reality, like a dancer.
According to the statement of the learned masters, "Thus you transform yourself into those various forms" (a.
sta. 18), the meaning is that by means of the worship of the Yoginīs who are parts of you, you alone are pleased. || 3/194 ||

One might object: "Since one could understand the meaning of the scriptures through the power of linguistic analysis alone and thus engage in the worship and other rites taught in the various tantras, what is the need for the instruction of a guru?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
But whoever should engage in this scripture without knowing the family tradition (kulācāra) and without having worshipped the sandals of the Guru—you will certainly cause him suffering. (3/195)

"The single form of Śiva is self-luminous; the single body is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that [Śiva]. The Supreme *Pādukā* is held to be the embodiment of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of these two, belonging to the Guru who is the very self of Paraśiva.
According to this method stated by us, regarding the Guru of the three abodes, one who has not understood the *Kulācāra*...

*Kula* refers to the Kaulika doctrine. Regarding that, the conduct (*ācāra*) prescribed in scriptures such as the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha* must be understood from the mouth of the Guru; one who would engage in this scripture or engage in this practice should be intent upon performing the activities as they have been taught. Such a person—
The "magnet" (cumbaka) is the lowest of practitioners; you, in the form of a fierce ḍākinī or yoginī,
afflict and seize the practitioner by means of drying up his flesh, marrow, and so forth—
of this there is no doubt, hence [the name].
The meaning is that one must engage in this treatise only after having understood the meanings of all the scriptures from the mouth of the Guru; otherwise, it would be fruitless. || 3/195 ||
Knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, one who is always devoted to the Kaula practice should offer us wine and meat, which appear as variegated [in form]. (3.196)
The form of the expansion of your fame should contemplate you alone.

Regarding the term *varārohā*, the lexicon (*nighaṇṭu*) states: "O fair-limbed one! A woman of excellent limbs, intoxicated with passion, most excellent, and of beautiful complexion" (Amarakośa 2.6.4). Having understood [this] in the manner thus described.

[This is] from the mouth of the Guru alone. Devoted to the Kaula practice—those who follow the Kaula path are defined by the characteristics mentioned previously (3/144, 191)—he is always intent upon performing those practices prescribed for them in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha* and other scriptures. Of us two...

According to the manner stated in the words of the learned, "Śiva is the spirit (*surā*) and Śakti is the flesh; bliss is said to be liberation," which consists of the nature of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), and takes on a variegated form (*śabalākāra*), [this occurs] by means of achieving a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) in the manner previously described (3/98–103).
Having offered wine and meat that have been purified and rendered nectarine, one should apply [the mantra] as "of us two.
"Forms consisting of the expansion of Your renown" means: Your renown is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*);
its expansion is vibration (*spanda*); the expansions thereof are those forms produced from it.

Those who are the presiding deities (āvaraṇadevatā) of those [mantras], being of such a nature, should contemplate you alone— not as having originated from anything other than you— as they have attained identity with that wheel of power (śakticakra) which has its source in the Root (mūla).
"One should contemplate [the deity] dissolved in that very immutable abode" (Su.

67). According to this statement by the learned authorities, those deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*), who consist of the manifestations of the power of discernment (*vimarśaśakti*) in its initial forms, [are to be contemplated] in that very [place].
The meaning is that one should contemplate [the object] as dissolved. || 3/196-197 ||
One should meditate upon you as the Goddess, whose form is will, appearing in the form of the Guru. || 3/197 ||
Having offered the remainder to the Guru, who is identical with you, one should unite it within oneself.

[One should offer it] to the Goddess, whose form is the universe, who has assumed a playful body (*līlā-vigraha*) out of a desire to favor the entire world—meaning, she whose body is her will (*icchā-vigraha*). To you alone.

One should contemplate [the Guru] as being the form of the Guru. Having offered that cause to the Guru—who is identical with you and possesses your very form—one should unite within oneself the remainder, which is the remnant offered to the deity and the Guru.
As long as the practitioner becomes one in flavor (*samarasībhavati*) with those two, so long should he [partake of] the remnant.
The meaning is that one should use it oneself. || 3/197 - 198 ||
He states the offering of the oblation:
"O Great Goddess, [the offering is] for the Yoginīs, for the Baṭuka who is the form of the Self. (3/198)
One should offer an oblation to me, the Lord of the Fields, for this reason:
because I am the self-nature of the rays of the knower, the known, and the means of knowledge, according to the previously stated manner (2.79) regarding the Yoginīs.
To Baṭuka, whose form is the vibration of supreme bliss; to the Lord of the Fields—“Fields” refers to bodies, and their Lord is the individual soul—to Him; for me, who am possessed by the ego of "I";
one should offer an oblation accompanied by the cause, which is wine.
Through the cessation of the two breaths and the union of the three Kuṇḍalīs,
that oneness of the individual soul (jīva) and Śiva is the internal sacrifice.

Thus, according to the method we have described, when the mind has been made to shine by accepting the "with-a-second" (*sadvitīya*) today, when the movement of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* has naturally subsided, and when the duality characterized by the triad has been dispelled,
the meaning is that the inner offering (*balis*) is "I am Śiva. (3/198–199)
Then, he says that one should become intent on acting according to one's own will:
"Constantly drinking, vomiting, and eating, one is oneself intent on acting according to one's own desire. (3.199)
One should wander happily, contemplating the identity of "I" and "this.
Daily and constantly, one should drink the remains of what has been offered to the deity and the guru;
one should eat the remaining food that served as the cause for that offering, and by implication, one should vomit both of these.

For one devoted to acting according to his own will, wherever there is satisfaction of the mind, there he should fix it; there, in that very place, the nature of supreme bliss shines forth. (Verse 73)

Thus, according to the method stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava, whatever desire arises in oneself at any given moment, that very thing is prescribed by the scripture; whatever desire does not arise is precisely what is prohibited by the scripture. Therefore, one should experience those objects that are favorable to one's own will.

The meaning is that one should abandon those objects that are contrary to that [realization]. Contemplating the identity of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*): *ahantā* is the attribute of the knower, while *idantā* is the attribute of the knowable;
their identity is such that wherever the rays [of consciousness] converge, there the all-pervasive Lord alone manifests.

In accordance with the manner previously established in [verses] 2.79 and 3.141, knowledge is characterized by the process of bringing the knower, the object of knowledge, and consciousness into a state of aesthetic oneness (*samarasīkaraṇa*); contemplating that very state as "I am," one should live happily. The meaning is that one becomes possessed of the bliss of perfect knowledge.
This has been stated by the venerable Vijñānabhairava:

"By the expansion of the bliss of aesthetic flavor arising from the exhilaration produced by eating and drinking, one should contemplate the state of fullness; from that, great bliss arises" (verse 71).
Thus [ends the section]. 3/199–200.
He concludes the primary subject at hand: "This divine and supreme triad of conventions has been told to you. (3.200)
This is clear. 3/200
Because it is the supreme of all knowledge, it must be kept strictly secret; thus he says:
"It should be guarded with effort, O lady of good vows, like one's own private parts.
Just as you guard your own private parts from other men with great care,"
In the same way, the meaning is that these three conventions must also be concealed from those who are unworthy. || 3/201 ||
Now, who are those unworthy ones to whom it must be concealed? To this he says:
"O sinless one, it must not be revealed by you to a flatterer nor to one greedy for knowledge. (3.201)
Lacking devotion and attached to many things, he is a mere seeker of knowledge (vidyāmātrapīṭha) who clings to various other tantras; greedy for knowledge, because knowledge is common to all,
he thinks that just as in the sciences of poetry, drama, and so forth, so too here knowledge must be acquired.
The meaning is that this secret of both of these must not be revealed by you.

Because that which is contrary to rule (anyāya) should not be performed due to the transgression of injunctions, he says: "O Maheśvarī, one should not give by an improper method to those who are nihilists.
Transgression of injunction is indeed what constitutes an improper method; those who believe that there is no other world are nihilists.
The "magnetizers" (cumbakāḥ) are the Buddhists and others; they are nihilists (nāstikāḥ).
To the question, "In that case, what is the injunction here?", he says:
"O Lord, I have been thus commanded by you, who are the embodiment of my own will. (3/202)

O Lord! O Thou who art endowed with the power that governs the course and order of the universe! For this very reason, according to the method taught in the *Catuḥśatī* scripture—“In the subtle Śiva, there exists neither name nor abode without Śakti”—I am unable to accomplish anything without You.

He was not capable of speaking. Therefore, he was commanded—impelled—by my will, which takes the form of the desire of me, the Lord of all, the speaker of all the scriptures and treatises; that is, by the power of the Unattached (Anāśrita-kalā) in the form of the intention to speak.
I have thus described knowledge as having the characteristics previously stated; therefore, the meaning is that your command alone is the injunction. || 3/202 ||
Therefore, he says that if one should transgress this, a great misfortune will ensue:
"But he who should give it by an improper method shall become a corpse.
Thus, whoever, having transgressed the rule of your command, [gives] this knowledge to Cumbaka and others—
If he should give [it], he will become a corpse.
He states the fruit of this thorough knowledge:
"He who understands the secret convention of the yoginīs shall become beloved by them. (3.203)

These are the three conventions. He who understands them solely from the mouth of the Guru is the beloved of the Yoginīs; "yoga" is union with Paramaśiva, and those [Yoginīs] are the powers (śaktis) who possess that [union], being rays of supreme consciousness. He is their beloved, Paramaśiva.

Because He possesses infinite power. As it is said in another Tantra: "The entire universe is His powers, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power. The meaning is that He is indeed Paramaśiva Himself. (3/203)
Now, one might ask: "If there is identity with Supreme Śiva, what is the human goal (puruṣārtha)? To this he says:
"The attainment of all desired fruits; it is the locus of the fruits of all desires.
For [it is] from this [identity] that all things desired—those being longed for by all people—are obtained.

Paramaśiva is the ultimate substratum of all fruits; therefore, the attainment of all desired fruits—that is, the acquisition of all those fruits that are wished for and longed for by everyone—occurs through the thorough realization of identity with Paramaśiva. This is the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha).
This is the meaning.
One might ask: "Where, then, is that seen? To this he says:
"O Goddess, from wherever it is seen! From wherever—that is, wherever at all—the mind extends, whether externally or internally, there [it is seen]."
He alone is perceived in the form of that experience, because He is omnipresent. As it has been said by the venerable Vijñānabhairava:
"O Beloved, wherever the mind goes—whether externally or internally—"

"In each and every [place], the state of Śiva will go nowhere, because of its all-pervasiveness" (verse 113), and "In each and every [place], the consciousness of the Lord is manifested through the path of the senses" (verse 114).
Now, one might ask: "Is this seen by everyone in that way? To this, he says:
How could a wise person not reflect upon this? (3.204)

Although He is seen as truth, yet they do not see Him; according to the manner stated in the Upaniṣads, "No one sees Me," [they fail to perceive] the Lord who is within the range of direct perception, and the world which churns the ocean.
Having seen this, the Śruti-śiras, being deeply distressed, feels compassion.

Thus, according to the method taught in other tantras, those devoid of instruction do not perceive even that which is being seen. One who possesses the direct experience (*aparokṣānubhava*) of identity with the partless Supreme Śiva, having realized the partless nature (*niṣkalatva*) in Śiva [as stated in 2/50].

The meaning is: how could one whose entire web of bonds has been severed by the glance of the Guru’s favor, and who possesses the vibrating realization of the supreme Śiva-consciousness of "I-ness," not contemplate this [reality], and how could he not perceive an equal state everywhere? (3/204)
O Mother! Because it was a secret, your form was spoken by Śiva in an indistinct manner;
we have now revealed it according to the words of our Lord—please forgive us for that.
Thus ends the third chapter, the "Secret of Worship," in the *Yoginīhṛdayadīpikā* composed by the eminent Yogin Amṛtānanda, disciple of the illustrious supreme lord of yogins, Puṇyānanda.
And this work is completed.
